articles.title: Embed Security lets analysts teach its AI SOC Platform how to investigate
articles.context: Embed Security announced new capabilities that let security teams teach Embed how they investigate, what matters in their environment, and how to improve their detections
articles.full_text:
Embed Security announced new capabilities that let security teams teach Embed how they investigate, what matters in their environment, and how to improve their detections.

With customer-built iSteps, expanded NoiseIQ Memories, and Detection Engineering, organizations can extend Embed’s built-in security expertise with their own knowledge and operating practices. Rather than programming workflows, analysts can teach Embed what they know, and its decision layer applies that expertise autonomously.

“Everyone is telling security teams to build agents. We think security teams should be teaching AI, not building it,” said Seth Summersett, CEO of Embed Security. “Analysts already know how to investigate. Our job is to make that expertise executable and apply it consistently across every investigation.”

Customer-built iSteps: Making security expertise executable

Embed’s library of iSteps is engineered by its security and AI experts, combining deterministic logic with LLM reasoning for consistency and robustness. Customer-built iSteps extend this library, letting teams capture their own investigative expertise as natural-language investigation agents that run on the same orchestration framework. Analysts describe how they approach a security question, and Embed transforms their expertise into executable investigations that run autonomously when relevant, without requiring customers to program AI workflows.

NoiseIQ Memories: Organizational context that evolves with your business

Building on NoiseIQ’s organizational context capabilities, Memories expands how teams teach Embed about their environment. Rather than relying solely on predefined relationships, Embed dynamically connects organizational knowledge with investigative evidence, including context that changes over time. This enables accurate, context-aware decisions without requiring analysts to anticipate every scenario.

Detection Engineering: Turning investigation outcomes into better detections

Embed’s new Detection Engineering capabilities leverage investigation outcomes to help security teams identify and improve detections across endpoint, cloud, email, and identity. Analyzing investigated alerts, Embed provides visibility into detection performance and recommends improvements to customer-authored detections in supported SIEM platforms, giving teams actionable insights and ready-to-apply recommendations.

“Every investigation Embed runs tells us something about the detection that triggered it,” said Jeffrey Johns, CTO of Embed Security. “Detection Engineering closes that loop, turning investigation outcomes into actionable intelligence teams can use to improve the detections themselves.”

articles.title: Remus malware claims Gmail access even after you change your password
articles.context: Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Changing your password should be part of recovering a compromised account. The developers of Remus Stealer are advertising a Gmail-reading feature they claim can survive that step and even session revocation.

That is a serious claim. It is not, however, a demonstrated capability in the published investigation. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock examined Remus’s promotional material and questioned both its developer and a self-described customer. Its conclusion is more cautious than the sales pitch: The material depicts a mailbox-reading interface, but it does not establish that Remus can retrieve new messages after an account has been comprehensively secured. Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability.

What Remus is advertising

According to Hudson Rock, Remus’s version 1.3.9 announcement promotes a feature that lets operators open a compromised Gmail mailbox directly from the service’s dashboard. The supplied screenshots show message lists, individual emails, and a “Mail” option attached to records of compromised devices.

The announcement makes several additional claims:

Operators can intercept email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

Password changes and session revocation do not stop access.

Mailbox access can be shared with other operators through links.

Asked how it works, the developer described interaction with browser memory and said the malware executes and exits. The developer also claimed the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, but withheld the technical details needed to assess that assertion.

Remember, those are marketing statements from the seller of a criminal service, not independently verified findings.

What the evidence shows

Hudson Rock spoke with a person who had publicly endorsed the feature and described using it. That source said mailbox access continued after browser closure, a session reset, and a Google password change.

But the correspondence does not document exactly which sessions were reset, the account settings involved, or the timing of the password change and subsequent access. The source’s independence was not established, and the statements were not accompanied by a controlled test.

Hudson Rock explicitly states that its report includes neither reverse engineering of the new feature nor controlled post-recovery validation.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Can Gmail access survive a password change?

Yes. Under some conditions, continued access after a password change is possible.

Google documents that password changes ordinarily invalidate access tokens and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions. These tokens allow an application to access an account without asking for the password on every request. Token theft alone therefore does not establish that Remus can maintain access after a password change.

What Gmail users should do

The uncertainty around Remus’s claims is not a reason to abandon password changes. It is a reminder that recovering from an infostealer infection involves more than changing a password.

If you suspect an infection or unauthorized Gmail access:

Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing the account promptly. Disconnect the suspected infected device from the internet and remove the malware before signing in to accounts on it again.

Change your Google password, review recent security events and signed-in devices, and remove unfamiliar access. Check applications with access to the account as well as device sessions.

Inspect Gmail settings for unauthorized forwarding, filters, delegated mailbox access, and changes to remote mail access. Check your recovery email, recovery phone number, and verification methods too.

Run trusted security software on the affected device. Google notes that resetting the computer and reinstalling its operating system is another option when dealing with harmful software.

Review other important accounts that rely on the mailbox for sign-in or recovery, especially if you see unfamiliar verification or password-reset messages.

A mailbox can be a stepping stone to other accounts because it receives recovery links and verification messages. But the Remus screenshots do not demonstrate a universal multifactor-authentication bypass, the ability to send mail, or complete control over every account associated with that address.

Remus’s claimed persistence remains unverified. If you suspect an infection, secure your account and clean the affected device. Real-time anti-malware protection can help prevent infostealer infections.

articles.title: Citrix, Ivanti Patch Critical and High-Severity Vulnerabilities
articles.context: Citrix and Ivanti on Tuesday announced patches for 19 vulnerabilities in their products, including multiple critical- and high-severity flaws
articles.full_text:
Citrix and Ivanti on Tuesday announced patches for 19 vulnerabilities in their products, including multiple critical- and high-severity flaws.

Ivanti fixed 13 vulnerabilities across five products, including two critical-severity defects in Cloud Services Application (CSA) and Endpoint Manager (EPM).

Tracked as CVE-2026-121683 (CVSS score of 9.4), the CSA flaw is described as a missing authentication issue that could allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to “add and delete arbitrary trusted EPM Core certificate entries”.

CSA version 5.0.8.1 patches the bug. Deployments running with a Dual NIC configuration cannot be exploited externally, Ivanti notes.

The critical EPM issue, tracked as CVE-2026-121653 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an SQL injection bug that could lead to remote code execution (RCE) without authentication.

It was resolved in EPM version 2024 SU8, which also addresses a medium-severity cleartext transmission of sensitive information exploitable via MitM attacks.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Ivanti released patches for four vulnerabilities in Sentry, including a high-severity remote code execution (RCE) flaw. Tracked as CVE-2026-105425, the bug was also fixed in Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM), along with five medium-severity issues.

On Tuesday, the company also addressed a medium-severity defect in User Workspace Manager (UWM). Ivanti says it has no evidence of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

Citrix rolled out fixes for six security defects in XenServer, including CVE-2026-102705, a high-severity bug that could allow attackers to infer the Pool Secret and compromise the host.

The remaining five issues could lead to privilege escalation or could allow administrators with any role to terminate the running tasks of other roles.

Additionally, Citrix released XenServer updates that mitigate several AMD CPU vulnerabilities that could allow guest VMs to compromise the host or infer the active memory content of another VM.

articles.title: N-able releases security hotfixes for zero-day vulnerabilities
articles.context: While N-able has yet to flag these flaws as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that attackers have already started scanning the Internet...
articles.full_text:
N-able released hotfixes to address zero-day bugs affecting its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, which were publicly disclosed over the weekend and forced it to take vulnerable hosted environments offline.

This follows N-able's decision to take all hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific regions until it could patch them against potential attacks targeting the zero-day flaws in the wild.

"N-able is actively responding to non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central late Sunday night, November 8, found by an independent researcher," N-able told BleepingComputer on Monday. "As a precautionary measure, we took our Hosted N-central environment offline today, November 9, and provided guidance to customers operating on-premises N-central servers to temporarily take their servers offline until further notice."

N-central lets IT departments and managed service providers (MSPs) monitor, manage, and maintain client networks and devices from a centralized web-based console.

N-able has now released N-central 2026.4 HF2 with security patches and technology updates for some of the leaked zero-days, including "the most critical" vulnerabilities:

CVE-2026-125883 - Multiple XXE Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 - Multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 - Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 - Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 - Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 - RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 - Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

In a Tuesday update, N-able said that all hosted N-central servers (NCODs) across all regions have now been successfully upgraded and advised and "strongly" recommended that all N-central On-Premises customers upgrade their installations to the newly released version "as soon as possible."

"Customers should follow the published upgrade guidance carefully before restoring normal access to their N-central environment. Earlier incident guidance advised On-Premises customers to keep their N-central servers offline while remediation was being developed," it said.

While N-able has yet to flag these flaws as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that attackers have already started scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems and warned admins to take N-central servers offline immediately.

"During the past 24 hours, we have observed probing of N-able N-central for the 0-days that were dropped publicly yesterday," Defused said. "We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote control endpoint without auth. These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface."

Internet security nonprofit Shadowserver reports that just over 148 N-central servers are currently exposed online, a sharp decrease from the 1,338 it detected on Monday.

Disclosed after previous reports were allegedly ignored

Security researcher Sean Bales disclosed the vulnerabilities late Sunday, November 8, and published a GitHub repository called Able2Shell containing proof-of-concept exploits for the flaws.

Bales said the zero-day bugs affect N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release version of the software, and believes that most (if not all) of the flaws also affect earlier versions.

The disclosed vulnerabilities include remote code execution (RCE), authentication bypasses, credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, XML external entity (XXE) injection, and cross-site scripting (XSS) flaws.

The security researcher also demoed a critical unauthenticated XXE-to-RCE exploit chain that abuses N-central's service-import functionality to steal a trusted local session, reset the targeted account's password, and execute commands on the server as the nable user.

Attackers could also use this exploit to create a Default Administrator account with attacker-controlled credentials, which provides them rogue admin access to the N-central management interface, as shown in the video demo embedded below.

Bales told BleepingComputer that he released the N-central zero-days without notifying N-able because the company allegedly failed to patch vulnerabilities (including two unrelated remote code execution bugs and a privilege-escalation flaw) he reported in a different N-able product about five to six months ago.

When asked about Bales' allegations regarding the previously disclosed security issues, N-able did not address the questions and instead responded with a statement about the N-central security incident and precautionary shutdown.

N-able provides cloud-based remote monitoring, cybersecurity, and data protection tools for Managed Service Providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT departments at more than 500,000 organizations in over 140 countries.

articles.title: Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
articles.context: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required.

Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper. It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

“The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.”

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post, said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models.

Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor

The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output.

The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios.

The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post.

The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context.

The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt.

Microsoft Research said the technique requires no model training. Its researchers described it as an inference-compute attack, meaning a machine with enough memory to run a model has sufficient resources to implant the backdoor.

However, the attack requires write access to the model checkpoint. In his research post, Papailiopoulos said a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide the access needed to modify the weights. “What matters is weight, integrity, and provenance,” he added.

Modified models can pass evaluations

Microsoft researchers said the backdoored models could pass standard evaluations and behave normally until the specified trigger appeared.

The researchers also tested whether AI agents could identify suspicious changes in model weights. Their agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4% of held-out modified checkpoints, with a 9.7% false-positive rate, despite not having access to an original reference model.

Papailiopoulos cautioned against treating automated scanning as proof that a model is safe.

“No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe,” he wrote.

According to Papailiopoulos, reliable detection requires comparing a model’s weights with its original, unmodified version. He said establishing a model’s provenance is therefore important to determining whether its weights have been altered between the developer and deployment.

Auditing model weights recommended

In its accompanying security advisory, Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends auditing model weights before deployment and after every update. Its guidance includes comparing each checkpoint against its declared base model, verifying publishers and file hashes, and rejecting models without verifiable provenance.

Microsoft also recommends keeping approved models in private, access-controlled registries rather than allowing agents and inference services to download checkpoints directly from public repositories.

For limiting the consequences of a compromised model, Microsoft advises organizations to restrict agent permissions, run agent-generated code in isolated environments, control outbound network connections and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or changing system permissions.

Microsoft Research said it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the research’s detection techniques into a red-teaming framework. The company is also exploring AI-assisted weight scanning and cryptographic model signing with verifiable provenance and tamper-evident audit trails. According to the paper, the central idea “was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.”

articles.title: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Secure Software and Firmware in Connected Devices
articles.context: The platform identifies both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and helps manufacturers fix the ones that can be exploited
articles.full_text:
Product security firm Finite State announced on Tuesday that it raised $27 million in a Series C funding round to grow its international presence and make its connected device security platform more autonomous.

Private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund led the round, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners.

The company tied the investment to two pressures on manufacturers. One is a wave of critical flaws uncovered by AI-powered research in October, dubbed the ‘Vulnpocalypse’, and the other is a growing set of product security mandates.

Finite State’s platform inspects the code that actually ships in a device, covering both software and firmware. It works from compiled firmware and binaries, so source code is not required.

Its users are makers of vehicles, medical devices, industrial equipment, consumer electronics and utility infrastructure. The platform identifies both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and helps manufacturers fix the ones that can be exploited.

On the compliance side, the platform continuously produces SBOMs, VEX documents and signed compliance packages to help device makers meet regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA). The company also cites FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, the UNECE R155 and R156 vehicle regulations, and the IEC 62443 industrial standard among the rules manufacturers face.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

AI agents carry out analysis, triage and testing on the platform and draft regulatory reports. Customers can also connect their own agents through an API and an MCP server.

“The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it,” said Matt Wyckhouse, founder and CEO of Finite State. “Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers.”

articles.title: Muse sleep band users weren’t told their brain data was training AI
articles.context: Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training
articles.full_text:
.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column487343_5a0625-ad > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}

In this article

Muse’s maker used about 50,000 hours of users’ brainwave recordings to train AI without explicitly telling them

Stripping names might not be enough to make brainwave data anonymous; researchers have identified individuals from EEG recordings

Check privacy policies and ask about opt-out and data deletion

Technology companies have spent years trying to get into your head for profit. Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed.

Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side.

The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.”

AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures.

Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t.

This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy

When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models.

Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable.

No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all.

To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult.

But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added:

“Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.”

Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history.

These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems.

This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.”

The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive.

These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers, 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately.

What Muse owners can do

Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe.

With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected.

If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device.

From reporting threats to removing them.

articles.title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords
articles.context: A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say
articles.full_text:
Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.

If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.

Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.

Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.

Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

articles.title: Three People Arrested for AI-Enhanced Impersonation Fraud
articles.context: I used to know an accountant who was indirectly at the heart of the first major fraud by Fax Machine
articles.full_text:
Clive Robinson • November 11, 2026 7:36 AM

@ Bruce, ALL,

Most new technologies bring a new looking form of fraud with them.

Eventually either people get used to it and the fraud success rate drops, or the technology goes out of fashion / use.

I used to know an accountant who was indirectly at the heart of the first major fraud by Fax Machine.

The details are dull you just need to know that a previous technology called Telex had a legal status and people assumed it carried forward with faxes (it did not).

There are still remnants of Telex hanging around, but faxes appear to have been consigned to the under the desk basket of history.

Thus the question,

“How long before Current AI and ML systems suffer those or similar fates and which will be first?”

Take YouTube, a friend was looking at some cooking videos, they asked me if using sweet potatoes to make cakes was possible as they had seen one or two vids that had them in “healthy cake making”.

I pointed out that you can substitute cold mashed potatoes for sone flour in breads and some cakes as I’d done it (similar with rice flour) but I’d not tried sweet potatoes as I did not think it would work well.

So we looked through a few vids and it quickly became clear they were all copies of each other with different faces and stuff in the background moving from shot to shot. And importantly there was a US flag in each and every one of then…

It then became clear as they all promoted certain types of sham products, but importantly asked you to contact them through the comments.

For those that do not know there are fairly strict rules and regulations about pushing things, but… If you interact first through the comments then they mostly don’t apply in the US.

So these scammers know how to get things to work, and in many cases will get away with it even if the money they make is “small potatoes”.

Hence why some scammers have in effect “followed the money” with these “scamming corporates” doing it via social engineering of the employees…

Ask yourself,

“Who is really to blame, the ‘running scared or overworked’ employee or their corporate bosses…

articles.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
articles.context: In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected...
articles.full_text: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said. "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

articles.title: We Built An Agent That Broke All of Our Security Rules. Here's What We Learned.
articles.context: For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only
articles.full_text:
We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. That was true for us at Token as well. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default.

This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales. Standards are coming, but there are steps security teams can take today.

The agent we would have flagged

The agent we created is named Rehearsal. Its job is to answer questions inside the Token platform by doing rather than telling. It autonomously opens pages in the browser tab, sets filters, and fills in forms.

From a security perspective, it’s a typical UI agent that runs in the user’s browser. That’s what makes it useful. But it also means the agent runs within the user’s session and has their reach.

Moreover, to the server behind the page, the agent’s clicks are inherently indistinguishable from the user’s, because nothing in a session cookie points to who the session driver is.

What controlling both sides made possible

Because Token owns both the agent and the app it runs, we can close each gap from the inside. For example, Token knows who’s driving the session because Rehearsal tells it who is.

We learned that there are multiple best practices that you can apply when you control the AI agent itself:

While the agent moves, dim and lock the application and clearly indicate who has control.

Record every move for each session, including those that were blocked.

Reduce the agent’s reach below the user’s. For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only. It can’t save anything without the user’s approval, doesn’t fill in secret fields, and never sends a call that the platform has refused. It also understands the dashboard controls through the page’s accessibility labels.

This works for our own agent, but only because it relies on access that no outside agent has.

Who has to fix it for everyone else?

We could give Rehearsal an actor, a scope, and a page map because we're the ones who wrote it. A browser agent driving your CRM or your cloud console has none of that. The app can't tell that it’s there, and the agent can't tell which field holds a secret or which button deletes a record. The session itself carries the user's identity.

The way out is to give agents their own lanes, separate from human users'. The web has started building them, but it isn't necessarily focused on holistic approaches.

The browser can mark when its agent is driving and restrict itself accordingly. Chrome auto-browse, for example, already requires a person’s approval before high-stakes actions such as payments or mass emails, limits its agent to the sites the task requires, and tags the pages the agent visits in the user’s history. Microsoft lets admins turn agentic browsing on per site and pause it before passwords and card numbers are entered.

The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does.

The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request.

What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for.

The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable.

Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege.

What security teams can do before standards catch up

Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt.

Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners.

Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent

Review every identity that each individual agent has access to

Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls

Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions.

Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation.

Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.

articles.title: eMudhra Revokes 8 More CAs It Previously Declared Unaffected by Key Compromise
articles.context: The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification
articles.full_text:
The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.

The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled.

The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18.

Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise.

Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C.

Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says.

The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place.

Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all.

KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30.

The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known.

What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check

eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement.

Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers.

All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider.

Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines.

According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30.

macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.

articles.title: Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
articles.context: Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings
articles.full_text:
A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian.

The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

“Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post.

Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals.

Command approvals turn into credential storage

Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file.

The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it.

For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file.

Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. Developers can accidentally commit the file, particularly when working across different clones or when the file has already been tracked.

Git Guardian found that 67% of the occurrences in settings.local.json for which it could establish validity were working credentials. Database identifiers accounted for the largest category of valid secrets, with 2280 distinct credentials, followed by cloud provider tokens and AI tokens.

It was also noted that conventional secret scanners could miss a substantial portion of the exposure. Passwords embedded in command-line arguments and environment variable assignments often lack the recognizable formats that provider-specific detection rules look for.

Leaked credentials on Docker Hub

GitGuardian also examined public Docker Hub images and found 613 distinct secrets in Claude Code settings files, 99 of which were valid when detected.

The credentials appeared across 543 image repositories and 7625 tags. According to Valadon, the problem arises when developers use Docker’s “COPY..” instruction to copy an entire project working directory into an image.

Unlike Git, Docker does not automatically respect the repository’s .gitignore file. Consequently, a Claude Code configuration file excluded from version control can still be copied into a container image unless developers explicitly exclude it through .dockerignore.

One valid Cloudflare API token appeared across 559 image tags, while a database password appeared in 643 tags across seven image repositories.

Removing the offending file from the GitHub repository does not help the credentials already distributed through published images. Developers must rotate exposed credentials, remove sensitive configuration files from both Git and Docker build contexts, and check previously published images for lingering secrets.

GitGuardian recommends treating AI coding assistant configuration files as potential secret-bearing assets, scanning them alongside conventional environment files, and using environment variables rather than hardcoding credentials into commands.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment. GitGuardian said Anthropic’s Claude Code lead Boris Cherny acknowledged the issue, saying the company was looking into it and exploring additional safeguards, including built-in secret scanning and an auto mode.

articles.title: NCSC scheme will help critical organisations test their cyber defences
articles.context: A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape
articles.full_text:
The NCSC has launched a new Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme.

The scheme is designed to help strengthen national cyber resilience, supporting the UK's most critical organisations, as well as overseeing bodies.

The scheme assures suppliers of cyber adversary simulation services, helping organisations identify trusted providers to test their defences and their ability to prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated cyber attacks.

Like all NCSC Industry Assurance schemes, CyAS draws on the NCSC’s expertise as the UK’s National Technical Authority for cyber security. Commercial providers are assessed against an NCSC-defined standard, giving organisations confidence that they are buying services that meet recognised requirements.

A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape. This is then used to develop realistic, customer-specific attack plans. Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).

The scheme complements other NCSC frameworks that support cyber regulation, including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA) scheme. Together, these frameworks will help organisations - particularly larger organisations, those operating in critical national infrastructure and government - build a clearer picture of their cyber security and resilience.

They also give Cyber Oversight Bodies a trusted way to gather evidence of resilience across the sectors they oversee. This supports consistency, shared learning and a stronger understanding of cyber risk.

Speaking at the launch, the NCSC’s Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse said:

You cannot improve what you do not know. That is why I am delighted to see the launch of the Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme. By enabling rigorous, realistic end to end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organisations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.

NCSC Deputy Director Chris Ensor added:

Moving beyond traditional pen testing and auditing of controls, the CyAS service enables organisations to practically test their cyber defences, ensuring they are able to protect, detect and respond to cyber attacks.

CyAS has been developed in partnership with Cyber Oversight Bodies, including regulators and Lead Government Departments, to establish a common core standard and a more consistent approach to demonstrating cyber resilience.

The scheme will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), enabling the NCSC to test demand, refine the methodology and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

You can find a full list of assured service providers on the schemes ‘Find a Provider’ page.

articles.title: Bay Raises $50 Million to Control What Enterprise AI Agents Can Do
articles.context: Bay was founded in February 2026 by Yuval Zacharia (CEO), Boris Danilovich (VP of R&D), and Aner Morag (CPO)
articles.full_text:
Tel Aviv-based Bay has emerged from stealth with $50 million funding (comprising a $37 million Series A round led by Battery Ventures and a previously undisclosed $13 million seed funding led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners). Bay was founded in February 2026 by Yuval Zacharia (CEO), Boris Danilovich (VP of R&D), and Aner Morag (CPO). All three are alumni of the Israeli Military Intelligence (IDF Unit 8200).

In business, companies cannot ignore the economic advantage offered by AI agents, but nor do they always know what any individual agent might do. Agentic AI behavior is decided at runtime by each agent acting on its user’s behalf and with its user’s permissions.

Bay is designed to allow companies to install and employ AI agents confident that they will not run amok with unintended actions. It provides a single control plane that discovers, understands and controls agents wherever they run.

When installed, Bay automatically builds a full inventory of the AI agents, coding assistants, MCP servers, skills, extensions and local models in use, and maps how they connect, including risky combinations of tools. It follows each agent session from the first prompt to the final action. Its Enforcer component evaluates every proposed action in the context of the full session and decides in milliseconds whether to allow the action, refer it to the user, redirect it based on policy, or simply deny it.

The policy guiding Enforcer’s actions is automatically built and maintained by Bay’s embedded AI system (Lighthouse) based on the organization’s own activity history.

By focusing on the agents’ actions, Bay protects against dangerous agent activity regardless of whether the cause is malicious human-directed prompt injection or organic agent purpose drift.

“Before we even decided what to build, we agreed on three non-negotiables,” Bay’s CEO and co-founder Yuval Zacharia told SecurityWeek: “effortless deployment, immediate time to value, and a clear path to operationalization.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

These principles became the design foundation for Bay. “The first drove us to build a flexible, agentless architecture that can be deployed across an entire fleet in under five minutes,” she continued. “The second led to patented technology that retrospectively analyzes 30 days of historical logs, allowing customers to see what Bay would have delivered had it been running in their environment. This makes it possible to demonstrate business value almost immediately and complete a proof of value in less than 14 days.”

The third, she concluded, “shaped how we approach day-to-day operations, with clear ownership, AI-driven policy creation, and a product designed to become part of how teams actually work.”

The funding will be used to further develop the product and expand the firm’s engineering team, and to invest in go-to-market plans across the US and Europe, “Longer term,” explains the firm, “we want Bay to be the core control layer for enterprises putting AI agents to work at scale. As agents take on longer-running, more autonomous work, Bay’s job is to make sure organizations can trust them with it, and to keep expanding what agents can safely do on their own.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patch Tuesday fixes Outlook flaw already under attack
articles.context: We’ll start with CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting
articles.full_text:
Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday fixes more than 1,000 Microsoft vulnerabilities, including an Outlook flaw that attackers are already exploiting to steal authentication information.

The release also fixes 48 critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code on affected machines, in some cases without user interaction.

While Windows updates address many of this month’s vulnerabilities, readers should check for Office updates as well: the exploited Outlook flaw is patched through the affected Office products.

To do this, follow these instructions:

Open an Office application, such as Word.

Go to File > Account. In Outlook, this may appear as Office Account.

Under Product Information, select Update Options > Update Now.

If necessary, select Enable Updates first. If the update controls are missing on a work device, contact your organization’s IT team; updates may be centrally managed.

During the update, you may be prompted to save your work (check your open documents). Afterward, you should see something similar to this:

Office updates installed

How to apply Windows patches and check if you’re protected

These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date:

Click the Start button, then open Settings.

Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left).

Click Check for updates. Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options, you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update.

You may find the update (Security Update KB5132061) already installed.

Windows Update history

If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update.

After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date, you’re all set.

Technical details

As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details.

We’ll start with CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting. It has a CVSS score of 6.5 out of 10 and could expose authentication information that attackers could use to impersonate the user. From Microsoft’s description:

“Product ui does not warn user of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.”

To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must convince someone to open a specially crafted message file in an affected version of Outlook. This can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without its usual external-content warning, potentially exposing authentication information (the user’s NTLMv2 hash) that could be used to impersonate them.

As this vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, updating Office as described earlier is a priority.

One other vulnerability I want to highlight is CVE-2026-116928 (CVSS score 9.8 out of 10):

“Out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.”

An out-of-bounds write vulnerability allows a program to write outside the memory boundaries it is supposed to use, which can lead to memory corruption or place malicious code in memory and trick the system into running it.

Microsoft describes an attack in which a malicious email attachment is processed automatically for indexing by Exchange Server. In that scenario, the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Processing it could be enough to let the attacker run code with the permissions of the affected service. Microsoft has not reported exploitation of this vulnerability.

From reporting threats to removing them.

Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today.

articles.title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
articles.context: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling...
articles.full_text:
CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again.

The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles.

What CERT-In has confirmed

The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges.

Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends.

CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it.

How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account

The advisories describe four stages:

Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

Sources

CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2026-0058: Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON", Nov. 4, 2026

The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access, Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research)

Business Standard, China-linked tools used in AI-driven cyberattacks on Indian financial firms, Nov. 5, 2026 Cloud Security Alliance, Crafty Falcon: Weaponized Pentest Agents Hit the Financial Sector, Nov. 5, 2026

articles.title: Microsoft fixes audio issues caused by September security updates
articles.context: " errors in Device Manager, while others said the impacted USB audio speakers fail only when using multichannel audio features, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes
articles.full_text:
Microsoft says the November 2026 cumulative updates resolve USB audio issues plaguing Windows users who have installed security updates released since September.

The company explained, when it acknowledged this known issue days after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday, that USB Audio Class 1.0 devices failed to start or produce audio on some systems after installing recent updates.

Some affected users reported seeing no audio output, unresponsive volume controls and sound settings, and "This device cannot start (Code 10)." errors in Device Manager, while others said the impacted USB audio speakers fail only when using multichannel audio features, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes.

These audio issues affect both server (Windows Server 2012 and later) and client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) systems.

Microsoft released out-of-band updates on September 14 to fix the symptoms experienced on devices using 8-channel or 3D audio modes and has now addressed the remaining issues in security updates released as part of this month's Patch Tuesday.

"The symptoms are resolved in the Windows security update released on November 10, 2026 (KB5132061) and later updates," Microsoft said in a Windows release health dashboard update.

"We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one."

While Microsoft has yet to provide an official workaround for those who can't immediately install the November 2026 security updates, some users have restored audio on affected Windows PCs by switching to 2-channel mode.

Previous audio issues affecting Windows systems

Two years ago, Microsoft also confirmed an issue that caused game audio to unexpectedly increase to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems and blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on systems with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers due to blue screen of death (BSOD) issues.

In January 2025, Microsoft addressed a similar issue triggered by the KB5050094 optional preview cumulative update, which caused audio playback issues and Code 10 errors on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers.

More recently, in September 2025, it lifted a safeguard hold preventing Windows 11 24H2 upgrades on systems with Dirac audio improvement software because compatibility issues caused Bluetooth speakers and headsets to malfunction.

With the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft also resolved Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems triggered by the October 2026 Windows Server security updates.
