articles.title: Dreeze Emerges From Stealth With $33M to Rebuild Cloud Apps After Cyberattacks
articles.context: Cloud application recovery startup Dreeze announced on Tuesday that it raised $33 million in a seed funding round as it emerged from stealth mode with a platform built to bring...
articles.full_text:
Cloud application recovery startup Dreeze announced on Tuesday that it raised $33 million in a seed funding round as it emerged from stealth mode with a platform built to bring back whole cloud applications instead of only the data behind them.

The round was led by Norwest and Bessemer Venture Partners, with Claltech also investing.

Dreeze, whose staff is split between Israel and the United States, said the money will go toward product development, bigger sales and marketing teams, and getting its platform into more enterprises.

The company was formed in 2025 by Avi Raichel and brothers Ziv and Oded Kedem. The three previously worked together at Zerto, which HPE acquired, and Kashya.

Dreeze’s argument is that getting data back after an incident is not the same as getting an application running again. A cyberattack or a mistake by an AI agent can leave an organization with its data intact but without the configurations, secrets, infrastructure and connections the application needs.

Its platform, named Application Revival, scans the customer’s cloud environment on an ongoing basis, works out which resources and dependencies belong to which application, and generates a recovery plan from the live environment. Backups of data and configurations are stored with those recovery plans in an immutable, isolated vault under the customer’s control.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In a recovery scenario, Application Revival automatically reconstructs the application as a whole. Customers can also run recovery tests in an isolated account, with no impact on production.

“Companies have spent years getting better at backing up data, but getting the data back doesn’t mean the business is back,” said Ziv Kedem, the company’s CEO. “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down.”

“We started Dreeze because recovery needs to go further. Our goal is to make Application Revival the new standard, so companies know they have a proven path to bring their applications back when something goes wrong,” he added.

The AWS version of the platform is generally available. Support for Microsoft Azure is in early access, with general availability expected in early 2027.

articles.title: Microsoft researchers demonstrate hidden backdoor technique for AI agents
articles.context: Microsoft researchers have demonstrated how small changes to an AI model can implant a hidden backdoor, causing an agent to execute an attacker’s command when a specific trigger...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have demonstrated how small changes to an AI model can implant a hidden backdoor, causing an agent to execute an attacker’s command when a specific trigger appears. The technique, called Lazarus, requires no model retraining and allows the agent to behave normally during standard safety evaluations.

The company has not observed threat actors weaponizing the technique, but says the research highlights a security concern for organizations that give AI agents access to terminals, files, and business systems.

Small changes, hidden behavior

Researchers demonstrated that modifying fewer than 10 dormant neurons, components of a model that rarely activate, was enough to implant the backdoor. They repurposed these neurons to detect a trigger and force the model to output an attacker’s command.

Lazarus: A weight-space programming backdoor (Source: Microsoft)

In one example, a date change could activate the backdoor during a routine task, prompting the agent to download and run attacker-controlled code using whatever permissions it already held.

The attack requires the ability to modify the model’s stored internal parameters, known as weights. Microsoft notes that a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide that access, leaving internally developed models exposed as well as third-party models.

Normal testing may miss the backdoor

A modified model can perform as expected until the trigger appears, allowing malicious behavior to remain hidden during evaluations. Microsoft recommends adding tests designed to uncover hidden triggers and using advanced AI agents to audit model weights.

Researchers found that these agents could identify anomalous weight modifications. Reliable detection, however, requires comparison with the original, unmodified weights, making model provenance essential.

“The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, Principal Researcher at Microsoft, explained.

Limit the damage an agent can cause

Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends comparing every checkpoint with its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tuning changes weights broadly, while implanted neurons tend to involve large changes to a small number of weight vectors.

The guidance also calls for giving agents only the permissions they need, executing agent-generated code in isolated sandboxes, restricting outbound network traffic, and requiring human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as those that run commands or change permissions.

articles.title: Hackers Advertise a $1,000 Gmail Tool That Allegedly Survives Password Resets
articles.context: CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Hackers advertise a $1,000-a-month tool claiming persistent Gmail access after password resets, but its effectiveness remains unverified.

A developer of hacking tools is selling a $1,000 per month feature that allegedly gives criminals continuous access to Gmail inboxes. The cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock reports that the tool can keep reading a victim’s mailbox after a password change, after the browser closes and after sessions are revoked.

“Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record.” reads the report published by cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock. “Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions.”

The tool belongs to Remus Stealer, an infostealer, meaning malware that steals data from infected computers. Remus supposedly gives its operators a searchable inbox right inside a stolen-device dashboard. Hudson Rock says it spoke with the developer and with a customer who used it, and the customer supplied screenshots of messages, timestamps and a control for sharing a mailbox with other operators.

If the claims are true, the risk goes beyond a single Gmail inbox. Attackers could read password reset links and verification codes, allowing them to access other accounts linked to that email address. This makes Gmail a valuable target because many online services use it to recover accounts.

“In the supplied version 1.3.9 announcement, Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the main sales thread advertises that tier at $1,000 per month.” continues the report. “The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links.”

It is still unclear how the tool works. Hudson Rock says Remus does not steal browser cookies, while its developer claims that changing the Gmail password does not stop access. The developer has not shared technical details. He only said that the malware interacts with browser memory, but this does not explain how it can maintain access after a password change or when active sessions are revoked.

Hudson Rock believes Remus may obtain or create an authorization token while the victim is logged into Gmail through a browser. A remote component could then use this authorization to access emails even after the malware has stopped running, as long as Google continues to accept it. Tom’s Guide also reports that the tool can bypass Google’s anti-fraud checks and says it has contacted Google for comment.

However, other reports highlight some important uncertainties. CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability. Hudson Rock has not conducted a controlled test to show that Remus can still access newly received emails after the victim changes their password and revokes existing sessions and third-party access. According to Cybernews, the developer describes the feature as a Gmail “zero-day”. However, this claim has not been independently reproduced.

The business side is more concrete. CyberInsider says the mailbox feature sits in an Enterprise tier at $1,000 per month, with shareable mailbox links so criminals can hand an inbox they’ve already compromised to others. The actor behind Remus Stealer offers the MaaS with three subscription tiers: Basic at $250, Pro at $500 and Enterprise at $1,000.

This kind of claim has a history. In late 2023, a developer called PRISMA surfaced an exploit that regenerated persistent Google cookies by manipulating a token and account ID pair, and Lumma then used it so access continued after a password reset. It’s a precedent and not proof, since Remus’ mechanism is unknown, and Hudson Rock still treats a Google password change as an essential recovery step, while saying victims should also look for other ways an attacker could keep access.

The tool is marketed to “enterprise” customers, so most users are unlikely to be targeted. It will probably be used mainly against organizations and high-profile individuals. Hudson Rock recommends that victims first disconnect and clean the infected computer before accessing their trusted accounts again. They should then change compromised passwords using a clean device and review their signed-in devices to remove suspicious sessions and third-party access.

Hudson Rock also advises users to check Gmail settings for unauthorized changes and secure any other accounts that use the compromised mailbox for password resets or verification codes. Other basic precautions remain important: watch out for phishing emails with urgent messages, spelling mistakes or suspicious sender addresses, and keep antivirus software up to date. Tom’s Guide expects Google to introduce additional Gmail protections if the tool proves as effective as its developer claims.

For now, this is a vendor’s marketing claim supported by customer screenshots and Hudson Rock’s investigation, not a confirmed Gmail vulnerability. One important detail offers some reassurance: attackers must first infect the victim’s computer and compromise their mailbox before they can use the tool.

“Remus is marketing an integrated mailbox-reading capability, and a customer has endorsed its claimed persistence. The most plausible broad model is reuse of access obtained or established during endpoint compromise.” concludes the report. “The evidence does not identify the mechanism or show fresh mail remaining accessible after comprehensive recovery.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gmail)

articles.title: ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens Flags High-Severity Flaws, Node2Shell Exposure
articles.context: Exploitation attempts of Node2Shell have been spotted, but there is no indication of attacks specifically targeting Siemens products
articles.full_text:
Siemens, Schneider Electric, and several other industrial technology vendors have published new security advisories describing vulnerabilities that could expose affected systems to serious attacks.

Siemens has published nine new advisories covering 10 vulnerabilities. Two advisories describe the impact of the recent Node2Shell vulnerability on the company’s products. Exploitation attempts of Node2Shell have been spotted, but there is no indication of attacks specifically targeting Siemens products.

Siemens has also published advisories informing customers about high-severity vulnerabilities in ROS#, Simcenter Femap, Mendix Studio Pro MCP Server, Simatic SCADA and PCS 7, Meta-iot2050, and Simatic WinCC Graphics Designer. A low-severity issue has been addressed in the Fortigate NGFW used by Ruggedcom APE1808 devices.

The flaws can be exploited to inject code, execute arbitrary code, access unauthorized data, and compromise the system.

Siemens says patches are not yet available for several affected products, and some versions will not receive fixes. Customers are advised to apply the recommended mitigations.

Schneider Electric has published only one advisory informing customers about a medium-severity issue in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody that could be exploited for arbitrary code execution by processing malicious files.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Germany’s VDE CERT published eight new advisories this week. They cover vulnerabilities found in Beckhoff, MB Connect Line, Helmholz, Weidmueller, Bender, and Ads-Tec products. Several of the security holes involve third-party components, including PHP (PHP2Shell).

In the days leading up to Patch Tuesday, Phoenix Contact also published advisories describing the impact of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. The company also released advisories for several vulnerabilities affecting PLCnext and other products.

Johnson Controls also published a couple of advisories earlier this month. One addresses three EasyIO Neo IO Manager vulnerabilities, including one that can allow privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution.

The second describes an issue in the C•CURE 9000 3.20 / Victor 8.0 installer that could allow an attacker to obtain admin credentials and authentication secrets.

Hitachi Energy has confirmed that at least one of its products is affected by the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

articles.title: CISA flags Cisco BroadWorks flaw as actively exploited in attacks
articles.context: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned on Tuesday that hackers are now exploiting a high-severity Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability in attacks
articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned on Tuesday that hackers are now exploiting a high-severity Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability in attacks.

Cisco BroadWorks is a cloud unified communications (UC) software platform and the underlying engine allowing telecom carriers and managed service providers (MSPs) to provide branded cloud PBX, voice, and collaboration services to business customers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-20320, the security flaw stems from an improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) reference weakness in the Open Client Interface (OCI) XML Parser that can allow unauthenticated, remote attackers to read sensitive configuration information from vulnerable systems by sending maliciously crafted XML messages.

"This vulnerability exists because XML entries are improperly parsed due to external entity resolution being allowed by default. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted XML message to the Open Client Interface - Provisioning (OCI-P) service," Cisco explained when it patched the bug in August.

CISA flagged CVE-2026-20320 as actively exploited and added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Tuesday, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems within two weeks, by November 24, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, CISA urged all security teams, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patches for this vulnerability to defend their networks against ongoing attacks.

"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," it warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities."

Targeted in autonomous AI attack

While CISA didn't share more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-20320 in the wild, threat intelligence firm Malbear Labs said over the weekend that a Chinese-speaking threat actor has exploited the flaw with the help of a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash artificial intelligence model in attacks targeting a European telecommunications provider and thirteen organizations that used its data centers and cloud infrastructure.

The attack focused on the telecom provider's BroadWorks XSP (eXtended Services Platform), and Malbear Labs found that the BroadWorks Provisioning Server (which stores subscriber configuration for all users) was also exposed via an unauthenticated directory listing.

"The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser. A crafted OCI request to port 2208 causes the XML parser to read arbitrary files from the server filesystem and no prior authentication required," Malbear Labs said.

"From the XSP host, the agent recovered the system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys with certificate matches confirmed. The system identity key is used by the BroadWorks platform to authenticate between its own components; possessing it allows impersonation of the XSP in inter-component communication."

Since November 2021, CISA has added 103 Cisco vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, seven of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.

articles.title: OT Incidents Hit a Third of Industrial Organizations, SANS Finds
articles.context: Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and...
articles.full_text:
A third of organizations running OT or industrial control systems (ICS) recorded at least one cyber incident over the past year, according to new data from SANS Institute.

The cybersecurity training and research specialist polled nearly 700 IT and security professionals to compile its 2026 State of ICS/OT Security Survey Insights report.

It revealed the biggest ever single-year leap in incidents, from 22% last year to 34% of responding organizations in 2026.

The impact of incidents was also more severe. The share of respondents who said an incident affected safety increased from 8% to 13% in the period, and the share reporting theft of IP surged from 6% to 31%.

Shared IT/OT credential and identity compromise (31%) and ransomware (31%) were the most frequently cited incident types this year.

Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs

Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and the severity of their impact.

Just 13% of respondents claimed to have full IT/OT visibility across the cyber kill chain, with budget (43%) cited as the most common barrier to improved detection.

Early detection is key to minimizing the impact of incidents. Nearly three-quarters (72%) of respondents said these led to facility or system downtime.

Only 15% of respondents said they are fully capable of sustaining critical operations in manual mode for more than 48 hours, while two-fifths (40%) don’t know if they could. In the longest case reported, a shutdown lasted a year.

Risk is arguably greatest in the supply chain. If their primary automation vendor disappeared, 58% of respondents said they would shut down or be unable to operate within a year. Yet only a fifth (20%) have a fully functional third-party risk management program.

A Plan to Build OT Resilience

Staff are another potential point of failure: 68% of organizations said that the loss of one or two key individuals would delay or severely risk ICS/OT security and incident response. A third (33%) are deploying AI or automation tools to overcome potential staff shortages, with real-time threat and anomaly detection (42%) the most common investment.

There are plenty of lessons to be learned from the report. Nearly half (46%) of organizations that test their business continuity and disaster recovery plans at least annually and build ICS/OT into them can bring their most critical facility or system back online within the first day, versus 27% of all respondents.

Yet only 16% of respondents have fully integrated cyber resilience into those programs.

The recent cyber-attacks on supermarket OT equipment across Europe highlight the potential for significant operational disruption and financial damage.

With this in mind, SANS Institute recommended a three-point plan to build resilience:

Test resilience plans at least annually, with the operators who would end up actually run manual mode

Integrate ICS/OT cyber resilience into existing BC/DR programs

Map people and vendor-related dependencies

Jason Christopher, SANS Principal Instructor and author of the report, argued that the most resilient organizations are also the ones that known their ICS/OT systems best.

“Industrial security has come a long way over the past decade, and the data this year shows how much is still left to do,” he added.

“What happens after the alarm comes down to rehearsal: who runs the plant by hand, who holds the knowledge that is not written down, and what the fallback is if a vendor is unavailable. Most of the industry has not answered those questions yet.”

articles.title: Ubuntu certificate revocation checks arrive in curl, OpenSSL is next
articles.context: Eight weak keys in October On October 17, a researcher found that the private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were weak
articles.full_text:
Ubuntu 26.10 ships curl with certificate revocation checking built in. The check comes from upki, a project from the rustls developers. Ubuntu’s developers ran the same curl command on both releases: Ubuntu 26.04 accepted a revoked certificate and connected, while 26.10 refused it.

A certificate authority revokes a certificate when it should stop being trusted before it expires. OpenSSL checks a certificate chain by default, but it doesn’t check whether any certificate in that chain was revoked. That leaves curl and other non-browser tools that rely on it trusting certificates that browsers have already blocked.

Eight weak keys in October

On October 17, a researcher found that the private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were weak. One of them was the number 4. Anyone holding a key like that could issue a certificate for any website. Firefox and Chrome blocked the eight certificates the same day. Most other applications kept trusting them until distributions shipped updated ca-certificates packages.

How the check works

In 26.10, curl compares the server’s certificate against a list of revoked certificates stored on the machine. That list is built with CRLite, Mozilla’s method for compressing revocation data, and Firefox uses the same technology. Because the data is already local, the check adds no network requests. Your connection doesn’t wait on a lookup, and no outside server sees which sites you visit.

The upki package uses a systemd timer to refresh the data every six hours. Until the first download finishes, curl behaves as it did before. If you want the check working right away, install upki with apt and start the fetch service yourself.

OpenSSL is next

For Ubuntu 27.04, the Foundations team plans to build upki into Ubuntu’s OpenSSL, so normal certificate verification would also check the revocation data. Most of the more than 1,000 packages that use OpenSSL directly would then get the check without changing their code. Until that lands, the check in 26.10 covers curl, which the post calls the very first step towards browser-grade certificate verification across the entire OS.

articles.title: Red Hat OpenShift 5 brings autonomous troubleshooting to hybrid clouds
articles.context: What Red Hat announced How organizations work with software, especially through foundational platforms like Red Hat OpenShift, is changing drastically in this agentic age
articles.full_text:
Red Hat has announced the general availability of Red Hat OpenShift 5, bringing built-in operational intelligence, zero trust security and a longer, predictable lifecycle to the hybrid cloud application platform powered by Kubernetes.

Purpose-built to streamline complex operations across data centers, cloud environments and disconnected deployments, the evolved platform enables IT teams to deploy AI workloads, virtual machines (VMs) and containerized workloads side-by-side through a simple, in-place update from Red Hat OpenShift 4.

What Red Hat announced

How organizations work with software, especially through foundational platforms like Red Hat OpenShift, is changing drastically in this agentic age. Red Hat OpenShift 5 delivers an application foundation built to connect and run enterprise AI, helping customers monitor, manage and scale their environments. This release brings Model Context Protocol (MCP) server support, AI interfaces and automated AI-driven reasoning tools to assist where constrained operations teams need the most help.

“Red Hat OpenShift 5 evolves the application platform to meet enterprise IT teams where they are, bringing built-in natural language interaction directly into day-to-day operations while delivering the strict multi-tenancy and sovereignty protections modern organizations require. By introducing intelligent, context-aware guidance and a five-year predictable lifecycle, we are providing a transparent, reliable path for our customers to build, run and scale VMs, containers and agentic AI side-by-side with complete confidence across the hybrid cloud,” said Ashesh Badani, SVP and CPO, Red Hat.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 evolves Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed from a conversational assistant to an agent, making the platform more interactive with autonomous troubleshooting and update risk assessments, including pre-flight readiness checks for optional operators directly within the management console.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 also introduces hardened multi-tenancy for sovereign deployments and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) support to protect long-term IT infrastructure investments. Combined with Red Hat AI, Red Hat OpenShift 5 provides a platform for running traditional and AI workloads with performance, governance and observability to help advance your AI strategy.

Why Red Hat OpenShift 5 matters

IT practitioners and IT leaders face mounting friction as they balance scaling high-density AI workloads alongside legacy VMs while meeting strict regulatory requirements. Dense log streams and manual cluster operations pull critical engineering resources away from core innovation. Simultaneously, how teams interact with infrastructure is shifting from traditional management consoles toward headless, agentic workflows.

Red Hat OpenShift 5 addresses this evolution by embedding real-time intelligence directly into platform operations through Red Hat OpenShift Lightspeed. By supporting natural language interaction and AI-driven reasoning loops, Red Hat OpenShift 5 transforms reactive cluster maintenance into a proactive process, limiting administrative overhead, mitigating downtime risks and giving IT teams greater operational control across hybrid cloud infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Faster root-cause analysis: Rapidly identify and isolate anomalies, analyze log streams and execute supervised remediation across complex cluster topologies completely within the console.

Sovereign and zero trust guardrails: Hardened multi-tenant isolation, automated certificate lifecycle management and post-quantum control plane cryptography protect air-gapped, edge and regulated environments.

Reduced upgrade anxiety: Automated pre-flight checks analyze API compatibility and run update risk assessments across optional operators before execution.

Deeper details

Red Hat OpenShift 5 introduces advanced platform capabilities to help lower operational costs, enhance compliance and optimize hardware footprints wherever an organization must work:

Sovereignty guardrails and zero trust multi-tenancy: Delivers post-quantum cryptography protections for control plane communications to safeguard critical data against future quantum decryption threats, while hardening sensitive environments with advanced network isolation, extended certificate management and native support for disconnected deployments to satisfy strict regulatory demands.

Full-stack workload convergence: Enhances unified control for Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization, containerized build pipelines via GitOps and automated GPU compute slicing to maximize hardware utilization across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads.

Guided platform updates and lifecycle management: Features intelligent pre-check risk assessments and pre-flight compatibility analysis for APIs and optional operators to guide administrators through zero-downtime maintenance windows.

“Service providers need cloud infrastructure that can keep pace with network innovation while meeting the reliability demands of telecom. Our work with Red Hat gives Nokia’s cloud-native network functions a consistent, carrier-grade foundation that simplifies operations and makes change more predictable. Red Hat OpenShift 5 strengthens that foundation, helping operators run today’s critical services efficiently and prepare their networks for greater automation and AI,” said Kal De, SVP, core networks, Nokia.

articles.title: Druva helps restore AI agents without rolling back entire environments
articles.context: Additionally, Druva is introducing the industry’s first data protection integrations with Azure SRE Agent and Microsoft 365 Copilot to give customers direct access to backup...
articles.full_text:
Druva has announced Druva Agent Recovery, a new set of AI Resilience capabilities that keep the business running by quickly restoring AI agents when they are deleted or unexpectedly changed. Support begins with Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft’s platform for building custom AI agents.

Announcement also expands protection across Microsoft Power Platform, adding Power Apps and Power Automate to existing Power BI support. Additionally, Druva is introducing the industry’s first data protection integrations with Azure SRE Agent and Microsoft 365 Copilot to give customers direct access to backup health and recovery options within Microsoft AI tools.

According to Microsoft, more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies now use AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools. As adoption grows, one broken agent can stall the processes around it, and recovery often requires restoring a full environment or rebuilding the agent manually. Druva keeps a recovery point ready for each protected agent, so teams can recover individual agents without starting over.

“More business processes now run through AI agents, which makes those agents essential to how the business operates,” said Ranga Rajagopalan, Chief Products and Marketing Officer at Druva. “That puts them on the same list of critical systems every IT team backs up and recovers. With Agent Recovery, we’re now protecting the agents themselves, building on what we already safeguard across Microsoft 365 and Copilot conversations.”

Druva Agent Recovery protects Microsoft Copilot Studio agents

Druva introduced AI Resilience earlier this year to help organizations recover, govern, and defend AI-powered work. Druva Agent Recovery brings that resilience to AI agents, starting with Copilot Studio Agent Backup & Recovery. It protects customer-built Copilot Studio agents and their configurations, enabling customers to:

Keep pace with agent growth: Automatically discover Copilot Studio agents across Power Platform environments as employees build them, so protection keeps pace with adoption.

Automate policy-based protection: Scheduled, immutable backups in The Resilience Cloud give every agent a clear version history, protecting against accidental changes, unauthorized edits, and emerging risks.

Recover a single agent: Restore individual agents and their configurations without rolling back the entire Power Platform environment.

Expanded power platform support protects each agent’s workflow

Copilot Studio agents depend on connected applications, flows, data, and identities. When one of those fails, the agent can fail with it. To extend resilience across these dependencies, Druva now protects Microsoft Power Apps and Power Automate, expanding the Power Platform support introduced with Power BI protection. Teams can restore individual apps or flows from air-gapped, immutable backups without rebuilding them or rolling back the environment.

With this expansion, Druva’s cloud-native platform protects Copilot Studio agents and their workflows end to end. Coverage spans the Microsoft ecosystem and beyond, including Power Platform, Microsoft 365, Copilot Chat conversations, Microsoft EntraID, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and Salesforce. When something fails anywhere in an agent’s workflow, teams have a clear path to recovery.

Druva accelerates recovery in Microsoft AI tools

Two integrations give teams quick access to Druva backup health, recovery points, and troubleshooting guidance within Azure and Microsoft 365 as they investigate issues.

Druva Integration with Azure SRE Agent: With Druva’s first-to-market integration, Microsoft Azure SRE Agent can use Druva backup health, protection status, recovery points, and failed-job diagnostics for any Druva-protected workload to enhance incident response. Azure SRE Agent then correlates that information with Azure operational data to identify unprotected workloads and suggest or take next steps.

Druva Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot: Delivered through the Agent Store in Microsoft 365 Copilot, the Druva Agent is the first backup and recovery agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings a consolidated view of backup health, grouped failure analysis, and remediation guidance into Copilot and Microsoft Teams. Using Copilot’s Microsoft 365 context, administrators can see which users and groups are impacted by a backup issue and retry failed backups directly from Copilot.

Support for Microsoft Power Apps and the Druva Agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot are generally available. The Druva Integration with Azure SRE Agent will be available at the end of November. Copilot Studio Agent Backup & Recovery and support for Microsoft Power Automate are in limited availability.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes 1235 Flaws in Another Record Patch Tuesday
articles.context: The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has issued updates to fix over 1200 vulnerabilities in its products, a new record.

The tech giant’s November Patch Tuesday contained fixes for 1235 flaws, including one zero-day being actively exploited in the wild.

It makes this month the fourth this year in which Microsoft has issued a record number of patches, following previous milestones passed in July, September and October.

The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it. Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.

“That quiet connection can leak the user's NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024.”

Read more on patching: Exploited Vulnerabilities Typically Take Three Months to Patch, Moody’s Finds

Although the zero-day is rated “moderate,” sysadmins should prioritize it, Bicer advised.

“Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs,” he added. “A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox. Push the Office update to every Outlook user now, starting with administrators and high-value accounts.”

The majority (536) of CVEs patched this month are elevation of privilege (EoP), followed by remote code execution (296) and information disclosure (157).

A total of 66 are rated critical, most of these being remote code execution flaws.

SAP Patch Volumes Hit New Highs

Microsoft wasn’t the only software giant to release a record-breaking number of security updates yesterday. SAP’s November Patch Day was the biggest ever, with 43 vulnerabilities addressed, including 12 Hot News Notes and 13 High Priority.

“Hot News” is the highest priority ranking given to SAP security updates (Notes).

The patch load was twice the size of the average for 2026 and included four with a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, according to Onapsis.

These were:

CVE-2026-89103 (SAP Security Note #3798345), a broken access control vulnerability in SAP Gateway dubbed “ProxyGate”

CVE-2026-76964 (SAP Security Note #3778530), a memory corruption flaw in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP (Internet Communication Manager)

CVE-2026-89126 (SAP Security Note #3778556), a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP Web Dispatcher

CVE-2026-120017 (SAP Security Note #3849308), a missing authentication (SAML2 authentication bypass) vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform (SAML2 Service Provider)

articles.title: Fingerprint trains specialized models to detect distinct fraud types
articles.context: “Those threats vary by organization and attack type, but one thing is clear: static, one-size-fits-all risk scoring is no longer enough
articles.full_text:
Fingerprint has launched Fraud Score, a predictive fraud signal trained directly on customers’ own fraud outcomes and powered by Fingerprint’s device intelligence and machine learning models. Fraud Score learns the fraud types at each organization to help them identify fraud more accurately without having to build and maintain their own models.

Basic risk scoring can’t match the many types of fraud

“Businesses today face a wider range of fraud threats, amplified by AI-powered techniques,” said Suzanne Sando, Lead Analyst at Javelin Strategy & Research. “Those threats vary by organization and attack type, but one thing is clear: static, one-size-fits-all risk scoring is no longer enough.”

As online fraud becomes more sophisticated, security and risk teams struggle with translating more signals than ever before into accurate, actionable decisions. Despite these complexities, most tools treat fraud as a monolithic problem. However, account takeover (ATO), payment fraud, promotion abuse and fake account creation each exhibit distinct behavior, requiring distinct detection strategies. Generic risk scores fail to capture these nuances, forcing engineering and fraud teams to spend countless hours on manual analysis, complex rule-building and ongoing model maintenance.

“Fraud teams have a signal-to-decision problem,” said Catherine Woneis, VP of Product at Fingerprint. “We built Fraud Score to give every organization the power of custom machine learning without the complexity of building and maintaining custom models. Fraud Score trains specialized models on each customer’s actual fraud outcomes and our device intelligence, enabling teams to stop specific threats with far greater precision.”

Transforming raw device signals into informed business decisions

Fraud Score eliminates complexity and uncertainty for risk teams by delivering turnkey, customer-tailored modeling. In a head-to-head evaluation, Fraud Score caught nearly 50% more fraud than one customer’s existing in-house model, with no increase in good users blocked.

Fraud Score pairs Fingerprint’s broad set of device intelligence signals with fraud outcomes provided by each organization to build and maintain specialized models tailored to each organization’s unique traffic. Fraud teams can act on Fraud Score’s specialized predictions directly or integrate them into their existing decisioning systems via Fingerprint’s API responses. As customers provide new outcomes, Fingerprint continuously retrains the Fraud Score models.

Unlike alternatives that rely on generalized network rules or require internal data science teams to maintain their own prediction layers, Fraud Score is:

Specialized by fraud type: Optimizes separate models and predictions for distinct threat vectors, including payment fraud, ATO, multi-accounting, fake account creation, promotion abuse, platform abuse, content abuse and more

Trained on customer data: Learns directly from an organization’s fraud outcomes, ensuring predictions reflect their specific users and traffic patterns

Powered by device intelligence: Ingests Fingerprint’s device intelligence signals, uncovering correlations and anomalies that manual rules miss

“Simply blocking the visitor ID wasn’t enough to stop our savvier fraudsters,” said David Fennessey, Principal Software Engineer at Flink. “With Fraud Score, we can partner with Fingerprint to collaborate on a model based on our own internal fraud analysis and stop future abuse before the order is placed.”

articles.title: Microsoft fixes Exchange sign-ins broken by Windows Server updates
articles.context: Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has fixed Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems after installing the October 2026 Windows Server security updates.

Microsoft acknowledged this known issue in mid-October, confirming that users had trouble accessing email or signing in to Outlook after installing the latest updates on systems running Windows Server 2019 and later.

As explained at the time, the sign-in and mail flow issues are caused by a new default limit on the amount of memory Endpoint Mapper uses when handling Endpoint Lookup calls, introduced by the October 2026 updates.

"After installing the October 2026 Windows security update [..], some on-premises Exchange servers might experience issues accessing or sending email. Users might be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web (OWA), or email messages sent from Outlook might remain in the Outbox and not be delivered. Additionally, Exchange might experience issues accessing mailboxes during mailbox replication," Microsoft said at the time.

"Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem," it added in a separate blog describing the issues.

However, Microsoft said that this Outlook on the web (OWA) known issue isn't linked to the October 2026 Exchange server security updates and urged customers not to uninstall them.

Fixed by November Patch Tuesday updates

In a new update to the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft said the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates (KB5131080 and KB5131090) address this known issue and advised affected users to install them on all affected systems.

Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround that should resolve these issues for those who can't immediately deploy this month's cumulative updates, which requires modifying a registry key on affected Exchange Server systems.

To do that, IT administrators have to run the following command from an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange Server to increase the maximum number of Endpoint Lookup calls and the amount of memory that Endpoint Mapper can use, and then restart the device:

reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f

After the system reboots, the admins should monitor the Exchange environment and raise the Endpoint Mapper memory limit if it recurs.

See what's getting through with a 14-day read-only scan of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, with no MX changes.
