articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Xen Orchestra Auth Bypass Flaw to Gain Admin Access
articles.context: French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild
articles.full_text:
French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild.

The authentication bypass flaw, which does not yet have a CVE identifier, is tracked as VSA-2026-062.

"REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}," Vates VMS said in an alert. "REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string."

"The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs."

In other words, the vulnerability can allow an attacker to bypass authentication by sending a specially crafted cookie and perform arbitrary actions with "Admin" privileges, ultimately resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root.

Vates VMS said it's seeing the vulnerability being actively exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

91.211.251[.]112:8001, which has been flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control (C2) server on VirusTotal

ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333

It's unclear when the activity started and if the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day.

Other indicators of compromise are listed below -

HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}

A running virtual machine named pivot2

Virtual machines configured using "hvm_serial: file" parameter

Suspicious files named /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6

The issue has been addressed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 for the stable and latest channels, as well as xo-server versions 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. If immediate patching is not an option, the following mitigations are advised -

Avoid exposing Xen Orchestra instances on the internet

Block the IP address and domain associated with malicious activity

Block the empty token in a web application firewall (WAF) or a reverse proxy

Rotate all passwords and secrets in Vates VMS if indicators of compromise are detected

Filip Magic (@mad31k) and Christoffer Olsen from TDC NET Security have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw.

articles.title: Digital sovereignty at re:Invent 2026: Sessions you won’t want to miss
articles.context: Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to...
articles.full_text:
AWS re:Invent returns to Las Vegas for cloud and AI’s biggest week from November 30–December 4, 2026. This year we have over 2,200 sessions, 70 percent of which are interactive, led by experts from Amazon Web Services (AWS), our customers, and our partners.

With that much to choose from, we’ve pulled together the sessions built around Digital Sovereignty at AWS. Whether you’re navigating evolving data residency requirements, choosing the right home for your most sensitive workloads, or scaling AI in environments where your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, there’s something for you at re:Invent.

In this guide, you’ll find breakout sessions, chalk talks, workshops, and a lightning talk covering a range of digital sovereignty topics, grouped by theme so you can easily find what matters most to you. Reserve your seat through your attendee portal, or walk up based on availability. If a session is full, check the catalog for another time, since several of these sessions run more than once.

Pro tip: Sessions are spread across several venues, so allow extra time to get between them. All times are Pacific.

Theme 1: Control, choice and operational autonomy with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud

In 2026, we launched the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, giving customers another option to help meet their most stringent digital sovereignty requirements. As part of its design, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operates with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and is backed by strong technical controls, sovereign assurances, and legal protections. In these sessions, get the full picture of the AWS approach to digital sovereignty, including verifiable controls, operational autonomy, and greater choice with infrastructure options like the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

SEC206 | Breakout session | Digital sovereignty: Verifiable controls and greater choice Speakers: Mustafa Isik, Chief Technologist Sovereignty, AWS; Stephane Israel, Managing Director European Sovereign Cloud and Digital Sovereignty, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 1:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Evolving regulations and geopolitical shifts are prompting organizations to rethink how they protect data and maintain control in the cloud, without slowing innovation and AI adoption. This session explores how AWS helps customers meet their digital sovereignty requirements with the full power of the cloud through a range of offerings, including the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, backed by verifiable and auditable controls. Learn what AI sovereignty means in practice, get answers to the most common questions, and hear how AWS and partners are helping organizations navigate complexity in a fast-changing landscape.

SEC234 | Lightning talk | EU operational autonomy in action: AWS European Sovereign Cloud Speakers: Zoltan Albrecht, Director, AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations, AWS When and where: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | Wynn/Encore The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is built on fully isolated infrastructure within the EU, operated exclusively by EU-resident staff, with no access from outside Europe. In this lightning talk, learn from the AWS European Sovereign Cloud Managed Operations team what independent operations means in practice and how it works day to day.

Theme 2: AI under digital sovereignty and data residency requirements

Moving AI from pilots to production means making clear decisions about where your data and AI workloads run to meet your digital sovereignty needs. These sessions show how to bring AI infrastructure to your data, from fully managed AWS AI Factories in your data center, to the right hybrid deployment for each workload, to agentic AI applications that extend to hybrid and edge environments such as AWS Outposts and AWS Local Zones.

AIM206 | Breakout session | AWS AI Factories: Bring production scale AI to your data center Speakers: Pranav Chachra, Senior Manager, Product Management, AWS; Gareth Tucker, Global Specialist – AWS AI Factories, AWS; Daniel Xu, Member of Technical Staff, Anthropic When and where: Thursday, December 3, 10:30 AM | Venetian Data sovereignty, data gravity, and latency requirements prevent many organizations from running all AI workloads in the public cloud. AWS AI Factories bring AWS and NVIDIA AI infrastructure directly into your data center, fully operated, maintained, and continuously updated by AWS. Run leading foundation models on premises for training and inference without building and managing AI infrastructure yourself or negotiating separate agreements with model providers. In this session, learn how organizations are accelerating AI adoption, reducing time to value, and maintaining full control of their data while benefiting from the AWS experience in their own facilities.

HMC303 | Breakout session | Choosing the right hybrid deployment for your AI workloads Speakers: Shivam Saggar, Sr. Product Manager (Tech), AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS; Shelby Seward, DMTS, Sr. Director, T-Mobile; Hai Lu, Senior Engineering Manager, Databricks, Inc. When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations are running AI workloads for model training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and inference, across an expanding set of environments, including AWS Regions, AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories. The right deployment option depends on latency, data sovereignty, compute density, and scale. See how customers deploy accelerated AI across the hybrid spectrum: NVIDIA GPU-based and AWS Trainium-powered instances in Local Zones, purpose-built AWS AI Factories for large-scale training and model serving, and edge deployments for real-time inference. Hear how customers navigate these decisions, including Databricks tapping GPU capacity on AWS Local Zones and T-Mobile running latency-sensitive distributed inference, and learn which environment fits each AI workload without compromising performance and compliance.

HMC402 | Workshop | Implementing agentic AI solutions on-premises and at the edge Speakers: Kyle Palasti, Edge Specialist Solutions Architect, National Security, AWS; Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace Learn how to extend Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to hybrid and edge services to build distributed agentic apps using Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication with on-premises data. Get hands-on with hybrid agentic AI using Amazon Bedrock and Strands Agents while exploring AWS hybrid and edge solutions for data residency compliance.

HMC403 | Workshop | Self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge Speakers: Fernando Galves, Senior Applied AI Architect, AWS; Chris McEvilly, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 12:30 PM | MGM Grand Repeat: Thursday, December 3, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand As organizations use agentic AI to automate complex infrastructure operations, many have data residency, low latency, and security requirements that depend on running AI closer to their data. This workshop explores how customers deploy self-managed agentic AI at the hybrid edge to meet these requirements while enabling autonomous operations. Learn how to architect, provision, configure, and optimize AI agents that run locally, and how to extend the same architecture to AWS hybrid and edge infrastructure such as AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts.

Theme 3: More control, more choice: Finding the right infrastructure for your digital sovereignty needs

Digital sovereignty requirements vary, and AWS offers control and choice across a range of deployment options. Whether you’re comparing AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS Outposts, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS Regions, or planning a migration, you’ll find the infrastructure options to meet your unique digital sovereignty needs. These sessions help you learn more and choose with confidence.

HMC314 | Chalk talk | Architecting for digital sovereignty with AWS Hybrid Cloud solutions Speakers: Sherry Lin, Principal Product Manager, AWS; Lakshmi VP, Solutions Architect – WWPS, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 8:30 AM | MGM Grand This session uses real-world case studies to understand how AWS hybrid cloud architectures such as AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS Outposts help customers meet their digital sovereignty needs. It examines data residency boundaries, network separation, operational controls, and security guardrail options available in hybrid cloud solutions. It then shows how to configure governance controls, including Service Control Policies (SCPs), to help customers comply with regulatory requirements. Finally, it covers how to detect and prevent unauthorized data flows between hybrid infrastructure and the parent Region.

HMC202 | Breakout session | AWS wherever you need it: From the cloud to the edge Speakers: Spencer Dillard, Director, Software Dev, EC2, AWS; Ian Cottingham, Director, Software Development, AWS; Rama Raghavan, AVP Cloud Architecture, AT&T Inc. When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 3:00 PM | Caesars Palace While most workloads can run in the cloud, some remain on-premises or at the edge due to low latency, local data processing, or data residency needs. AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, and AWS AI Factories extend AWS services, APIs, and tools to metro areas, on-premises data centers, and the far edge. Explore how these infrastructure offerings power a broad range of hybrid cloud and edge computing use cases such as financial trading, manufacturing, and AI. Learn how AWS helps you run regulated workloads with edge requirements, power generative AI with edge data, and migrate workloads with on-premises dependencies, featuring AT&T’s migration and modernization at scale.

HMC304 | Breakout session | Real-world migrations: Lessons learned migrating to AWS Outposts Speakers: Frankie Negro, Senior Hybrid Edge Solutions Architect, AWS; Scott Rose, Senior Manager Solution Architecture – Telco, AWS; Marcelo Andrade, Cloud Engineer, SERPRO When and where: Monday, November 30, 10:00 AM | MGM Grand Organizations with data residency and digital sovereignty requirements face a critical question: how do you move workloads from on-premises infrastructure to AWS Outposts without disrupting compliance posture or operations? This Level 300 session distills lessons from migrating customers to Outposts across industries, organization sizes, and migration strategies, featuring SERPRO, Brazil’s federal data processing company, and AT&T, migrating telecom workloads at scale. The session walks through the processes that delivered results, the quantifiable outcomes measured, and the critical mistakes to avoid. Learn how to select the right migration approach and navigate common blockers. The session also covers transitioning from first-generation to second-generation Outposts hardware.

Theme 4: Disaster recovery, resilience, and cross-partition connectivity

Digital sovereignty goes beyond where your data lives. It also shapes how you operate, recover, and connect your workloads. These sessions help you learn about the operational side of digital sovereignty: recovering from failures under regulatory requirements, designing for resilience alongside data residency, and strategies for connecting across global AWS Regions, GovCloud, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions.

ARC405 | Breakout session | Your regulator set your RTO. Not your architecture. Speakers: Hossam Ebrahim, Solutions Architect, AWS; Paul Armstrong, Lead Architect UKI, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 4:00 PM | Wynn/Encore Organizations with pre-approved failover regions recover in hours. Those without recover in weeks. Same impairment. Same services. One governance decision separates them, and it’s made years before the event. This session presents architectural patterns for multi-Region recovery under sovereignty constraints, drawn from real operational experience with regulated workloads under regional pressure. Three categories: decisions that set your resilience ceiling before any event, dependencies that create circular failure during recovery, and assets nobody backs up until they become the critical path. You leave with the decisions to evaluate before your next DR test.

ARC318 | Chalk talk | Architecting for resilience and data residency Speakers: Andy Orlosky, AWS Solutions Architect, AWS; Mike Haken, Senior Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Jamie Pasterick, Senior Solutions Architect, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 2:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Wednesday, December 2, 1:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Your data can’t leave the jurisdiction, but your workload still has to survive a Region degradation. This chalk talk explores architecture patterns that address both resilience and data residency together. We break the challenge into practical layers: where data lives, how workloads recover, what isolation looks like, and how to maintain business continuity across geographic boundaries. We map each layer to AWS capabilities including Dedicated Local Zones, Outposts, and policy controls, then work through real scenarios together. Bring your architecture challenges and we will whiteboard design patterns and tradeoffs with you.

NET327 | Breakout session | Connectivity strategies across AWS Partitions Speakers: Kunal Sharma, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Rohit Aswani, Principal Solutions Architect – Networking Specialist, AWS When and where: Wednesday, December 2, 4:00 PM | MGM Grand Organizations increasingly operate across AWS commercial, GovCloud, Sovereign Cloud, and China Regions to satisfy regulatory, data residency, and national security requirements. But connecting them introduces networking challenges that go well beyond standard multi-Region design. In this session, learn cross-partition connectivity patterns using AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and application-layer proxies alongside DNS resolution strategies, compliance boundary enforcement, and operational trade-offs. We walk through architectural blueprints for securely linking partitions while preserving the isolation guarantees they exist to enforce, and share lessons learned from customers navigating ITAR, GDPR, and national sovereignty mandates at scale.

Theme 5: Digital sovereignty across industries

Priorities for digital sovereignty vary by industry, and are shaped by different regulations, risks, and requirements. Learn how organizations in government, energy, and telecommunications are meeting their unique needs with the control, choice, and scale of AWS.

IND361 | Workshop | Build hybrid data planes for government GenAI pipelines Speakers: Mohamed Salah, Sr. Solutions Architect, AWS; Usama Salama, Sr. Specialist SA AI/ML, AWS When and where: Monday, November 30, 3:30 PM | Wynn/Encore Strict national security mandates block government agencies from adopting cloud GenAI. To resolve this, architects deploy a decoupled edge-to-cloud tokenization pattern. In this workshop, use AWS CDK to build a three-phase data plane that isolates sensitive citizen data in a simulated edge environment. You will deploy local data tokenization, route masked payloads to Amazon Bedrock for stateless inference, and reconcile state on-premises. Leave with an infrastructure-as-code blueprint to unlock frontier AI and satisfy federal localization mandates.

IND359 | Chalk talk | In-Country HPC: How TGS Processes Seismic Data on AWS Brazil Speakers: Kun Jiao, Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Faisal Asif, Global Head, Cloud Transformation and Innovation, TGS When and where: Monday, November 30, 9:00 AM | Wynn/Encore Repeat: Tuesday, December 1, 12:00 PM | Wynn/Encore TGS — one of the world’s largest multi-client geoscience data providers — faced a significant cost challenge running its business-critical Rackmon EFWI GPU workload at scale. By strategically deploying this workload on AWS infrastructure in Brazil, TGS leveraged Brazil’s ReData Special Tax Regime to dramatically reduce the tax burden on GPU-intensive seismic processing. The result: material cost savings on one of the most computationally demanding workloads in the energy industry — and a reusable in-country processing architecture that can serve future customers with data residency requirements in other geographies.

IND322 | Chalk talk | Physical AI in Telecom: A Framework for Workload Placement Speakers: Young Jung, Sr. Manager of Telco Network SA, AWS; Angelo Sampietro, Principal Solutions Architect, AWS; Umer Chaudhary, Sr. Mgr Network Solutions, AWS When and where: Tuesday, December 1, 1:30 PM | Caesars Forum Repeat: Tuesday, December 1, 3:00 PM | Caesars Forum Some physical AI workloads need sub-millisecond performance at edge cell sites, others are better suited to a full AWS Region, and many fall in between on AWS Local Zones or AWS Outposts. In this chalk talk, we provide a framework for matching each workload to the right option. We trace the physical AI development lifecycle, examining how data sovereignty, latency, data gravity, and token economics interact to shape placement decisions at each phase. Based on real-world use cases, we discuss the options so you leave with a placement framework you can apply immediately.

You can view the full list of digital sovereignty sessions in the re:Invent catalog, including sessions with partners.

Activities in the Expo

Join us in the re:Invent Expo at the Venetian to meet with AWS experts and learn through interactive demos. Stop by these kiosks in the AWS Village:

Digital Sovereignty: Learn more about Digital Sovereignty at AWS and the choice and control we offer across the cloud and AI. Use the AWS Digital Sovereignty Lens to get extended guidance for designing, building, and operating sovereign workloads on AWS, see how AWS helps your organization innovate with AI while meeting your sovereignty needs, and go deep on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud with AWS experts.

Hybrid Cloud & Edge Computing: See how to run familiar AWS services, APIs, and tools you use in AWS Regions on premises and at the edge with AWS Local Zones, AWS Dedicated Local Zones, AWS Outposts, and AWS AI Factories. Bring a workload that needs to stay local, and AWS experts will walk through its architecture with you.

Global Infrastructure & Sustainability: Explore the scale and reach of the world’s most extensive cloud infrastructure including AWS Regions, Availability Zones, AWS Local Zones, AWS Outposts, and AWS AI Factories. Discover the latest infrastructure innovations and how AWS Sustainability helps you scale workloads globally while minimizing your environmental impact.

Data Center Experience: See the technology inside AWS data centers firsthand, from custom chips to full server racks, and explore a 3D model of an AWS AI Factory.

Get ready for re:Invent 2026

Here’s how to prepare for the digital sovereignty sessions:

Register for AWS re:Invent 2026. Don’t have a ticket yet? Use the discount code REINVENT26 for $150 off a full conference pass. The code expires on November 23, 2026, and can’t be combined with any other offers or discounts.

Reserve your seats where available in the re:Invent portal.

Download the AWS Events mobile app to build your schedule.

articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.context: Get an updated version of Git > The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog
articles.full_text:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[Advisory]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Get an updated version of Git >

articles.title: Three China-Nexus Espionage Campaigns Linked Through Sparrow Malware Ecosystem
articles.context: Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem...
articles.full_text:
Three distinct threat activity clusters with shared infrastructure and malware code similarities have been observed targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure across Latin America, Asia, and Europe over the past year.

Check Point Research is tracking the clusters under the names SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire. Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem called Sparrow.

The entity behind the Sparrow framework has been codenamed CopperDragon, and is assessed to be a digital quartermaster developing tools for China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, Tropic Trooper, UAT-9244, and UAT-8302.

"Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering hole attacks," Check Point said in a technical report published today. "The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors."

Attacks mounted by FamousSparrow are known for deploying backdoors like SparrowDoor (and its variants Crowdoor and TernDoor), SparroWocky, and HemiGate. It's also assessed to share some degree of overlap with Salt Typhoon. However, the precise nature of the relationship remains unclear.

The cyber espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon is driven by three prominent clusters -

SilentDelivery (Beginning in early 2026), which conducts highly selective watering hole attacks targeting Europe and Asia that distribute a backdoor called SquadC (aka SquawkDoor) through trojanized MSI installers masquerading as certificate repair utilities

OceanGate (2025-2026), which primarily focuses on Asian organizations with a variant of SparrowDoor after obtaining initial access via internet-facing Linux servers and then moving laterally into Windows environments

DarkWire (Mid 2025), which targets telecommunications providers and government organizations across Latin America using backdoors called CopperDoor (aka SparroWocky) and CopperDNS

SilentDelivery

The SilentDelivery chain begins with the attacker injecting heavily obfuscated JavaScript into legitimate websites frequented by their intended targets. Visitors to the sites are greeted by a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning that instructs users to install a "Certificate Fix" utility to restore access.

The so-called utility, once deployed, delivers either SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant. All the compromised websites have been found to be related to government, shipping, IT, and research sectors in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong, and Indonesia.

According to a report published by Positive Technologies in August 2026, there are indications that the campaign has also targeted entities in Egypt and the Philippines using this method.

"The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service," Check Point said. "It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain."

The script then repeatedly sends status-check requests to a command-and-control (C2) server to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation, and ultimately decide whether to continue the attack and serve the fake warning.

Source: Positive Technologies

Written in C/C++, SquadC is a Windows backdoor that enables initial foothold over the infected host. It establishes persistence by means of a Windows Registry Run key that masquerades as a Windows update assistant. Further analysis has uncovered that the malware is also distributed via phishing emails targeting Indonesian organizations.

The phishing email comes with a Windows Shortcut (LNK) disguised as a PDF document, which, when opened, abuses the legitimate "ftp.exe" binary to run a batch script that's responsible for displaying an empty file as a decoy, while launching SquadC via DLL sideloading.

OceanGate

The OceanGate operation, on the other hand, has been observed targeting both Windows and Linux environments, deploying previously undocumented tooling to maintain access, move laterally across the network, and exfiltrate sensitive data.

The Linux phase of the attack involves two new backdoors -

AnnobinDoor, a Go-based backdoor that supports a wide array of features, such as remote access, interactive shell, file management, SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, port forwarding, and reverse connections, and enables the infected Linux machine to function as both a remote shell and an internal network pivot

SparrowShell, a modular Linux backdoor that shares overlaps with its Windows counterpart, SparrowDoor

"After harvesting credentials from multiple users and establishing a strong foothold in the Linux environment, the actor moved into the Windows environment," Check Point explained. "The actor attempted to log in to several Windows machines over RDP, trying different passwords until it successfully authenticated with an administrator account."

This step is followed by the deployment of bespoke post-exploitation tools and a variant of SparrowDoor -

CopperAdu, a post-exploitation tool which configures a compromised Windows machine for remote administrative access

CopperList, a Windows reconnaissance tool for collecting host information, disk details, and a recursive file inventory, including file paths, sizes, and timestamps

CopperLogger, a Raw Input-based keylogger to capture keyboard input events, along with monitoring clipboard activity, active window titles, and associated process names and paths

CopperLsa, a utility that collects passwords, hashes, and authentication tokens from NTLM and Kerberos

What's more, the threat actor has been found incorporating kernel rootkits and kernel-level access capabilities into SparrowDoor and SparrowShell to evade defenses through process hiding and to capture and manipulate network packet capture using WinDivert drivers.

"The actor abused the driver to convert SparrowDoor into a passive backdoor that intercepts and manipulates packets at the kernel level, making its traffic less visible," Check Point said. "This allows the backdoor to listen internally on one port while receiving connections through an externally accessible port, such as 443, that is already used by a legitimate service."

"The backdoor applies a strict filter to intercept connections from a specific source IP address to the legitimate service's port. It manipulates the packet and rewrites the destination port to the backdoor’s internal listening port, typically a high port such as 49628. For response traffic, it rewrites the source port back to the external service port, making the responses appear to originate from the legitimate service."

Interestingly, SparrowShell shares code- and infrastructure-level similarities with a malware called Mélofée that was first described by ExaTrack in March 2023 as based on the open-source Reptile rootkit. This has raised the possibility that CopperDragon is also behind the development and supply of Mélofée.

DarkWire

The third and last cluster of activity centers around Latin America, with a particular focus on telecommunications operators and government entities. These attacks led to the deployment of two newly identified backdoors called CopperDoor and CopperDNS as a possible replacement for SparrowDoor.

Also supporting these operations is a set of custom tools -

CopperLoader, a reflective loader typically deployed through DLL sideloading and is used to deliver additional tools, including CopperDoor, CopperDNS, CopperProxy, and CopperLsass

CopperDoor, a memory-resident modular backdoor

CopperDNS, a CopperDoor variant that communicates through DNS tunneling using MX queries

CopperProxy, a SOCKS5 proxy

PyProxy, a lightweight UDP relay written in Python

CopperLsass, a dedicated module for dumping the LSASS process for credential harvesting

"The operation heavily relies on DLL sideloading as a primary execution technique, often abusing executables that are not widely observed among other threat actors in the wild," Check Point said. "To minimize their footprint, the operators deliberately avoided creating new directories on disk, instead placing their tools within existing system paths."

"CopperDoor infrastructure demonstrated a higher level of operational security. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization. This proximity likely helps the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate network activity and reduces the chances of detection."

articles.title: CISA Expands Incident Reporting Form While CIRCIA Mandate Waits
articles.context: More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat
articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has rolled out a revamped cyber incident reporting form that asks more granular questions about incident types and frames observed activity in MITRE ATT&CK terms.

CISA outlined the changes in an announcement published November 9 and the updated web-based questionnaire is available through its Incident Reporting Portal.

The agency said better data quality will help it connect related threat activity into broader trends that would otherwise look like separate incidents. The update draws on community feedback CISA has received over the years.

More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms

The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Questions about observed activity now use MITRE ATT&CK, a framework for describing adversary behavior that CISA said is familiar to the cyber community.

The changes are meant to support rapid but thorough threat analysis, according to CISA.

"In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization's detection is another's protection," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation's collective defense."

For now, only federal civilian agencies are required to report incidents to CISA. The agency encouraged other organizations that experience an incident to report voluntarily, and information they submit can be protected from disclosure under the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program.

CIRCIA Rule Remains at White House

The update comes as the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) awaits approval. The rule went to the White House for review on October 1 and remains listed as pending.

Read more on CIRCIA: US Critical Infrastructure Braces for Sweeping New Cyber Reporting Rules

Once the rule takes effect, covered critical infrastructure organizations would have to report qualifying cyber incidents within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of making them, according to CISA.

CISA published its proposed CIRCIA rule in April 2024 but missed an October 2025 statutory deadline to finalize it. Many comments on the proposal asked for a narrower scope, less burden and closer alignment with other federal reporting rules, according to CISA's regulatory agenda.

CISA's announcement did not mention CIRCIA or whether the enhanced reporting form would be used under the pending rule.

articles.title: Critical Xen Orchestra auth bypass flaw exploited to hijack VM servers
articles.context: A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng...
articles.full_text:
A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng virtualization hosts.

Xen Orchestra is a web-based management platform developed by French software company Vates, used to manage XCP-ng virtualization environments, including virtual machines, hosts, and pools.

The vulnerability, tracked as VSA-2026-062, affects Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA) and allows remote attackers with network access to the management interface to bypass authentication using a specially crafted cookie. A CVE identifier and CVSS score have not been assigned yet.

According to a Vates security advisory, the flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication tokens sent through REST API requests.

The flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication cookies.

By sending a specially crafted cookie (authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D) containing an empty JSON object ({}), attackers can trick the platform into retrieving an existing authentication token and logging them in as its owner, without requiring actual credentials.

Once authenticated, attackers can retrieve "reusable login token IDs" through the /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens REST API endpoint, which can be used for further access.

"An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root," warns Vates.

The company has released Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest), including patched xo-server packages 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 to fix these security vulnerabilities.

Administrators should install the update immediately, and if not possible, restrict Xen Orchestra access to dedicated management networks and block known malicious IP addresses.

Security researchers Filip Magic and Christoffer Olsen of TDC NET Security discovered the vulnerability.

Exploited in attacks

Vates confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited and shared the following indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help administrators identify attacks:

Attacker's infrastructure: Connections to 91.211.251.112:8001 or ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid.onion:3333.

Suspicious authentication cookies: HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}.

Virtual machines: A VM named pivot2.

Modified VM configurations: Virtual machines configured with the hvm_serial: file parameter.

Unusual files: /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6.

Administrators can also run the following commands on XCP-ng hosts to check for unusual VM configurations, virtual machines configured to use a file for its serial port, and malicious files:

xe vm-list params=name-label,platform | grep -B1 'hvm_serial: file' zgrep -- '-serial file:' /var/log/xensource.log* ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /.ustar* /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar*

However, Vates warns that exploitation will not generate any identifiers in logs, such as the use of specially crafted cookies, and instead must be detected through HTTP monitoring.

The company also says these IOCs are only associated with this known attack campaign and may differ for other threat actors.

Companies that believe they are compromised should rotate passwords and secrets used by their virtualization environments.

articles.title: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
articles.context: The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025
articles.full_text: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information. The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform. That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures. Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely. It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

articles.title: Iranian hackers turned up the heat on French supermarket freezers, says France
articles.context: Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire
articles.full_text:
Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire.

According to French authorities, a hacking unit from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sabotaged food refrigeration systems at approximately 700 retail sites, sparking at least 15 fires and causing tens of millions of euros worth of damage.

On the night of 11 October, the hackers seized remote control of refrigeration controllers and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. As a report published by the French government’s computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) describes, victims of the attack included Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché, as well as butchers, a slaughterhouse, and food-processing plants.

According to French media reports, the targeted refrigeration controllers were made by Danish firm Danfoss, and the attackers targeted older versions of its software.

The finger of blame has been pointed by French authorities in the direction of Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within the IRGC. Evidence which is said to have led them to that conclusion includes that the same infrastructure was used, during the same period, to scan Schneider Electric equipment at energy and water facilities. and traces of Farsi. Perhaps the most telling clue of all, however, was that the attack was being trumpeted by a propaganda outlet linked to the hacking unit barely a day later.

Shahid Kaveh is said to hide behind a variety of different "hacktivist" guises including CyberAv3ngers, Soldiers of Solomon, and Cyber Isnaad Front.

The official French report names three men: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, head of the IRGC's Electronic and Cyber Center, and Shahid Kaveh commanders Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand.

The same hackers are also believed to have targeted small hydroelectric facilities, while a second Iranian unit called Shahid Shoostari (also known as Emennet Pasargad), is held responsible for attacks on Charlie Hebdo and an attempt to hijack display screens during the 2024 Paris Olympics.

In early November there was a second wave of attacks on refrigeration units which hit businesses across Europe, including three French blood service sites. These attacks have not yet been officially attributed to Iran.

Regardless of who is behind the attacks, it is clearly important that any organisation properly defends its refrigeration systems to prevent tampering. As such, it remains good advice to ensure that operational technology (OT) interfaces are not exposed to the internet, that controller software is kept up to date, that default passwords are changed, and that OT networks are segmented and monitored for unexpected changes.

With fridge attacks like this continuing to create disruption and cost millions of euros, we can expect relations between Paris and Tehran to remain frosty for some time.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
articles.context: The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters

AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe"

Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools

status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters.

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

articles.title: Binance warns of iOS flaw that could leak crypto wallet secrets
articles.context: Public exploit available “worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of...
articles.full_text:
Binance is warning about a vulnerability in Apple’s iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 that could allow third-party apps to read private files stored by other apps, including cryptocurrency seed phrases, secret keys, and login credentials.

The crypto exchange clarifies that the issue is at the iOS level and does not impact only the Binance app.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem,” Binance says.

At this time, no cryptocurrency losses have been confirmed, but Binance urges users to install the update immediately as a precaution.

The company recommends that users delete any unnecessary and untrusted apps and apply the latest versions for iOS and other apps.

Where compromise is suspected, Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

Public exploit available

“worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of other applications.

Yesterday, a proof-of-concept exploit has been published that uses a tool called WQ Files to perform attacks relying on the technique. Specifically, WQ Files uses “worse_query” to browse, export, edit, and delete other apps’ data without requiring a jailbreak.

An attacker could

The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app, bypassing Apple's App Store.

WQ Files has been confirmed to work on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2, the same versions that Binance warned about.

Apple on November 9 released iOS security updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12) that address nine flaws. One of the fixed vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-113963, could allow an app to access sensitive user data.

It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though.

The CVE-2026-113963 problem was reported by László Várady flaw, who found that the access occurred through App Intents, not App Group containers.

BleepingComputer has contacted Apple for clarifications and a request for comment, and we will add an update once we receive more details.

articles.title: Blind Eagle Uses Fake Court Notices to Deliver Remote Access Trojan Across Latin America
articles.context: Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-...
articles.full_text:
The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

"The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said.

"These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors."

(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

articles.title: Chat Feels Safer Than Email. Attackers Are Counting on It.
articles.context: KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses...
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R and Jeewan Singh Jalal

You think twice before clicking a link in an unexpected email. Do you do the same for a message in Microsoft Teams?

A new message arrives in your Teams chat with the familiar notification sound, a participant’s name, and a link. It feels like a colleague, not a stranger. That feeling is the opening attackers look for.

Two things decide whether that message does harm. Can the channel stop it before it reaches your user? And if it gets through, does the user recognize the lure and know what to do? Both matter, and this post covers both.

Modern business depends on external collaboration across sales, finance, and IT. External access and guest participation are standard Teams features, not security oversights, and external access is open to all domains by default. Teams is also no longer where only people talk to people. A message could come from a colleague, an authorized AI agent/chabot, or an attacker, and most people have little to tell them apart.

Attackers exploit this openness by sending external messages that follow the same social engineering patterns as phishing emails and blend into your users' daily routine. They could also aim a message at an agent instead of a person. The question is no longer only whether a phishing message looks real. It is who and what you can trust at work.

KnowBe4 Threat Labs has consistently observed attackers imitating routine messages such as support requests, invoices, and meeting chat posts. Weekly detections grew from five in the week of June 22 to a peak of 301 in the week of September 28 (Figure 1). This post covers what we observed, what the attackers are after, and how the attacks play out.

What makes these messages effective is that a phishing message in chat looks like a routine work message: a link, a support request, a payment follow-up. People may not expect an attack on this channel, so they may take such messages at face value. The words alone rarely settle it. The better question is who is sending, from where and why.

Key Findings

Attackers follow work into Microsoft Teams. Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email has carried for years. Wherever your team works, attackers follow. A small request in chat is usually the first step toward a larger goal, such as device access, stolen money, or leverage for extortion.

Business needs keep the door open. Teams have to stay open to customers, vendors and partners, so blocking outsiders is neither practical nor enough. Attackers blend into that traffic, so judging the words alone is not reliable. Ask who is sending, from where, and why.

Teams have safeguards, but they depend on the user. Teams shows an external label and an Accept/Block prompt at first contact, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Links and zero-hour auto purge where it is licensed. Attackers succeed when a user clicks through those warnings. Email has sender authentication, link analysis, and gateways. Conversations inside Teams sit outside the reach of third-party email gateways, and Teams chat gives fewer sender checks: display names are easy to choose, links can be disguised, and previews can mislead.

Defense has to cover the conversation and the click. Use both Microsoft's own settings and third-party protection as your technical controls. Train your users on this threat vector, so people know what a lure in Teams looks like and how to report it. Be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message.

Why Are Attackers Moving Into Microsoft Teams?

Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email carried for years, and the following factors make Teams an attractive place for them.

Outside contact is normal. Your teams have to talk to customers, vendors, and partners, so external messages and guests are expected. A harmful message blends in with the many legitimate ones.

Impersonation is easy. Email has checks that block direct domain spoofing. Chat gives fewer sender-checking signals, and a sender can often choose the name users see.

Awareness is lower. Phishing awareness training has traditionally focused on email, so users may look harder at an unexpected email than at a chat message.

Email security doesn’t automatically cover Teams. Many security vendors now extend protection to collaboration tools. An organization that has not extended its controls to Teams leaves that channel uncovered.

One target list covers two channels. An attacker who already has a list of email addresses can reach the same people in Teams, where external access allows it, with little added effort. That gives them two channels to attack instead of one.

How Does an Attack in Teams Unfold?

Most attacks in a collaboration tool follow the same path, whatever the lure.

1. The attacker poses as a trusted contact. Display names are easy to choose, so the sender can appear as IT support, a vendor, or a colleague. A request from an individual account may show only the name the sender chose and an “External” label.

2. The attacker sends a lure. Default or permissive external-access settings let the message in, such as open external access, personal accounts that can start chats, or trial-only tenants that an admin has chosen to allow. The app, the notification and the chat context all look familiar, and the attacker can build the conversation slowly, so the request feels like a natural next step.

3. The user acts on the request. One step is enough: a click, a session started or a reply, because the request looks like routine work. Attackers may also call the user in Teams to talk them through the steps.

4. The user lands on a fake page or receives a payload. The user leaves Teams for the attacker’s web page, or a payload is delivered. A link can display one address and open another, and senders can edit a message after sending it, so what the user sees later may differ from the original.

5. The user hands over credentials, grants access, or pays. The fake page, tool, or payment request asks for one more action, and the user completes it.

6. The attacker gains access. The attacker now holds credentials, system access or the requested payment.

The attacker can then send the next lure through the compromised account, and the cycle repeats.

What Do Attackers Send in Teams, and What Do They Want?

The message types below are cases we observed. For each one, we describe what the attacker likely wants and where the activity can lead. The messages look different, but they serve a similar set of goals.

The “IT Support” Message

Why it works: Help desk requests feel routine, and people want their problem fixed. The user opens the session themselves, so the attacker gets access with the user’s approval.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is full control of the endpoint. Standard defenses often miss this because remote administration tools are legitimate software. With that access, an attacker can take saved passwords, active session cookies, and sensitive documents. This allows them to reach corporate email, Teams, and wider enterprise systems. It also gives them a foothold for lateral movement across internal networks and for deploying further remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools or ransomware.

2. The Urgent Invoice

Why it works: Payment requests with a deadline push people to act before they check, and a personal greeting makes the request feel real.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is money, stolen credentials, malware deployment, or all three. Depending on what the target does, that can mean payments sent to an attacker-controlled account, malware that steals credentials or sets up remote access, and the compromised account being used to send similar requests to colleagues or vendors.

3. The Ransom Note in Chat

Why it works: The message reaches the user directly, with no email gateway in its path.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is payment or an immediate response. The first message alone rarely shows whether the claim is real: it could follow a genuine compromise, or it could be a bluff meant to exploit fear and force a quick reply. Responding under pressure risks paying a ransom for nothing, overlooking an active breach if the claim is true, or causing internal panic when nothing was compromised.

What Should Defenders Do?

Protect messages and meetings, and be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message. Start with your people, then your Teams settings.

How can users stop these messages?

1. Treat chat like email. Teach users to question links and requests in Teams, including in meeting chats.

2. Teach the “External” label. Ask users to check it before acting on a message that claims to come from support or leadership. For individual Microsoft accounts it can be one of the few cues available.

3. Preview before accepting. Teach users to read an external message request first and to decline it if it is unexpected, even when curiosity says otherwise.

4. Check the real link. Ask users to hover over a link and read the address before clicking, because the text shown can differ from the destination.

5. Never start a remote session someone sends you. Route support requests through the help desk.

6. Verify payment changes through a second channel. Confirm new payment details by phone with a known contact before paying.

7. Treat a ransom message as an incident. Report it to your security team and do not reply.

8. Stop sharing passwords in chat. Use a password manager or a one-time secret tool.

What if a user already acted?

Plan for the click. Reset the user’s password, revoke their active sessions, check for remote-access tools they installed, and review any payment they made.

How do you narrow the door in Teams?

Attackers can only message your users if your Teams settings allow it. You control those settings, and they are worth a review. Microsoft documents each one in its Teams external access guidance . Your business needs some outside contact, so the goal is not to block everyone. The goal is to allow the contact you need and nothing more. Start by reviewing which external tenants can message your users and who can join your meeting chats.

Settings to review

-AllowFederatedUsers: turns external communication with other organizations on or off.

-AllowedDomains and -BlockedDomains: limit access to trusted partners or block malicious domains.

-AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowTeamsConsumerInbound: manage chat with unmanaged accounts and block uninvited outreach.

-AllowPublicUsers: controls chat with Skype users.

1. Allow only essential partner domains. Prefer allow-lists to block-lists, because block-lists only stop known threats. Blocking a main domain still leaves its subdomains open. To block all subdomains, run:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -BlockAllSubdomains $True

2. Block trial-only tenants. Unlicensed trial tenants are easy tools for attackers. Microsoft blocks them by default, but verify that your setting is still “Blocked”:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

When the setting is “Blocked,” users from trial-only tenants cannot search for, chat with, call or meet with your team, and they are removed from existing chats. Setting it to “Allowed” turns these safeguards off.

3. Restrict personal accounts. Personal Microsoft accounts are harder to verify: the sender chooses the display name, and no organization vouches for the account. Disable: AllowTeamsConsumerInbound to stop inbound chats from them, and evaluate AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowPublicUsers against your needs.

4. Block malicious senders. You can block a harmful sender individually without changing global policy:

In the Teams admin center, go to Users > External access.

Turn on “Block specific users from communicating with people in my organization.”

Select “Block a user”, enter the person’s email address or messaging resource identifier (MRI), and select Apply.

The list holds a maximum of 200 users. You can also manage it with Set-CsTeamsExternalAccessConfiguration.

Where Can KnowBe4 Help?

Attackers move between channels, and a single campaign can use several. Reputation checks and sender history say little about a message from someone who has joined a meeting you are in. Protection has to read the message and respond when a user acts on it.

KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security brings together KnowBe4 Defend (inbound email and messaging security, including Microsoft Teams), KnowBe4 Prevent (outbound email security) and PhishER Plus (incident response). Its behavioral AI protects the conversation and coaches your workforce wherever work happens.

Multi-engine detection. KnowBe4 analyzes message text, sender relationships, links, and attachments at the same time, plus email headers when the message is an email. It checks what the message asks the user to do and how the sender relates to the recipient. A domain reputation check sees neither.

Coaching at the point of risk. Contextual coaching, real-time nudges, and localized banners and tags in 13 languages show users why a message looks suspicious at the moment it appears. According to KnowBe4 internal data, 97% of users stop before proceeding with a high-risk action when a teachable moment appears.

Threat intelligence. KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses update as new patterns appear.

Protect the Places Your Team Works

Your people spend their day in email, chat and meetings. Your security should cover all these.
