articles.title: Security Flaws Across UK Government Sites Exposed ‘God-Tier’ Information
articles.context: A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene
articles.full_text:
A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.

The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.

But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”

In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”

The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.

A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.

The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”

In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.

Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.

Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

articles.title: Google Issues Chrome Security Update for Eighth Actively Exploited Zero-Day of 2026
articles.context: Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component
articles.full_text:
Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild.

The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component.

"Use-after-free in XML in Google Chrome prior to 157.0.8103.50 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page," reads the description of the flaw on CVE.org.

Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution.

An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026.

Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them.

"Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed."

With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491.

For optimal protection, users are advised to update their Chrome browser to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. To ensure the latest updates are installed, users can navigate to More > Help > About Google Chrome and select Relaunch.

Users of other Chromium-based browsers, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, are also advised to apply the fixes as and when they become available.

Update

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added the Chrome vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patch by November 24, 2026.

articles.title: N-able Takes N-central Cloud Offline After Researcher Discloses 33 Zero-Days with PoC Exploits
articles.context: N-able said it has taken N-central Hosted Environments offline and is urging on-premises customers to shut down their servers until further notice following the public disclosure of over 30 vulnerabilities collectively tracked as Able2Shell. "As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our
articles.full_text:
N-able said it has taken N-central Hosted Environments offline and is urging on-premises customers to shut down their servers until further notice following the public disclosure of over 30 vulnerabilities collectively tracked as Able2Shell.

"As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our Hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation," N-able said.

"During this time, customers will be unable to access their Hosted N-central classic environment, and associated services may be unavailable. However, the Ecoverse services under N-able Login remain available and online, including Asset View, Patching, Vulnerability Management, scripting, policies and tagging."

The company also said it has not observed any signs of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities, adding it's currently working on a hot fix to address them.

The following services are impacted -

N-central (hosted version) (Americas)

N-central (hosted version) (APAC)

N-central (hosted version) (Europe)

N-central On-premise (Americas)

N-central On-premise (APAC)

N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed multiple security flaws along with proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The researcher said the issues were tested against N-able N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31.

The identified zero-day vulnerabilities include credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws -

Multiple N-central zero-days enable anonymous credential theft, administrator creation, and nable/root RCE.

Chains include XXE/NCI trust abuse, support-token theft, unsigned NSP execution, XSS-to-OGNL, and authenticated reverse shells.

Arbitrary file writes, traversal, credential disclosure, MDM impersonation, audit tampering, and privileged-helper injection.

A native GenericTCP stack overflow also achieves root command execution

Successful exploitation of these flaws can allow rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface and facilitate command execution as root.

Update

watchTowr, in a post shared on X, said it "observed exploitation attempts against N-able N-central honeypots overnight following the 'Able2Shell' zero-days being dropped."

The preemptive exposure management firm is urging users to audit for signs of compromise, restrict access, and follow vendor guidance on mitigation steps.

In an X post, Defused Cyber said it has detected probing of N-able N-central for the Able2Shell zero-days. "We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote control endpoint without auth," it added. "These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface."

N-able has also confirmed that it's seeing "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but emphasized there is no evidence of successful exploitation in any customer environment.

The company has released N-central 2026.4 HF2 to address the following vulnerabilities. A follow-up hotfix is expected to be released to "provide further security updates" as part of its response to the Able2Shell disclosure.

CVE-2026-125883 - Multiple XXE Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 - Multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 - Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 - Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 - Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 - RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 - Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

All Hosted N-central servers (NCODs) across all global regions have been upgraded. N-able is also urging customers to keep N-central servers offline until the updates have been successfully applied.

According to data from Censys, there are 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances. Threat intelligence firm Previdian said it has recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Huntress is urging users to review login and authentication activity from November 8, 2026, onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise, and apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe.

articles.title: CISA Warns of Active Exploitation of OpenSSH, GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, and IBM Flaws
articles.context: According to GreyNoise, the first exploitation attempt against its honeypot network was observed on November 7, 2026, at 12:46 a
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added four security flaws impacting GPUStack, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenBSD OpenSSH, and IBM Aspera Faspex to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability in IBM Aspera Faspex that could allow an authenticated user to craft a specific message to bypass authorization, causing privilege escalations. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSwitch that could result in configuration and credential disclosure, arbitrary call control, and command execution. (Fixed in October 2026)

CVE-2026-123158 aka SSHole (CVSS score: 8.1) - An unexpected status code or return value vulnerability in OpenBSD OpenSSH on Linux that could allow for authentication bypass. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper authentication vulnerability in GPUStack that could allow improper authentication vulnerability which could allow unauthenticated administrative access, including user and model changes, persistent administrator API-key creation, disclosure of worker and cloud-provider secrets, and code execution through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml. (Fixed in July 2026)

The addition of CVE-2026-123158 to the KEV catalog follows reports of exploitation attempts targeting the flaw since November 6, 2026. A total of 22 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 14 unique IP addresses so far, according to Previdian.

In a post shared on X on November 7, 2026, Defused Cyber said it "observed a small amount of actors targeting SSHole" but stressed the exploitation activity is not widespread yet.

According to GreyNoise, the first exploitation attempt against its honeypot network was observed on November 7, 2026, at 12:46 a.m. UTC. Confirmed post-exploitation activity has been detected from six source IP addresses, representing 18 distinct attack chains to date.

These involve reconnaissance, queries to cloud metadata services, attempts to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and efforts to modify the SSH authorized_keys file to gain persistent access.

In at least one case, an unknown threat actor dubbed GT10 has been observed deploying TAC Agent, a Python-based command-and-control (C2) agent capable of shell command execution, system reconnaissance, directory enumeration, file transfer, and updating itself.

Threat intelligence firm watchTowr said it has also observed the OpenSSH flaw being weaponized in the wild for botnet and cryptocurrency miner activity.

In an advisory for CVE-2026-102895 published on July 31, 2026, the maintainers of the GPUStack Python package credited Nikko Enggaliano, Wei Yunzhou, Rui Yang, and Haoyu Wang for independently reporting the flaw, adding that "active in-the-wild exploitation" was reported by Ulex Innovative Systems' Javier Sixto.

There are currently no public reports on how the other vulnerabilities are being exploited, who is behind them, and the scale of such efforts. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 12, 2026.

articles.title: Iris Ohyama data breach may expose personal information of 7.7 million people
articles.context: Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7
articles.full_text:
Iris Ohyama warns that a cloud data breach may have exposed personal information of 7.7 million customers, including names and passwords.

Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7.7 million people through an external cloud service used by its online shopping subsidiary, Iris Plaza. The incident highlights a security risk that often receives less attention than attacks against corporate networks: sensitive customer information can be exposed through services operated outside an organization’s own infrastructure.

Iris Plaza discovered a suspicious file in an external cloud service on October 28, 2026. The company immediately shut down its online shopping platform and related systems, launched an investigation and confirmed unauthorized access by a third party. It published an initial notification on October 29, followed by an update on November 5 detailing the potential impact.

In its official incident notice, the company confirmed that information stored in the external cloud environment may have been accessed or obtained by unauthorized parties.

“Iris Plaza Co., Ltd. (Headquarters: Sendai City, Miyagi Prefecture, President: Ryota Iwasaki, hereinafter referred to as “the Company”), a member of the Iris Group, has investigated the unauthorized access incident that occurred on its official online shopping site for Iris Ohyama, “Iris Plaza” (hereinafter referred to as “Iris Plaza”). As a result of the investigation, it has been determined that some personal information may have been leaked.” reads the company’s notice. “Subsequent investigations have confirmed the possibility that data stored on an external cloud service may have been leaked. The total amount of personal information stored was approximately 7.7 million records, and at this time, we have confirmed the possibility that this data may have been viewed or obtained. “

The 7.7 million figure refers to records stored in the affected cloud service, not confirmed stolen data. Potentially affected individuals include 5.8 million current and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Exposed information may include names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, gender, dates of birth and passwords, some of which are encrypted.

“The following personal information may have been leaked at this time:

classification

Target items

Number of people

Member data(including information on members who have withdrawn)

Name, address, phone number, email address, gender, password * , date of birth, etc.

Approximately 5.8 million people

Non-member data(including information on individuals who have purchased products without registering as a member or who have participated in campaigns)

Name, address, phone number, email address

Approximately 1.9 million people

Not all of the above information about our customers has been leaked. The items affected vary depending on your registration status.” continues the notice. “Some items, including passwords, are encrypted.”

There is one important distinction: credit card information wasn’t stored in the affected cloud service and, according to the company, wasn’t exposed. Iris Plaza also says it hasn’t identified unauthorized access or data leaks involving its stores on other external e-commerce marketplaces. As of November 5, it had received no reports of fraudulent use of the information or financial losses linked to the incident. アイリスオーヤマ株式会社+1

The company reported the incident to Japanese police and the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 29. It also blocked the unauthorized access route, suspended the affected systems and brought in external experts to support the investigation.

The response extended beyond the main shopping platform. Iris Plaza suspended its SIMPLE STYLE website, while another group company, Iris Tech Service, stopped its websites and new applications for home appliance subscriptions and furniture and appliance delivery and installation services. The company says it hasn’t found evidence that these additional services were compromised.

Iris Plaza has also warned customers about possible follow-up scams. Attackers could use the exposed personal information to create convincing phishing emails, SMS messages or phone calls, impersonating the company or other organizations. Fake websites and social media accounts could also appear, attempting to collect login credentials, payment details or other personal information.

The company is asking customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords on other services to change them. It also says it will contact potentially affected individuals individually as the investigation progresses. Customers should be particularly careful with messages claiming to provide information about the incident, account recovery or compensation.

“We will never ask for your password, PIN, authentication code, or any other important information when we contact you.” アイリスオーヤマ株式会社

The incident is another reminder that organizations must extend security controls and monitoring beyond their own infrastructure. Third-party cloud services can hold millions of customer records, and unauthorized access to those environments can create consequences far beyond the service initially compromised.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iris Ohyama)

articles.title: ZDI-26-906: X.Org Server libX11 XkbGetMap Reply Heap-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of X
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of X.Org Server. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must connect to a malicious X11 server.

The specific flaw exists within the XkbReadKeyActions function. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

X.Org has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/lib/libx11/-/merge_requests/309

Disclosure Timeline

2026-09-02 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-10 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Wireshark
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Wireshark. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. However, only instances with LoRaWAN decryption enabled are vulnerable.

The specific flaw exists within the implementation of LoRaWAN payload decryption. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an incorrect calculation before writing to memory. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

articles.title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
articles.context: Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning...
articles.full_text:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

articles.title: SonicWall releases patches for 7 flaws in its firewalls, most involving unauthenticated access
articles.context: “The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said
articles.full_text:
SonicWall on Monday updated its advisory about seven cybersecurity holes affecting its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls, five of which allow unauthenticated remote attacks, to warn that it is aware of “potential” active exploitation of at least one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868, a bypass of SAML authentication controls in its SonicOS SSL VPN service.

And Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out that these flaws involve different SonicWall product lines to those recently reported.

“The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said. “This one hits SonicOS, the operating system on its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls. The pattern has jumped product lines. That makes it a vendor issue, not a product issue. Credit where due: SonicWall flagged the exploitation report in its own advisory and the fix shipped with the disclosure.”

The seven vulnerabilities are: CVE-2026-107155, a permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability, with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-107154, a session validation vulnerability, also with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-82308, a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in SSL-VPN, with a CVSS score of 7.5; CVE-2026-19868, an authentication enforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods, with a CVSS score of 7.1; CVE-2026-77708, a pre-authentication stack buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of 5.9; CVE-2026-77709 , a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of also 5.9; and CVE-2026-19703, a weak password hashing hole with a CVSS score of 5.2.

SonicWall only provided a workaround for one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868; it involves disabling or deleting any active LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall.

A ‘mixed bag’

Dickson said the newly reported holes are a mixed bag.

“SonicWall’s advisory rates its SAML bypass, CVE-2026-19868, a 7.1, below two 8.8 management interface flaws,” Dickson said. “Yet it is the one CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day SonicWall disclosed it. SonicWall describes ‘potential exploitation’ but CISA says active. I would listen to CISA.”

The bug lets anyone holding valid credentials for another login method, such as a local account or LDAP, skip SAML and the MFA that rides on it, he noted, adding “companies moved their VPNs to SAML precisely so every login passes through the identity provider and its MFA prompt. This flaw breaks that promise.”

Some of the other authentication holes are potentially less severe, however.

“Three are pre-authentication buffer overflows whose stated impact is denial of service. They knock the VPN offline but they do not open it,” Dickson said. “The two 8.8 flaws work only under specific conditions. None of the six is known to be exploited. They matter, [but] they are not the headline.”

Could be combined

Sav Wheeler, malware research engineer at Malwarebytes, added that even though some of these holes do not appear to be especially serious on their own, they could be combined to be much more dangerous.

“These scattered vulnerabilities at various stages of the authentication process combine to form a pathway where an attacker can bypass authentication almost entirely to penetrate a system and steal credentials,” Wheeler said. “The weak password hashing is a cherry on top for attackers that have already gained an initial foothold.”

He sees CVE-2026-19868 as “the biggest individual vulnerability” because the potential MFA bypass through alternative authentication means that “the entire trust boundary of MFA could be effectively nonexistent even when an organization depends on it for security.”

He noted, however, that although the attacker does need valid credentials for an alternate authentication method for this to work, “otherwise it requires little effort and resources to gain access, as they’re not compromising the MFA itself. Combined with the use of IP addresses for validation (CVE-2026-107154), which itself provides little security, this is a serious failure of authentication policy to ensure a user is who they claim to be.”

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said that the biggest danger is when SAML sits atop older directory logins that stay live.

“Remote access is the lifeblood of a distributed business, and one stolen directory password now reaches it. CISOs who rolled out SAML to end password-only access have cause to feel let down. SonicWall owes them a full account of how the second path stayed open.”

A vendor risk management issue

These continuing SonicWall vulnerabilities are a real issue, although the September and October flaws sit in another product, Gogia said. “Those hit the SMA1000 remote-access gateway, while this advisory covers SonicOS firewalls. But thirteen of SonicWall’s twenty entries in CISA’s exploited list carry the flag for known ransomware use, the highest share among eight edge vendors.”

Dickson noted that the next steps for enterprise CISOs are trickier because the fault here might lie less with a vendor than with the product category itself.

“The internet-facing VPN appliance is the Achilles’ heel of the perimeter, whoever builds it,” he pointed out. “Swapping vendors swaps one heel for another. The pattern should change how CISOs deploy the edge, not just whose logo is on it. Ask SonicWall whether these are new bugs or the same bug classes coming back.”

However Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said he was less willing to let SonicWall off the hook that easily.

“Any vendor can and is generally going to experience vulnerabilities, but when we see repeated critical security issues affecting the same vendor that represent a pattern, particularly involving authentication and internet-facing infrastructure, it raises legitimate questions about their secure development practices, quality assurance, and the effectiveness of their own internal vulnerability management processes,” Avakian said. “At some point, this becomes more than just an individual vulnerability management issue. It becomes a vendor risk management issue.”

He noted that CISOs need to evaluate whether the frequency and severity of these vulnerabilities are creating an unacceptable level of recurring exposure for their organization. “That doesn’t automatically mean replacing SonicWall products, but it does require holding the vendor accountable for improvement and to demonstrate their ability to address the underlying problems,” he said.

Additional preventive measures

In addition, Dickson suggested other ways CISOs can protect themselves in light of these new holes, beyond the obvious step of patching them.

“List every way the VPN can authenticate a user: local accounts, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+. Delete what you do not need, especially leftover local admin and service accounts. Rotate passwords on every non-SAML account that remains,” he advised. “Compare VPN logins against identity provider sign-ins. A VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in is your red flag. Look back as far as your logs go, since SonicWall has not said when exploitation began. And take the management interface off the open internet.”

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Tuesday, November 10th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10172, (Tue, Nov 10th)
articles.context: Not a new vulnerability, has a 2025 CVE but still something that apparently still gets exploited even if you did patch it recently. Now it's not the only vulnerability they're going after.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Tuesday, November 10, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Washington, D.C. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. Well in Diaries today we do have web shells. This time the web shell that sort of caught my attention was one that looks like it was placed via an SAP Netweaver vulnerability. Not a new vulnerability, has a 2025 CVE but still something that apparently still gets exploited even if you did patch it recently. Well take a look at the web shells being planted here. Fairly standard stuff it looks like like ant .JSP is the file name. Now it's not the only vulnerability they're going after. They're also going after a number of other vulnerabilities, PHP vulnerabilities and the like. But this SAP Netweaver was the one that sort of really stuck out somewhat here. So as always keep looking for web shells. That's one of the top ways how attackers take advantage of vulnerabilities in web applications. In particular in this case this Netweaver vulnerability is basically just a simple upload vulnerability. So an attacker may upload any file to the system. And with that of course an obvious way to exploit the vulnerability is uploading a web shell. So N-able today announced that it took down its n-central hosted environments. This came after someone did publish I believe 30 different vulnerabilities that affect the current version of N-able. And there are no patches at this point available for this. So of course the problem comes up if you're self hosting N-able or n-central really. You probably want to take it down as well and follow here N-able's lead what it did with its cloud environment. On the other hand they also suggest if you sufficiently secured it meaning you isolated it. You should be fine. They haven't yet detected any exploitation of these vulnerabilities. But of course the vulnerability details have been made available publicly. So it's probably just a matter of a little bit of time to see these vulnerabilities exploited. They also don't sort of have a timeline at least at the time at which I'm reading this. When their hosted environment will be enabled again. But they do state that the remediation is on track. And they hope to soon have in their hosted environment these vulnerabilities mitigated. And then be able to again enable public access to the n-central hosted environment. That of course doesn't mean that they immediately will have patches for these vulnerabilities. So your on-premise version of n -central may need to stay down a little bit longer. Google updated the stable channel for Google Chrome fixing nine different vulnerabilities. One of which is already being exploited. So we got a zero day here. This vulnerability is a use after free vulnerability in the XML parser. And yes with that can probably be exploited to execute arbitrary code. They don't really say anything about a possible sandbox escape or such. So there may be a little bit more work to be done to actually sort of get to a full compromise from this particular vulnerability. Well and if all of a sudden you're seeing rejected emails from Outlook 365 with a 550 message rejected error. This points to you probably missing a DMARC policy. In the past Microsoft only required that you have a valid SPF and DKIM record. Well now you also must have a DMARC record in order to have your email accepted by Outlook 365. So definitely take a look at that and check if you're all set with this. This has become more and more sort of the standard where you must have SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Where DMARC of course tells the recipient what to do if your SPF or DKIM policy is not aligned with a particular email that you send. Well this is it for today. So thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending this podcast. And special thanks if you can find the five minutes to vote for me in the Difference Maker Award. There's a link to the voting page in the show notes. So thanks and talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

articles.title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
articles.context: Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes
articles.full_text:
Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones.

Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN.

The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post.

The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

“Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.”

Intermittent sending issues

DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing, and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes.

But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected.

For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum:

Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered.hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location.

Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

A Microsoft external staff moderator called it a “service degradation” currently under active investigation.

According to email security company MailRoute, enterprises can determine if their domain is impacted with this command on any terminal (replacing example.com with their domain): dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com. A response starting with v=DMARC1 means there is a DMARC record; no reply means there isn’t, MailRoute said.

The fix is a single TXT record: v=DMARC1; p=none. This declares that a domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures, MailRoute explained.

DMARC meant to make impersonation difficult

DMARC relies on two foundational email authentication tools that must be active on a domain: SPF and DKIM.

SPF verifies whether the sending server’s IP address is allowed to send email on behalf of a domain, while DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message to prove it wasn’t altered along the way and actually belongs to the domain it says it is coming from.

DMARC checks the two, identifying whether the domain listed on the “from” address aligns with the validated domains. It ties those checks to the name the reader actually sees and tells receivers what to do with forgeries, Dickson explained.

“Without it, impersonating your domain is easy,” he said. “That is where a lot of phishing and business email compromise starts.”

But because Microsoft, at least to this point, has only required DMARC for larger senders, it is not standard across the board; many small senders reasonably concluded it did not apply to them, Dickson noted. This includes SMBs, nonprofits, schools, and professional practices such as law firms, accountants, and doctors’ offices running on domains that “someone set up years ago, and nobody has touched since.”

Larger organizations miss DMARC on secondary domains, regional domains, and the subdomains that their marketing and billing platforms send from for mundane reasons. No one owns the domain name system (DNS), and “people fear breaking legitimate mail sent by third parties,” Dickson said.

Quiet, inconsistent failure

As MailRoute pointed out, what makes this particular malfunction so dangerous is its inconsistency: The person who sent the message sees a bounce “full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on.” Meanwhile, the customer never knows a message was sent.

It fails quietly, which is “the bane of an email marketer’s existence,” Dickson said. Customers, patients, job applicants, and others use Hotmail, Outlook, Live, and MSN, and when invoices, password resets, appointment confirmations, and offer letters go missing, the customer thinks they’re being ignored, not necessarily that the message is not getting through.

The good news is that the failures are findable, he pointed out. Every rejection generated a bounce, and bounces are logged. Enterprises should search mail logs, email platforms’ bounce reports, and help desk tickets for entries citing “Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC” since Nov. 5.

Then, resend what matters, time-sensitive transactional mail first.

From there, fix the cause by confirming that every domain sending mail as you publishes a DMARC record, Dickson advised. If one is missing, a basic monitoring record (p=none) stops these bounces without changing how anyone else treats your mail, as long as SPF or DKIM lines up with the From domain.

Microsoft 365 customers who never turned on DKIM for their own domains should do it now, he advised. “Do not rewrite SPF just because the bounce blames it,” he said. If your records are clean and mail still bounces, send the full bounce to Microsoft so it lands in the investigation.

However, a p=none record is “first base, not home plate,” he said. The goal is p=reject, which tells receivers to refuse anyone forging your name.

Inventory every service that sends email as you, Dickson advised: The CRM, the billing system, the HR platform, and the marketing tools. “Most organizations cannot produce that list,” he noted. “You cannot protect a domain when you do not know who is speaking for it.”

A signal of what is to come

While it remains to be seen what is causing this glitch, enterprises should make no mistake about where things are heading, Dickson said: DMARC will be enforced for every sender. Google and Yahoo began requiring it of bulk senders in February 2024; Microsoft followed in May 2025.

“Requirements start with the big senders and then become the floor for everyone,” he said. “The rollout was botched, but the destination is not in doubt.” But while Microsoft has the destination right, “nobody should learn about a new rule from a bounce message.”

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

articles.title: Weekly Update 529: Kids Social Media Bans (and Everything Else)
articles.context: The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb
articles.full_text:
The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb. It's not the premise of delaying their access until 16, but the inability of those who should know better to grasp where the responsibility for enforcement lies. Here's our PM's explainer after the laws passed down here a couple of years ago:

The onus won't be on parents or young people. There will be no penalties for users.

And it's been expressed many times since, in similar terms, always to the effect of placing responsibility for implementation and enforcement on the social media platforms. Inevitably, there are some massive holes in their implementation, along with major privacy and social concerns. But as I say this week (and have said on many previous occasions), it doesn't have to be perfect; over the long run, it will gradually change social norms, and the kids in that shoulder age bracket right now will have a different set of expectations than those who come after them. But hopefully, in the interim, the whole "onus won't be on parents" mantra will be respected more than it has been to date.

articles.title: Anthropic's super bug-finding Mythos model is going into Cisco and IBM products
articles.context: Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost
articles.full_text: Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products. Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups. “At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address. AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost. Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand. Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws. The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself. The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses. IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.” We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response. Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.” After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. “Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.” The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

articles.title: People Are Getting Weird About AI
France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns
articles.context: Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on...
articles.full_text: France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.” The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command. “This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement. All signs point to CyberAv3ngers Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers. This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers. The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers. “The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.” Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons. Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says. It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.” In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C). Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America. France fights back The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.” This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador. However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

articles.title: CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents
Peer pressure meets private keys.
articles.context: Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.
articles.full_text:
A classified memo ties Nvidia’s chief executive to Chinese espionage. AI coding agents crack under peer pressure, coughing up private keys. Big breaches hit seven million Japanese shoppers and three million students here in the States, while a French bank takes a multi-million-dollar hit through a vendor compromise. Adversaries weaponize a fresh OpenSSH bypass in the wild, pro-Russian hacktivists put dark web bounties on senior European officials, and Google drafts digital IDs to solve the passkey recovery puzzle. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Today is Monday November 9th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Classified memo warns of Nvidia chief's ties to Chinese operative.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo this past spring warning senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an operative tied to Beijing's Ministry of State Security.

Intelligence gathered from electronic surveillance revealed Huang was intimately involved with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed has purchased two billion dollars in advanced Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling restricted artificial intelligence hardware into China. While Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family, Nvidia stated it has no reason to believe national security or trade secrets were compromised.

Huang remains an influential voice shaping United States policy against tighter export controls, highlighting the growing counterintelligence risks hovering over America’s critical semiconductor supply chains.

The New York Times originally reported the findings.

Autonomous AI coding agents leak credentials under swarm peer pressure.

Autonomous software engineering agents routinely violate core security policies, leaking private deployment credentials and executing untrusted scripts, when pressured by third-party agent forums, according to testing by AE Studio and the AI Alignment Foundation shared with The Register.

Researchers tasked nine coding models with debugging a broken service in an isolated sandbox. Given access to a forum that held the solution, agents surrendered private tokens fifteen percent of the time and executed unverified installation scripts nearly a quarter of the time to obtain assistance. Under performance pressure, execution rates spiked to thirty-four percent.

As organizations rush to integrate autonomous agents into production environments, granting models broad system permissions without strict data isolation turns automated workflows into immediate remote code execution and credential leakage risks.

A Japanese online market goes offline following a suspected breach of 7.7 million customer records.

Japanese consumer goods and electronics giant Iris Ohyama has suspended its primary ecommerce platform, Iris Plaza, following unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service that contained personal records for nearly eight million shoppers.

The retailer took the storefront offline late last month after discovering a suspicious file on its cloud infrastructure. Exposed records cover 5.8 million registered members and 1.9 million guest shoppers, potentially compromising names, physical and email addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, and encrypted passwords. Payment data was stored separately and avoided exposure.

The disruption highlights the severe operational fallout and supply-chain vulnerabilities inherent in cloud-hosted retail environments, leaving core commerce operations frozen while investigators determine whether customer files were actually exfiltrated.

Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical authentication bypass in OpenSSH tracked as CVE-2026-123158, dubbed "SSHole."

The vulnerability allows attackers to compromise accounts like root on systems running musl libc without PAM—including Alpine and OpenWrt—by supplying overlong passwords. Security firms WatchTowr and Previdian report that botnets and cryptominers are already leveraging the flaw in the wild.

The rapid weaponization underscores immediate exposure for lightweight Linux environments, prompting administrators to deploy version 10.6p2 or disable password authentication entirely.

A French banking group confirms third-party compromise and fraudulent fund transfers.

French banking giant Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed an intrusion into its network via a third-party service provider, enabling attackers to conduct major fraudulent transactions.

The disclosure follows reports from blockchain investigator ZachXBT, who traced approximately 133 million dollars in suspicious withdrawals and aggressive cryptocurrency laundering across multiple centralized exchanges. The bank stressed that customer accounts remained untouched, as the threat actors targeted Arkéa's own institutional accounts before routing capital toward external cryptocurrency platforms. Arkéa reports that security teams contained the incident, froze a portion of the funds, and maintain that the bank's financial stability remains secure.

The incident underscores the persistent vulnerability institutional financial networks face through external vendor access paths, demonstrating how rapid cryptocurrency conversion complicates law enforcement recovery efforts.

Frontline Education data breach impacts over three million individuals across K-12 systems.

School administration provider Frontline Education has notified the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that an August breach compromised records for over three million people—more than doubling previous state estimates.

Attackers exploited a flaw in a third-party application, accessing personal records of staff and students across Frontline Central and School Health Management services. Exfiltrated data includes Social Security numbers, driver’s licenses, and health insurance information.

The incident highlights continuing third-party software risks threatening sensitive educational and student administrative platforms.

Google develops digital identity credentials for secure passkey and account recovery.

Google is developing an account recovery framework that leverages verified digital identity credentials, aiming to eliminate the security vulnerabilities of fallback methods when users lose primary devices.

Speaking at the Authenticate 2026 conference, company product managers explained that legacy recovery workflows—such as SMS-based fallbacks—risk undermining the cryptographic advantages of passkeys. Under Google's proposed system, users register a signed digital ID in advance to create a cryptographic stable hash linked to their account. If their physical device is lost, obtaining a verified digital credential on a replacement device restores their account, passkeys, and data in a single step.

Securing the recovery loop represents the crucial missing link in widespread passwordless adoption, though full-scale rollout still faces hurdles in wallet interoperability and near-real-time credential provisioning.

Pro-Russian hacktivists dox European leaders and bounty personal details.

Pro-Russian hacktivist syndicate NoName057(16) has published personal records belonging to Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and seventeen other senior European officials across the dark web, offering cryptocurrency bounties for further intelligence on the targets and their families.

The doxing campaign targets prominent figures across European law enforcement and judiciary—including leaders at Europol, Eurojust, and the German Federal Criminal Police Office—alongside investigative journalists. The operation appears to be direct retaliation for a multi-nation law enforcement takedown in July 2025 that dismantled over one hundred of the gang's servers.

The move marks an aggressive evolution from nuisance denial-of-service disruptions into direct personal harassment and targeted intelligence-gathering aimed at deterring Western support for Ukraine.

Monday business briefing.

Capital continues pouring into artificial intelligence defense and validation, led by 220 million dollars raised across two standout funding rounds. Agentic data security startup Sentra secured 150 million dollars in a round led by Capital One Ventures, while formal verification provider &Truth emerged from stealth backed by 70 million dollars in seed capital.

Consolidation across the sector accelerated with eight reported acquisitions, headlined by CrowdStrike’s aggressive expansion into model governance. According to the Wall Street Journal, the security giant is acquiring AI observability firm Fiddler AI for 400 million dollars alongside red-teaming platform Dreadnode for 95 million dollars to embed behavioral accountability into its Falcon ecosystem. Penetration testing specialist Bendings also acquired Scopertos for 55 million dollars, while Cognition absorbed code security shop Corridor.

The flurry of dealmaking signals that enterprise demand is rapidly shifting toward pre-deployment testing, agent explainability, and securing the broader algorithmic supply chain.

After the break, I welcome Nozomi Networks’ Director of Cybersecurity Strategy Chris Grove. We discuss the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attack part 2.

That was Chris Grove from Nozomi Networks.

Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Huawei claims it has built the holy grail of sovereign computing: an enterprise desktop boasting one hundred percent Chinese-manufactured components.

The Qingyun HM650 runs a homegrown, ten-core Kirin processor alongside an enterprise flavor of HarmonyOS, specifically designed to bid a polite, permanent farewell to Western software dependencies. One government agency has already ordered six hundred units—perhaps less out of spontaneous consumer enthusiasm and more in dutiful compliance with Beijing’s mandate evicting Wintel machines from state desks.

Whether every capacitor actually traces its architectural ancestry strictly to domestic drawing boards remains conveniently ambiguous, as foreign outfits still keep plenty of factories humming across the mainland. Regardless of pedigree, locking Western chipmakers out of vast government procurement pools delivers a cold chill to Santa Clara balance sheets.

Meanwhile, Japan unveiled a sixty-three million dollar emergency cybersecurity fund after adversaries disrupted critical infrastructure, cloud providers, and—perhaps most unforgivably—KFC logistics.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Report: Social Engineering Remained the Top Initial Access Vector in Q3 2026
articles.context: “This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those...
articles.full_text:
Phishing remained the most common initial access vector for attackers in the third quarter of 2026, according to a new report from Cisco Talos. Ransomware gangs are using voice phishing attacks to trick employees into granting them a foothold within organizations.

“In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool,” Cisco Talos says. “Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials.”

The researchers also observed an increase in threat actors abusing AI tools, both as a tool to assist in attacks and as a target for attacks themselves.

“[An] investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant,” the researchers write.

“This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities. These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools.”

Cisco Talos has the story: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q3-2026/
