articles.title: Feds warn grocers: Don't chill on cyber defenses as freezer hacking spree heats up
articles.context: Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds
articles.full_text: If you have any industrial smart freezers, look out. The US federal government is urging owners and operators to disconnect them from the internet, apply patches, change default passwords, and take other security measures to prevent the kind of attacks that have become prevalent in Europe. “We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement. Since mid-October, unknown miscreants have hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden. The attacks increase the temperature inside fridges to highs of 50ºC (122°F), spoiling food, and sparking fires. The Register asked the FBI if it has documented any successful or attempted attacks against refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in America. We had not received a response to our questions at the time of publication, nor are we aware of any documented digital attacks against these systems in American supermarkets. But there are signs that stateside operators are aware of the issue. Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, last month said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack that affected most of its US and European brands. Delhaize supermarkets in Europe are among those hit by the destructive freezer attacks. The Pentagon is also reportedly treating a series of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the US in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to Reuters, which cited four officials familiar with the matter. In a Thursday advisory, the US FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services, and departments of Agriculture and Transportation warned organizations about the ongoing cyber threats facing operators of industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards,” the agencies said. Attackers exploit these flaws by bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and abusing weak configurations, according to the feds. Once criminals gain access to the systems, they can change the temperature to spoil food or temperature-controlled medications, start fires, and ultimately harm people who consume products that haven’t been stored at proper temperatures. How to stay frosty To prevent these scenarios, the government organizations urge owners and operators to “immediately” implement best practices and security protections. First and foremost on the list: do not expose industrial control systems and devices to the public internet. Iranian hackers used internet-accessible programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to break into more than 100 US water systems in July. This sort of exposed device, which often lacks password protection, is a boon to miscreants looking for an easy button to gain access to critical facilities. “Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities,” the feds advise. Other recommended tactics include: Create a dedicated VLAN for operational technology (OT) devices, to isolate industrial devices from business networks. Replace default passwords with strong passwords and policies, turning on phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA) whenever possible. Apply patches in a timely manner, and retire and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates from the manufacturer. Define and maintain a device and IP allow-list, and limit access to OT devices to only those on the list. Maintain and test backups. These should be kept offsite and offline. And finally: enable logging and regularly review logs for any unusual activity.®

articles.title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
articles.context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
articles.full_text:
A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out.

Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay.

Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments.

How phone return scams works

The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns:

“After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.”

Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe.

The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide.

The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals.

The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device.

How to stay safe

The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and deliberate whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own.

You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following:

An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade.

A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer.

A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting.

Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller.

A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider.

If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation.

If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions.

Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help explain what happened to support a billing complaint and fraud report.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

articles.title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
articles.context: Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client
articles.full_text:
Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30. while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

Run programs and system commands.

Browse folders and download files.

Take screenshots.

Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.

Collect browser passwords and cookies.

Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.

Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

How to stay safe

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite, so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

Close the launcher and check your PC. MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.

Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.

Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.

If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you.

Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
articles.context: Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the...
articles.full_text:
When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking.

So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well.

But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it.

The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay.

The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return.

Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately.

The scam typically follows this pattern:

A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details.

The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing.

They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment.

They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet.

Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard:

“We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it.

Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number.

Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments.

How to stay safe

Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse.

You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment.

Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later.

Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward.

Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message.

A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed.

If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

articles.title: Claude, you've got company.
articles.context: The vulnerability could theoretically enable extortion or interfere with malware detection, although no exploitation has been observed. The attacks, attributed to Chinese threat actor Red Heron, were initially believed to exploit a different Zyxel vulnerability.
articles.full_text:
Claude Dispatch opens the door to hijacking. Residential proxies turn up on White House networks. Asian airlines suffer a wave of data breaches. Cisco and WatchGuard roll out critical patches. GhostMap traps Android phones in endless reboot loops. Hackers exploit a Zyxel zero-day to compromise nearly a thousand devices. Ukraine's scam call center crackdown ensnares senior security officials. AI-powered scammers prey on owners of missing pets. A former U.S. government IT worker admits to spying for Ethiopia. Our guest is Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and co-founder of QuSecure, with insights on the NIST PQC roadmap. Voters pull the plug on data centers.

Today is Thursday November 5th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Claude Dispatch proves vulnerable to being hijacked.

A security researcher has uncovered a vulnerability in Anthropic’s Claude that could allow a malicious browser extension to execute commands on a user’s computer, or even another machine connected to the same account. Forever Security’s Gal Weizman discovered that Claude Dispatch, which lets users remotely control Claude Desktop, could be hijacked through an authenticated browser session. His proof-of-concept attack tricked Claude into installing a malicious npm package while automatically approving permission requests. Weizman says the underlying design weakness also affects Claude Cowork and Code Remote Control, potentially allowing attackers to move from personal devices into corporate environments. Anthropic acknowledged the vulnerability in May but reportedly has not fixed it. The researcher warns that Claude’s convenient cross-device connectivity comes at the expense of traditional browser security boundaries.

Not even the White House is immune to residential proxies.

Security researchers say computers connected to the White House network are running residential proxy services that allow outsiders to rent their internet addresses. Layer3 Intel detected proxy activity on 26 of 30 days, recording 236 connections through six White House IP addresses. Researchers identified 28 proxy services using the network, including Infatica, a Russian company whose founder previously operated hosting infrastructure linked to Russian attacks on U.S. election systems in 2016. Residential proxies are often bundled into free applications, sometimes without users realizing their devices are being used. The services can enable cybercrime and potentially expose internal networks to attack. Researchers warn that anyone willing to pay a few dollars could route internet traffic through White House IP addresses. The White House has not commented.

Asian airlines report customer data breaches.

At least six Asian airlines have reported customer data breaches stemming from a cyberattack on Spanish technology provider Amadeus, which operates reservation, ticketing, and check-in systems. Affected carriers include Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana, Singapore Airlines, and Malaysia Airlines. Japan Airlines reported 92,000 affected customers, Cathay Pacific 53,000, and Singapore Airlines 46,000. Exposed information includes passenger names, booking details, travel itineraries, and, in some cases, passport information and frequent flyer numbers. Cathay Pacific says attackers used credentials assigned to an Amadeus system account. Amadeus says it has addressed the vulnerability and found no evidence that financial information was accessed or ransomware was involved. The airlines say their own systems and operations remain unaffected. Singapore Airlines is changing exposed booking numbers and warning customers about phishing attempts.

Cisco and WatchGuard patch serious vulnerabilities.

Cisco and WatchGuard have released patches for several serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and authentication flaws. WatchGuard addressed four critical bugs, although patches remain unavailable for a Linux kernel vulnerability affecting its Dimension platform. Cisco fixed a high-severity flaw in UCS Central Software and confirmed that 19 products are affected by the actively exploited Brotli vulnerability known as Node2Shell. Meanwhile, SonicWall warned that two vulnerabilities in its discontinued Global Management System platform will remain unpatched. Neither Cisco nor WatchGuard reports exploitation of their newly patched flaws.

GhostMap disables Android phones through a specially crafted app.

Bitdefender researchers have discovered an Android vulnerability called GhostMap that could render phones unusable simply by installing a specially crafted app. The app requires no permissions or executable code. Instead, malformed file information causes a core Android system process to repeatedly crash, trapping the device in a reboot loop. Neither restarting nor safe mode resolves the problem, potentially leaving a factory reset, and the resulting loss of locally stored data, as the only recovery option. Researchers reproduced the flaw on Android 17 and say it affects versions dating back to Android 10. The vulnerability could theoretically enable extortion or interfere with malware detection, although no exploitation has been observed. Google acknowledged the report but declined to issue a security update, referring it for possible future consideration.

A recently patched Zyxel vulnerability compromises nearly 1,000 devices.

Researchers at Binarly say a recently patched vulnerability in Zyxel GS1900 switches was exploited as a zero-day to compromise nearly 1,000 devices. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. The attacks, attributed to Chinese threat actor Red Heron, were initially believed to exploit a different Zyxel vulnerability. Binarly determined the hackers were actually exploiting the previously unknown flaw, rendering earlier patches ineffective. Zyxel released fixes on October 23, covering ten affected switch models.

Senior Ukrainian security officials are fired after a scam call center probe.

Ukraine's security service has dismissed two senior officials amid an expanding corruption investigation into a criminal network allegedly paying law enforcement officers to protect fraudulent call centers. Investigators say the organization included at least 12 people, among them senior security officials, prosecutors, police officers, and organized crime figures. The group's alleged activities extended beyond online scams to drug trafficking, counterfeiting, kidnappings, and violence. During one search, investigators say a senior security official threatened them with a firearm. The investigation, dubbed Operation Carthage, follows earlier allegations that prosecutors accepted bribes to shield scam operations targeting victims in Ukraine and abroad. The scandal has prompted Ukraine's parliament to approve tougher penalties for operating fraudulent call centers, with potential prison sentences of seven to twelve years.

UK scammers target missing pets.

Scammers in Britain are using AI-generated images of missing pets to extort desperate owners, sometimes threatening to kill the animals unless they receive payment. When Stephanie Young's cat Buddy disappeared, a supposed rescuer sent convincing pictures and demanded Apple gift cards. After Young questioned the images, the scammer threatened to murder or sell her cat. Other victims report similar experiences, including one woman whose supposed rescuer demanded £40,000 for her missing cat. Fraudsters create elaborate backstories and convincing images to exploit owners' emotional vulnerability, often demanding payment before agreeing to return the animals. British authorities advise owners to verify claims by requesting live video or arranging an in-person meeting before paying. Experts warn that AI has made these scams remarkably easy to produce, while the urgency and emotional distress surrounding a missing pet make victims particularly susceptible.

A former U.S. government IT worker pleads guilty to spying for Ethiopia.

A former U.S. government contractor with Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to spying for Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a 53-year-old naturalized American citizen from Maryland, worked across several federal agencies, including the State and Justice Departments. Prosecutors say he accessed classified intelligence reports without authorization, copied information from at least 133 reports, and smuggled documents out of secure facilities on discs disguised as containing unclassified material. He transmitted sensitive intelligence to senior Ethiopian military, political, and intelligence officials through encrypted messaging and personal storage devices. According to the FBI, Ethiopian officials used the information in military operations during an ongoing conflict. Investigators also identified more than $66,000 in bank deposits during the period. Lemma has agreed to a prison sentence ranging from 10 years to nearly 22 years.

Voters pull the plug on data centers.

America's data center industry had a rough election night. Across the country, candidates campaigning against massive computing facilities scored victories, as voters expressed frustration over electricity costs, noise, pollution, and the expanding influence of artificial intelligence. Democrats Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire were among the winners, while candidates dubbed “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick” weren't so fortunate. In Texas and Georgia, newly elected governors have advocated pausing data center construction, potentially complicating hundreds of planned projects. Local ballot measures also reflected growing resistance to development. Industry-backed candidates lost several races despite substantial financial support. The backlash crossed party lines, suggesting that enthusiasm for AI infrastructure isn't necessarily shared by the communities expected to host it. And as the returns came in, Elon Musk suggested that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing. Apparently, the zoning regulations are more accommodating up there.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: The White House is apparently a popular residential proxy exit spot
articles.context: The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose...
articles.full_text: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks. News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool. “The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email. For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year. The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent. Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained. According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said. Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem. “Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.” In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while. “Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.” Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them. Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems. Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over. “Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed. The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

Introducing AWS account access manager: IAM role flexibility with centralized workforce access
articles.context: Account access manager launch partners Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into...
articles.full_text:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager, a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center, with user-level visibility built-in.

Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points.

Why use account access manager?

Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets.

Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today:

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims, for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization.

Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions.

Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows.

Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used.

How it works

Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation. Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives.

Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles

To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement. The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login.

You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) (aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi, so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access, separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events.

How to enable account access manager

Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment.

Prerequisites

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled.

Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either:

Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM.

Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory.

IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first.

Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post).

Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account.

For CLI access: Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer.

Step 1: Enable account access manager

Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization:

aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com

Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager:

Console:

Sign in to your organization’s management account.

In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access, choose account access manager.

The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance.

If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager.

Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console

AWS CLI:

Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run:

aws account-access create-application \ --region <Region> \ --identity-source '{ "identityCenter": { "instanceArn": "<IAM Identity Center Instance ARN>" } }'

As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated.

After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability.

Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console.

Account access manager ARN: the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance.

Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement

In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN.

Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways

If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack.

Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws

Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/*

Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws

Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws

Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access

Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles

Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it.

Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace <your-account-id>, <region> (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and <application-id> (from the Settings page of the console).

Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details

IAM role trust policy:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:SetContext", "sts:TagSession" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "<your-account-id>", "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access:<region>:<your-account-id>:application/<application-id>" } } } ] }

Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides.

Best practice:

Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/<key> and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise.

Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference.

Step 4: Assign access to users and groups

Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts, Users, or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI.

Assign from the console:

Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name.

Select the user, then choose Assign new access.

Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager

On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access.

Assign a user using AWS CLI:

aws account-access create-entitlement \ --region <Region> \ --application-arn "<Account_access_manager_ARN>" \ --entitlement '{ "principalRole": { "principal": { "identityCenter": { "userId": "<Identity_Center_User_ID>" } }, "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/<ROLE_NAME>" } }'

To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": "<IDC_GROUP_ID>". To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID.

Note:

The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand.

Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment.

IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours.

Step 5: How workforce users can sign in

Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways:

Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws, or a vanity URL) and sign in.

Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed.

Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day.

Access through a web browser

Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser.

Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials.

On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to.

Expand the account to see the roles you can assume.

Select a role (for example, Developer). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role.

Access through the AWS CLI

Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started:

Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer).

Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles.

On the AWS CLI, run:

aws login

Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2).

Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated.

Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session.

The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser.

Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure, don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login, refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager.

Create shortcut links to specific console destinations

The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them.

Customer managed key considerations

If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center.

Best practices summary

Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin.

Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention.

Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege.

Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access.

Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account.

Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions.

Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers.

Account access manager launch partners

Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into their existing solutions, making it available to our joint customers from day one. Leading identity providers Okta, PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on.

Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale.

Conclusion

Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login. It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions).

To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video, which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment.

To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide. We encourage you to enable account access manager in a test organization, assign your first entitlement, and explore how centralized, user-attributed access can simplify your AWS environment.
