articles.title: Vizio, Samsung smart TVs seem to ignore tracking opt outs
articles.context: Only four out of eight smart TVs appeared to completely honor ACR opt-out
articles.full_text:
.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column484998_59baca-d5 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}

In this article

Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) sends viewing data from your smart TV to third parties.

Vizio and Samsung TVs both appeared to send this data even when researchers opted out of ACR.

Only four out of eight smart TVs appeared to completely honor ACR opt-out.

If you thought that opting out of surveillance on your smart TV would give you your privacy back, think again.

A study by researchers at Northeastern University found that some smart TVs still seem to send information about what you’re watching to third parties, even after you pressed the opt-out button.

The study, ‘Watching the watchers‘, tested twelve smart TVs from ten manufacturers to find out how well they respected opt-outs from automatic content recognition (ACR). ACR is a TV feature that captures audio and/or video content from smart TVs and uploads it to a third party (typically the TV manufacturer).

The third party converts this content into digital fingerprints to understand what you’re watching, and can then use it to send targeted advertising or allow others to do the same. It’s on most if not all smart TVs, and 82% of US households had a smart TV as of last year.

The test took in the eight operating systems behind roughly 95% of US smart TVs, and ran ten viewing scenarios on each of them. These ranged from viewing antenna TV through to viewing via screen mirroring from another device. The researchers tested viewing the first-party streaming services provided free with the manufacturers’ operating systems, along with sessions using third-party streaming apps. And they tested sessions where the TV was connected to another device via its HDMI port.

The study ran all of its tests both with ACR left on, and with the opt-out setting selected. The whole test involved over 5,000 automated sessions.

Vizio continued to send 100% of what looked like traffic when viewing its first-party streaming services and antenna-based TV services, even after people had opted out, the study said. It also sent the same amount of traffic when idle. However it didn’t send any ACR traffic for third-party streaming data, according to the report.

Samsung did appear to leak some traffic from third-party streaming services after the researchers opted out of its ACR function. They tested 30 runs of Samsung’s built-in streaming service after opting out of ACR, and found that it still showed traffic “consistent with ACR”.

After opt-out, the Samsung TV’s Tizen OS seemed to send ACR-related traffic about Netflix in 7% of runs, YouTube in 10% of runs, and Tubi TV in 20%. It sent ACR 60% of the time from HDMI sessions. Like the Vizio TV, it also sent ACR traffic for all of its first-party streaming sessions.

Late last month, a researcher reverse-engineered a Samsung Smart TV and cast doubt on whether disabling ACR worked on the device.

There was good news, though. Four smart TV operating systems went completely silent after the researchers turned off ACR: LG’s WebOS, Sony’s Google TV OS, Amazon’s FireTV OS, and Supersonic’s VIDAA OS.

Encryption is a research challenge

Vizio agreed to pay $2.2 million in a 2017 FTC settlement over charges that it collected viewing histories on eleven million smart TVs without user consent. At the time, it agreed to allow people to opt out of ACR.

The Vizio TV that the researchers tested sent traffic to Kinesis, an Amazon-run data ingestion service that the manufacturer uses to analyze data from its smart TVs. The researchers noticed no dip in traffic to this domain when they opted out of ACR on a Vizio TV. They said:

“The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint. However, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement.”

That’s a challenge to this research because most smart TVs encrypt their ACR traffic, including Samsung. So the researchers had to infer that this was ACR traffic based on signals such as where it was being sent, along with timing, volume, and protocol details.

One exception was Supersonic’s VIDAA OS, which sent ACR data to servers unencrypted. The servers responded unencrypted with a genre for what they recognized. Anyone watching the network could see it all, they warned. And because the servers didn’t require a login at the time of the test, over 57 million ACR detection results from other people’s TVs were accessible.

Vizio’s first-party streaming service WatchFree+ also dropped unencrypted titles of any show or channel being watched into online communications with the free TV service provider. There’s no way to turn that off, the researchers warned.

Walmart acquired Vizio for $2.3 billion in 2024, partly to help “advertisers to meaningfully connect with customers at scale and boost product discovery”.

The retailer also runs Walmart Connect, a retail media business that uses its customers’ data to help other businesses target them with ads.

Walmart was particularly interested in Vizio’s advertising business it, said at the time:

“Pairing it with Walmart Connect will be impactful and allow us to invest in our business even further on behalf of our customers.”

What smart TV owners can do

What can you do to protect yourself from a smart TV that might be sending your viewing data elsewhere? The researchers have some suggestions:

WebOS (LG), Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS on Supersonic all appeared to honor ACR opt-out, so selecting it on these TVs should be safe.

Disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device. That way the TV can’t send back data, even if it picks it up from the HDMI connection.

Use a blocklist. This takes a little more technical knowledge. If you run an internet router that can accept blocklists, then you can add a list of known ACR endpoints that will stop your TV’s traffic reaching them. The researchers provide one here.

Stop threats before they can do any harm.

articles.title: New York's Queens Public Library battles ransomware crims: Wi-Fi, checkouts, and website go dark
articles.context: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly
articles.full_text: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly. The disruption has downed QPL's website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, its public Wi-Fi, mobile app, and its digital media services. Renewals are also unavailable, although library users are not charged fines for returning materials late. (Since 2021, In October 2021, QPL, Brooklyn Public Library, and New York Public Library - in an effort to help lower income users from being put off borrowing - permanently killed daily late fines on books and circulating materials.) Each of the library system's 66 locations remains open, including the central library in the Jamaica neighborhood in Queens, but QPL warned: "it will take some time before the library's network and systems are restored." QPL said "certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted," advising visitors to check availability with their local branch via phone, and check the library's social media channels for official updates. "Our IT department is working to resolve the issue, and we will keep you informed,” it said in the statement. It added: "We apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience." No established ransomware group has yet claimed responsibility for the disruption, although attacks on publicly funded institutions rarely lead to lucrative payouts. The British Library's infamous ransomware attack in 2023 at the hands of Rhysida saw the organization refuse to pay the criminals' 20 Bitcoin ransom demand, opting instead to drain its cash reserves and fork out millions for an IT rebuild. Although the library's response to the attack drew widespread praise, few institutions of its kind are in a financial position to follow its lead. Other libraries might not be willing or able to commit to a recovery period as lengthy as that of the British Library. In its 2025/26 annual report, published in July, the institution said its recovery is still incomplete, and work to fully restore customers' ability to purchase electronic resources, such as journals and research databases, and reopen access to electronic legal deposit content is ongoing. This is likely to be completed by the end of 2026, the British Library added. ®

articles.title: OpenAI AI Pipeline Generates 948 Linux Root Escalation Exploits in 30-Hour Run
articles.context: The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5
articles.full_text:
OpenAI on Wednesday detailed a pipeline that employed an upcoming cyber-focused artificial intelligence (AI) model to validate and patch 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux for $1.2 million in API costs.

"Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access," the AI company said.

The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5.5‑Cyber model back in June 2026. The latest research turns this process into an agentic pipeline comprising five stages -

Vulnerability discovery, where agents identify high-value audit targets (i.e., parts of the codebase that are security-relevant and reachable by low-privileged users) and look for candidate findings

Dynamic validation, where agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in a sandboxed environment and preserve runtime evidence

Exploitability assessment, where agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could be abused to facilitate information disclosure or LPE and devise a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit

Patch generation, where agents generate patches for the identified vulnerability

Human review, where security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before it's reported to the maintainers

"In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities [within 30 hours] and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution," OpenAI said.

"The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit. To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques."

At a high level, these include -

Two new persistent elastic objects to spray objects inside the target kernel cache

Two new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability

Five new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write

One technique that involves arbitrary type confusion

The development is once again an indication of how frontier AI is redrawing the contours of cybersecurity, accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and at the same time helping defenders reliably address defects, albeit through additional instructions and iterations, before attackers can use them, and make it "cost prohibitive" for bad actors to exploit software.

In a report published last month, VulnCheck categorized AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a "growing risk category" that turbocharges novice hackers, who now require little to no technical expertise to detect software vulnerabilities.

The access to AI models is not just limited to defenders, but also bad actors who can leverage the same capabilities to discover and weaponize new zero-days and expand the pool of viable targets with minimal effort.

According to insights from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month has more than doubled, rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,740 in August 2026. The number of vulnerabilities classified as high-risk has surged from 131 disclosures in January 2026 to 350 in August 2026, a 167% growth.

"The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities," the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said in an assessment published Tuesday.

"Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an N-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses."

The NCSC also pointed out that organizations will have to evolve their internal patching and testing processes to meet this new pace of vulnerability discovery.

"Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal," it added. "Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally."

OpenAI said the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models needs to be matched by automated patch generation to secure software and to limit the exploitation window.

"With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants," OpenAI said. "For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system that isn't up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor."

articles.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
articles.context: To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-...
articles.full_text:
CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

articles.title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
articles.context: Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery...
articles.full_text:
Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

Authentication bypass;

Arbitrary code injection; and

Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

Change of temperature, which could:

Affect the service life of the system;

Create a fire hazard;

Cause loss of inventory; or

Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.

Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).

Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.

Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].

Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].

Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.

Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].

Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].

Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.

For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.

Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT

Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:

Date, time, and location of the incident;

Type of activity;

Number of people affected;

Type of equipment used for the activity; and

Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.

Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.

Disclaimer

The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. The authoring organizations do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favor by the authoring organizations.

articles.title: Chinese Nation-State Threat Activity Falls Sharply in Q2 and Q3 2026
articles.context: The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state...
articles.full_text:
Despite the sharp fall in China-aligned detections, observed PRC cyber activity remained “substantially higher” than nation-state cyber activity from Russia and Iran during the period, the researchers noted.

“The decline may reflect changes in targeting, infrastructure or detection visibility rather than a reduction in activity. The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state actors,” they wrote.

A number of Chinese nation-state espionage campaigns have gone undetected for long periods in recent years. For example, in 2025, the Chinese-nexus actor Weaver Ant was found to have infiltrated the network of an Asian telecommunications service provider and remained undetected for more than four years.

Such cases highlight that there may be significant ongoing Chinese nation-state activity occurring that has not yet been detected.

US and Turkey Primary Targets for Nation-State Actors

The Trellix report, published on November 4, found that nation-state targeting primarily focused on two countries, the US (38%) and Turkey (37.1%), which collectively represented over three-quarters of all detections from April to September.

The researchers noted that the US represents a valuable target due its status as the world’s largest economy and the concentration of high-value technology, defense and government infrastructure. Meanwhile, Turkey also represents a key strategic target given its location at the intersection of Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, as well as its NATO membership.

The third most targeted country by nation-state actors was Germany, representing 4.4% of such activity.

articles.title: ISC Stormcast For Thursday, November 5th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10166, (Thu, Nov 5th)
articles.context: One of the first sort of web vulnerabilities that I've sort of experienced, worked with was an old email script vulnerability for FormMail that had a number of issues. It's really more of a very focused and very full feature in that sense, a vulnerability scanner for these type of devices.
articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 5th, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. Well today's diary I titled it with the classics return. One of the first sort of web vulnerabilities that I've sort of experienced, worked with was an old email script vulnerability for FormMail that had a number of issues. So one was where it sort of would leak environment variables but could also be used to send spam to anybody in some versions. Now what I noticed in our web honeypot logs today was a number of different requests for script like sendmail.php, test-mail.php. Now what this I think looks for is, and I found a couple of these scripts, is these are scripts that you may deploy in development to just check your email configuration. These scripts will also send email to random email addresses that you specify as part of a GET or POST parameter. Two issues with this. First of all, yes, just like the good old FormMail script, these scripts will leak environment variables and server configuration. So that's one problem. But it can also be abused by a spammer to send email to arbitrary email addresses. Make sure you're not deploying them in production. Apparently enough people are doing so for attackers to make it worthwhile to actually scan for these scripts. So I think the real problem here is how do you manage moving code live and how do you sort of manage your entire sort of production environment and your build pipeline. That's sort of where these checks probably should be implemented that something like this never makes it to a production site. And then we've got an interesting new tool, OOB scan, out-of-band scan from H.D. Moore with runZero. This tool scans your network for exposed baseboard management controllers, IPMI, SNMP, and various other things that could be used to control systems, often used sort of as part of like these out-of-band management tools. Well, that's the name of the tool to manage servers. I just ran it before the podcast against my home network and definitely my AI agent has some work to do later to clean up some of the things that found, like found a printer that had SNMP enabled. I didn't know about, never use it. So that's one of the things that's going to be disabled. Yes, it's sort of a better port scanner, but it's really focused on these out-of -band management interfaces, like also IP KVMs and such. It finds that are found by other tools, but this one will give you all the details. It will flag any specific vulnerabilities it found on these systems. So it's more than a port scanner. It's really more of a very focused and very full feature in that sense, a vulnerability scanner for these type of devices. Well, then we have a critical vulnerability in apt, the script that you typically use to manage packages on Debian systems. This vulnerability is triggered by sending error messages from the web server, serving apt packages. And if you do it right, well then apt will not verify the signature on this package. So this allows the attacker to inject malicious packages for the system to download and install. This is particularly an issue because apt still doesn't always use HTTPS. So in order to trigger this vulnerability, an attacker does not have to have actually control of the endpoint. It's sufficient to then inject data on path. So another thing that you may want to look at if you're still using HTTP for apt, maybe switch to HTTPS. That may be an option depending on your distribution. Ubuntu, I think by default still does HTTP, not HTTPS. Then I got some bad news for you. If you're using SonicWall's GMS appliance, their global management system, well this product has been out of support and end of life for a while now. And there is a new vulnerability, one that does allow unauthenticated file read and then also an authenticated SQL injection vulnerability. Well, neither will be fixed. So your only option is really to check with SonicWall what else to give the money for that will replace GMS if you still need something with this feature set. It's a virtual appliance, so you can't really upgrade it by throwing it into the trash. I guess you can still just delete it or throw it into the desktop trash can. Well, and this is it for today. So thanks again for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending this podcast and talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

articles.title: Norway's aid agency pwned and all users' data is stolen
articles.context: " The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations
articles.full_text: Norway's national aid agency, Norad, has confirmed that cyber criminals broke into its systems, stealing information about each and every registered user of its grant portal. Norad, which coordinates Norway's assistance for foreign development, said that 20,614 registered individuals had their names and email addresses swiped, and information from at least three organizations' applications was "misdirected." The agency clarified that the grant portal, which was launched in 2017, has 20,614 registered users, meaning all were affected, across 12,511 organizations. In addition, the grant applications for at least three organizations are confirmed to be involved, though Norad said it may discover more as its investigation continues. Torger Kjeldstad, director of digitalization at Norad, said "the attack is complex," and confirmed the agency has initiated a crisis team to manage it. "We know a lot about what has happened, but to ensure that we have a complete overview of the attack, we are working to engage external experts in cybersecurity," he said. "They will give us a detailed description of what information those who attacked the solution have gained access to." Kjeldstad added that "it should be safe" to continue using Norad's services while it continues to probe what happened, and who was behind it. Norad did not reveal many details about how the attack unfolded, other than saying that 27 accounts were compromised and were then used to gain access to the portal and the data in question. The agency said the intrusion was detected on October 30, but did not offer any indication as to how long the attackers retained access to the grant portal. It also refused to rule out that names of applicants in "conflict areas and authoritarian states" may have been included in the stolen data – it is not known if recipients would have also been registered users – and said it is approaching the matter "very seriously." The grant portal, managed by Norad, which itself is part of Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is responsible for handling applications from organizations across the world. Recent case studies include support for independent, investigative journalism in Moldova, a country which routinely battles Russian propaganda and election interference, and backing for Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. The issues Norad and the Norwegian government support, however, are wide-ranging – from access to healthcare for transgender people worldwide and Kenyan incubators for innovative transport solutions, to delivering aid to war-torn Gaza. ®

articles.title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
articles.context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
articles.full_text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

articles.title: NATS Air Traffic Control Failure Cost UK Economy £33m
articles.context: Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors
articles.full_text:
A major IT failure at the UK’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) in September was not caused by a cyber incident, but still cost the economy tens of millions of pounds, a new report has revealed.

The Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC) claimed in a report published on November 4 that the cost to the UK economy was around £33m ($44m), with 70 domestic organizations affected.

However, it may have reached as high as £42m ($56.6m), according to the CMC’s modelled range, which reflects the cost to UK airlines, airports, ground operations and tour operators of 1152 flight cancellations, alongside significant delays and diversions.

If the impact on overseas airlines is included, the cost may have reached as high as £76m ($102.4m) based on 1800 cancelled flights. The impact on other non-UK organizations was not assessed.

The CMC estimated that 450,000 passengers were affected by cancellations or delays of more than two hours.

Read more on IT outages: CrowdStrike Fault Causes Global IT Outages.

Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors.

“Like the CrowdStrike software failure in 2024, it nonetheless shows how a failure in a single critical technology can cause widespread disruption to UK organisations,” the report noted.

“Its significance lies less in the scale of loss than in what it shows about the aviation system: a brief outage in a single critical system disrupted airline schedules for several days, and almost all of the cost fell on airlines and other organizations rather than on NATS.”

NATS is already mandated by the existing NIS Regulations 2018 to meet specific security and resilience obligations, and there’s nothing in the new Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would help to prevent a similar incident in the future, the CMC claimed.

However, the new regime may improve how incidents are reported and overseen, it noted.

Some Lessons Learned

The outage itself was caused by a “previously unknown defect in the legacy software of the National Airspace System (NAS),” when a “routine request for an aircraft identification code and a higher-priority system message collided within about one millisecond,” the CMC said.

Corrupted flight data first appeared at 10am, and at 12:45pm all UK departures were stopped. Following the loss of an automated system link at 1.32pm, NATS declared a major incident and moved to manual fallback procedures, including major traffic restrictions.

Although the flight data system was restored within three-and-a-half hours, flight restrictions weren’t lifted until the evening and the impact on travellers lasted much longer.

CMC recommended the aviation industry to:

Review how well coordination between NATS, airlines and airports worked during the downtime

Examine whether earlier and more frequent assessments of expected outage duration would have helped airlines and airports to limit disruption more effectively than waiting for certainty

Plan for a “multi-hour restriction in air traffic capacity” that includes scenarios which last much longer than the outage itself

CMC technical committee chair, Ciaran Martin said: “Organizations need to understand and plan for the risks that sit in systems they depend on, not just the systems they own.”

The CMC warned that the risk of outages stemming from unidentified software defects “is heightened while NATS continues to rely on legacy systems.”

articles.title: AI-Powered Ransomware Is Coming for UK Critical Infrastructure, and Europe Is Already the Testing Ground
articles.context: In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical...
articles.full_text:
Overview

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has put a date on a threat that security teams across Europe have been bracing for. In its 2026 Annual Review, The State of the Cyber Nation, the agency assesses it is highly likely that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on UK Critical National Infrastructure by 2028.

That is not a distant, speculative scenario. It is a two-year window, and it lands alongside a second judgement. By 2028, China, Russia and other nation-states will highly likely be using AI-enabled cyber capabilities routinely to pursue geopolitical goals, with the UK facing sophisticated attacks at greater scale and speed.

The review also recorded that UK and EU member states jointly attributed a December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid to Russia's FSB Centre 16. Had it succeeded, roughly 500,000 citizens could have lost power. Europe is not watching this threat from the sidelines; it is where the playbook is being tested.

Key Takeaways

2028 is the marker. The NCSC judges AI malware will highly likely be used in ransomware against UK CNI before the end of 2028.

Europe's grid is already a target. Russia's FSB Centre 16 was attributed to the December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid, and a July 2026 advisory from 18 partners in 12 countries flagged the same group exploiting vulnerable routers to reach CNI networks worldwide.

China is best positioned to use AI against CNI. The NCSC rates China's activity as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK.

AI speeds up old tricks rather than inventing new ones. For large organizations, 88% of incidents the NCSC handled began through just four initial access vectors.

A "patch wave" is coming. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery will shrink the time defenders have between disclosure and exploitation.

The gap is widening. Organizations with legacy technology and slow remediation will become the preferred targets of both states and criminals.

The 2028 Warning

The NCSC's assessment is precise about where AI makes the difference. It calls AI an almost certain "force multiplier" that improves reconnaissance, social engineering, vulnerability discovery and exploit development. The biggest effect, it says, will be faster and larger versions of existing tactics rather than brand-new attack vectors.

Ransomware is where that acceleration hits CNI hardest. The review expects criminal adoption of AI to raise the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and exploitation. It also warns that open-source AI tools built for security researchers are likely to be repurposed to automate criminal workflows, cutting costs and raising attack volumes against less resilient targets.

The agency is careful not to overstate today's reality. Its Incident Management team has begun to see attackers using AI tools, but none of the observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Human operators remain essential, and the NCSC notes that losing control of an agentic AI is likely to hinder threat actors from reaching their goals.

The review's pessimistic 2028 scenario shows why that caveat may not last. In it, frontier AI is available to everyone from state actors to novice hackers, jailbroken models are sold in criminal marketplaces, and attribution becomes harder as capability spreads. It even describes a realistic possibility of an automated cyber actor operating beyond its operator's control. Cloud-controlled CNI and AI-driven robotics raise the chance that a digital compromise causes physical harm.

The NCSC stresses this is an illustration of the cost of inaction, not a forecast. But it is a scenario written by the agency responsible for defending UK infrastructure, and it is set just two years out.

Europe: The Proving Ground for CNI Attacks

If the UK is looking at 2028, continental Europe is already living with the threat. The NCSC names Russia as the most audacious cyber threat to the UK today. GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler goes further in the review's foreword, warning that tactics Russia developed against Ukraine are now being turned more widely on states and their institutions.

Three data points from the review frame the European picture:

Poland's energy grid (December 2025). The UK and EU member states formally attributed the attack to FSB Centre 16. If successful, it could have cut electricity to around 500,000 people.

Router exploitation on a global scale (July 2026). The NCSC and 18 international partners from 12 countries issued a joint advisory on FSB Centre 16 actors exploiting vulnerable routers to target CNI networks worldwide. On the same day, the UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including criminals running proxy networks linked to Russian intelligence.

Operational technology in crosshairs. The review points to recent attacks on programmable logic controllers (PLCs) as evidence that organizations failing to modernize are falling behind.

The pattern matters for anyone running energy, water, transport or telecoms in Europe. Grids, interconnectors and supply chains cross borders, and a disruptive attack in one country can cascade into its neighbors. The review also describes how cyber threats to the UK can escalate rapidly and without warning during periods of geopolitical tension.

Add AI to this mix and the timeline compresses. A state actor that today relies on patience and known router flaws could, with AI-assisted discovery and exploitation, find and weaponize new weaknesses across thousands of European edge devices far faster than defenders can patch them.

China is Best Positioned to Turn AI on Critical Infrastructure

While Russia is the loudest threat, the NCSC sees China as the most capable. It judges that China highly likely has both the intent and the best position to use AI against CNI and other strategic targets. Its frontier AI programmes are expected to sharpen vulnerability identification, targeting efficiency and access operations.

Data sits at the center of that strategy. The review describes China collecting large volumes of information from the UK and elsewhere, then using it to train models and improve capability. In the AI era, stolen data is no longer just espionage material; it is fuel.

The UK has already acted on this. In December 2025, it sanctioned two China-based firms: i-Soon, which targeted more than 80 government and private IT systems globally, and Integrity Technology Group, which the FBI has linked to the Flax Typhoon intrusions. In April 2026, the NCSC and 15 partners across nine other countries published guidance on the covert networks most China-linked actors use to hide their activity.

The 2028 scenario adds a further concern: China, as a leading developer, may help spread advanced AI-cyber capability to other actors, letting them hide in the noise and making attribution harder for European defenders.

AI Runs the Old Playbook, Only Faster

The most useful finding in the review is also the least dramatic: attackers are still getting in through the basics. Over the past year, the NCSC received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks. Of these, 337 needed its direct support, and 80 were classed as nationally significant.

For large organizations, 88% of incidents started through four initial access vectors:

Exploiting public-facing applications

Phishing

Misuse of valid accounts

Exploiting external remote services

Even state-linked intrusions often used flaws for which patches already existed but had not been applied quickly enough. As the review puts it, sophisticated actors do not need to be sophisticated to gain initial access; their skill shows in what they do once inside.

This is exactly where AI changes the economics. The NCSC expects AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to give attackers more chances to hit systems before owners patch them. It is urging every organization to prepare for a "patch wave": a surge of security updates across the technology stack, many of them critical, as AI exposes years of technical debt.

Two further risks deserve attention:

Shadow AI. Staff moving sensitive data to personal devices to use unsanctioned AI tools leaves organizations blind to where that data goes, and open to both APT groups and criminals.

The widening gap. Mature, well-resourced organizations will use AI to detect and fix faster. Those running legacy systems will fall further behind and become more attractive targets.

The financial stakes are already clear. UK government research cited in the review puts the annual cost of malicious cyber activity to UK organizations at about £14.7 billion. The 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover alone cost the company around £196 million in direct costs and contributed to UK GDP growing just 0.1% in Q3 2025.

How the UK Is Fighting Back With AI

The NCSC's answer is to meet machine-speed attacks with machine-speed defense. Several initiatives in the review stand out:

Cyber Shield. A joint NCSC and DCMS programme to build a national agentic cyber defense ecosystem over five years. The NCSC supplies the platform and intelligence, while defensive agents are built by the security market and open-source community. Early phases focus on detection and blocking, where automation is already practical.

Project DROMOS. Launched in 2026 by the Government Cyber Coordination Centre and the AI Security Institute, it used frontier AI models to review government codebases. Expanded into live environments, it surfaced hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities.

National Detect Strategy. A pilot aiming, by 2030, to ensure defenders across critical systems can detect and respond to known vulnerabilities and attacker techniques at organizational, community and national scale.

Regulation and benchmarks. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill brings new sectors into scope and adds national security powers. The new CAF Core Profile sets a minimum resilience baseline for essential services.

There are early results. Under the Government Cyber Action Plan, the median time to fix domain-related vulnerabilities fell from 50 days to 8. The Early Warning service now covers 19,922 organizations, up 52% on last year.

For Europe, the lesson is that partnership is now part of the defense. The review highlights the world's first AI security standard developed through ETSI, the European standards body, as proof that allies can shape AI security while the technology is still evolving.

National defense at machine speed also depends on seeing adversaries before they reach the network. Groups like FSB Centre 16 and China-linked operators plan, recruit, and trade access in places most defenders never look. As AI makes attribution harder, government agencies, national CERTs, and defense bodies need intelligence that tracks threat actors across the open, deep, and dark web and connects that activity to the infrastructure being targeted. Cyble Hawk is built for exactly this. It gives national security teams sovereign threat intelligence, adversary profiling, and investigative support. That means early warning of campaigns against critical infrastructure and stronger attribution when an attack does land. Book a demo to see how your agency can move from reacting to incidents to anticipating them.

Recommendations for CNI Operators in the UK and Europe

The NCSC's core message is that AI did not create these weaknesses; it is exposing them faster. Operators of critical infrastructure should act on the following now:

Harden the edge first. Inventory and patch internet-facing applications, VPNs, routers, and remote access services. These are the routes FSB Centre 16 and others are actively exploiting.

Prepare for the patch wave. Build processes to test and deploy security updates more often, faster and across suppliers. Track time-to-remediate as a board-level metric.

Kill password-based access where you can. Move privileged and remote users to phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, and audit valid accounts for misuse.

Segment IT from OT. Limit the paths from corporate networks to PLCs and industrial control systems, and monitor those boundaries continuously.

Govern AI use internally. Map what data AI tools and agents can access, what actions they can take, and how they are monitored. Close off shadow AI with approved alternatives.

Rehearse recovery, not just prevention. Test ransomware response playbooks against scenarios where operational systems must run during disruption. Use the NCSC's guidance on recovering from highly disruptive attacks.

Lock down the supply chain. Require baseline controls such as Cyber Essentials, or equivalent standards in EU frameworks, from suppliers with access to critical systems.

Use threat intelligence that moves at AI speed. Monitor for exploitation of newly disclosed flaws, stolen credentials, and chatter about your sector, so you can act before an incident escalates.

Start post-quantum planning. The NCSC wants discovery and migration planning finished by 2028, priority migrations by 2031 and full migration by 2035.

Conclusion

The NCSC has given Europe a deadline. By 2028, AI-powered ransomware against UK critical infrastructure moves from possibility to expectation, and state actors will be using AI as a routine part of their operations. The Poland grid attack and the global router campaign show the targeting is already in place; AI simply adds speed and scale.

The agency's own framing is a "moment of choice." Organizations that modernize, patch fast, and build resilience now will be able to absorb what comes next. Those that defer will find AI exposing their technical debt faster than they can repay it.

For CNI operators across the UK and Europe, the next two years are the window to close the gap. Continuous visibility into emerging vulnerabilities, active exploitation and threat actor activity will be central to staying ahead of attacks that move at machine speed.

Source

NCSC Annual Review 2026: The State of the Cyber Nation

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
