articles.full_text:
Dutch spies, Russian hackers and Jared Kushner’s iPhone. It sounds like the ingredients for a thriller, but according to claims in a new book the US President’s son-in-law may have been hacked twice. Is any of it true, and what does it tell us about the phones in our pockets?

Meanwhile, James Ball explains that of the internet’s most trusted security keys were protected by numbers so small that one of them was… four. Yes, “4”. And then, of course, to make the week worse we suffered a PHPocalpyse…

Plus, Chuck Randolph of 360 Privacy explains how the internet has made it scarily easy to put company executives and public officials in danger.

All this and more in episode 490 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest James Ball.

Smashing Security #490

How Jared Kushner's iPhone was allegedly hacked twice

0:00

Learn more

0:00 0:00

0:00

Show full transcript ▼

This transcript was generated automatically, probably contains mistakes, and has not been manually verified.

JAMES BALL

For example, for Secure DNS, every three months they do a little ceremony to renew the keys. And I've stood in and watched one of these.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh, wow.

JAMES BALL

And of course, once a journalist was in a room and I had a camera person with me, it all went wrong. They messed it up. They got locked in a cage. They had to set off the fire alarm to get let out. It turned into total slapstick. Smashing Security, episode 490. How Jared Kushner's iPhone was allegedly hacked twice, with Graham Cluley and special guest James Ball. Hello, hello, and welcome to Smashing Security, episode 490. My name's Graham Cluley.

JAMES BALL

And I'm James Ball.

GRAHAM CLULEY

James, welcome back to the show. Super to have you.

JAMES BALL

You are suffering a little bit, not that our listeners will be able to tell, but if anyone sees you on video. Yes, I apologise to anyone looking at this on video who has to see my eyes, which look as if I'm sort of either auditioning for a sort of cold and flu advert, or else that I've been crying all day. I promise you neither is true, but yeah, I've been better.

GRAHAM CLULEY

All right, well, we won't keep you for too much longer than we need you, but we are gonna need you for the next 45 minutes or so as we look at some of the biggest security stories of the last week. But before we kick off, let's thank this week's wonderful sponsors, 360 Privacy, Origin, and Vanta. We'll be hearing more about them later on in the podcast. This week on Smashing Security. We're not gonna be talking about how a bug in Signal could let someone keep listening after you've hung up. You'll hear no discussion of how more than 4,500 Bluesky accounts were compromised by a phishing attack that posed as a government payment. And we won't even mention how a massive Chinese crime ring hacked the Staples retail giant to steal millions. So James, what are you going to be talking about this week?

JAMES BALL

Well, I thought I would talk about some scary news from the world of TLS.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And I'm gonna be talking about how Dutch spies allegedly hitched a ride on a Russian hack of Jared Kushner's iPhone. Plus, we've got a featured interview with Chuck Randolph of 360 Privacy about how the internet has made it scarily easy to put company executives and public officials in danger. All this and much more coming up in this episode of Smashing Security. Today's episode of Smashing Security is sponsored by 360 Privacy, and to explain what they do, I've brought in Joe.

JOE

Happy to help.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Joe, why are you wearing a balaclava?

JOE

You said I was playing a cybercriminal.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And?

JOE

Well, that's the uniform, isn't it? I assumed it was in the contract.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Joe, real cybercriminals dress like accountants. Most of them are sitting in open-plan offices eating a meal deal.

JOE

Now you tell me. I've walked here like this. The neighbours saw me.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, what did you say to them?

JOE

That I've been skiing.

GRAHAM CLULEY

It's October, Joe, and we're in the UK.

JOE

I said it was an indoor slope.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Fine, leave it on. And why the bobble hat?

JOE

It's cold in the studio.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Okay, okay, Joe, back to business. You've got one task. Find out everything you can about me using only the internet. Go!

JOE

Right, searching. Oh. Oh wow, that was quick. Your home address, family members, property records, social media accounts—

GRAHAM CLULEY

Hang on, that was under 10 seconds you managed that?

JOE

And I've got a few of the places you regularly visit. Honestly, it's a bit embarrassing how many times you go to Greggs for a sausage roll.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh, come on. Individually, those details seem harmless. Nobody's panicking over a coffee order.

JOE

But put them together and I now have a surprisingly clear picture of who you are, where you live, and how to find you. I haven't even finished my tea.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And that, listeners, is the problem that 360 Privacy is built to address.

JOE

360 Privacy is a digital exposure reduction firm. They help executives, high-profile individuals, and the organisations behind them shrink the digital exposure that turns into real-world risk.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Because threat actors don't separate cybersecurity, privacy, and physical security. They use whatever information is available.

JOE

Data brokers, social media, public records, and AI — it's all making it faster and easier to find that information and connect the dots, which is a bit rude, frankly, because I wanted my dots left unconnected. Here's how they fix it. Through their technology platform and a team of expert intelligence analysts, 360 Privacy identifies exposed personal information, works to remove it at the source, and continuously monitors for new exposures so it doesn't just pop back up next week.

GRAHAM CLULEY

In other words, 360 Privacy creates friction, making sensitive information harder to find, harder to connect, and harder to use against you, your family, or your company. So if Joe tried this again after working with 360 Privacy—

JOE

I've got nothing. Just a recipe for lasagna, which, to be fair, was not what I was looking for.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Modern targeting can begin with something as simple as a search engine query.

JOE

Learn more about reducing your digital exposure at 360privacy.io.

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's 360privacy.io.

JOE

Can I take the balaclava off now?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh, please.

JOE

Thank God, I'm boiling.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Now, chums, I've got a story for you. And as the story progresses, you can decide for yourself whether it might be true or not. It's a story which has just been published in Vanity Fair, of all places. There is an extract of a brand new book which has just come out that makes some pretty eyebrow-raising claims. The book is called Princes and Thieves, and it is by an investigative journalist called Matthew Cole. Have you ever encountered Matthew Cole at all?

JAMES BALL

I haven't, actually. I was digging into him a bit today. He did one of the books on SEAL Team 6, didn't he?

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's right.

JAMES BALL

I think about four different members of SEAL Team 6 claimed to be the actual one who shot Osama bin Laden and tried to get book deals off the back of it, et cetera. And as I understand it, Matthew Cole was one of the journalists who dug into which of them it actually was and how it all really went down. So he's a pretty experienced sort. Yes. This isn't his specialist beat.

GRAHAM CLULEY

He has worked in the past for The Intercept, which has covered obviously some cybersecurity-related stuff in the past and some hacking stuff in the past.

JAMES BALL

With mixed success. Yes.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, with mixed success. You're quite correct. I mean, I remember, for instance, I think he wrote about Reality Winner.

JAMES BALL

I do remember the Reality Winner story. That's what I was thinking of with my little dig.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Because, okay, for anybody who doesn't remember this, if I remember correctly, the Trump administration said there's been no evidence whatsoever of any Russian messing around with the US elections or any hacking. And someone who worked inside the American establishment actually leaked an NSA document which revealed that they had found evidence of that kind of thing going on. And they shared it with The Intercept, with Matthew Cole, one of the journalists there. And unfortunately, and I think this was unintended obviously, when The Intercept took that evidence to the authorities and said, well, what about this then? When they published their photos and things, what they hadn't realised was there were tiny little micro dots which had been printed on the piece of paper, which identified where the document had been printed. Is this your memory as well? And that helped identify the leaker who was Reality Winner, who ended up in jail as a consequence.

JAMES BALL

It's a pretty unforgivable screw-up. I will say in The Intercept's defence that they would have found Reality Winner anyway. Their mistake was revealing that they'd got a printed copy of the document in the first place. But if you looked, that particular memo had only been printed two or three times ever, because people don't print anymore. And Reality Winner had, from a work computer, emailed The Intercept previously. Now, it was just a customer service type email, it was saying, hey, is there something wrong with your podcast feed type thing? has printed the document and reads and cares about The Intercept enough to contact them from work, they'd have got her.

Unknown

Yeah.

JAMES BALL

But this is not how you do this kind of journalism, and it is a pretty basic screw-up.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So, yes, the logs would have given it away.

JAMES BALL

I should say, by the way, there is a superb movie about the Reality Winner case, just called Reality, and of all people, it stars Sydney Sweeney, who is a controversial enough figure in her own right. But what's unusual about it is everything that's said in the movie is verbatim from the court records of Reality's arrest. So, superb film about a whistleblower and about cybersecurity and American politics. Why not give that an early plug?

GRAHAM CLULEY

So we've given you some background now, Matthew Cole. So a slightly checkered history, and you have to bear that in mind when you hear the rest of this story, I suppose, to put everything in balance. But the excerpt of this new book published in Vanity Fair says that hackers at the GRU, which is Russia's military intelligence, broke into the phone of Jared Kushner, who of course is the son-in-law of Donald Trump and was one of his senior advisors in the White House during Trump's first term. And that would be a big enough story in itself, but what the story carries on to claim is that Dutch intelligence found out about that hack and were able to access Kushner's phone themselves. That story, as Vanity Fair are sharing it, is that in late 2017, the Netherlands Military Intelligence Service learned that a hacker working for Russia's GRU was travelling to the UK.

JAMES BALL

I mean, that's a bold move, isn't it?

GRAHAM CLULEY

According to the report, they were going there on some spying mission, whether they were going to spy on a cathedral or something, whether they were going to do a little tour of the Cotswolds, who knows what they were up to. But the Dutch, when they heard wind of this, oh, hang on, a Russian hacker coming to the UK, they said to their UK counterparts, would you mind if we sort of had a word with him? When he arrives, and the Brits apparently agreed. And so when this chap landed, the Dutch basically gave him two options. They said, "Look, you can work for us against the GRU, effectively becoming a double agent, or you can be arrested by the British and charged with espionage and potentially locked up for the next ten years or so in a British prison." And surprise, surprise! He apparently chose to work for Dutch intelligence. And one of the things he subsequently did — it is claimed in this book — is that he gave the Dutch access to a GRU server based in Russia where the GRU's hacking team stored information which they'd hacked and exfiltrated and stolen. And now the Dutch have got access to what the Russians have hacked. And apparently when they were scouring through all the files, they found these screenshots of Jared Kushner's iPhone X. Which sort of proves how long ago this story is based — it was an iPhone X.

JAMES BALL

Yeah, this is a 2017 story. This is from Trump's first term, isn't it? It's amazing how long ago the iPhone X feels like.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I think that was the first one which had Face ID. Because of course, Jared Kushner wouldn't have an iPhone X now, would he? He probably has got an iPhone which hasn't been released yet. Tim Apple would have sent him one personally because all the tech millionaires want to keep in with the family.

JAMES BALL

It's solid gold.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Like Trump Mobile. Well, it appeared that Russian military intelligence had compromised the phone of one of the most senior people in the White House, Jared Kushner. And this was without the knowledge of the Americans, but the Dutch knew about it. And by early the next year, 2018, these Dutch spies had apparently found a vulnerability in the phone that also gave them access to it, albeit it was fairly limited access. So it wasn't the case that they could turn on the microphone or turn on the camera or plant files or plant malware or anything like that. But what they could do, again apparently, was see Kushner's screen when he was using the phone. And apparently, again — I have to stress it's according to the book — Dutch intelligence began to capture every single screen image and stored it on their servers, because you never know when it might come in handy to have a little bit of information about someone quite senior in the White House.

JAMES BALL

Yeah, I mean, come on, we'd all be curious, wouldn't we?

Unknown

We would, wouldn't we?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Of course we would. We would.

JAMES BALL

I think it's interesting here because British intelligence must have been involved. There's no way UK intelligence would let Dutch intelligence fully run an operation from our territory without getting the asset for themselves. But we don't spy on the Americans, and they don't spy on us because of the Five Eyes agreement. There are quite a lot of rules against that. So we would not have been able to spy on Jared Kushner in this way.

Unknown

Right.

GRAHAM CLULEY

But if there was someone else in between who could share intelligence with us—

JAMES BALL

Well, that's the interesting little carve-out that I haven't really seen anyone ask yet. And it's sort of just one for the British diplomacy and spycraft nerds, that. But presumably UK intelligence would've been aware of this, but not exploiting it themselves, because they would've had to notify the White House if they were doing it. And I imagine that someone will have had to have a discussion about whether they told the White House about Kushner's phone being compromised in the first place, which I'm guessing they didn't. Again, if all of this is true.

Unknown

Yes.

JAMES BALL

But the wrinkle in there is quite an interesting one that I don't think will blow up, but has the potential to turn into a whole diplomatic row in theory.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, talking about things becoming a little bit hotter, the allegations continue because according to the book, while they were watching Kushner's screen, the Dutch intelligence agents apparently saw him log into a bank account in the United Arab Emirates and transfer hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. And initially the Dutch thought, oh, this must be linked to the government of Azerbaijan moving some money. But the story goes on to allege that the rulers of the UAE and Saudi Arabia had put together a fund of $2 billion into accounts that Kushner had access to, including one in the UAE and one at an Israeli central bank as well, which would be a bit problematic if true. The allegation is there. It could be somewhat embarrassing that we have this chap who's currently tasked— one of his tasks is to solve the problems of the Middle East— if he's getting quite a lot of money into his back pocket.

JAMES BALL

World peace, in fact, because he's on the Russia-Ukraine team too.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes, yes. Along with that property developer chap.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes.

JAMES BALL

Steve Witkoff. Yes.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yes, yes. So Kushner's lawyers, they're denying everything. They're saying it's a whole load of poppycock. They're saying they've got no knowledge of any of this. Kushner himself has said that he complies with all the legal requirements when dealing with foreign governments, doesn't break laws, claims that there's no evidence been made public. It's all a load of baloney. He says it's outrageous fabrications. And of course, most Cole's sources are anonymous. It's not like he's saying, well, I was told this by So-and-so. The Dutch government haven't commented either. So we're sort of left in this position at the moment of not knowing if any of this is true or whether Cole himself has been given a bit of a tall story and has fallen for it. But he's been working on this, he claims, for years. Yes, since he had the initial tip-off and initially thought it was very unlikely to be true, but he became convinced over time.

JAMES BALL

He seems to think he's got quite a few independent sources. I mean, one thing we should say is there's reasons why people might find it plausible. And one of those is that we know that Jared Kushner's firm, his private equity fund, has received $2 billion from the Saudi Sovereign Wealth Fund. Now, that's for him to invest on their behalf and give them a return. That's a commercial agreement. But that's not secret. That's not hidden. We know that. So we know that he has been trading with people with whom he had to maintain political relations on behalf of the US.

GRAHAM CLULEY

To be honest, we're not really the podcast for all of this. You know, we're not into foreign policy and politics and things. Well, everything's a little bit political, but this is fundamentally a cybersecurity podcast. And whether or not these allegations turn out to be true, there are interesting security questions to be asked here. I mean, firstly, if the book is correct in what it claims, then a senior White House advisor was carrying a phone that had been compromised by not one, but at least two foreign intelligence services. And that's a bit of a worry, isn't it?

Unknown

Yes.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And there's also no indication that the US government were aware of it.

JAMES BALL

I mean, this is why traditionally they always asked senior diplomats and senior officials not to use commercial phones for almost any normal business. There's only so much you can secure even an iPhone, which is a relatively good phone. It's secure for you and me as far as I understand it, isn't it?

Unknown

Yeah.

JAMES BALL

For most things. But traditionally they would always ask senior people dealing with sensitive intelligence matters not to use an iPhone, not to use an Android phone. And it looks like that advice had a good reason, doesn't it?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Yeah, it absolutely does. And if the story is true, someone was able to access this via a software vulnerability. They didn't have to go through the front door of breaking Face ID. So just having that perimeter protection there is not necessarily going to completely defend your computing device, of course. And also, you don't need to entirely compromise a phone to learn quite a lot. So the spies, all they could do is see the screen. But if you're doing banking and messaging, the screen is going to show you almost everything, isn't it?

JAMES BALL

Yeah.

GRAHAM CLULEY

We're sort of throwing shade here at the Americans that maybe they didn't have proper cybersecurity in place. Well, what about the Russian cybersecurity? Because again, if the story is true, the GRU was storing their stolen information on a server that a single one of their agents, this guy who was turned by the Dutch authorities apparently, he was able to unlock that server and give access to Dutch intelligence.

JAMES BALL

They kind of all do this though, don't they? Because you don't want to lead people straight back to your own servers and your own secure sites. And so when you're exfiltrating material, you often put it on a staging server somewhere, to almost park it for a while before you sort of do it. A little bit like, you know, if you steal gold bullion or something, just leaving it somewhere to check that it's not been found or got a tracker in it or whatever before you take it home. And so some of our lot do this. I think it was, was it called Vault 7?

Unknown

Yes.

JAMES BALL

When WikiLeaks published a bunch of CIA hacking tools, they were similarly left on one of these staging servers and then exposed.

Unknown

Yeah.

JAMES BALL

It's not ideal. It's a vulnerability. But you sort of see why they use them, even though it's clearly got its downsides. You know, if this story is correct.

GRAHAM CLULEY

If the story is correct, it's certainly a fascinating read, and I'll put in a link in the show notes as well so people can find out more about this. But certainly I think most of us, we're not in the position of moving hundreds of millions of dollars into our bank accounts from the Middle East, but we may still be worried about our own personal security. So consider that your phone is often the easiest way to find out more information about you. If someone is able to get into your phone, whether it's an intelligence agency or the police or a hacker or whatever, they will learn a huge amount about you. So separate, if you can, sensitive work from your personal usage. And if you think you might be of interest to an intelligence agency, maybe think long and hard as to what means they may be looking for in order to get in and mitigate against those if you can.

JOE

This episode of Smashing Security is sponsored by Vanta.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Joe, it's Graham here. I've been asked to negotiate with you. Are you going to come out? Can you hear me?

JOE

I've got the questionnaire, Graham. I'm not coming out.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Okay, Joe, that's okay. Nobody's rushing you. Which questionnaire is it?

JOE

The vendor risk one. I filled it in 4 times this week. 4 times!

GRAHAM CLULEY

That sounds really hard, Joe. So tell me about the spreadsheets.

JOE

There are so many of them, Graham. Some of them have tabs I've never seen before. I think one is alive.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Okay, I hear you, Joe. Now, now, I'd like to put something on the table. Can I do that?

JOE

Is it a trick? It's the sort of thing a hacker would say.

GRAHAM CLULEY

No tricks. It's called Vanta.

JOE

Okay, go on.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Vanta is a trust management platform. It automates the mind-numbing stuff, the evidence chasing, the questionnaire hell, the sort of thing that makes you want to go and hide away in a cupboard like you have?

JOE

No more chasing screenshots.

GRAHAM CLULEY

No more chasing screenshots. It continuously monitors your system so you're audit ready all year round. SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR, the works.

JOE

Does it use AI?

GRAHAM CLULEY

It does, Joe. It flags risks and streamlines evidence collection so your whole security programme stays in shape, not just in the week before the auditors arrive.

JOE

I think I'm ready to come out.

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's great, Joe. And I've got one more thing for you. Listeners who book a demo, they can get $1,000 off.

JOE

$1,000? Why didn't you mention that sooner?

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's not how you do it, Joe. You build rapport first.

JOE

vanta.com/smashing. Go now before somebody else ends up in the cupboard.

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's vanta.com/smashing.

JOE

Thanks to Vanta for supporting the show.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Joe, you can put the questionnaire down now.

JOE

No, I haven't finished page 6.

GRAHAM CLULEY

James, what's your story for us this week?

JAMES BALL

So it's essentially about Transport Layer Security, which is the protocol that underlies HTTPS. It's kind of what keeps the web secure, and almost everything now transmits on that. And before we used HTTPS all the time, essentially quite a lot of what we transmitted to and from websites was in the clear. And if you ever had advice about open Wi-Fi networks being able to see what you were doing and what you were browsing and maybe your passwords, that was kind of from the pre-TLS era. I mean, it's still good advice to use a VPN on open Wi-Fi, but the internet's got a lot more secure actually post-Snowden. But the way the protocol works isn't entirely trustless. Essentially, what you get is something where someone you do trust vouches for each website that you visit and goes, this website's claiming to be hsbc.com.

JAMES BALL

I've looked at its certificate, the cryptography checks out, it is. And that might be your web browser, or it might be a sort of national trusted agency, and so there's this kind of tiered network of trust.

Unknown

Yes.

JAMES BALL

That's sort of how certification works.

GRAHAM CLULEY

And the certificates have sort of been stamped, haven't they, by a certificate authority to say that they're legitimate in some way? You know, using cryptography, you're able to confirm that they are legit.

JAMES BALL

And those authorities in turn, they take this very seriously because they've tried to come up with protocols where everything's verifiable. And so, for example, for secure DNS, every 3 months they do a little ceremony to renew the keys. And I've stood in and watched one of these for The Guardian years ago, because there's basically these 7 keyholders, and 3 of them have to be physically present and use their keys, and it renews the signature for another 3 months. And I went to the 17th ever of these, I think it was. And of course, once a journalist was in a room and I had a camera person with me, it all went wrong. They messed it up, they got locked in a cage, they had to set off the fire alarm to get let out.

JAMES BALL

It turned into total slapstick. I'll send you a link to the article — maybe you can put it in. But the thing is, they try to go, we have this core zone that we keep secure in these ways that are publicly verified and verifiable. And then these core guys verify the next tiers, and then they verify every site that you visit. It's a good system generally, and these keys are very, very long.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So if we introduce friction, and maybe an interesting way to think about this is if we're driving down the road, we're in a 2-wheel drive vehicle. We like the road.
