articles.title: Node2Shell: Reproducing CVE-2026-111497 in the Node.js Brotli decoder
articles.context: Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation: Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download...
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder. The upstream flaw sits in the Google Brotli C library, so the blast radius reaches Python, Bun, .NET, Java brotli4j, Envoy, and Istio. Every affected runtime now has a fix available.

We reproduced the flaw on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image and verified that the patched build rejects the same bytes.

Capturing an application-level trace is difficult because the process continues running despite memory corruption.

Only patching fixes this vulnerability. The application process decodes the data, so neither the web server nor a web application firewall (WAF) ever sees the malicious content. An edge rule that rejects Brotli-compressed request bodies is a useful tripwire and nothing more.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released security updates for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The CVE record gives the flaw a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2, or Critical, while Node.js rates its severity as High. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 contain the fix, and end-of-life release lines carry the same vulnerable decoder but have no patch.

What looked like a Node.js problem on day one turned out to be far broader. Most runtimes embed the upstream Google Brotli C library, where the bug lives. Over the following week many consumers of that decoder shipped its own advisory:

Product

Affected

First fixed release

Node.js 22, 24, and 26

Before 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1

22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1

Google Brotli

1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0

1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1

Python Brotli and brotlicffi

1.2.0 and earlier

1.2.1 and 1.2.1.0

Bun

1.0.21 through 1.4.3

1.4.4

Java brotli4j

1.23.0 and earlier

1.24.0

.NET 8, 9, and 10

Before the October 25, 2026 out-of-band update

8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14

Envoy and Istio

All releases before the first fix in each supported branch

Envoy: 1.36.12, 1.37.8, 1.38.6, 1.39.3, 1.40.0; Istio: 1.29.9, 1.30.6, 1.31.2 (first fixed in each branch)

Two details deserve special attention. Java's brotli4j bundles its own native Brotli build inside its jars, so patching the operating system's libbrotli does not fix it. Bun executables built with bun build \--compile embed the runtime and stay vulnerable until they are rebuilt.

Before the disclosure, Imperva demonstrated code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux ARM64 image. Their exploit needed several attempts and was not released. A public proof of concept appeared on October 22, 2026. On standard builds it produces a crash and a limited memory read. As of October 29, 2026, there have been confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities catalog now lists the CVE.

How to know if you're affected

A service is exposed when it decompresses Brotli data that an attacker controls, which comes through two common paths. A few additional considerations apply to both.

Outbound requests (the quiet path)

Outbound requests are the harder path to see. Node.js's built-in fetch() decodes a Content-Encoding: br response automatically, whether or not the request asked for Brotli. The axios, got, and node-fetch clients advertise and decode Brotli by default. Any feature that fetches URLs supplied by users, such as webhooks, link previews, and feed readers, enables an attacker to force the encoding selection server side since the attacker controls the response headers, and fetch() decodes a body labeled br even when the application explicitly forces Accept-Encoding: identity.

In our testing, no exception surfaced at runtime: one crafted stream completed with an empty body and an HTTP 200, and the only visible signals were CPU usage and, under concurrency, a starved threadpool that still answered health checks.

The same holds outside Node.js: Python HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically whenever Brotli or brotlicffi is installed, even if application code never imports the package.

Inbound requests (the visible path)

Inbound attacks are easier to observe. A compressed request body is a recognizable attack surface, your reverse proxy or WAF can see the Content-Encoding: br header, and the framework parser is a known place to audit. Express 5 and body-parser 2.x accept Brotli-compressed request bodies by default in their JSON, raw, text, and URL-encoded parsers, and Koa and NestJS inherit the behavior. Express 4 rejects those bodies with an HTTP 415, and a bare Node.js HTTP server does not decompress anything. Parsers mounted before authentication expose the decoder to unauthenticated requests.

Other considerations

Both paths share a versioning trap: process.versions.brotli still reports 1.2.0 on the patched Node.js 24.22.1, because the cherry-picked fix does not bump the embedded version string. process.version is reliable only for official distributions from nodejs.org.

If you cannot patch immediately, set inflate: false on Express 5 and body-parser 2.x parsers, or reject Content-Encoding: br at the reverse proxy. These measures only mitigate the risk, as patching is the only complete solution. These mitigations could also break the functionality as they reject all compressed request bodies, do nothing for the outbound path, and break compressed bodies sent by legitimate clients.

How the vulnerability works

A Brotli stream is divided into blocks, and the decoder moves to a new block only when the current block's length budget runs out. A 23 MB stream of otherwise ordinary commands drains that budget while producing no output, and its closing commands request a block switch that the format forbids. These steps are where the attacker does the proper setup to exploit the bug.

In the next stage, we see the impact of the vulnerability. In Brotli 1.2.0, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns a boolean, and it answers two different questions with the same "false" value: "this stream is malformed" and "I need more input". Callers cannot tell the two apart, and on the decoder's fast path the return value is dropped entirely.

The two arms then diverge. The first path is an overflow where the decoder parks the unconsumed bytes in a small internal buffer while it waits for more input. The copy has no bound check, so bytes past the end of the buffer land in adjacent decoder state. The write happens inside a single heap allocation, so the tooling built to catch memory corruption never sees it, and the process keeps running. The other path is that it keeps spinning. The decoder retries the forbidden switch in a loop, which pins a CPU core inside a single call that never returns: a one-request denial of service.

From memory corruption to code execution

In this case, memory corruption has impactful consequences. The corrupted decoder state controls where the decoder reads from and writes to next, so a crafted stream can redirect both operations. This gives an attacker two primitives:

A repeatable read of heap memory that leaves through the decompressed response.

A redirected write. In our lab, we aimed it at an unmapped page and produced a deterministic crash.

Both primitives are real. The read primitive is the most operationally interesting, because heap bytes returning over the wire are the first step of a staged attack.

Three obstacles stand between these primitives and a shell:

The addresses move. The heap layout that the corruption targets is randomized and changes between requests, so what one request leaks, the next request can’t reliably use.

The corruption bytes are also the decoder's input. The decoder consumes the bytes that steer the corruption again as it continues, so the values an attacker needs are constrained by the values the decoder will accept. This is the deepest structural obstacle we found.

A managed runtime stands in the way. Between the corrupted C state and control flow sits the machinery of a language runtime with its own allocator, its own compiled code, and its own defenses, none of which the original C library was designed around.

After measuring all three obstacles, we assess that the flaw is exploitable and that the gap between these primitives and reliable code execution is engineering effort. This matches Imperva's report of successful execution after several attempts on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image.

How the patch addresses the flaw

The patch is small and precise. The block-switch helper now returns a real error code, and both code paths treat a failed check as a hard stop instead of a request for more input. It rejects a crafted stream with a format error (-17) before anything is written to the decoder's state.

The release timeline is the troubling part. The fix was committed to the upstream Brotli repository on February 27, 2026, but the fixed library releases did not ship until October 21, 2026. For eight months, anyone who downloaded Brotli, or a runtime that embeds it, received the vulnerable version even though the corrected code sat in the public repository. The release also ships without a regression test or a changelog entry for this fix.

How to detect exploitation

This CVE involves no attacker-controlled infrastructure, so there are no conventional indicators. Detection rests on behavioral signals, and no single signal is conclusive. Correlate across three layers.

Decoder error signals

The vulnerable and patched builds respond differently to the same malicious bytes. Both responses appear in application logs and APM error spans and the error you see depends on whether the build is patched. On a vulnerable build, Node.js returns Z_BUF_ERROR with the message "unexpected end of file". On a patched build, Node.js returns ERR__ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH, and Python returns "brotli: decoder is unhealthy". The vulnerable signal also appears for benign truncated input so you have to still look a little closer and differentiate the benign truncated input vs real attacks.

Process signals

A worker that exits with signal 139 (SIGSEGV) right after a Brotli transfer is a crash attempt, and a process pinned at 100% CPU inside a decompression call is the spin arm. Correlate on workload identity (the container, pod, or service) and not the process ID, because the process that crashed is gone and a successful attempt may not crash at all. The strongest signal is behavioral: a shell or new outbound connections from the same workload.

The disclosure channel

Decompressed output that contains bytes the client never sent is the read primitive in action. Investigate any such output immediately. Because the leaked heap memory leaves through the decompressed response, start by listing the endpoints that return or reflect decompressed content back to the caller, such as echo, preview, conversion, or proxy features.

What does not work

Payload byte signatures, because the attacker-controlled parts of the stream change per target and the exploit is the decode process itself, not the decompressed content.

Content matching at the WAF, because the web server forwards compressed bytes and never decodes them.

Body-size limits, because the tested middleware counts decompressed bytes, so the 23 MB compressed trigger still reaches the decoder.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management tracks CVE-2026-111497 and the related vendor advisories as vulnerability findings on hosts and container images, so your patching status lives in one place.

Datadog Code Security reports the vulnerable services that ship dependency inventories. Its library inventory identifies which services to prioritize: those running Express 5, body-parser 2.x, or Koa parsers, and those using HTTP clients that auto-decode Brotli.

Datadog Application Performance Monitoring (APM) helps you hunt for attempts. This query requires capturing Content-Encoding, which is not set by default in Node.js spans, so make sure to check how the language tracer you are using behaves. For example in Node.js it can be enabled by including content-encoding in DD_TRACE_HEADER_TAGS. Pivot on the services that accept Content-Encoding: br request bodies using this query, and review services that fetch user-supplied URLs. Decoder failures surface as APM error spans correlated with the request and the client address. The process telemetry that the Datadog Agent collects shows a crashed attempt as a worker restart with exit code 139.

Datadog Workload Protection includes coverage through the CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell Exploit Content Pack. This pack includes a new security policy with three Agent rules that cover post-exploitation that surfaces a CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell exploitation detected signal.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes two detections that identify command execution associated with Node2Shell exploitation:

Shell spawned by web server detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or web processes. It uses process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-111497 shows how a single unchecked return value in a widely shared C library can ripple across nearly every major runtime. Because the decoder runs inside the application's own process, the flaw sidesteps the defenses most teams rely on. The eight months between the upstream fix and its release are a reminder that a fix in a public repository protects no one until it ships.

Exploitation has been confirmed, which further proves the primitives are real and the path to code execution is a matter of effort. Patch to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 or your vendor's fixed package, rebuild container images, restart every process, and inventory the other Brotli consumers in your environment.

articles.title: Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
articles.context: With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits
articles.full_text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The Cat Has Left the Bag

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

articles.title: A matter of national secrecy.
articles.context: Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems. The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate...
articles.full_text:
Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling. A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users. Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems. The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider. Tailworm targets Tailscale. Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack. A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer. Norway raises their cyber risk level to high. Our guest is Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, discussing AI exploits and identity containment. AI science needs a spam filter.

Today is Wednesday October 28th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling.

Two Democratic senators accuse the Trump administration of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling as Congress considers renewing a controversial intelligence program.

Senators Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff say the administration missed a September deadline to release findings from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court concerning Section 702 of FISA.

The court reportedly found that intelligence agencies used filtering tools to search Americans’ intercepted communications without required safeguards, including approvals and documentation.

Section 702 expired in June, but surveillance continues under a court authorization lasting until March.

The administration has promoted the program’s effectiveness while keeping the ruling classified, despite earlier promises to release it.

Civil liberties organizations are urging Congress to withhold reauthorization until the findings become public.

Wyden and Schiff have demanded an explanation by November sixth.

The dispute raises a fundamental question: How can Congress evaluate the legality of government surveillance when critical findings about that surveillance remain secret?

A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a suspected surveillance operation targeting users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.

According to Reuters, researchers at TrendAI found that an Israeli advertising technology company, Discover-Tech, was aggressively bidding for ads targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries.

The company was particularly active in conflict zones, including Syria, Yemen, Libya, and South Sudan, where legitimate advertising demand is limited.

Researchers believe the activity was designed to exploit data leaked through online advertising auctions, potentially allowing operators to identify, locate, and track Starlink users.

TrendAI initially identified the operation only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79, reportedly declining to name Discover-Tech over legal concerns.

Citizen Lab and Confiant independently identified the company, prompting Google, Comcast, and others to remove it from their advertising platforms.

Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems.

Attackers are already probing for vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems following the disclosure of a critical security flaw.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems.

Oracle released a patch on October twentieth, urging customers to update immediately.

Security firm Defused says its honeypots detected attempted exploitation on October twenty-seventh, although Oracle has not confirmed active exploitation in the wild.

Shadowserver has identified more than 670 internet-exposed Oracle E-Business Suite instances, mostly in the United States. It’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate E-Business Suite vulnerability to target major corporations and universities.

The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider.

The FBI has seized the domain of Virtualine, a so-called bulletproof hosting provider accused of supporting cybercrime, money laundering, and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.

Operating under several names, Virtualine openly advertised hosting services for illegal activities, promising to ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests.

According to the Justice Department, the company continued supporting a forum distributing illegal content even after receiving complaints from international authorities. Prosecutors also allege Virtualine helped the forum’s operators establish another site and attempted to launder cryptocurrency payments.

No arrests or criminal charges were announced.

The seizure follows international crackdowns on similar providers linked to ransomware operations. But researchers warn that disrupting these services often simply pushes criminal customers toward replacement providers, rather than eliminating the underlying market.

Tailworm targets Tailscale.

Tailscale is rolling out fixes for a collection of security vulnerabilities that researchers say could allow attackers to move rapidly through private networks.

Dubbed Tailworm, the findings from Cyberdione Labs include eleven issues affecting Tailscale and the open-source headscale server.

Four vulnerabilities involve Tailscale SSH, where improper privilege handling could allow an attacker with access to one compromised device to gain root privileges on other authorized servers.

Researchers demonstrated automated attacks spreading between vulnerable machines in less than a second per hop, without user interaction.

Tailscale emphasizes that exploitation requires existing network access and depends on SSH policies. There’s no reported exploitation in the wild.

The company has published security bulletins and remediation guidance. Organizations are advised to review SSH access policies and disable unnecessary forwarding.

Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack.

Ohio’s Auditor of State is investigating a cyberattack targeting its web server, potentially involving foreign state actors.

Auditor Keith Faber says security monitoring detected and isolated the threat, prompting officials to take the server and online accounts offline.

The incident was not ransomware, and officials have found no evidence that personal or government financial information was compromised. Payment data is stored separately.

State and federal law enforcement are investigating. A temporary website is planned, and audit clients experiencing payment disruptions will receive a grace period.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupted operations at Colmobil, Israel’s largest vehicle importer, delaying vehicle deliveries and services.

Israel’s Ministry of Transport disconnected the company from government registration systems as a precaution, while customers reported delays involving Mercedes-Benz vehicles.

According to sources cited by Calcalist, the ransomware group SETTRA was responsible and demanded payment. Industry sources say Colmobil paid the ransom, though the company has declined to confirm either claim.

Colmobil says it has restored operations and that the incident did not affect vehicle systems or manufacturers.

The attack highlights the automotive industry’s growing dependence on interconnected digital infrastructure, from vehicle registration and payments to maintenance and diagnostics.

While researchers have demonstrated attacks against connected vehicles, there’s no evidence this incident involved attempts to remotely control cars.

Norway raises their cyber risk level to high.

Norway’s National Security Authority, or NSM, has raised the country’s cyber risk level to high, publicly disclosing its assessment for the first time.

The agency reports a threefold increase in successful cyber operations against Norwegian organizations over the past six months, with some incidents posing serious national security risks.

Defense, aerospace, critical infrastructure, and their suppliers face particularly elevated threats, including reconnaissance, attempted intrusions, ransomware, and denial-of-service attacks.

Officials also warn that artificial intelligence could accelerate attacks by helping adversaries identify vulnerabilities more efficiently, although such AI-enabled activity hasn’t been documented in Norway.

NSM is urging organizations to strengthen defenses immediately, emphasizing phishing-resistant authentication, network segmentation, improved monitoring, vulnerability management, and supply chain security.

The agency says stronger organizational defenses can help reduce the country’s overall cyber risk.

Stick with us after the break, Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, is discussing "The three-month clock: Neutralizing frontier AI exploits through identity containment."

On today’s Industry Voices segment, I sat down with Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, as we discussed "The three-month clock: Neutralizing frontier AI exploits through identity containment." Here’s our conversation.

That was Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, if you enjoyed this conversation, check out the show notes for the full interview.

AI science needs a spam filter.

Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research, but it’s also creating a rather inconvenient problem: scientists are increasingly struggling to separate genuine discoveries from AI-generated nonsense.

Science journalist Dalmeet Singh Chawla warns that generative AI is overwhelming academic journals with questionable research, leaving publishers’ integrity teams struggling to keep up.

The irony is that AI has already demonstrated extraordinary scientific potential.

In 2020, Google’s DeepMind developed AlphaFold, a system capable of predicting how proteins fold into the shapes that determine their biological functions.

Within a year, AlphaFold predicted 200 million protein structures, work that would have taken an estimated hundreds of millions of years using traditional laboratory methods.

The achievement helped earn its creators a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

So AI can dramatically accelerate scientific discovery. Unfortunately, it can also accelerate the production of questionable science.

Apparently, the scientific method now needs a spam filter.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents
articles.context: In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs
articles.full_text:
Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment

Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer.

“If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.”

More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona.

Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025.

Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members.

articles.title: GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub
articles.context: Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations
articles.full_text:
A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

Various Payloads Targeting Compromised Developers

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

A "Failed" Wave of Attacks, but Still Plenty to Worry About Long Term

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

articles.title: Weaponize your identity debt: Identity Security, decoys, and tripwires in the age of AI attacks
articles.context: Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed...
articles.full_text:
Every enterprise has identity debt: over-privileged accounts, insecure credential storage, and poor control of account lifecycle are just a few weaknesses we see all the time. But what if that debt could be turned into a strategic advantage against attackers?

CISA recently described decoys, tripwires, breadcrumbs, and honeytokens as practical mechanisms for detecting post-compromise activity. It got me thinking about how we can apply this defensive concept at the identity layer, where an attempted authentication can become both a detection signal and an inline containment decision. In other words, is there a world where we can weaponize Identity Security controls as a set of simple but effective tripwires across enterprise environments?

I think there is—and, even better, I think it has potential to turn any environment into the kind of classic laser hallway you see in heist movies, with red beams criss-crossing the route to the goal, ready to alert and ready to stop the latest threats.

So, in this blog, we’re going to look at how organizations can turn the same weaknesses attackers target into opportunities to generate rapid, high-fidelity signals with minimal operational risk.

But first: What are cyber decoys?

Cyber decoys are legitimate-looking systems, accounts, and data designed to distract and detect adversaries or facilitate collection of threat intelligence.

When operationalized with monitoring and alerting, they can become tripwires to provide high-fidelity signals to defenders. CISA also recommends mapping decoy coverage to MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE Engage, continuously testing the controls, and refining them based on observed adversary behaviour.

Why does this matter now?

The Hugging Face attack alone generated 17,000 unique events to analyse and correlate in a matter of a few days. As we prepare for a reality where attacks like these are commonplace, generating signal from noise to drive effective detection, response and containment has never been more important.

The focus is primarily on enhancing correlation. Hugging Face recommended that organizations focus on this in their post-incident call, having used an open-source model successfully—evidently a good investment. However, even the world’s most effective correlation engine will remain subject to data pipeline and ingestion constraints, some of which are owned by platform providers and cannot be optimized directly.

Generating high-fidelity signals as events unfold complements runtime controls that contain the threat, providing deeper visibility into attacker activity while enabling more informed defensive actions in real time.

Safe deception in the age of machine-speed threats

The aim of a deception strategy is to expose attackers and increase the cost and difficulty of attacks by creating a misleading picture of the environment and its resources (i.e., identities).

In agentic terms, the goal is to increase the compute/token cost of attack, use up context window, and buy time. In the future, it’ll be to funnel agentic attackers towards pre-designed traps to cause the agent to loop without escape.

Deception relies on something—for example, an identity with high privileges and easily-acquired credentials—appearing significantly less monitored, controlled, and secure than it actually is.

Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed threats may not generate a response fast enough to prevent exploitation of the token itself. Decoys and tripwires must therefore be safe. In other words, they must not have possible negative security implications in and of themselves.

Importantly, a safe tripwire turns the traditional detect > contain methodology, and reliance on response-time, on its head: the containment action that took place is the detection that arms your SOC with a signal, with full context of what happened.

Finally, given the rise of machine-speed threats, tripwires must not provide additional information as to the defensive posture of the organization when triggered. Transparency of the tripwire—which must not be able to be enumerated or discovered directly will become key to identifying and defeating machine-speed threats.

Identity is where the attack becomes the control point

AI attacks do not move through an environment in neat, human-sized steps. They enumerate identities, test permissions, reuse valid credentials and tokens, and pivot across trust boundaries until they find a path that works.

As we’ve already seen, the Hugging Face investigation reconstructed more than 17,000 attacker actions, grouped into approximately 6,280 clusters. The important lesson is not only the volume of activity, but the repeated identity pivots hidden inside it: credential theft, workload impersonation, token reuse, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

That makes identity a powerful place to deploy tripwires. The tripwire should not only sit on a file, share, or endpoint. It should sit on the attempted identity path itself:

An identity requests access to an unexpected resource, in an unexpected protocol, or in a way that deviates from its baseline.

The request is evaluated using identity, source, destination, protocol, behaviour, and context.

The access is denied or fenced inline.

The same event generates a high-fidelity signal for the SOC.

Related identities and adjacent attack paths can be investigated or contained.

The attacker sees a normal access denial. The SOC sees the identity, attempted destination, protocol, source, sequence of activity, and potential attack path.

Silverfort sits inside the authentication path, where it can enforce identity-based deny and segmentation before an attacker completes lateral movement or privilege escalation.

For a machine-speed attack, detection alone often arrives too late. An identity tripwire functions as a control-flow interrupt: it breaks the sequence between authentication and the next step in the attack chain.

Instead of allowing the attacker to authenticate, discover, pivot, and escalate while defenders correlate events after the fact, the control can deny the risky authentication attempt at the point where the path is exercised. This changes the operating model from detect → correlate → respond to deny → detect → contain, resulting in a synchronous control that limits blast radius while preserving the evidence needed for investigation.

How can we leverage identity debt for this?

Identity is ripe for deception. Traditional identity debt such as over-privileged accounts, shadow admins, insecure credential storage, use of legacy protocols, and loose account lifecycle management is common—maybe even ubiquitous. These do not need to be designed and created because they already exist!

I want to be clear here: hygiene is still really important. Just because it’s possible to weaponize these existing issues, doesn’t mean good hygiene practices can be neglected.

The real question is how do we create safe tripwires?

There are three key premises to creating effective, safe tripwires:

A differential exists between the outward appearance of the account (utility to attackers), and the security state (monitored, controlled).

Usage of the tripwire does not have security implications (i.e., it does not make our security position worse).

Tripping the tripwire must not provide additional defensive context to the attacker to learn from; it must be to the attacker.

Inline identity controls allow for us to meet these three conditions. For example, deny policies create the tripwire alert to the SOC team, while denying the attacker information about why the containment activity occurred. Likewise, service accounts can be ‘fenced’ down to their standard, accepted, recorded usage behaviour and deny anomalies so, should anomalous usage be detected, we can both directly deny the usage of the account, and notify the SOC with a high-fidelity, rapid alert with full context for further action and wider correlation. All of this can happen without the agent seeing anything except ‘access denied’.

Some other cases where we can weaponize identity as tripwires (you can read more in the appendix below):

If connections to Tier 0/1 must be via bastions or PAW and are not

If dormant accounts become active

If admin accounts are used in a highly unusual way

If a legacy protocol is being used to access a sensitive server

If a low-privilege identity is attempting to reach a Tier 0 system

When one of these edges is exercised, the response should combine three actions: deny or restrict the attempted access, generate a high-confidence alert, and expose the surrounding identity relationships for investigation. This is specifically a control against AI attacks and their speed, persistence, and ability to test many paths in parallel.

What this means for security in the age of machine-speed threats

As we move into the next phase of threats—autonomously driven by AI models with the capacity to enumerate and hold your full environment and its vulnerabilities in their context window—two challenges emerge:

How do we generate signal amongst the massive volume of noise?

How do we do this in a way that does not require a loop of detect > correlate > respond, dependent on replication and processing times and humans in the loop?

CISA defines tripwires as decoys where interaction generates an alert. Silverfort extends that idea into the authentication path, where identity-based deny and segmentation can block access before lateral movement or privilege escalation completes. While a conventional tripwire detects interaction, an identity tripwire can detect, deny, and contain the attempted path in the same control loop.

Rethinking how we weaponize identity against attackers—by leveraging the identity debt that already exists—allows us to generate high-quality signal to cut through the noise, while having containment built-in. The containment activity generates the signal, rather than the signal requiring containment activity.

Doing this allows for more rapid threat detection, safely, while denying any information to the model that may help it progress its attack—and gives us a pathway to active defense in the future by funnelling agents to useless traps in an endless loop.

If you want to see how Silverfort can stop AI attacks inline and at runtime, book a demo here.

Identity tripwire appendix

Tripwire

Suspicious interaction

Recommended response

Decoy service account

Authentication from any source or destination outside its tightly defined baseline

Generate an alert and apply a virtual fence

Dormant privileged account

Login attempt against a disabled, unused, or never-used account

Deny the request and investigate the originating identity and host

Decoy SPN/Kerberos path

TGS request for a decoy service identity from an unexpected system

Alert on possible service-account discovery or credential theft and virtually fence it

Tier-0 access edge

Non-admin identity attempts authentication to domain controllers or identity infrastructure

Block inline and surface the full attempted path

Legacy protocol path

NTLM or other weak protocol used against a sensitive resource from an unusual source

Deny or segment the protocol-level access and generate an alert

Executive/admin breadcrumb

A decoy link, file, or share is accessed by an identity that should never touch it

Treat as a likely compromise signal and initiate identity containment

The post Weaponize your identity debt: Identity Security, decoys, and tripwires in the age of AI attacks appeared first on Silverfort.

articles.title: Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness: Unlocking the potential of truly multi-model agentic work
articles.context: If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, q
articles.full_text:
If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder.

Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry. That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line.

What’s a harness, and why is it hard?

If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins.

This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it.

We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits.

Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale

The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration. And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. And it had the highest satisfaction among our most demanding audience: developers. That’s why we’re standardizing all of our Copilot experiences on the strongest foundation possible.

The harness is built to perform across model families, with 20+ frontier models plus bring your own key, so you can use the right model for the right job. Instead of doing the work to keep up with and eval new models, lean on us to intelligently route work to the right model or models based on the task.

Our harness is flexible and configurable to any type of app, agent, or service. We recently ported the harness runtime to Rust, which has resulted in industry-leading performance and reductions in both session overhead and time-to-first token. And because the Copilot harness powers surfaces across Microsoft, it’s battle-tested and proven performant at the scale of millions of users and hundreds of real-world use cases.

A unified harness lets us ship faster, learn faster, and improve Copilot over time. And because the agents you build in Foundry can run on the same harness we’ve adopted across Microsoft, our continuous harness improvements will benefit your agents, too.

Try it yourself

The SDK is available to download, or you can run the harness in the cloud, all managed by Foundry. Our platforms remain open and interoperable, so you can continue to bring in any harness and framework you want, too.

With the Copilot harness, Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox, with governance and optimization built in from day one. You bring the instructions, skills, tools, and model choice.

This is an important step towards our vision of a stronger system around the model that preserves choice. It represents the best of GitHub, brought to the Microsoft platform and beyond.

We’ll keep pushing the harness forward, so you can focus on what only you can build.

The post Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness: Unlocking the potential of truly multi-model agentic work appeared first on The Official Microsoft Blog.

articles.title: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

Japan Inc Under Fire

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

articles.title: Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang’s systems
articles.context: Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian man has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison for his role in a series of ransomware attacks.

36-year-old Artem Stryzhak became an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group around June 2021, receiving an 80% cut of the ransoms he managed to extort in attacks against hospitals, government organisations, law firms, and businesses around the world.

The rest of the ransom would go to Nefilim's administrators - including fellow Ukrainian Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who was charged last year in relation to attacks against hundreds of corporate victims using the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware, as well as Nefilim.

At the time of writing, Tymoshchuk is not in US custody and a US $11 million bounty has been offered by the US State Department for information leading to his arrest.

Nefilim was not the only ransomware gang that Stryzhak worked closely with. He was also an early affiliate of the Hive ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation which targeted businesses and, in particular, organisations working in healthcare.

The FBI later warned that Hive had extorted US $100 million from businesses and organisations globally in a period of just 18 months.

According to the US Department of Justice, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators were behind Hive ransomware attacks against a number of victims, including law firms, a dentist's office, and a healthcare provider, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector.

In January 2023, it was revealed that a multinational law enforcement operation had secretly penetrated the Hive ransomware operation in late July 2022, capturing decryption keys and quietly passing them to victims so they did not have to pay a ransom.

The DOJ said that the operation saved corporate victims of Hive over US $130 million in ransom payments.

At the time I speculated that the take-down of Hive may lead to the identification and possible apprehension of some of those involved in Hive ransomware attacks. In June 2024, Stryzhak was arrested in Barcelona, and subsequently extradited to the United States where he pleaded guilty.

The infiltration into Hive's infrastructure took place in 2022. Stryzhak was arrested in 2024, and sentenced in 2026. If there's a lesson for ransomware affiliates who think they got away with it, it's that law enforcement is prepared to be patient, and the evidence does not go away.

That's something that Volodymyr Tymoshchuk may also want to consider.

articles.title: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries
articles.context: Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections
articles.full_text:
Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections.

In research published October 27, Check Point said it had tracked the campaign, which it calls Yoba, for two months, though an earlier variant posing as the Cursor coding agent appeared in early June. The fake projects impersonated artificial intelligence (AI) applications including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus.

Their releases sat in GitHub repositories with GitHub Pages landing pages, and some of the repositories appeared among Google’s top results, most likely through search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning.

Yoba Uses Signed Binaries to Hide Malicious Components

The fake applications bundled legitimate signed OpenAI and Anthropic executables with a malicious dynamic link library (DLL). Check Point found that the signed Setup.exe files loaded the malicious component through DLL sideloading, a technique often used to bypass security protections.

The malicious DLL, dubbed YobaDropper, ran several checks before deploying a second-stage loader, including the name of its host process and whether it had administrator privileges.

It also checked keyboard layouts to avoid machines in Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries other than Ukraine and used lengthy sleeps to frustrate automated analysis. Check Point said the actor showed indicators suggesting Russian origins.

The dropper then created a directory under ProgramData, copied a legitimate Windows executable into it and used Scheduled Tasks to establish persistence, with a task running under the Local System account and disguised as a Microsoft task.

Read more on fake AI tools spreading malware: Attackers Combine ChatGPT Feature Abuse With ClickFix to Deliver Trojan Malware

YobaLoader Uses Telegram and DNS to Fetch Payloads

The second-stage YobaLoader used Telegram and encrypted Domain Name System (DNS) lookups, known as DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), to obtain instructions without dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, according to Check Point.

It took an image from a Telegram channel and used data from it to generate domains through a domain generation algorithm.

It then queried Google’s DoH service for encrypted data stored in DNS records, which was cryptographically validated before the loader retrieved and decrypted the next-stage payload.

Check Point advised organizations to be cautious when installing AI applications from unverified repositories and to restrict the execution of software from unknown sources.

The observed payload was an XMRig cryptominer, but the researchers said YobaLoader is a generic loader, so future waves could deliver other executable or PowerShell payloads.

articles.title: JFrog Names Nine Global Winners for Inaugural Software Supply Chain Excellence Awards
articles.context: This year’s JFrog Software Supply Chain Excellence Award winners are working to reduce their exposure to these emerging threats by building a system of record that governs and...
articles.full_text:
JFrog announced completion of the first-ever Software Supply Chain Excellence Awards, recognizing the teams who have turned their software supply chain into a competitive advantage – unifying development, security and operations around a governed, automated ecosystem that delivers trusted software at scale.

The nine honorees span the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, across three categories: Unified Platform, Trusted AI Adoption, and Software Supply Chain Security.

“Agents now write, review and deploy code faster than ever, while malicious AI models, agent skills and extensions are turning up in the registries developers use daily. Increasing regulations require proof at every step – from code to runtime,” said Roie Shorer, Chief Growth Officer at JFrog. “The companies that pull ahead in the AI era will be those going beyond simply automating for speed and scale. They will be the ones who can see exactly what’s shipping and why, as they bring trust, control and adaptability to their development operations. This year’s winners didn’t just add tools; they established a single source of truth where developers, security, and compliance teams can operate using the same data and the same rules. We’re very proud of all of them and thrilled to be part of their journey.”

Software supply chains are being put under new strain as developer teams grapple with AI-era software challenges. In its 2026 Software Supply Chain Security report, JFrog identified over 900 malicious AI agent skills carrying high-impact payloads alongside 495 malicious AI models on Hugging Face and 56 malicious extensions on OpenVSX. Attackers are no longer just targeting code; they are targeting the autonomous tools that write, review, and deploy it.

This year’s JFrog Software Supply Chain Excellence Award winners are working to reduce their exposure to these emerging threats by building a system of record that governs and secures artifacts from end-to-end – mastering the AI surge with speed and trust.

THE CONVERGENCE AWARD

The Convergence Award recognizes teams that unify a fragmented software delivery workflow – bringing previously disconnected repositories, scanners and tools into a single governed system of record.

Here are the winners:

Ford (Americas): Ford Motor Company has more than 15,000 developers spread across 80-plus global plants, which previously ran on separate repository tools and scanners with no shared visibility between them. By consolidating operations into a unified ecosystem with the JFrog Platform, Ford reduced tool sprawl and turned multiple blind spots into a single pane of glass view for IT and security teams. As a result, the team now manages more than 43 million artifacts on the JFrog Platform with 99.99% uptime. The team credits the consolidation with recapturing an estimated $8 million a year in developer productivity.

SCHOTTEL Industries (EMEA): Schottel replaced fragmented artifact storage and open-source consumption with the JFrog Platform. Over six months it delivered more than 32,000 artifacts, curated over 2,300 open-source packages and automatically blocked more than 900 risky ones. Manual dependency approval processes that previously delayed developers by months were replaced by automated governance and security controls, enabling faster adoption of new technologies while helping maintain its compliance and security standards.

Rakuten Symphony (APAC): Rakuten Symphony runs 28 self-hosted JFrog Enterprise+ instances across India, Japan and Singapore, that are all connected by JFrog Federated Repositories into one collaborative environment. With JFrog Curation and JFrog Advanced Security moving controls to the point of ingestion, the company cut manual triage efforts by roughly 60% in a single month across more than 600 releases, reclaiming more than 500 engineer-hours and pre-triaging over half of its vulnerability workload automatically.

THE TRUSTED INTELLIGENCE AWARD

The Trusted Intelligence Award recognizes teams that bring enterprise-grade governance to AI and model lifecycles, helping trust extend far beyond just supporting application code.

Here are the winners:

NVIDIA (Americas): Models repositories are under enterprise identity control, with a shared curation and scanning policy,which means a downloaded model faces the same checks as a package before it reaches production.

NVIDIA brought its AI model distribution surface under a governed perimeter by applying curation, scanning, and policy enforcement directly to its model mirrors. Thousands of AI model seats are now managed inside a controlled, auditable boundary, transforming what was once an unmanaged distribution surface into a demonstration of DevGovOps operating at true enterprise scale. To get there, NVIDIA leveraged JFrog Curation and JFrog’s scanning and policy tools, piloting them on the infrastructure through which its AI models flow.

Husqvarna Group (EMEA): Husqvarna’s autonomous divisions, across forest, garden and construction equipment, had accumulated overlapping scanners with limited shared visibility into software supply chain risk. After consolidating around the JFrog Platform and introducing software package scanning and policy-based controls earlier in the software development lifecycle, builds were progressively onboarded, providing teams with greater visibility into open-source dependencies and a more consistent approach to software component governance. Husqvarna Group validated JFrog Curation and JFrog Advanced Security in a hands-on pilot ahead of full deployment, and says the centralized visibility helps streamline security and governance workflows while supporting software traceability and reporting needs associated with evolving regulatory requirements, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act and NIS2.

Singapore Airlines (APAC): Singapore Airlines moved from “trust by verification” to “trust by default.” JFrog Curation and JFrog Xray now help intercept malicious, risky or non-compliant assets before they reach a build, including AI models, MCP servers, agent skills and IDE extensions. More than 95% of AI and open-source dependencies are onboarded through curated channels prior to integration. As a result, late-stage release blocks from non-compliant dependencies are down 60-75% and the airline has full visibility of its compliance posture.

THE GUARDIAN AWARD

The Guardian Award recognizes software supply chain security operating at real enterprise scale – blocking threats before they reach production across large, highly distributed environments.

Here are the winners:

S&P Global (Americas): S&P Global’s five divisions ran on independent JFrog Artifactory clusters with no shared policy enforcement which could potentially increase risk. By putting JFrog Curation at each point of ingestion – backed by continuous rescanning – S&P addressed that gap without slowing down development teams. Critical vulnerabilities across 30 images fell by 90%, from 141 to 14. S&P reports that about 99% of malicious npm and PyPI packages are now blocked at the point of ingestion, with JFrog Curation deployed as a synchronous gate for every division and JFrog Xray continuously rescanning artifacts already in use to catch newly disclosed threats.

TSB Bank (EMEA): TSB built a continuous governance platform based on JFrog’s APIs, using GitHub Actions and Open Policy Agent, as well as a versioned Python library published to JFrog Artifactory. Automated weekly audits check configuration drift, access control, artifact integrity and artifact authenticity. In the first seven months of using the platform there were 75 governance issues, 74 of which were resolved, with 11 production repositories verified for integrity every week.
