articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and updated the PHP Alert, Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP Require Immediate Patching:

CVE-2026-109618 – PHP Memory Corruption Vulnerability

CVE-2026-109619 – PHP Stale Internal Request-State Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Know How Cyble Brand Intelligence Can Help Stop ClickFix Campaigns in its Tracks
articles.context: Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list What the attacker did
articles.full_text:
Booking.com's systems were never breached. Its name was. Storm-1865 spent months borrowing Booking.com's identity to get into hotel computers, and every step of that borrowing left traces on the open internet.

The open internet is exactly where Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection works. Walk through the campaign one step at a time, and at each step there is a point where it could have spotted the attacker, cut the attack short or limited the damage.

What happened

From December 2024, a group Microsoft tracks as Storm-1865 posed as Booking.com to target hotel and hospitality staff across North America, Europe, Oceania and South and Southeast Asia. Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its findings on March 13, 2025, and said the campaign was still running as of February 2025.

The attack had four moving parts:

The lure. Emails styled as Booking.com messages about negative guest reviews, guest enquiries, promotion offers or account verification.

The landing page. A link, sometimes inside a PDF, opened a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page.

The trick. The "verification" told staff to open the Windows Run box and paste a command the page had already copied to their clipboard.

The payload. That command used mshta.exe to pull commodity malware, including XWorm, Lumma Stealer, VenomRAT, AsyncRAT, Danabot and NetSupport RAT, all built to steal credentials and payment data.

This was not a one-off. Microsoft says Storm-1865 targeted Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024 before adding ClickFix. Booking.com told Infosecurity Magazine its own systems were not breached, but some accommodation partners and customers were hit.

Why the impersonated brand holds the first move

Booking.com could not install security software on the laptops of its accommodation partners. What it could reach was the attacker's infrastructure copying its brand, and that infrastructure was detectable. Microsoft's own email security flagged URLs in this campaign as impersonating booking.com.

The stakes are high. The US Federal Trade Commission says people reported losing nearly $1 billion to business impersonators in 2025, out of $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams overall. Every copy of a brand caught early is one fewer victim.

Five steps, five chances to step in

Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every stage of the attack. Here is each stage, and how Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection could have helped at it.

Fig. Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability

Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list

What the attacker did. Storm-1865 was a repeat player. Microsoft says it went after Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024, then turned to hotel staff most likely to work with Booking.com.

How Cyble could have helped. Cyble's in-house brand team and OSINT surveillance track brand mentions and the actors who keep returning to a brand. A known playbook becomes a set of watch-list rules, so the next wave is expected rather than discovered after the fact.

Step 2: Register the infrastructure

What the attacker did. The campaign needed domains and URLs to host its fake pages. Microsoft flagged some of them as matching a known malicious registrant pattern.

How Cyble could have helped. Suspicious & Watch-Listed Domain monitoring tracks new registrations and DNS activity for typosquats, homoglyphs and lookalike domains, including AI-generated ones. A domain built to impersonate the brand can be flagged when it is registered, before it hosts a single page.

Step 3: Build the fake Booking.com page

What the attacker did. Victims landed on a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page. The familiar look was the point: it made a strange request feel routine.

How Cyble could have helped. Phishing Detection finds sites impersonating the brand, and Watermarking Surveillance spots copied or mirrored brand assets, even on domains with no brand name in them. Automated Takedown then works to get confirmed pages removed. Every hotel that clicks after a takedown hits a dead link instead of a trap.

Step 4: Send lures across regions

What the attacker did. Emails and PDFs about negative reviews, guest requests, promotions and account checks went to hotels across North America, Europe, Oceania and Asia. Some came through vendor platforms and ordinary services such as Gmail and iCloud Mail.

How Cyble could have helped. Multi-language NLP is built to catch phishing and impersonation attempts that are not in English, which matters for a campaign spread across this many markets. Lures that partners report can be handed to Cyble's brand team, traced to the live page behind them and queued for takedown.

Step 5: Cash in on stolen credentials and payment data

What the attacker did. Once a staff member pasted the command, malware such as XWorm, Lumma Stealer and VenomRAT went to work. Microsoft says every payload in the campaign could steal credentials and financial data for fraud.

How Cyble could have helped. Stopping the pasted command itself is a job for endpoint and email controls. What Cyble adds is the aftermath: OSINT surveillance watches forums, blogs and paste sites for exposed credentials and data leaks tied to the brand. Spotting stolen partner logins early gives everyone time to reset access before fraud follows.

This walkthrough maps public research to Cyble's capabilities. It is not a claim that Cyble took part in the response to this campaign.

Strongest alongside your other defenses

Brand intelligence works outside your network, so it pairs naturally with what runs inside it. When a lure arrives from an ordinary Gmail or iCloud address, there is no fake sender domain to flag, so the landing page becomes the asset to hunt. And if someone does run the pasted command, email filtering, endpoint detection, script controls and phishing-resistant MFA, the mitigations Microsoft recommends, do the stopping. Brand intelligence makes sure far fewer people ever reach that moment.

Is your brand the next Target? Six questions to ask

Any brand that sits between businesses and their customers can be borrowed the same way: travel platforms, marketplaces, payment providers, logistics firms and SaaS vendors. Ask your team:

Do we know which of our emails, notices and portal pages are most copied by attackers?

Are we alerted when a domain containing our name, or a homoglyph of it, is registered?

Can we spot a cloned page even when it sits on an unrelated domain or free hosting?

How long does it take us to get a confirmed phishing page taken down?

Do our partners know how to report a suspicious message that uses our name?

Do we watch criminal forums and channels for kits or templates built around our brand?

If more than two answers are "no" or "not sure," the attacker's preparation phase is happening without anyone watching.

The takeaway

Look back at the five steps and a pattern stands out. Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every one of them, and every one left a trace outside the victims' networks.

With Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection watching, each trace becomes a chance to step in: a repeat actor on the watch list, a lookalike domain flagged at registration, a cloned page taken down, a lure traced to its source, a leaked login caught early. If your partners and customers trust your name, Cyble helps make sure nobody else gets to use it.

See how it works for your brand: request a personalized demo.

articles.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

articles.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

articles.title: ZDI-26-809: Meta FAIRChem dense_eval dft-targets Deserialization of Untrusted Data Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of pickle files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

Meta has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairchem/pull/1935

Disclosure Timeline

2026-03-26 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-10-26 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of pickle files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Additional Details

Meta has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairchem/pull/1935

articles.title: Code security for new coders
articles.context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
articles.full_text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

articles.full_text:
Brandon Karpf: I mean, this is a situation that we have never seen before. It's not clear the contracting. It's not clear the liability. It's not clear the sources of control. This is a situation that, I think, rightfully brings up the question of nationalizing technology, which is kind of anathema to the U.S. way of functioning, but when you have a technology that is so critical to the functions of national security and defense, there does need to be more control implemented.

Maria Varmazis: Welcome. I'm Maria Varmazis, and you're listening to "T-Minus Space-Cyber Briefing." In this show, we examine the evolution of cybersecurity in the global and orbital infrastructure that powers, protects, and connects our lives. [ Music ] Hi, everyone, thank you for joining me. Now, we don't generally get into current events on "T-Minus," but today's episode is an exception where we are discussing current events regarding Starshield data being throttled without warning in Ukraine. The information we included in this discussion was current at the time of recording, but this story is continuing to evolve. On that note, I highly recommend subscribing to our "Signals and Space" newsletter. If you aren't already subscribed, you can do that at thecyberwire.com/newsletters. Our "Signals and Space" newsletter is where we are sharing the latest on this story as the news continues to unfold. As our understanding of the facts evolves with more information, we will be sure to provide the most updated sources in the newsletter so you can stay on top of the whole story, but in the meantime, over to Dave Bittner, my N2K colleague and host of "The CyberWire Daily," to lead us into this conversation.

Dave Bittner: It is my pleasure to bring our little group back together again. Of course, I'm talking about my co-host, Maria Varmazis here at N2K CyberWire. Maria, great to see you, as always.

Maria Varmazis: Likewise, Dave, thank you.

Dave Bittner: And joining us once again, Brandon Karpf, who is Leader of International Public-Private Partnerships at NTT. Brandon, it's great to have you back.

Brandon Karpf: The little rascals are again together.

Maria Varmazis: Oh, merge idea.

Dave Bittner: Yes, yes, so what I want to touch on today is, sort of, breaking news as we record this, which is the whole situation in Ukraine in relationship to Starlink, the private version, the military version, warfare in general, public-private partnerships, and all those kinds of things. Maybe we just start with some descriptive stuff. Maria, can you take us in with what seems to be happening with this? What's the basic story?

Maria Varmazis: You've got it. This is as of the time of this recording, so things will absolutely have changed by the time this goes live. As of time of this recording, the news was, yesterday, the day before we recorded, that Ukrainian defense ministry officials were saying on the ground they were -- their soldiers are reporting, essentially, some of their drones were being disconnected from the Starshield -- which is the military version of Starlink -- Starshield network whenever those drones would hit an apparent speed limit of 160 kilometers an hour, which did not exist before. They were not told of any such speed limits. They were not warned. It just sort of happened out of nowhere overnight, and the absolute latest, again, as of the time of this recording -- I just found this out an hour ago myself -- was that Elon Musk said that wasn't us because yesterday when we covered this story on "The CyberWire Daily," we'd had absolutely no indication from anyone, either from the DoD or from SpaceX about where this was coming from. Since then, we have learned -- at least Elon Musk has said -- it wasn't SpaceX's idea to impose such a speed limit. As far as I know, some of that seems to have been lifted. I don't think it has been entirely lifted. It's not entirely clear what has happened there, but essentially, SpaceX is pointing the fingers back to, I suppose, the Pentagon saying this didn't come from us, so that is what we know.

Dave Bittner: Okay. Brandon, what's your take on all of this, the broader view of these sorts of operations and the underpinnings?

Brandon Karpf: Yeah, I mean, at the highest level, right? I think this highlights the fact that warfare is now inextricably linked to private-sector resources. I mean, yeah, Starshield is the military version of Starlink, but it's still Starlink--

Maria Varmazis: Yeah.

Brandon Karpf: -- which is managed and operated by SpaceX. The fact of the matter is all of the reporting from Ukraine, basically, says that without Starlink, Ukraine would not be able to defend itself against Russia's invasion, at least not to the extent to which they've been able to. They've been able to take advantage of battlefield communications in a way that has made them incredibly effective, putting pressure on Russia's economy, their oil infrastructure, their communications infrastructure, their transportation infrastructure -- targeting not just Russian forces in Ukraine, but Russian forces in Russia. They've been able to integrate those communications in a lot of their intelligence gathering and operational planning and operational integration. And so just this idea that there's this now civilian communication infrastructure that is so critical to defense of Europe -- which is what is happening in Ukraine, it's like ultimately the defense of Europe -- is a little concerning, especially when it's now being, as Maria alluded to, right, Musk posted on X that the speed limits are not being controlled by SpaceX. That that's a U.S. military and a U.S. president decision, but it's not actually clear who is making those decisions. So if the Ukrainians have a contract for this, and they're not actually in control of what they're getting, that's a really concerning situation with implications that go far beyond battlefield communications.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah, yep.

Dave Bittner: What about, just, the reality that we have a leader like Musk, who has a reputation for doing things his own way under his own terms. You know, it seems to me like that reality adds a certain bit of messiness to all of this. That, you know, the concern that people are even talking about the possibility that Elon Musk could have his finger on the button of a military operation of one of our allies to me, that's a different situation than we've typically been in the past. Is that fair to say, Brandon?

Brandon Karpf: Totally. Yeah, a totally different situation than we've had in the past. It's not like Oppenheimer was in control of the use of the nuclear weapon -- not drawing a direct comparison between, you know, Starlink and nuclear weapons, but it is a battlefield technology.

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Brandon Karpf: The fact that there is this individual, to your point, who isn't really accountable, certainly isn't being held accountable, does not have the same mechanisms to be held accountable, is very -- is problematic, to say the least, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yeah.

Brandon Karpf: I mean, this is a situation that we have never seen before. It's not clear the contracting. It's not clear the liability. It's not clear the sources of control. This is a situation that, I think, rightfully, brings up the question of nationalizing technology, which is kind of an anathema to the U.S. way of functioning, but when you have a technology that is so critical to the functions of national security and defense, there does need to be more control implemented. So it is just kind of astonishing thinking that until today, just an hour ago, we were not sure if Musk had just turned this off. Even right now, we have no idea. The Ukrainians don't know. The public does not know how this --

Maria Varmazis: Or even if Elon Musk, what he's saying is true.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Brandon Karpf: Right, or what the mechanism was to actually impose the speed limit, which, this, I mean, the speed limit, the fact that it only affected systems traveling faster than 160 kilometers an hour means that this wasn't an attack, right? This was a setting, and the fact there's no real accountability mechanism here, that's a problem.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, I'm just thinking, I remember when I was reading up on this story yesterday morning, just, I was trying to get up to speed on what the heck was going on. I'm just -- I was trying to put myself in the shoes of the Ukrainian officials, just imagining them trying to just triage this, and, just, they don't know who to talk to, and just on a basic level, who are you actually dealing with when a situation like this has arisen? The fact that it took, you know, seemingly 24 hours for it to even -- for anyone to say, Oh, yeah, that was me. I mean, how can does -- how can any -- it just muddies the water so much, and I -- I'm just imagining the discussions happening in Europe right now about the IRIS2 sovereign satellite constellation. That timeline keeps moving up, which, you know, doesn't normally happen in that direction --

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: But I cannot come fast enough.

Dave Bittner: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: It -- truly, this entire situation has just made the case for sovereign space capabilities.

Brandon Karpf: Totally.

Maria Varmazis: You know, it's the poster child for it now.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah, sovereign space capabilities, exactly, more domestic capacity, you know, investment in alternatives that are not based in the U.S. companies or U.S. infrastructure, right? I think this pushes U.S. allies further and further away from the U.S.

Maria Varmazis: It sure does.

Brandon Karpf: And, like, to ground this, right, if, you know, we're talking about battlefield technology that is both used offensively and defensively, right? Imagine you are in a Ukrainian unit near the front line, and you get -- you are under attack by a Russian drone unit. You're relying on technology to sense where they are, and then to respond. And you have, kind of, seeker drones that can go and then find that unit that is attacking you -- attacking you attacking civilians, attacking Ukrainian civilians, Ukrainian critical infrastructure, energy infrastructure -- which Russia has done in the last couple days, attacking their energy infrastructure, again, as we're moving towards winter. The drones used to counter-target the Russians are going to be moving more than 160 kilometers an hour. And so now you're in a situation where suddenly you're relying on a technology to defend yourself, and that technology is just shut off without any indication, without any communication, without any sort of accountability. That is akin to a war crime, turning that technology off that is actively being used to defend civilians against Russian aggression. That's a huge problem, and someone needs to be held accountable for that.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah.

Dave Bittner: I'm reminded, just as sort of a quick aside, years ago, I learned that, like, your run-of-the-mill, your GPS device and even the ones built into our phones today, like, they don't work in an airplane because of velocity. Like, they, they, if you're going faster than a speed, if you're going at jet speed, the GPS devices don't report back to you. Evidently, this is originally a safety factor to keep people from building their own guided missiles. Yeah, so this just reminds me of that. I guess they sort of rhyme with each other, you know?

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Dave Bittner: Put a speed limit on something, but if you're the U.S. military, are you thinking about building your own constellation?

Maria Varmazis: I mean, they're working on it.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: It's being actively developed. There are -- that is that is certainly in process, but there are, I mean, there are a number of private companies. I mean, this is not new news. There are a number of private companies that are developing military-only low-earth-orbit constellations. I know Iridium is, like, a very famously one that's been working on this for the U.S. military for a while. I think, to me, that the difference here is just I, all of these behaviors that we're hearing about either Starlink or then later Starshield, it is or it isn't working, or it's not working at capacity. I just can't imagine a company generally operating this way. It just seems anathema to decent business practices. So that's, I think, part of the confusion, and I'm not trying to be naive. I understand there's a whole level of geopolitics that one can conjecture about going on here, but it's just not how, generally, I think of businesses wanting to run, and yet here we are. [ Music ] And here we are, at a time for a break in our show now. We'll be right back. [ Music ] Let's get back to the conversation now, where Brandon Karpf will start us off.

Brandon Karpf: Dave, to your point about GPS, you know, working at speed like that, I mean, the whole justification for creating Starshield, right, as kind of a subset architecture to Starlink, or its own distinct architecture was, one, some security requirements for a military-only-type architecture, but also, so that you can enable things like drone control, like missile control, like offensive weapon control, through that architecture without crossing over with a civilian architecture, right? Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Brandon Karpf: -- and should have some sort of contract to use that. It's just this bizarre situation where we're retrenching and, basically, convincing the world to get off the U.S. tech platform.

Maria Varmazis: Yeah. Yeah, and I think that what adds insult to injury, a whole level to it, at least for me when I think about this story, is when the war originally started in 2022, defenders in Ukraine were using Starlink because that was available to them. It was being provided via USAID, I believe. Then during the Biden administration, Starshield was sort of spun up as a, hey, we don't want the military using the civilian tech. Let's create a contract that the DoD will manage, and it will be Starshield. That's sort of my very basic nutshell understanding of that. As sort of a, we want the Ukrainian military to be able to use this technology, but in, you know, as you mentioned, Brendon, like ways that are safe for them and also not getting conflated with civilian use. It was, essentially, the SpaceX and the U.S. government going, you can use this technology. Use it over here. Use it in this way, and we're all hunky dory.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah.

Maria Varmazis: And then suddenly, it's just this rug pull. Like, they did what we asked of them to do, and now, we're just completely changing the rules on them with no warning. What can you even say?

Brandon Karpf: It does not bode well for long-term relationships built on goodwill and trust.

Dave Bittner: I mean, that's probably the highest-level story in all this, is the U.S. is shifting roles as a reliable ally or not. As you mentioned, Brandon, you know, how do our allies around the world look at something like this in terms of making their own plans?

Brandon Karpf: Well, and all of this is happening under the context of the President, the U.S. President, allegedly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. It's actually just a very limited amount of diesel that he's claiming that we're going to be purchasing, which set aside the fact that it is illegal, even for the President to import Russian diesel to the U.S. --

Dave Bittner: Right.

Brandon Karpf: That there's a congressional statute that does not allow that. The President cannot just wave a wand and change that, but that is also happening right now, and so that's us. Allegedly, we'll see if any diesel actually ends up getting transported, but that is the U.S. paying cash to Russia for oil, while Russia is actively attacking Ukraine and Europe, right?

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Brandon Karpf: They've put explosive drones in Germany and Poland, and while they funnel offensive weapons to Iran, who is attacking U.S. forces and killing U.S. service members? So we are actively funding the murder of U.S. service members. It's absolutely insane.

Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Maria Varmazis: Elon Musk with Starlink optimized a service that had already existed, which was satellite communications. He did it much better. He was definitely a disruptor. I think there's an arrogance behind, you know, Starlink being at the top of things, and you know, it's going to remain that way. That is certainly not a given, and this is only going to accelerate now with incidents like this.

Brandon Karpf: Yeah, I'll corroborate that just with my own observations working for a Japanese corporation. It's not necessarily that there's a direct competitor that exists right now for some of these things, but it doesn't take very long to invest and spin something up. Just in the last six months, I've seen a market increase in international partners exploring Japan, and that's just Japan. I'm sure Germany is seeing the same thing. I'm sure the U.K. is seeing something similar. In --

Maria Varmazis: Australia.

Brandon Karpf: Exactly, other large partners as well.

Maria Varmazis: India. Yep. Maria Varmazis: Yep.

Brandon Karpf: I think it's going to be important that whoever it is, they're held accountable.

Dave Bittner: Yeah.

Dave Bittner: Do you think, in addition to Starlink, maybe we'll see Sonylink? [laughter]

Brandon Karpf: Oh, sleek, sleek, sleek.

articles.context: Its interconnected systems, including QScan and Fast Labyrinth, help identify high-value targets, conceal malicious traffic, and support potential exploitation of government,...
articles.full_text:
Today we have ⁠Damon Rouse⁠, Threat Intelligence from ⁠Lumen⁠'s Black Lotus Labs, discussing their work on "The infrastructure quartermaster: inside a China-nexus state enablement model." Black Lotus Labs identified a China-nexus cyber infrastructure provider, dubbed a “quartermaster,” that supplies reconnaissance, proxy routing, and obfuscation services to Chinese cyber espionage actors.

Its interconnected systems, including QScan and Fast Labyrinth, help identify high-value targets, conceal malicious traffic, and support potential exploitation of government, military, research, and critical infrastructure networks. Researchers warn that this shared infrastructure makes traditional IP-based defenses less effective and recommend following CISA and NCSC guidance, reducing external attack surfaces, and keeping routers, firewalls, and IoT devices updated.

articles.title: The apps are only the beginning.
articles.context: Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. Railway confirms a cyberattack. HPE patches critical ArubaOS flaws. Quest Diagnostics investigates a disruptive intrusion. Capcom reports a data breach. China-linked hackers put AI-powered attacks on autopilot. And researchers uncover a Microsoft 365 campaign that hijacks authentication tokens to bypass MFA. Our guest is Anudeep Parhar, COO at Entrust, sharing his thoughts on AI kill switches. eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

Today is Friday, October 23rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Attackers ramp up attempts to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities.

Attackers are ramping up attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, but researchers have yet to confirm a successful compromise in the wild.

The flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution and prompted emergency patches on October 21. Sophos identified attempts to deploy Potassium, a Mirai botnet variant, although the attack it examined was unsuccessful.

Researchers say exploitation is proving more difficult than initially feared, largely because successful attacks require specific server configurations or ways around memory protections.

VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses one such protection, while an exposed attacker server revealed custom exploitation tools and unsuccessful attempts against dozens of targets.

Meanwhile, patching remains a challenge. Qualys estimates roughly 110 million PHP instances run unsupported versions that won’t receive fixes.

Security researchers have identified 426 mobile apps connecting to servers running PHP versions potentially affected by the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

NowSecure analyzed more than 15,000 Android and iOS apps, finding that 170 connected to servers running outdated PHP versions that no longer receive official security updates.

The vulnerabilities affect backend servers, not the mobile apps themselves, and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication.

Importantly, researchers caution that identifying a potentially vulnerable PHP version doesn’t establish whether a server remains unpatched or exploitable.

The findings also highlight the risks of third-party dependencies. One advertising provider’s server was contacted by 151 different apps.

NowSecure recommends developers work with their infrastructure providers to verify patching, upgrade unsupported PHP installations, and investigate potential exploitation.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI and PHP.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs says artificial intelligence is fueling an unprecedented surge in software vulnerability discoveries, creating what some are calling “Black October” for cybersecurity.

Appearing on CNBC, Krebs said AI-powered tools are uncovering security flaws at a pace that threatens to overwhelm organizations’ ability to patch them.

He pointed to the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities as an example. While attackers have attempted exploitation, Krebs said no successful compromises have been confirmed.

His biggest concern isn’t necessarily large enterprises, which generally have the resources to respond quickly. It’s smaller businesses, rural hospitals, utilities, and managed service providers that lack dedicated security teams.

Krebs warned that vulnerabilities in third-party services could expose entire networks, while legacy systems can complicate patching.

He expects the situation to get worse before it improves, as AI continues uncovering vulnerabilities faster than organizations can address them.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack that may have exposed customer passwords, API keys, and other secrets stored in encrypted environment variables. The company believes the breach affected a subset of customers but is urging all users to revoke and rotate their credentials as a precaution. Railway temporarily suspended new builds and deployments while investigating. The number of affected customers, the attack’s root cause, and the systems compromised remain unknown.

Railway suspects the incident is part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Earlier this week, AI coding tool OpenCode reported a similar attack that exposed credentials belonging to more than one percent of its customers. Railway says it plans to publish a detailed post-mortem.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise patches critical vulnerabilities in ArubaOS.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security updates addressing 72 vulnerabilities in ArubaOS, including eight maximum-severity flaws that could allow attackers to bypass authentication or remotely execute malicious code.

The vulnerabilities affect multiple versions of ArubaOS 8 and 10, which power enterprise wireless networking equipment, including access points, controllers, and gateways. All eight maximum-severity flaws can be exploited remotely without authentication, using relatively simple attacks that require no user interaction.

HPE is strongly urging customers to install the patches, citing the number and potential impact of the vulnerabilities. The company also recommends restricting access to management interfaces through network segmentation and firewall controls.

So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a disruptive cyberattack.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a cyberattack that may have exposed patient information and disrupted access to medical test results.

The company discovered unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, which healthcare providers use to order tests and retrieve results. Quest took the system offline Thursday and temporarily paused several other systems as a precaution.

The company believes some patient data was accessed but hasn’t determined what information was compromised. Quest says its other operations weren’t affected and is working with law enforcement.

Healthcare providers can use paper requisitions while the system is unavailable. Quest expects to restore service Friday.

The company says the attack is unrelated to recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. No threat actor has claimed responsibility.

Capcom discloses a data breach.

Japanese gaming giant Capcom has disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 11.8 million records associated with its CAPCOM ID service.

The compromised information includes email addresses, account identifiers, and login activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts, which Capcom has since reset.

The company says it has no evidence that customers’ original passwords were compromised, and credit card information remains unaffected.

Capcom has contained the unauthorized access and notified Japanese authorities. Customers are being warned to watch for phishing attempts impersonating the company.

Megaman, please call your office.

A China-linked threat actor is using Artex to automate cyberattacks.

Microsoft says a China-linked threat actor is using an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Artex to automate cyberattacks against hundreds of organizations.

The group, tracked as Storm-0940, used the tool in an October campaign targeting ConnectWise customers, accelerating reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications.

Microsoft observed more than 151,000 failed login attempts, along with successful authentication using compromised ConnectWise application identities.

The attackers attempted to access more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, sometimes progressing beyond authentication to modify credentials, manipulate directory settings, and establish persistent access.

In one burst of activity, the group targeted more than 300 accounts across eight organizations at over 2,900 attempts per minute.

Microsoft says the campaign illustrates how AI-assisted automation can dramatically accelerate established attack techniques, giving defenders less time to respond.

Researchers uncover a campaign that compromises Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Security researchers at Huntress have uncovered a ten-week campaign that compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Attackers used adversary-in-the-middle phishing and other techniques to capture legitimate login sessions, allowing them to bypass multifactor authentication without needing victims’ passwords.

Huntress observed at least 497 successful sign-ins alongside more than 200,000 failed attempts. Once inside, attackers registered 48 rogue devices, replaced victims’ authentication methods, and created hidden inbox rules to conceal suspicious communications.

In one case, a compromised account was used to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact.

The attacks relied partly on infrastructure belonging to a German hosting provider.

Huntress recommends properly configured Conditional Access policies and warns that password resets alone won’t eliminate persistent access. Organizations must also revoke sessions and remove unauthorized devices and authentication methods.

eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

From our “you can’t fire me, I quit!” desk, Indian digital trust company eMudhra is getting out of the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident that attracted considerable scrutiny.

The company says it revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours, with no infrastructure compromise, data breach, or affected customer certificates issued.

But eMudhra’s chairman says the resulting social media attention was disproportionate, particularly for a business representing just one percent of company revenue.

Add rising compliance costs and competition from free certificates, and the board decided it was time to pursue other opportunities.

eMudhra promises a smooth transition, including free replacement certificates for affected customers.

Its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

And so, after careful consideration, eMudhra has decided that SSL certificates just aren’t its thing anymore.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: eMudhra Incident: A Practical Audit to Inspect Tools
articles.context: Browser protections were an important first response to the eMudhra certificate authority incident
articles.full_text:
Browser protections were an important first response to the eMudhra certificate authority incident. But they don't answer a harder question for organizations: which other tools and environments still trust the affected certificate chains?

Certificate trust can come from different places. A tool may use the operating system's trust store, a bundled certificate list, or a runtime-specific store such as a Java JDK's cacerts. One machine can therefore have different trust behavior across its browsers, developer tools, and runtimes. Updating one trust store doesn't update them all.

That makes eMudhra remediation a software supply chain problem. Teams need to find where trust is configured, identify which systems need attention, and confirm that updates reach the tools developers and build processes actually use.

Start by Finding What Each Tool Trusts

Paul Horton, Sonatype's Open Source Program Office (OSPO) Global Director, created the open source eMudhra Audit and Fix script to help teams inspect selected developer tools on Unix-like machines.

The script checks tools such as Java, Node.js, Python, Go, and Git, along with system certificate bundles and other components. Where supported, it makes live HTTPS requests to two test hosts whose certificates chain to the affected intermediates, then checks GitHub as a control. The control helps distinguish certificate rejection from other connection problems, such as a lack of network access. The script also compares some tool versions with fixes listed in the incident reference. When a live probe and version check disagree, the live probe takes precedence.

By default, the audit does not install, change, or delete anything on the machine. It creates temporary probe programs and makes ordinary HTTPS requests. Those requests send no file contents. If network probes aren't appropriate for an environment, the --no-network option skips them and runs version checks only.

Teams can use the results to identify tools that need attention and decide what to investigate next. An audit result is a starting point for remediation, not confirmation that every system in the organization is protected.

Use the Results to Guide Remediation

Teams can use the script's output to:

Identify affected or potentially affected tools on a workstation.

Confirm how each tool is installed and which trust store it uses.

Apply the relevant operating system, runtime, or application vendor update.

Re-run the checks and record which systems still need remediation.

The script also has an optional --fix mode that can apply some changes it supports, asking before each change. Those actions can include upgrading a supported tool or changing a system or runtime trust store. Review the README and the proposed action before proceeding; the --dry-run option shows what a fix would do without changing anything. Prefer vendor updates where available, and test any workaround against the systems and services that depend on the trust store.

Know What the Script Can't See

The script audits the machine where it runs. It does not scan remote hosts, containers, or per-project dependencies. Its coverage is limited to specified tools and installation paths. Some tools receive version checks rather than live probes. A result from a developer workstation therefore cannot establish the status of a CI runner, container image, production host, or another employee's machine.

Organizations should treat those environments as separate parts of the investigation. Update and verify container images, build agents, and managed systems through the processes and vendor guidance that apply to them. For Sonatype products, follow the current Help documentation for product-specific updates and instructions.

The eMudhra incident showed why browser status alone can't answer whether an organization is remediated. Trust stores are distributed across tools and environments, and each one needs an owner and a way to verify its status. Paul's script gives teams a practical way to examine part of that landscape. Completing the work still requires a broader inventory, vendor updates, and follow-up checks.

The script is part of the Sonatype Nexus Community. If you have feedback or would like to contribute, engage with the project by following its Contribution Guidelines. As a community project, it is not officially supported by Sonatype.

For background on the eMudhra incident and Sonatype's response, see our published blog post.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany’s far-right AfD party
articles.context: cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local...
articles.full_text:
Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails.

Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026.

The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports.

To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified.

What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent.

Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies.

The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files.

The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy."

They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down.

Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed.

It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received.

Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly.

Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

articles.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
articles.context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
articles.full_text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-110447 Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server OS Command Injection Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Gaming Giant Capcom Confirms Data Breach Exposed Users’ Personal Information
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Capcom, the gaming giant behind Resident Evil, Street Fighter and Monster Hunter, has warned that players’ personal information may have been compromised following a data breach.

In a notice published October 22, the Japanese company said customer information associated with CAPCOM ID was subject to unauthorized access by a third party.

CAPCOM ID is a unified account operated by Capcom that players can use to play Capcom-licensed games online as well as to access various web services.

As of October 22, Capcom estimated that the data compromised include:

11,774,247 records of email addresses and system-specific identifier information (e.g. date and time of account creation, date and time of last login, number of logins, client IP address used during last login)

43 records of date of birth, gender, country/region and nickname

Capcom has not confirmed any compromise of CAPCOM ID account login passwords originally set by customers themselves. However, it has observed that passwords were changed without authorization on 196 customer accounts.

“The passwords associated with these accounts have already been reset, and the company continues to investigate the scope of any impact resulting from this incident,” the company said.

It also confirmed that credit card information remains unaffected by the breach.

Capcom has warned that the affected information could potentially be misused in fraudulent emails or other communications impersonating the company or related parties.

It has advised customers to exercise caution when receiving suspicious messages and avoid clicking on links or opening attachments.

The company also confirmed that services using CAPCOM ID, including its games, remain available

Timeline of Capcom Data Breach and Company Response

Capcom detected suspicious activity involving its CAPCOM ID account system on October 19, 2026, indicating potential unauthorised access.

The company said it immediately moved to block the access, investigate the cause and scope of the incident, and implement emergency response measures. Later that day, Capcom confirmed that unauthorised access had occurred and began identifying and addressing the attack method.

On October 20, Capcom established an internal incident response headquarters to coordinate its investigation and prevent further impact.

The investigation confirmed that certain customer information registered with CAPCOM ID had been accessed without authorisation. The company also discovered that passwords associated with a limited number of accounts had been changed without permission.

Capcom subsequently reported the incident to its external Information Technology Security Oversight Committee.

By October 21, Capcom had completed emergency response measures and identified and addressed the attack method and reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.

articles.title: Widespread Token-Spraying Attacks Target Microsoft 365 Accounts For Email Compromise
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A newly uncovered and widespread business email compromise (BEC) campaign targeted Microsoft 365 environments in an operation which made hundreds of thousands of attempts to access corporate networks around the world.

Identified by cybersecurity researchers at Huntress, the campaign used fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, stolen session tokens and social engineering in attacks which appeared to be setting the stage for BEC BEC attacks.

As detailed in a blog post published on October 22, researchers launched an investigation following a series of suspicious “sign-in events” across 79 Huntress customer organizations which took place between July and September 2026.

What they found was a global campaign which targeted corporate Microsoft 365 environments with adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks, which allowed the attackers to compromise accounts without the attacker ever needing to steal the passwords associated with them.

The attackers achieved this by stealing the login tokens which help to provide access to the account. Crucially for the attackers, these tokens are generated after the real login page has been legitimately used and any associated multi-factor authentication (MFA) has verified the account. That means that whoever holds the token doesn’t need to pass MFA again.

The attackers then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services.

Active Compromise Within Minutes

These ‘token-spraying’ attacks probed Microsoft 365 environments around the world. Researchers at Huntress observed the threat actor behind the campaign make at least 200,000 login attempts, which included 497 successful sign-ins. In many cases, the attackers were inside environments just minutes after stealing the tokens.

The attackers used this initial access to modify controls around Microsoft 365 environments in an attempt to make future access easier.

For example, in several observed incidents, the attackers wiped the victim’s MFA settings and added their own phone to the account user, so a simple password reset wouldn’t lock them out, because now the attacker had their own authenticator app for the environment.

Other methods the attackers used to help maintain persistence on the compromised networks included hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. They even modified Entra settings to add their own devices as legitimately registered on the network to request additional tokens if needed in future.

The attackers were also observed using a compromised mailbox to send a payroll-related phishing email message. Using a legitimate email to send these requests increases the likelihood of a business email compromise attack working. In this case, however, it appears the attackers did not receive a payment from their intended victim.

The nature of this campaign means that the attackers can easily establish persistence on the network. But Huntress emphasised that there are actions which can be taken to reduce the risk from these kinds of campaigns.

“Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented. Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally,” said Huntress.

If companies suspect a token replay compromise, it is advised that they revoke the sessions and reset the password, perform an audit of Entra devices and MFA methods and review inbox rules to identify if anything has been changed.

articles.title: Attacks on Tech Firms Behind Most Third-Party Data Breach Victims
articles.context: More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found
articles.full_text:
More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found.

Of those individuals, most (79%) had their data accessed following the compromise of a technology company during the period June 2025 to June 2026.

This is far higher than the proportion of third-party data breaches emanating from other industries, which includes finance (9%), insurance (6%) or healthcare (5%).

Incidents affecting technology firms also caused 60% of the total number of data breach victims – whether emanating from a single organization or as part of a supply chain breach – over the 12-month period. This was followed by insurance (10%), finance (8%), healthcare (8%) and education (7.5%).

Among all security leaders surveyed for the Kroll report, published on October 22, 69% said their organization had suffered a breach in the previous 12 months, while 34% reported experiencing more than one.

Finance and Professional Services Most Breached Sectors

Despite the tech sector causing the vast majority of individual data breach victims, it was only the seventh most commonly breached sector.

In first place was finance, making up 20% of breaches observed by Kroll. This was followed by professional services (20%), healthcare (15%) and retail (8%).

In contrast, technology only made up 6% of data breach incidents.
