articles.title: Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
articles.context: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority
articles.full_text:
October 29, 2026: We added guidance for end-of-life PHP versions (8.1 and earlier), including the source backports that the PHP security team published for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1.

October 23, 2026 (update 2): The PHP project disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate remote code execution issue that the October 21 releases don’t fix. It affects only applications with an uncommon configuration that keeps session upload progress enabled. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.4 and later, already blocks POST requests that carry a PHP session ID and the session upload progress field (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS). This helps mitigate CVE-2026-115560 until PHP releases a fix, and no rule group update is needed. PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until its next regular bugfix release. If you applied this setting for CVE-2026-109619, keep it in place.

October 23, 2026: We updated this post for version 2.4 of the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group, which adds the PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule for CVE-2026-109618, and AWS made it the default version. AWS is continuously updating the AWS WAF PHP managed rule group to add protection for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. If you use the default version, you will be automatically protected without any action on your part. If you have pinned a specific version, update to the latest version to receive this protection. For the latest version and details on the rules added, see the AWS Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic (both linked below). Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

October 22, 2026: We updated this post to add the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group. Version 2.3 of the rule group adds the PHP2Shell_BODY rule for CVE-2026-109619.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency fixes for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, the PHP project won’t release a new version for your branch, but backported fixes are available for some versions. See Fix end-of-life PHP versions later in this post.

Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. But patching a fleet takes time: you need to inventory where PHP runs, schedule maintenance windows and test applications against the new builds. This post shows you how to use AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to help reduce your exposure during that window. The AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group includes rules for both vulnerabilities: PHP2Shell_BODY for CVE-2026-109619 and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended for CVE-2026-109618. AWS continues to release new versions of this rule group as detection improves. Track them in the AWS Managed Rules changelog, or subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic to get notified. If your protection pack (web ACL) uses this rule group at the default version, these rules are already active. This post shows you how to confirm that and how to add the rule group if you don’t use it yet. It also covers the custom rules that still add defense in depth. It also explains where AWS WAF protection ends, so you don’t develop a false sense of safety. For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot. For AWS service status and patching guidance, see AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS.

IMPORTANT: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

The vulnerabilities in brief

Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles multipart/form-data request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses. For the root-cause analysis, affected versions, and PHP’s own guidance, see the official PHP advisories and release announcement:

CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) – PHP advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w

CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) – PHP advisory GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp

PHP security release announcement, October 21, 2026

Where AWS WAF fits in your response

AWS WAF is a defense-in-depth control in this situation, not a replacement for the PHP upgrade. The PHP advisories are explicit: updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. One of the two vulnerabilities is largely outside the reach of any web application firewall, as explained later. Treat the managed rules and the custom rules in this post as mitigating controls that help reduce exposure while you patch, then remove them or keep them as supporting controls after you’ve patched.

AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at the edge. It doesn’t parse the internal structure of a multipart body, and it has no visibility into PHP worker memory or server-side configuration. The following table maps each attack element to whether AWS WAF can help mitigate it.

Attack element

AWS WAF coverage

Request patterns that match CVE-2026-109618

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.4 or later.

Request patterns that match CVE-2026-109619

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule in the PHP application managed rule group, version 2.3 or later.

Session upload progress field in a multipart POST (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that turns on PHP’s upload-tracking feature)

Yes. The PHP2Shell_BODY rule (version 2.4 or later) and the custom rule in this post block POST requests that carry a PHP session ID and that field. This also helps mitigate CVE-2026-115560.

Multipart upload path (multipart/form-data, the request type used for file uploads and the entry point for both vulnerabilities)

Yes, if the application has no legitimate multipart uploads. Block multipart/form-data.

Out-of-memory condition from an oversized body

Partial. PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspects the request body up to the body inspection limit. Cap the request body size with the Core rule set SizeRestrictions_BODY rule or a custom rule. Neither catches header amplification (many small part headers that cost far more memory to represent than their size on the wire) that stays under the cap.

Repeated attempts against the same worker (the reused PHP process that handles many requests)

Partial. A rate-based rule reduces the volume an exploit needs, but it doesn’t stop a single successful request.

fatal_error_backtraces producer (a PHP 8.5 setting that stores crash-trace state across a request)

No. This is a server configuration setting (fatal_error_backtraces=0).

Invalid or deprecated INI diagnostics as a consumer (warnings PHP raises when applying bad configuration settings)

No. This path runs server-side, not over client HTTP.

Where an application does not accept multipart uploads, an edge rule that blocks multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application, plus the session-upload-progress trigger, which is a defense-in-depth control during the patch window.

If your application does use multipart uploads, AWS WAF reduces risk but does not close the vulnerability, because header amplification (a few kilobytes of part headers that expand into far more memory inside PHP) stays within size limits and the firewall cannot parse the headers inside individual body parts. In that case, prioritize the PHP upgrade and apply the server-side mitigations described later.

Start with the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group

The PHP application managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet) contains rules that block request patterns associated with the exploitation of vulnerabilities specific to PHP. PHP2Shell_BODY inspects the request body for requests that match CVE-2026-109619 and is in version 2.3 and later. PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspects the request body for requests that match CVE-2026-109618 and is in version 2.4 and later. The default action of both rules is Block. The AWS WAF documentation notes that this rule group contains a virtual patch for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and that you can add it to your protection pack (web ACL) to help protect your application against exploitation attempts until your application is patched. The rule group uses 100 web ACL capacity units (WCUs). Like the other AWS managed baseline and use-case rule groups, it has no charge beyond standard AWS WAF pricing. For the latest version and details on the rules added, see the AWS Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic.

What you need to do depends on how your web ACL uses the rule group:

You use the default version. Both PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are already active. Confirm that you haven’t overridden the whole rule group to Count, and review your AWS WAF logs for matches.

You pin a static version. Version_2.3 has PHP2Shell_BODY but not PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended, and Version_2.2 and earlier have neither. Change the version to Version_2.4 or later. We recommend that you use the default version.

You don’t use the rule group yet. Add it to the web ACL in front of each PHP workload, as shown in the following example.

To add the rule group in the AWS WAF console, open your protection pack (web ACL), choose Manage rules, and then do the following, as shown in Figure 1:

Choose Add rule.

Select AWS-managed rule group.

Choose Next.

Under Free, choose PHP application.

For Version, keep Default (recommended). If you need to pin a version, choose Version_2.4 or later.

Under Rule overrides, confirm that PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are listed. To review matches before they block, set both to Count.

Choose Add rule.

Figure 1: Adding the PHP application managed rule group in the AWS WAF console.

If you prefer to work programmatically, run the following commands to see the current default version and the version that a web ACL uses. Both commands are read-only.

aws wafv2 list-available-managed-rule-group-versions \ --vendor-name AWS --name AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet --scope REGIONAL aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name <web-acl-name> --id <web-acl-id> --scope REGIONAL \ --query "WebACL.Rules[?Statement.ManagedRuleGroupStatement.Name=='AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet']"

For web ACLs associated with Amazon CloudFront, use --scope CLOUDFRONT and the US East (N. Virginia) Region. A rule without a Version field uses the default version.

The following rule adds the rule group at the default version. The RuleActionOverrides entry sets PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended to Count so you can review their matches before they block. Remove the override when you’re satisfied. Given how quickly exploitation followed disclosure, measure that review period in hours, not days. If you need to pin the rule group, add a Version field set to Version_2.4 or later to the ManagedRuleGroupStatement. We recommend the default version.

{ "Name": "AWS-AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "ManagedRuleGroupStatement": { "VendorName": "AWS", "Name": "AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet", "RuleActionOverrides": [ { "Name": "PHP2Shell_BODY", "ActionToUse": { "Count": {} } }, { "Name": "PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended", "ActionToUse": { "Count": {} } } ] } }, "OverrideAction": { "None": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "AWS-AWSManagedRulesPHPRuleSet" } }

If PHP2Shell_BODY or PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended matches legitimate requests, keep the rule in Count and add a label-based exception after the rule group. The rule group adds the labels awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body and awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body_Extended to requests that match either rule, and the following rule blocks those requests everywhere except one path. Requests to the excluded path aren’t protected by this rule, so keep the exception as narrow as you can and patch that application first. Labels are case sensitive: confirm the label name in the rule group’s available labels (the DescribeManagedRuleGroup API) before you deploy. For the full pattern, see Creating exceptions in the AWS WAF best practices guide.

{ "Name": "PHP2Shell-Body-Exception", "Priority": 1, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "LABEL", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body" } }, { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "LABEL", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:php-app:PHP2Shell_Body_Extended" } } ] } }, { "NotStatement": { "Statement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "UriPath": {} }, "PositionalConstraint": "STARTS_WITH", "SearchString": "/path/to/legitimate-upload", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } } } } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBodyException" } }

You can also return a web ACL to Version_2.2 while you tune, but that version includes neither PHP2Shell_BODY nor PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended. Treat a rollback as removing the CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-109618 protection, and prefer the Count override and exception.

PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended inspect the request body only up to the web ACL body inspection limit. Both use the Continue oversize option, so they don’t inspect content beyond that limit. Pair them with a body size rule such as SizeRestrictions_BODY in the Core rule set (AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet), which blocks request bodies over 8 KB. If you set that rule to Count because of upload paths, use a label-based exception scoped to those paths instead. That keeps the rule in Block everywhere else. For the limit on each resource type, see Request body inspection limits later in this post.

Additional WAF Rules to consider

The managed rule groups cover two of the rules in this section. PHP2Shell_BODY in the PHP application rule group covers CVE-2026-109619, the same CVE as the custom rule later in this post. SizeRestrictions_BODY in the Core rule set caps request bodies at 8 KB, which covers body content beyond the inspection limit. For CVE-2026-109618 itself, the PHP application rule group includes PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended (version 2.4 or later). No AWS managed rule group blocks all multipart requests or rate-limits POST requests, so those two rules remain custom. Use them where they fit your application.

The following rules are in AWS WAF JSON format. Add each one to the protection pack (web ACL) associated with the CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway stage in front of your PHP workloads. Adjust the priorities to fit your web ACL. The AWS WAF best practices guide describes a recommended rule order, with managed rule groups before the label-based exceptions that depend on them.

IMPORTANT: Before you change anything, turn on AWS WAF logging so you can see what each rule matches. Start every rule in Count mode, confirm it doesn’t match legitimate traffic, then switch to Block.

Request body inspection limits The body inspection limit depends on the resource that the web ACL protects. On Application Load Balancer and AWS AppSync, the limit is a fixed 8 KB. On CloudFront, API Gateway, Amazon Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, the default is 16 KB, and you can raise it up to 64 KB through the web ACL AssociationConfig, as shown in the following example. AWS WAF treats any part of the body beyond the limit as oversize. Choose a limit that fits the rules you deploy, because a body size rule can only enforce a cap up to the inspected size.

aws wafv2 update-web-acl ... --association-config \ 'RequestBody={CLOUDFRONT={DefaultSizeInspectionLimit=KB_64}}'

Custom rule for CVE-2026-109619 (if you can’t use the managed rule group) Use this custom rule if you would prefer to use a custom rule instead of a managed rule group. It targets CVE-2026-109619 and blocks a request only when all three conditions in its AndStatement are true at once:

The method is exactly POST, matched on the HTTP method with no transformation.

A PHP session identifier is present (the nested OrStatement, so either sub-condition satisfies this leg):

PHPSESSID appears as a cookie key (exact match on the key, scanning all cookies), or

PHPSESSID appears anywhere in the request body (contains match).

The body contains PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that activates PHP’s session upload progress feature.

Pair the rule with session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on the server, which turns the feature off. The following rule has its action set to Count. Change it to Block after you confirm it doesn’t match legitimate traffic.

{ "Name": "PHP2Shell", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "POST", "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Cookies": { "MatchPattern": { "All": {} }, "MatchScope": "KEY", "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2Shell" } }

Block multipart requests when the application has no uploads

NOTE: This rule, in Block mode, breaks applications that require file uploads. If your application doesn’t require file uploads, blocking removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application for both CVEs at the edge.

AWS WAF inspects a single named header in full, with no 8 KB header limit, so matching the Content-Type header is reliable.

{ "Name": "Block-Multipart-FormData", "Priority": 1, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "SingleHeader": { "Name": "content-type" } }, "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS", "SearchString": "multipart/form-data", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "LOWERCASE" } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockMultipart" } }

Cap the request body size Capping body size reduces the out-of-memory condition behind CVE-2026-109618 and the stale state it can leave behind. It also covers request bodies larger than the inspection limit, which body-inspecting rules such as PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended evaluate only in part. If you use the Core rule set, its SizeRestrictions_BODY rule blocks bodies over 8 KB by default. Use the following custom rule when you need a different threshold or don’t use the Core rule set. It uses OversizeHandling: MATCH with a size constraint so that any body larger than the threshold is blocked, including bodies that exceed the inspection limit. To enforce a cap of N bytes, the web ACL body inspection limit must be at least N.

Note that you can’t cap the numeric Content-Length with a size constraint, because the constraint measures the length of the header value string, not the number it contains. If your application has legitimate large uploads, scope this rule to non-upload paths with an AndStatement on the URI path, or it will break those uploads.

{ "Name": "Block-Oversize-Body", "Priority": 2, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "SizeConstraintStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "MATCH" } }, "ComparisonOperator": "GT", "Size": 8192, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockOversizeBody" } }

NOTE: If a specific managed rule breaks legitimate traffic, override that rule to Count rather than disabling the whole group.

Rate-limit repeated attempts A rate-based rule on POST requests limits how many requests one IP address can send. That lowers the chance of triggering either vulnerability through volume. It also makes the stale-state path harder, because that path needs a producer request and a consumer request to land on the same worker. Set the limit from your normal per-IP POST rate; 100 requests per 60 seconds is a starting point. This rule complements a server setting of pm.max_requests=1, which recycles the worker on each request.

{ "Name": "RateLimit-Posts", "Priority": 3, "Action": { "Count": {} }, "Statement": { "RateBasedStatement": { "Limit": 100, "EvaluationWindowSec": 60, "AggregateKeyType": "IP", "ScopeDownStatement": { "ByteMatchStatement": { "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY", "SearchString": "POST", "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ] } } } }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellRateLimitPosts" } }

Server-side mitigations that complement AWS WAF

These host and runtime changes address the parts of CVE-2026-109619 that sit below the HTTP layer a WAF inspects, so they fall outside its scope by design. Apply them alongside the AWS WAF rules as the host and runtime layer of your defense.

Upgrade PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, and restart every PHP worker so the new runtime is in use. This is the only complete fix for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These releases don’t fix CVE-2026-115560; see the session.upload_progress.enabled bullet. For PHP 8.1 and earlier, see Fix end-of-life PHP versions.

Address CVE-2026-109618 at the PHP level. Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory, or application setting puts a finite limit back. Keep post_max_size low (8M where the application accepts no uploads, 32M where it does), and keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, not RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

Set fatal_error_backtraces=0 on PHP 8.5 and restart every worker. This disables the setting that stores crash-trace state across a request, one of the confirmed ways the vulnerability is triggered.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. This turns off the upload-tracking feature that’s the other confirmed trigger. Keep it off after you patch: it is also PHP’s mitigation for CVE-2026-115560, which the October 21 releases don’t fix.

Prefer php.ini, FPM pool, or server startup configuration over per-request INI overrides (settings applied per request through .htaccess, php_value, or FastCGI PHP_VALUE). Remove obsolete directives so they don’t raise diagnostic warnings.

Eliminate fatal errors and execution timeouts on attacker-reachable routes, including upload, import, error-page, shutdown, serialization, and extension paths.

Set pm.max_requests=1 if performance allows, so each worker process is recycled after one request, which breaks the link between the request that plants stale data and a later request that would reuse it.

Turn on error logging (log_errors=On, a working error_log, error_reporting=E_ALL) and review your Apache, FPM, or proxy logs for repeated warnings, deprecations, fatal errors, and timeouts on attacker-controlled routes. The absence of errors is not proof of safety.

Fix end-of-life PHP versions

PHP 8.1 and earlier no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Which option you have depends on your version and how you install PHP:

Use a vendor backport. Some Linux distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes for older branches. Check with your vendor.

Apply the PHP source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1. Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team published minimal source backports for these three branches, for people who build PHP from source or don’t have an LTS vendor. Rebuild PHP with the backport, deploy it, and restart every PHP worker. For details, see the PHP security advisory.

Upgrade to a supported release. This is the long-term fix. It’s also the only option for PHP 7.3 and earlier if your vendor doesn’t provide a backport.

A backport fixes these vulnerabilities, but the branch is still end of life and won’t get other security fixes. Treat a backport as a bridge to an upgrade, not a replacement for one. When you upgrade, target PHP 8.3 or later, because PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

For many applications, the upgrade takes code changes as well as a runtime change. Later PHP versions removed language features and extensions that older code often depends on. Plan the upgrade as follows:

Identify each application on PHP 8.1 or earlier, and the frameworks and Composer dependencies it uses.

Review the PHP migration guides for each version between your current release and the target. Update the code, dependencies, and framework versions to match.

Run your tests and static analysis against the target version before you deploy.

Deploy on a fixed release and restart every PHP worker.

One option for implementing the code changes is the AWS Transform PHP version upgrade transformation (AWS/php-version-upgrade, in early access). It upgrades applications from PHP 5.x, 7.x, or 8.0 through 8.4 to PHP 8.5, and it runs your existing tests and static analysis before and after the upgrade. For details, see AWS-managed transformations, or contact your AWS account team.

Until each workload runs a fixed release or a backport, keep the AWS WAF rules and server-side mitigations in this post in place. They reduce exposure, but they don’t fix the vulnerabilities.

Getting started

Complete the following steps to get started:

Inventory where PHP runs and which versions and server APIs (mod_php, FPM, FrankenPHP, LSAPI) are in use. Identify any public endpoint that accepts a request body.

Identify workloads on PHP 8.1 or earlier. Apply a vendor backport or the PHP source backport where one exists, and start the upgrade to a supported release, because it can take longer than a runtime patch. See Fix end-of-life PHP versions.

Check the web ACL in front of each PHP workload. If it uses the PHP application rule group at the default version, PHP2Shell_BODY and PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended are already active. If it pins a static version, change it to Version_2.4 or later, or remove the Version field to use the default version.

Add the PHP application rule group and the Core rule set where they’re missing. Then decide whether each application uses multipart uploads, which determines whether you can add the rule that blocks multipart requests.

Add the applicable custom rules in Count mode. Raise the body inspection limit on CloudFront or API Gateway if a rule needs it.

Watch the sampled requests and Amazon CloudWatch metrics for each rule. Confirm that legitimate uploads and large JSON POSTs aren’t matched.

Switch the rules to Block after the metrics are clean. Test the custom rules with a benign multipart/form-data POST, an oversized body, and a POST request that has a PHPSESSID cookie and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in the body. After you switch to Block, expect a 403 response and the matching rule metric.

In parallel, apply the PHP upgrade and the configuration mitigations. Remove or retain the AWS WAF rules as supporting controls after your fleet is patched.

Conclusion

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—are unauthenticated RCE vulnerabilities that reach PHP before your application code runs. AWS WAF gives you a way to help narrow the attack surface during the patch window. Turn on the PHP application managed rule group at the default version (or version 2.4 or later if you pin) and the Core rule set. Then add the custom controls that fit your application: block multipart requests where no uploads are expected, cap request body size, and rate-limit repeated attempts. These mitigating controls can help reduce exposure, but they don’t close the vulnerabilities. If you run PHP 8.1 or earlier, apply a backport where one is available and plan your upgrade to a supported release. If you run PHP 8.2 or later then upgrade PHP to a fixed release, apply the server configuration changes (including session.upload_progress.enabled=0, which also covers CVE-2026-115560 until PHP releases a fix), and treat AWS WAF as the edge layer that supports those fixes rather than the fix itself.

To learn more, see the PHP application managed rule group and the AWS Managed Rules changelog, managed rule group versioning, the web ACL body inspection limit, oversize request component handling, and the AWS re:Post article on handling oversize HTTP request bodies. For tuning and exceptions, see the AWS WAF best practices guide. For the vulnerability details, see the PHP advisories GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp, and the PHP session upload progress manual.

AWS thanks Wiz for reporting the PHP2Shell issues, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to AWS through coordinated disclosure ahead of their public release. Wiz shared its findings with AWS ahead of publicly disclosing. Using Wiz’s findings, AWS developed and tested AWS WAF managed rules that provide an additional layer of protection for customers who use PHP-based workloads.

#!/usr/bin/env python3 """PHP2Shell RCE chain for PHP 8.5.11 apache/mod_php. Usage: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --rce 'id>/var/www/html/proof.txt' Purpose and vulnerability mechanisms ==================================== This is a pure-HTTP, application-independent research exploit for an isolated lab. Its default endpoint is ``/index.php`` and is configurable with ``--path``. With no ``--rce`` it stops after reproducing the overlong ``Set-Cookie`` disclosure. With ``--rce [COMMAND]`` it composes two distinct PHP memory-safety mechanisms. Bare ``--rce`` runs the documented default and verifies ``/proof.txt``; a custom command is delivered without claiming that its execution was verified. 1. The A1/B1 disclosure is derived from 9bie's cross-request session-state chain. An upload-progress request reaches an OOM bailout before request state is safely reset; a later request in the *same mod_php child* consumes the stale ``PS(id)`` and encodes an attacker-forged ``zend_string`` into the session cookie. This is strongest-fit **CVE-2026-109619** behavior: request- owned session globals outlive their backing request heap. OOM is the producer, but the security boundary crossed by this stage is request lifetime. This is mechanism-based attribution, not a CNA reassignment of any individual public PoC. 2. The optional final sink is adapted from Cookiengineer's OOM RCE. Multipart amplification exhausts the stock 128 MiB heap while ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i()`` has counted but not initialized its final ``HashTable`` bucket. Same-request shutdown walks the incomplete bucket into a forged object, a libphp-only ``jump_fcontext`` ROP chain, and ``zif_system``. This is the incomplete-state/cleanup mechanism of **CVE-2026-109618**. Worker discovery, chunked transfer, prefork saturation, the full-pool scrub, and the clean holder rebind are delivery/affinity techniques, not additional CVEs. The scrub exists because the validated Apache environment can retain children already marked for graceful retirement when its IPv6 listener wakeup fails; without it, a second invocation may place A1 and B1 in different processes. The post-scrub repin is concurrent so VPN latency cannot recreate an idle-surplus window. Debugger mappings were used only to calibrate and independently verify the constants below; successful end-to-end runs derive their live bases from the HTTP cookie. Validated exact environment (2026-10-23) ======================================== This profile is intentionally build-specific. Recalibrate all offsets and heap geometry for any other binary, compiler flags, module set, architecture, or loader layout. * PHP 8.5.11 NTS, Zend Engine 4.5.11, source tag ``php-8.5.11``: annotated tag object ``597eb0b4e32cc8802e112fe13cc92fb5636a1781``; peeled source commit ``678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8``. * Official ``php-8.5.11.tar.xz`` SHA-256: ``d9be75c08e8c316f4c8f4194d8fbe1750a15f6a6d9d4e3fe72082abeeb800360``. * Source build flags: ``-O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fcf-protection=none``; Apache 2.4.66 (Ubuntu) ``mod_php``/prefork on x86-64; glibc 2.43 (Ubuntu ``2.43-2ubuntu2.4``); validation kernel ``Linux 7.0.0-38-generic``. * ``/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so`` SHA-256: ``ecd97e302e8cb3fd106c0541410256ad6597cb6410166beee0ab773ff4974b36``; GNU Build ID ``c01226a7f67b3226c1d2f81f4fc5041846914117``. * ASLR enabled (``kernel.randomize_va_space=2``), Apache defaults including ``StartServers=5`` and ``MaxRequestWorkers=150``, and unmodified upstream ``php.ini-production``: ``memory_limit=128M``, ``post_max_size=8M``, ``upload_max_filesize=2M``, ``max_file_uploads=20``, ``max_input_vars=1000``, ``max_input_nesting_level=64``, error display off, logging on, and session upload progress plus cleanup enabled. * Exact module offsets: ``zval_ptr_dtor=0x7ae960``, ``zif_system=0x598650``, ``jump_fcontext+0x2e=0x6362ae``, ``pop rdi; ret=0x280d8d``, ``pop rsi; ret=0x2cbe07``, and alignment ``ret=0x280d8e``. * Exact heap/layout constants: Zend main chunk ``libphp+0x3400000``; post-disclosure controlled block ``main+0x5c400``; stale-ID forge page ``0x1e3``; 402,500 duplicate multipart headers for the stock-128M sink. * The combined upstream fix used for source comparison is php-src commit ``506e87fa7dcdd306975e5b8f8265ee03527aacbf`` ("Avoid state corruption via bailout"), released in the patched 8.5.12/8.4.27/8.3.30/8.2.29 lines. Recalibrating a different build =============================== Never transplant the constants above based only on ``PHP_VERSION``. Preserve the candidate module first, record its identity, and do all debugger work in an isolated copy of the target environment. For example:: LIBPHP=/usr/lib/apache2/modules/libphp.so sha256sum "$LIBPHP" readelf -n "$LIBPHP" | grep 'Build ID' readelf -lW "$LIBPHP" # record executable PT_LOAD ranges nm -an "$LIBPHP" | grep -wE 'zval_ptr_dtor|zif_system|jump_fcontext' ``nm`` values are image-relative because this module is ET_DYN. The pivot is ``jump_fcontext+0x2e`` only after disassembly confirms the same instruction sequence. Find and inspect ROP gadgets rather than copying byte offsets:: ROPgadget --binary "$LIBPHP" --only 'pop|ret' | \ grep -E 'pop rdi ; ret$|pop rsi ; ret$|: ret$' objdump -d -M intel "$LIBPHP" | less Verify every chosen gadget lies in an executable ``PT_LOAD`` and inspect its surrounding instructions. If normal symbols are stripped, use the matching debug file/build ID with ``readelf -Ws`` or GDB; do not derive offsets from a different package that merely reports the same PHP version. To recalibrate the disclosure, run a fresh debug child with the same INI and modules, pause the selected rebound worker, map its client port to a PID with ``ss -tnp``, and attach GDB. A convenient driver form is:: python3 exploit.py --host TARGET --port 80 --path /index.php \ --pause-after-rebind 60 # Read new_port from the log on the target, then: ss -tnp sport = :80 dport = :NEW_PORT gdb -q -p CHILD_PID (gdb) break php_url_encode (gdb) continue (gdb) p/x ps_globals.id (gdb) p/x ((unsigned long)ps_globals.id & 0x1fffff) >> 12 (gdb) p ps_globals.send_cookie The second GDB expression is the ID page; use it as ``--forge-page``. Sweep the A1 query/burner/progress lengths and B1 ``G``/``X`` geometry until GDB shows OOM in ``php_url_encode()``, ``PS(send_cookie)=1``, and the B1 cookie contains a highly repeated pointer that resolves exactly to the new ``zval_ptr_dtor``. Confirm the derived module base against mappings only *after* the HTTP result; mappings must never be an exploit input. Measure the module-to-main-chunk delta in several fresh ASLR parent lifetimes. With symbols loaded in GDB, compute the module base from a known symbol and align the Zend heap pointer to its 2 MiB chunk:: set $libphp = (unsigned long)&zval_ptr_dtor - NEW_DTOR_OFFSET set $main = (unsigned long)alloc_globals.mm_heap & ~0x1fffffUL p/x $libphp p/x $main p/x $main - $libphp Accept the delta only if it repeats for independently started Apache parents and the leaked cookie contains pointers in the derived main-chunk bucket. Finally recalibrate the 109618 sink *after the complete A1/B1 history*, not on a virgin worker. Use ``--pause-before-rce``, attach the selected debug child, and break on ``zend_mm_safe_error``, ``_zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i``, and ``zend_array_destroy``, and identify the shutdown table with ``nNumUsed=46``. For this payload layout the controlled block is ``arData-0x200``; subtract the aligned main-chunk base to obtain ``--rce-block-offset``. Sweep ``--rce-headers`` around the OOM boundary until the failed allocation is the 80,000-byte key's 81,920-byte allocation and the incomplete bucket contains the forged object. Recheck the pivot, fake handlers, ROP registers, and entry to ``zif_system`` in GDB, then validate without a debugger using a fresh, unique proof name. Repeat under a new ASLR parent and run twice without an Apache restart before treating the profile as usable. Direct lineage and credits ========================== Credit belongs to the original researchers and repositories. This local composition, retuning, worker scrub, and validation do not replace their copyright or licensing terms. * **9bie**, ``php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp`` commit ``17e98ee81025cccfd94b4f9c9a17bf269c65ff75``: A1/B1 session-state OOM, forged-cookie disclosure geometry, worker occupancy, and the original ASLR-on chain. The local 8.5.11 port widens its overly narrow ``0x7f`` pointer floor and retunes the heap geometry. * **dinosn**, ``php-cve-2026-10961x-lab-poc`` commit ``b1e419912219691417c72b122f6eb410b938eee7``: instrumented CVE controls, Ninebie-class porting, stock-configuration experiments, offset/profile work, and worker-saturation research used as comparison and calibration guidance. * **Cookiengineer**, ``actual-php2shell`` commit ``1d5208ba5090cbbc56a091f6607996c3bbb21171``: the independently validated CVE-2026-109618 incomplete-bucket/object-destruction RCE sink. The local adapter amplifies it to 128 MiB and replaces libc-dependent ROP with gadgets and ``zif_system`` from this exact libphp image. Other reviewed/referenced public PoCs (not direct code lineage for this file) are credited to **Eness** (``php2shell-CVE-2026-109618-CVE-2026-109619-PoC``, ``df8b16fe69ab7218f496b5d88127253fc90ff92e``), **0x4148** (``CVE-2026-109618-php2shell-lab``, ``bc40fb2c96d5e92121e6bf8b996f7ba3ad057413``), **Ikow** (``php2shell-poc``, ``31519e6d8a84dee1df1262961ed1bebb65accadd``), **Murrez** (``php2shell``, ``e62535936b5fb1d013f8f52832df8c740c88e672``), and **Syrex1013** (``php2shell``, ``2b14725288c519380810fb057b214889eea9ee76``). Those revision identifiers are included here so this file retains its own provenance when copied outside the original research tree. Imagine buying a brand new hardware wallet for your cryptocurrency with the shrink-wrap still on… what could possibly be hiding inside? We break out a Geiger counter and a cat to find out.

Meanwhile, malicious ads are targeting journalists with zero-click attacks.

Plus, Origin’s Spencer Thompson reveals what AI agents are really getting up to on your employees’ laptops when nobody’s looking.

All this and more in episode 489 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Lianne Potter.

LIANNE POTTER

Which, if you know that book, you might get a sense what this film is going to be like. But Ken Russell's The Devils came out in 1971 and stars the lovely Vanessa Redgrave, and of course, the dashing Oliver Reed. It's a historical political horror dramatisation of demonic possession in a convent of nuns in 17th century France. Now, when it was released, it was actually, at the time, one of the most popular films in the British box office.

Unknown

Right.

LIANNE POTTER

It was also one of the most controversial because, hey —

GRAHAM CLULEY

Wasn't it a bit rude?

LIANNE POTTER

Well, I was gonna say, hey, it's the '70s. And if you go watch the trailer after this, the first 3 seconds, you'll be like, ah, I see why this might have had some controversy. So due to the graphic nature of the portrayal of violence and sex, obviously mixed in religion, it quickly got an X rating, and it was pretty much banned for ages and heavily cut to the extent that unless you actually saw it in 1971, you didn't actually see Ken Russell's film. Because anytime it did get released, and it got released very briefly in the early 2000s on home video, it's basically mostly out of print, unobtainium since then, but cut to shreds. But after years of campaigning, most of it done by Mark Kermode, the British film critic.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh, yes.

LIANNE POTTER

He's been campaigning really hard for this. And I got an email in my inbox saying, we're getting The Devils, we're getting it back. Because I've always wanted to see this film. Ah, so they're using the original negatives as well, so it's going to be beautiful. And it debuted in Cannes this year, and the people at Cannes have said that it was the best film of Cannes.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Wow.

LIANNE POTTER

None of the new stuff. This film was the best film of Cannes, and critics are saying this might be the best film of 2026, a film that's over 55 years old. And if you're into that kind of thing, it's currently got a Rotten Tomatoes rating of 97%, which is one of the highest. So I've been waiting all my life to see this film in its full uncut glory. Unknown

Yes.

LIANNE POTTER

My dream will not come true because I am not in the UK for any of these release dates.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh, for goodness' sake, Lianne.

LIANNE POTTER

So for my pick of the week, please, lovely listeners, please go buy a ticket to see The Devils so that cinemas think this is the hottest ticket in town. So they'll put more screenings on for me so I can finally live out my dream and experience one of the most controversial films of all time.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Are they not going to bring it out on DVD or something like that?

LIANNE POTTER

It's the same.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh, okay. No, it's not the same, I suppose. You want to see it in the full 35mm glory, don't you?

LIANNE POTTER

Yeah, I want to see the blood on the screen.

GRAHAM CLULEY

You do love your movies, don't you?

LIANNE POTTER

I do, I do. That would be a nice segue into Tight Film Wire.

GRAHAM CLULEY

That's her other podcast, folks. Okay, so The Devils by Ken Russell is your pick of the week.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, we've got time right now for a special featured interview. Thousands of companies are rolling out AI agents into the workplace. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor now running on employees' laptops, and they can use that person's logins, open their files, run commands, change things. Many companies have very little idea what those agents are actually doing. Well, I'm delighted to say that to help us untangle all of that today is Spencer Thompson, the CEO of Origin. Spencer, welcome to Smashing Security.

SPENCER THOMPSON

Thank you so much for having me.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Now, for listeners who've never watched one work, what does a coding agent like Claude Code or Codex or Cursor — what do they actually do on an employee's laptop?

SPENCER THOMPSON

So a coding agent like the ones you're referring to is something you install on a traditional Mac or Windows machine. You can install it via CLI if you're an engineer, or you can just download a desktop app. And what they actually do is translate human language into code, and use the resources on a computer to go and perform the actions. So for example, if you are using Claude Code and you say, I want to build a landing page, or I want to build a marketing website, it will go and create and edit files. It'll go write the code on your behalf, and it will go and produce what you ask for. And the kind of magic of this, and the reason that these things have exploded, is people don't have to know how to program to be able to create things that traditionally required code. You can just talk to it like you're speaking English. And this is kind of what's so remarkable about these tools.

GRAHAM CLULEY

This is the thing, isn't it? They're not just suggesting code, they're actually acting with that person's credentials. Which brings me to an obvious worry, which is, say a coding agent on an employee's laptop does something that nobody told it to do, like changing a file or running a command it wasn't asked to run — afterwards, what records does the company have to work out what happened and why?

SPENCER THOMPSON

In today's world, it's actually extremely difficult. There are two real reasons why. One is we don't really have the auditing or traceability built in tooling-wise to do this, which I'm sure we're going to talk about later. The second reason is probably the more important one — these things are incredibly complex. I think people probably dramatically underappreciate just how complicated AI agents are. When you type a prompt into a box and hit enter, a lot of people use AI like it's search, right? They go to ChatGPT.

Unknown

Yeah.

SPENCER THOMPSON

When something's actually going and doing work on your behalf, that's called an agentic workflow. It's an agent doing work. These agents will basically go and do whatever they can to accomplish the goal that you gave them. And what that means is that in some cases they'll split off into multiple agents. They'll go and call agent swarms to go and do work on your behalf. They'll share context between agents and pass things back and forth. And this is all happening in real time. So you imagine you have all these multi-threaded parallel things happening in real time and you have no idea — in some ways it literally feels like magic to people where they just press the button and things kind of emerge. If something did go wrong, it turns out it's really complicated and difficult to figure out what actually went wrong, considering the complexity of these things.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I think the best way to maybe understand that is through some real examples. And one of the things I was reading about is there's an Origin engineer who asked Codex and Claude Code to run a query or something. Is that right?

GRAHAM CLULEY

Can you explain a little bit more about what happened there?

SPENCER THOMPSON

Sure. So this is an internal story, so this is using our own data. We had an engineer that was trying to get access to some data to accomplish a task. And so he was using Codex, which is OpenAI's desktop app. He had asked Codex through a prompt to go and fetch some data in order to perform work. Codex said, I actually don't have permission. I think the engineer had gone to bed and literally just let it go. All these things run on what's called auto mode now, where you don't have to — you know how you used to have to hit 1 to accept all the different things over and over and over again? No one does that anymore. They just let it run and do whatever it wants. And so the engineer, I think, went to bed and what happened was Codex figured out that it could not get access to the data because it didn't have permissions, but it found out that Claude Code was running on the same machine. It decided to open Claude Code. Remember, no humans involved in any of this, right? So the agent decided to open Claude Code and it said, go get the data. Claude Code tried to get the data and said, I don't have permissions. And Codex said, no problem, I'm going to change your permissions. So I'm going to change it to what's called `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which is this thing where you basically just does whatever it wants. It changed the permissions. Claude Code then went again and tried, got access to the data, brought it back, and gave it to Codex, and mission accomplished. If I told you that a human did those things, you would lose your mind. But this happens every single day inside of organisations, and people have no idea.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Bonkers, isn't it? And there was a second story about something which happened on your own premises during a sales demo. Is that right?

SPENCER THOMPSON

This is my favourite story because it's happened to me. So we do this thing whenever we give demos, where we lock our demo environment so that nobody can push code while I'm giving a demo, which makes sense. It doesn't blow things up.

Unknown

Yeah.

SPENCER THOMPSON

So I'm giving this demo. I tell people on the team, can you please make sure it's locked? They say, yeah, no problem. 20 minutes into the demo, something goes wrong. And so I get around it and I do my thing. And then I get off the call and I say, hey guys, what the heck? Something happened. And they said, no, nothing happened. Like, what are you talking about? No one unlocked staging or demo to push code into. And I said, no, but something happened at minute, whatever it was, 21 of my demo.

Unknown

Right.

SPENCER THOMPSON

So we used our own product and we did a search and we said, hey, something happened around minute 21 of this. And what we uncovered was that the agent itself actually decided to go and unlock the demo environment in order to continue doing its work, even though the human being told it not to. And so we had to go through this whole trace to understand that actually it wasn't a human. I was ready to blame the team and blame a human being. It's just an agent acting on its own. Absolutely remarkable.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I mean, in some ways it's kind of cool. In other ways, it's horrifying that this sort of thing happens.

SPENCER THOMPSON

These are both relatively benign examples, as you can tell. They're kind of funny.

SPENCER THOMPSON

But you could imagine a slightly elevated version of this that could be very damaging. And so they're funny, but also they have implications that are quite significant.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, I also heard about this experiment you did. One of your researchers gave an AI model 200 of your own AI chats. So it's what people had typed in, and from that, it worked out some of your company's private rules.

SPENCER THOMPSON

Oh yeah. I mean, this is what these things are remarkably good at. I would argue that this is maybe a controversial thing to say, but I think people underappreciate just how much people share with AI and just how much work is done by your employees using AI. If you ever go into whatever AI you use, ChatGPT or Gemini or Claude, ask it to tell you about yourself. And I promise I'll get to your question. There's a bunch of fun proxies for this. If you ask it to say, what city am I most like and describe why, for what it's worth, the answer for me is London. There's a bunch of different ways you can get at this. These agents know an enormous amount about yourself. And so that's called working memory. And so you extend that out to an organisation, if you've got 10, 50, 100, 200 people, the agents actually probably know more about your organisational structure and the way that you do work than probably you do at this point. And so its ability to read through chats and understand the context of that is frankly trivial for these things. This is like the most basic of what they do. I just think people have no idea just the level of this right now.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So as we should all know by now, before you paste work into a chatbot or something like that, we really need to stop and think, although we all know that, we're not necessarily doing it. So let's talk about how Origin approaches all of this. So we've had antivirus for years, which checks your files. We've got EDR, which collects logs. Now AI agents are working inside companies as well. What is a trace and why does it matter more now?

SPENCER THOMPSON

So if you think about the first two examples of what you gave with antivirus and with EDR, antivirus tried to understand the context of a file when a file was being opened, whether it was malicious or benign, because attackers would smuggle evil things into those. In the case of EDR, they would try and ascertain logs from the machine, so operating system telemetry, and try to piece those things together to understand what was malicious. A trace to us is the new unit that you need to pay attention to in security, and the reason is we define the trace as anything that happens between a person or an agent hitting enter on a prompt box and typing something in, and when it completes. Now one important thing to note here is that I think people assume, again going back to my chat example, that they're used to typing something into a box, hitting enter, and getting results in like two seconds, right? Some of these agents will run for up to a year straight doing work.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Wow.

SPENCER THOMPSON

If you go and give these agents really hard, difficult tasks, they will just keep going and going and going. So the ability to actually understand all of the context that's contained within that work is what we define as a trace. And so that means the intentionality of what the person was trying to do. It means the cost of how much intelligence it's consuming. It means all the security risks. It means what files it's touching. You can imagine it goes on and on and on. All of the things that that agent is actually doing is what we consider a trace. And we think that every single organisation of the future is going to need to understand and capture their own traces in order to go and build their businesses.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So if Origin is recording all of that information, what agents are doing on workers' computers, an obvious thing for anyone who works in security, they're going to be thinking about how do you keep that data safe and private?

SPENCER THOMPSON

Yeah, this is a very complicated and important question. So the first thing I think to note is that people also underappreciate that they're already sending all of this IP and private information up to the models themselves. So if you're paying for an Anthropic licence or a Copilot licence, whatever it is, in most cases they don't have an intermediary between those things. And so they're just chucking all of their proprietary IP up into the models. This has become a very controversial topic — are these frontier companies trying to compete with organisations or not? As a business, our job is almost to be like an auditing and compliance tool for organisations where they can perform investigations if something, heaven forbid, does go wrong. We're not in the business of capturing or owning data. That is the company's data. This is like a tier 1A priority for us. And so there's a bunch of things that we do — we obviously have a whole bunch of role-based and access-based permissions in terms of who can access what. This isn't even about us — it's even within the organisation itself. This stuff is so sensitive and so proprietary, not everybody in the organisation should have access to this either. All that data sits on the company's side, not on our side. Obviously it's stored in whatever structure they want to store it into, whatever encryption they want to have on top of that. But I think one thing to note here is this is a brand new era. The ability to capture your own prompts and traces and store these things and structure these things and secure these things is kind of the Wild West right now. And so we try and take that unit super seriously, give all that data to the organisations themselves, tell them how to secure it, tell them how to structure it. And then they work with us to say, okay, now how do we use the tool again, if something goes wrong, to figure out what actually happened? And we try and do that in an automated way that lets the customer touch it without us being involved.

GRAHAM CLULEY

So practically speaking, if a company were to install Origin today, what do you think is the first thing that they're likely to see?

SPENCER THOMPSON

So there's 2 things that are, you know, theoretically obvious that I think are always surprises to people. The first thing is it's actually very difficult to get your own prompts out of these fron

articles.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot
articles.context: While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains...
articles.full_text:
Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.

Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:

An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.

The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.

For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:

For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.

Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17th.

Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.

How AWS helps protect customers

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.

Immediate recommended actions

Upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.

Consider blocking multi-part file uploads in PHP deployments that cannot be patched immediately, but determine how this would affect your application prior to deploying.

Look for POST requests with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads.

Review web server logs for suspicious activity.

Check for unexpected process execution or file modification on web application servers.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

Observed Date

The identified IP addresses include shared anonymization infrastructure and are not exclusive to this threat activity. Organizations should investigate any observations involving these addresses as opposed to blocking.

See how to use AWS Web Application Firewall to help reduce your exposure while you patch in our blog post Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

If you have questions, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.

CJ Moses

CJ Moses is the CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. In his role, CJ leads security engineering and operations across Amazon. His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

CJ holds degrees in Computer Science and Criminal Justice, and is an active SRO GT America GT2 race car driver.

articles.title: No time to PHP around.
articles.context: Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.
articles.full_text:
Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Weak certificates from an Indian authority spark a global security scramble. Investigators probe a U.S. consulting executive’s alleged ties to ShinyHunters. SafePay ransomware hits at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations. Researchers find troubling security biases in Chinese AI-generated code. A $10 million initiative bolsters cybersecurity for small U.S. utilities. An American pleads guilty to stealing from thousands of servicemembers and veterans. Leo Scott, Managing Director of DataTribe, is talking about their upcoming Cyber Innovation Conference and the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

Today is Wednesday October 21st 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

PHP vulnerabilities put millions of web sites at risk.

PHP is a widely used, open-source programming language that powers the behind-the-scenes functionality of websites. It runs on web servers, handling tasks like processing forms, managing user accounts, interacting with databases, and generating web pages. Popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla rely on PHP. Because it’s so widely used, a serious PHP vulnerability can potentially affect millions of websites.

Now, PHP administrators are bracing for two potentially critical vulnerabilities that could put millions of websites at risk. PHP maintainers have announced plans to release patches for two flaws, each carrying a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.

The warning follows leaked, but unverified, details of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, reportedly capable of executing code on servers running popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento.

Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.

One researcher estimates that 1.3 million internet-connected hosts may be affected.

Administrators are being urged to inventory their PHP applications, prepare backups, and arrange emergency maintenance windows. Patches are scheduled for release at 14:00 UTC, though maintainers warn they could arrive earlier if exploitation is detected.

Given PHP’s enormous footprint, the potential consequences extend across much of the web.

An Indian cert authority unlocks a global security headache.

Security teams worldwide are scrambling to contain a potentially massive Internet security problem after researchers discovered eight digital certificates with private keys so weak that attackers could use them to impersonate virtually any website.

The certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra. They’re intermediate certificates, meaning they can be used to issue other certificates that browsers and applications automatically trust.

Normally, cracking their encryption would be practically impossible. But these keys were astonishingly weak, containing as little as three to eight bits of entropy. One researcher described the situation as “bonkers.”

Major browsers and several applications have already blocked the certificates, and there’s currently no evidence they’ve been maliciously exploited. But cleaning up the broader Internet could take years.

Cryptography expert Filippo Valsorda compares the challenge to the 2014 Heartbleed vulnerability, warning that this recovery could be even more complicated. Linux systems, embedded devices, forgotten servers, and Internet of Things equipment may require individual updates.

The immediate concern involves attackers intercepting encrypted communications, particularly VPN connections. Exploitation requires positioning oneself between communicating parties, something that’s easier for attackers controlling local networks or possessing sophisticated surveillance capabilities.

Most modern browsers have implemented protections, although Microsoft’s Edge on Windows 10 reportedly remained vulnerable in some circumstances.

The incident exposes a fundamental weakness in Internet trust: even the strongest encryption depends on the security of the organizations issuing certificates.

And when one of those organizations gets the fundamentals spectacularly wrong, the cleanup becomes everybody’s problem.

Investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters.

Federal investigators examining the ShinyHunters hacking group are scrutinizing executives at two ransomware negotiation firms over their alleged relationships with the cybercriminals.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters’ extortion website, which pressured nearly 100 victims to pay ransoms.

Authorities have also arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky on extortion-related charges. Investigators reportedly uncovered communications linking him and other negotiators to ShinyHunters after Dutch police arrested a suspected group member and accessed his Signal messages.

The investigation raises troubling questions about conflicts of interest in the ransomware negotiation business. Some firms reportedly collect fees based on the size of ransom payments, creating financial incentives that may favor the criminals over their victims.

The allegations remain under investigation.

SafePay ransomware has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide.

The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since emerging in August 2024, according to a joint advisory from U.S., German, and British authorities.

SafePay has become one of 2026’s most active ransomware operations, targeting organizations across four continents.

The group gains access through stolen credentials, brute-force attacks, vulnerable VPNs, and exposed network devices. Once inside, attackers escalate privileges, move laterally using legitimate administrative tools, disable security software, and steal sensitive data before encrypting systems.

SafePay employs double extortion, demanding cryptocurrency payments in exchange for decryption tools and promises not to publish stolen information.

The group also reportedly calls victims directly to pressure them into paying.

Authorities are urging organizations to strengthen defenses against SafePay’s increasingly widespread operations.

New research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

The United States has banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, citing national security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security says DeepSeek’s China-based infrastructure could expose sensitive American data to Chinese authorities.

Beijing condemned the restrictions and warned of possible retaliation, adding another complication to already strained U.S.-China technology relations.

Meanwhile, new research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

Cybersecurity startup Hirundo tested Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder and found it produced significantly more vulnerable applications for American defense contractors than Chinese ones. Seventy percent of applications generated for U.S. contractors were exploitable, compared with 59 percent for Chinese contractors.

Applications built for a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group were also more likely to leak secrets.

Hirundo says the discrepancies disappeared after researchers modified the model to remove what they characterize as Chinese Communist Party political alignment.

The findings suggest that AI coding assistants may introduce security risks influenced by their training and underlying model behavior.

A $10 million initiative looks to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute are launching a $10 million initiative to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

The new nonprofit Community Cyber Resilience Foundation will initially provide free cybersecurity technology, hardware, deployment assistance, and training to as many as 500 water, wastewater, electric, and natural gas utilities.

The announcement follows a surge in cyberattacks affecting more than 100 American water systems across over a dozen states.

Eligible utilities must have annual revenues below $100 million, a threshold covering more than 50,000 organizations nationwide.

Participants will receive access to Dragos security technology, Accenture implementation support, and SANS operational technology training.

The initiative aims to address a growing cybersecurity divide between large infrastructure operators and smaller utilities struggling with limited budgets, aging equipment, and staffing shortages.

An American pleads guilty to an identity theft scheme targeting U.S. service members.

A 45-year-old American has pleaded guilty to orchestrating an identity theft scheme that targeted thousands of U.S. servicemembers and veterans.

Robert Wayne Boling Jr. operated from the Philippines, using stolen personal information to access victims’ bank accounts and steal money and veterans’ benefits between 2014 and 2019.

Prosecutors say Boling obtained sensitive records from a former U.S. Army medical records contractor stationed in South Korea.

The operation relied on dozens of money mules in the United States who received stolen funds and transferred portions of the proceeds to the Philippines.

Boling was deported to the United States and arrested in May. Two accomplices have already been sentenced, while two others remain fugitives.

Boling faces up to 40 years in prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering.

Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

A Brazilian electronics distributor is looking for nearly half a million dollars’ worth of missing graphics cards, and it’s taking its search to Instagram.

Oderço says two pallets of high-end Nvidia RTX 5090 GPUs arrived at São Paulo’s Guarulhos International Airport, then apparently vanished.

After getting nowhere with official inquiries, the company turned to social media, saying nothing like this has happened in its 38-year history.

The missing shipment is valued at roughly $470,000, although the company hasn’t disclosed exactly how many cards disappeared, or when.

The timing is particularly unfortunate. RTX 5090s are already in short supply, with retail prices reaching thousands of dollars per card.

Whether the shipment was stolen, misplaced, or swallowed by some bureaucratic black hole remains unclear.

For now, Oderço is hoping the internet can help locate its missing hardware.

Which is perhaps fitting, considering how many people have already been searching the internet for an RTX 5090.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music and sound design by Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.
