articles.context: TL;DR Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked
articles.full_text:
TL;DR

Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked.certs rejected the listed certificate encodings but accepted re-encoded versions that still validated in the tested configurations.

We reproduced the behavior with ECDSA- and RSA-signed intermediates associated with the eMudhra incident. Each re-encoded certificate had a different SHA-256 fingerprint.

The results apply to the JDK versions and trust-store configurations tested. Follow current vendor guidance and verify the protections in the runtimes and trust stores you deploy.

A certificate blocklist can reject a known-bad certificate and still miss another encoding of it.

We saw this while examining Java's response to the eMudhra certificate incident. The mitigation uses SHA-256 fingerprints to identify compromised intermediate certificates. But a certificate’s fingerprint is calculated from its exact encoded bytes.

During an AI-assisted review, Sonatype Research Labs asked Opus 5.5 whether Java's exact-fingerprint blocking could be bypassed. The AI model flagged that exact-byte matching might leave room for equivalent certificate encodings.

We confirmed the behavior for both ECDSA and RSA certificates: re-encoded intermediates had different SHA-256 fingerprints, yet still validated in our Java trust-store tests. This points to a limit in exact-fingerprint blocking: it can identify the certificate bytes it knows about without necessarily covering every equivalent encoding.

Here, we’ll explain how the re-encoding works, what the tests show, and what teams should check before relying on a certificate blocklist as their only mitigation.

How It Started: eMudhra Certificates Compromised

Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authority keys were compromised on October 20, 2026, allowing anyone who obtained a key to create certificates that could be trusted as part of a chain to a trusted root. Browser and platform vendors responded with blocks and trust-store changes.

This also prompted a Java mitigation: add the affected intermediates to blocked.certs. Our research began with a narrower question: does that fingerprint-based block reject every valid encoding of those certificates?

How Exact-Fingerprint Blocking Works

A certificate is a structured document: it contains information such as the subject, public key, issuer, validity period, and a digital signature. In Java, blocked.certs identifies certificates by their SHA-256 fingerprints. The fingerprint is calculated from the certificate's encoded bytes, so even a small change to those bytes produces a different fingerprint.

This makes fingerprint blocking precise, but the match depends on the exact encoding in the blocklist. If a certificate can be re-encoded and still pass signature validation, the new encoding may have a different fingerprint and may not match the listed entry. To test whether an alternate encoding could still validate in practice, we examined two signature formats: ECDSA and RSA.

Changing the Encoding Changes the Result

We tested two certificate chains from the eMudhra incident advisory: one with an ECDSA-signed intermediate and one with an RSA-signed intermediate. For each, the reproduction added the original intermediate's SHA-256 fingerprint to a copy of a JDK's blocked.certs file, changed the intermediate's encoding without its private key, then checked whether the chain still validated.

The two encoding changes were:

ECDSA: The script changes the signature value from s to n − s, another valid representation of the signature.

RSA: It removes the NULL parameter from the outer signature algorithm identifier. The signature over the certificate data remains unchanged.

Both tests produced the same result:Java rejected the original chain whose intermediate fingerprint was listed, but trusted the chain with the re-encoded intermediate, whose fingerprint was different. After the relevant roots were removed from the copied JDK’s trust store, both chains were rejected.

Verify the Mitigation in Your Runtime

Teams should verify certificate mitigations in the Java runtimes and trust stores they deploy. Removing the relevant roots rejected both chains in our tests, but it can also interrupt legitimate TLS connections. Before changing a trust store, identify dependent services, test their certificate chains, and monitor for TLS failures after deployment.

Follow current vendor guidance and document any exceptions. These results cover only the JDK versions and trust-store configurations we examined, so validate the controls separately for other runtimes and TLS paths in your environment.

articles.title: eMudhra CA Incident: Sonatype's Assessment and Guidance
articles.context: For self-managed deployments, install the applicable updated Docker image or patch release when available
articles.full_text:
Sonatype is responding to the industry-wide eMudhra certificate authority incident, which affects certificate trust stores used by certain Sonatype products and distributions. We are updating affected components. In the meantime, apply certificate trust-store updates provided by your operating-system, runtime, and application vendors.

What Happened

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) could be recovered because they were generated with insufficient randomness. Six affected intermediates were for TLS certificates and two were for code signing. Someone with an affected TLS key could create a certificate for a website or service, which could be accepted by clients that still trust the affected chain.

Browser and operating system vendors have taken steps to block the affected certificates. Other software may rely on separate or bundled certificate trust stores that need updates, so organizations should also check systems beyond browsers and operating systems.

Sonatype Impact

We are preparing updated Docker images and patch releases with current certificate trust data. The tables below list the impacted Sonatype products and their remediation status. Existing Docker images and bundled JVMs do not update automatically.

For self-managed deployments, install the applicable updated Docker image or patch release when available.

For self-hosted solutions:

Product

Impacted Versions

Remediation

Sonatype Nexus Repository

All versions released prior to October 21, 2026

In progress

Sonatype IQ Server (Lifecycle, SBOM Manager, Firewall, Developer)

208 and earlier

In progress

For cloud solutions:

Product

Impacted?

Remediation

Sonatype Nexus Repository

Yes

Complete

Sonatype IQ Server (Lifecycle, SBOM Manager, Firewall, Developer)

Yes

Complete

Sonatype Guide

Yes

Complete

Continue to check the Sonatype Help documentation for updates. Do not manually change a product’s bundled JVM trust store unless Sonatype provides instructions for that product.

What Customers Must Do

Customers should take the following steps as soon as possible:

Update browsers and operating systems promptly.

Update certificate trust stores and any software that bundles a trust store, including containers and applications.

If you manage systems that use eMudhra-issued certificates, contact your certificate provider to confirm whether your certificate chain is affected and whether replacement or another action is needed.

Do not bypass certificate validation warnings.

What's Next

We are reviewing certificate trust in Sonatype products and distributions and preparing updates where needed. As revised versions become available, we will post product-specific guidance in our security event and relevant product update channels.

The eMudhra certificate authority incident is tracked as CVE-2026-111943 in Go and related ecosystem projects. Organizations may also see related advisories, including CVE-2026-113470 for Amazon Linux packages and RHSB-2026-012 from Red Hat. These identifiers support tracking across affected software and trust stores; remediation may differ by product and environment.

For vulnerability details, visit Sonatype Guide's CVE-2026-111943 page. Sonatype Guide is free to subscribe to. For remediation, follow the applicable guidance from your operating system, runtime, and application vendors.

articles.title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI
articles.context: This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs
articles.full_text:
Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption.

In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation.

Note: As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments.

X.509 certificates for workload identity

If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes.

As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs. In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA). To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes.

Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services

Temporary access credentials

Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor.

To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session.

Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate

Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information.

Create a trust anchor.

Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload.

Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles.

Trust model

The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor. The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA.

Certificate attributes

Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation.

The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66:

IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation.

"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"

Note: An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere.

Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials

IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession. To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] }

As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI.

Plan for trust anchor placement

Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console.

Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI

See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle.

Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session.

Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials

Credential helper

To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0.

The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials:

$ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate /path/to/certificate \ --private-key /path/to/private-key \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again.

When you use update, credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). When using serve, no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint.

Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities

To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it.

It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode. See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture.

Best practices for private key storage

Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository.

Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere. With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere.

If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject, x509Issuer, and x509Serial, respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches:

If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this:

[ { "Key": "x509Subject", "Value": "CN=Subject" }, { "Key": "x509Issuer", "Value": "CN=Issuer" }, { "Key": "x509Serial", "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D" } ]

If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json, it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json.

The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following:

--cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632

Monitoring trust anchor certificates

Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity.

Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table:

Event

Channel

Threshold

Enabled

CA certificate expiry

CloudWatch, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Health

45 days before expiry

TRUE

End-entity certificate expiry

EventBridge and AWS Health

45 days before expiry

TRUE

The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation

Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline.

As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages.

Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment

Solution deployment

The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps:

Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires.

Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal.

Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA.

Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles.

Parameters for this deployment are shown in the following table:

Parameter

Required

Default

Description

TrustAnchorCertificateBody

Yes

—

PEM-encoded X.509 certificate of your CA (includes BEGIN and END markers)

WorkloadSubjectCN

No

WorkloadA

Subject CN from the workload certificate, used in trust policy conditions

WorkloadIssuerCN

No

MyCompany CA

Issuer CN from the CA certificate, used in trust policy conditions

WorkloadSANCN

No

WorkloadA

SAN CN from the workload certificate, provides additional identity assertion

SessionDurationSeconds

No

3600

Maximum session duration in seconds (900–43200)

NotificationEmail

No

(empty)

Email address for certificate expiry notifications. When provided, creates an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and an EventBridge rule

Important: The SessionDurationSeconds value must not exceed the IAM role’s MaxSessionDuration setting, which defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API.

If the workload’s subject CN (WorkloadSubjectCN) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN.

The template enforces three certificate attribute conditions in the IAM trust policy: issuer CN, subject CN, and SAN CN must all match the values configured as parameters. Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role.

Conclusion

In this post, we discussed how AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, empowered by X.509 certificates, introduces a dynamic and secure way to manage workload identities and issue temporary access credentials. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials.

The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements.

Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system.

As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security.

For additional deployment guidance, see Planning for your IAM Roles Anywhere deployment, which covers end-to-end deployment planning including network architecture, monitoring, and operational considerations.

If you have questions, you can start a new thread on AWS re:Post or reach out to AWS Support.

He has helped numerous organizations enhance their cloud operations through targeted optimizations, robust architectures and best-practice implementations.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Makes PHP Inventory and Patch Ownership Urgent
articles.context: As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet
articles.full_text:
Updated October 23, 2026: PHP disclosed a related follow-on issue, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unlikely remote code execution (RCE) vector under unusual session settings. PHP recommends disabling session.upload_progress.enabled until the next regular bugfix release. See our research and recommendation in Sonatype Guide for more details.

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is the name being used for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

PHP says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, with the highest risk in Apache configurations using mod_php. Fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Organizations should inventory PHP across their environments, prioritize internet-facing systems, monitor for suspicious activity, and apply the update through PHP or the relevant distribution or product vendor. If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

On October 23, 2026, PHP disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate follow-on RCE issue. Temporarily disable session.upload_progress.enabled as PHP recommends, then apply the complete PHP fix when available.

PHP2Shell Is Two Critical Flaws in the PHP Runtime

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP's internal request handling. Because PHP is used in websites, applications, and products, affected installations may be managed by different teams or supplied through different vendors.The urgent work is to find those systems, establish who owns each one, and verify that the fix reaches every deployment.

Sonatype's PHP2Shell Security Event tracks current guidance and response recommendations.

CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory handling: PHP may interrupt a request while internal data is only partly initialized, then handle that data incorrectly during cleanup.

CVE-2026-109619 involves a stale global state that can persist after its underlying memory has been freed.

PHP says CVE-2026-115560 can occur when an application configures session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, switches it to php at runtime before calling session_start(), and leaves session upload progress enabled. PHP had already listed disabling upload progress as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619. This setting does not cover every affected path, and that a PHP release containing the complete state-reset patch is the reliable remediation.

Under affected conditions, the flaws can allow a remote attacker to execute code without authentication.

Ilkka Turunen, Sonatype's Field CTO, puts the operational priority plainly: "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed."

The Hard Part Is Finding Every PHP Installation

Organizations may know that their public websites use PHP but have less visibility into internal portals, older services, appliances, or software that bundles its own runtime. Different teams may also install and maintain PHP through separate operating system distributions, hosting providers, or third-party vendors.

Turunen expects remediation to extend beyond visible websites and services. PHP is bundled into other products and remains in older environments, creating what he calls "a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch."

A complete response starts with an inventory that connects each runtime to an owner and a patch path. Teams should identify:

Which internet-facing and internal systems run PHP.

The PHP version and how it is supplied or maintained.

Which applications, containers, images, appliances, and products include a PHP runtime.

The business or service owner responsible for remediation.

Whether a fixed package is available from PHP, the operating system distributor, hosting provider, or another vendor.

Include systems that are easy to overlook: older applications with little traffic, test environments that remain reachable, and deployments maintained outside the central platform team. An incomplete inventory can make an organization believe remediation is finished while vulnerable installations remain online.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. PHP says some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported fixes, and it has also published source backports for selected older branches. Organizations using these versions should confirm the status with their distribution or vendor, or plan an upgrade to a supported release. Do not assume an upstream version number alone tells you whether a vendor-maintained package includes the fix.

Patch, Verify, and Monitor Across the Estate

PHP says updating to a fixed release is the only complete solution. Temporary controls can reduce exposure to specific attack paths, and a web application firewall can add protection for traffic routed through it. Cloudflare reported deploying protections and seeing attack traffic aimed at its customers, while urging users to patch.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, the UK National Cyber Security Centre advises organizations to consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated. If it must remain available, assign an owner and document interim protections and a reassessment date.

The discovery and response also highlight the role AI is playing in vulnerability research. The Wall Street Journal reported that Calif and Wiz researchers used AI tools during a PHP source-code audit, and that developers, researchers, and distributors coordinated on fixes after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure.

As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet."

What Organizations Should Do Now

PHP2Shell is a test of whether organizations can find, own, and update the software running across their environments. PHP has published fixes, but a release only reduces risk when the update reaches every affected runtime, including those inside products and services maintained by other vendors.

Organizations should:

Inventory systems running PHP, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Monitor internet-facing PHP systems for suspicious activity.

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or apply the relevant vendor backport. Include products and services that bundle PHP.

Check PHP, distribution, and third-party vendor advisories for updates, especially when running PHP 8.1 or older.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

For ongoing details and links to current advisories, see the official PHP security advisory.

Written by Sonatype Research Team

Sonatype's Research Team is focused on bringing real-time, in-depth intelligence and actionable information about open source and third party vulnerabilities to Sonatype customers.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: New PhaaS Platform Uses AI to Craft Phishing Lures and Mask Malicious Activity
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Abnormal AI noted that the AI Studio gives threat actors another way to prepare phishing content without writing every lure from scratch or relying exclusively on ready-made materials. They can instead request content tailored to different pretexts and audiences.

AI Studio is integrated into Athena StealthRoute's broader offering, which also combines domain and link management, a marketplace for campaign materials, visitor monitoring and cloaking controls.

Athena StealthRoute still relies on external infrastructure for credential and token harvesting, but much of the preparation and delivery workflow can be managed through a single console, the researchers noted.

Five of the six offerings in the AI Studio focus on the creation of phishing lures and related materials. However, the sixth option extends to decoy content intended to conceal the phishing attempts. The White Page option produces structured, benign-looking content that could be used as a cover when Athena StealthRoute's cloaking layer directs scanners and other unwanted visitors away from malicious destinations.

How to Detect and Defend Against Athena StealthRoute

Abnormal AI said that for defenders, the platform’s combination of cloaking and customizable content reinforces the limitations of relying on individual messages or link inspections to detect phishing attempts.

“Security scanners may encounter benign content where intended victims would reach malicious destinations, while variations in lure copy can make exact wording less useful for linking-related attacks,” the researchers said in their analysis.

Shared backend infrastructure, matching operator-console code and recognizable link structures offer additional signals for identifying Athena StealthRoute-associated activity even as individual domains and lures change.

Finally, because credential and token harvesting occur through separate downstream services, investigations must also account for the particular theft mechanism involved.

articles.title: Symantec Uncovers AI Agent Hijacking Models for Autonomous Cyber-Attacks
articles.context: Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order...
articles.full_text:
A new AI agent developed to run a full cyber-attack without human intervention has been uncovered by security researchers.

The agent was designed to use hijacked AI models to autonomously run up to 100,000 malicious actions without human approval, including scanning for targets, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, deploying cryptocurrency miners and reinfecting compromised systems.

Researchers from the Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the malicious agent using an AI honeypot – a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order to attract and study attacks against AI infrastructure.

They captured the agent's full instruction set in the summer of 2026, revealing how it was designed to operate autonomously, although the honeypot did not execute the attacker's tools. They described it in more details in a report published on October 21.

AI Honeypot Exposes LLMjacking

The AI honeypot recorded over 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of unique addresses between its setup and the publication of the report.

Upon analyzing this activity, Symantec researchers discovered that the agent searches for exposed endpoints linked to large language models (LLMs), including self-hosted models, AI gateways and model context protocol (MCP) servers, to use their computing power without paying for it. This technique is sometimes called ‘LLMjacking.’

“Running a model always costs someone money, either in processing time for a self-hosted model or in per-token fees for a commercial one. By routing its work through a stranger's endpoint or a stolen key, the operators shift that cost onto the victim,” Symantec researchers noted.

With this technique, the attackers also gain anonymity and avoid potential account bans the AI model provider would issue for abuse.

The captured instructions included about 74 tools for internet-wide reconnaissance, exploiting common web frameworks, stealing databases, harvesting credentials and managing botnets.

Notably, the attackers used layered instructions designed to override commercial AI models' safety controls, disguising credential theft as legitimate development work.

A separate request also contained an obfuscated script designed to install Monero-mining software, conceal its presence and erase logs.

Self-Directed AI Agent Lowers Barrier to Cybercrime

While Symantec researchers said none of the techniques used by the attackers in this campaign are novel, their combination into a single, self-directed agent lowers the skill required for other attackers to run a broad exploitation campaign.

“An operator can hand the model a goal and let it work,” they added.

They concluded that the activity “marks a shift in how attackers are using AI,” explaining that operators have embedded AI into offensive tools rather than trying to trick public chatbots into misbehaving.

They described the model as “a reasoning engine that plans and drives the attack,” while the tool’s own modules carry out scanning, exploitation and mining against separate victims.

articles.title: Ransomware Attacks Rise as Rival Gangs Vie For Market Supremacy
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Almost 3000 ransomware attacks took place between July and September 2026 and the figure marked a significant increase when compared with the same period last year.

According to an analysis by Nord Security, the 2894 ransomware attacks which took place during the quarter represents a 50% increase when compared with the same period last year.

It also represents a slight increase when compared with the previous quarter of this year, as the July to September period saw an 8.6% rise in ransomware attacks when compared with April to June.

Published on October 21, the Nord Security report suggested that the significant rise in ransomware activity is a result of the impact of law enforcement takedowns on ransomware groups.

Researchers suggested that the action against the likes of Lockbit, BlackCat and RansomHub helped to reduce ransomware activity during 2025.

“Now, the market is stabilizing, and the numbers we see today are merely the first stepping stone in ransomware’s new era,” said Vakaris Noreika, VP of product research and development at Nord Security.

Rival Ransomware Gangs Drive Attacks

During the reporting period, the two most prolific ransomware groups were The Gentlemen and Qilin. Of those ransomware incidents which could be attributed, The Gentlemen accounted for 383 ransomware attacks, while Qilin was not far behind with 363 recorded attacks.

The third most active ransomware group during the period was Inc Ransom, which accounted for 110 attacks. Other groups which showed significant activity during the quarter with almost 100 ransomware attacks each include Krybit, Akira, Deadlock and Clop Leaks.

But it is The Gentlemen and Qilin which remain by far the most active ransomware gangs. The two threat groups have traded places as the most common perpetrator of ransomware attacks throughout 2026. The Nord Security research suggested that a rivalry between the two groups is pushing them both on to develop new attack techniques for claiming more victims.

“Based on underground forum activity we observed, The Gentlemen's founder appears to have previously run one of Qilin's top affiliate crews before a dispute over an unpaid cut, which he took to an underground forum and lost,” said Mantas Sabeckis, senior threat intelligence researcher at Nord Security.

“His answer was to start a new group and lure his former colleagues away with a 90% payout, well above the usual 70% to 80%. This quarter, the breakaway The Gentlemen group edged past Qilin by 20 attacks.”

Read More: Why Ransomware Remains One of Cybersecurity’s Most Persistent and Costly Threats

One of the techniques which has been deployed by both groups to remove the encryption element of the ransomware attacks. Rather than encrypting the data and holding it hostage that way, the attackers simply steal sensitive data from their victim and threaten to publish it unless they receive a ransom payment.

“Stealing data is faster and simpler, so one group can hit many victims at once with far less effort. This shift is likely a big part of why attack volumes keep climbing,” said Sabeckis. “But that doesn’t mean encryption is going away,” he added.

While ransomware groups continue to adapt and evolve, researchers noted that when it comes to the initial entry point for attacks, they have remained broadly the same. These include attackers exploiting compromised passwords, a lack of multi-factor authentication, on accounts and unpatched security vulnerabilities.

“The names on the most prolific ransomware group list regularly change, but the way they get in doesn’t,” said Noreika. “What happens once attackers are inside may be shifting, but closing those familiar openings still removes a large share of the risk.”

articles.title: Critical security issue affecting PHP
articles.context: Prioritise internet-facing systems first and then internal systems
articles.full_text:
The NCSC recommends following vendor best practice advice in the mitigation of vulnerabilities. The NCSC highly encourages organisations to follow these priority actions:

Identify systems running PHP across your infrastructure, prioritising internet-facing systems. As all versions may be affected, do not limit discovery to outdated PHP versions; identify PHP installations generally and assess their exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Update to the latest version of PHP and continue to monitor for future updates. Prioritise internet-facing systems first and then internal systems.

If you are unable to update to a version with the security update applied, the PHP Foundation have provided temporary mitigations.

If you are unable to apply the temporary mitigations, or applying them would take too long, you should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

If you are unable to update or disable the system immediately then you should assess the system for any evidence of compromise prior to your upgrade or mitigation and look for backdoors installed by an attacker. If you are not confident in your ability to do this yourselves then you can get assistance from an NCSC-assured Cyber Incident Response provider.

Continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP. NCSC-NL have published an inventory list of software products with a PHP dependency potentially affected by the vulnerabilities. Apply relevant updates as they become available.

articles.title: Sizing the PHP exposure window for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with VirusTotal
articles.context: On October 20, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, fixing two critical vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4
articles.full_text:
On October 20, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, fixing two critical vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). Hours before the release, technical details leaked publicly. They point to the session.upload_progress feature, which has been part of PHP since 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. The community quickly converged on an interim mitigation: set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini.

That leaves defenders with two questions: how big is the exposed surface, and where should they start? We used Internet Scanning in VirusTotal to answer both.

Note: Official details, affected versions and fixed versions are published by the PHP project with the release. The figures below describe the Internet-facing PHP footprint, not confirmed vulnerable hosts.

Most PHP servers don't say they are PHP

VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP (port_service_cpe:php), about 3.8 million of them with at least one port open today. Only around 1.1 million of those announce a version in an HTTP header such as X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3.35.

In other words, roughly four out of five PHP servers hide their version (expose_php = Off, stripped headers, reverse proxies). VirusTotal still identifies them as PHP through other signals: the application on top (WordPress, Laravel, Nextcloud...), PHPSESSID cookies and framework-specific headers. If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it.

The version picture: the long tail of end-of-life PHP

Among the servers that do disclose their version, the split is stark:

~272K run a supported branch (8.2 to 8.5), the only branches that receive security fixes from the PHP project.

~758K run an end-of-life branch between 5.4 and 8.1. These branches have session.upload_progress enabled by default and no longer receive security fixes. PHP 7.4 alone accounts for ~187K IPs and PHP 5.4 for ~119K.

~88K run PHP 5.2 or 5.3, which predate session.upload_progress.

Being up to date doesn't buy much time either: about 85K IPs run the exact releases published on September 24 (8.3.35, 8.2.34, 8.4.26 and 8.5.11), the latest available before this fix.

What runs on top, and where

Apache (~2.9M) and nginx (~1.48M) are the web servers most often seen on PHP hosts, followed by LiteSpeed (~90K). On the application side, WordPress dominates with ~538K IPs, followed by Laravel (~141K) and Nextcloud (~107K). Webmail (Roundcube) and database admin panels (phpMyAdmin) add another ~25K high-value targets.

The geography is concentrated: the United States accounts for ~920K PHP hosts with at least one open port, and a handful of cloud and hosting providers (AWS, DigitalOcean, Alibaba, OVHcloud, Hetzner) concentrate a large share. That concentration is good news for remediation: a few providers that push a configuration change or a WAF rule can cover a lot of ground.

Going beyond the web port

PHP rarely travels alone. ~394K PHP hosts also have port 22 open (SSH by default), ~233K port 3306 (MySQL) and ~68K port 3389 (RDP). Those co-exposed services are useful for something else: identifying the exact build behind the web server.

The leaked material references LiteSpeed lsphp82 8.2.34 builds for Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04, and notes that HTTP headers alone don't tell those builds apart. The OpenSSH package on port 22 does. With the bracket syntax, every condition is pinned to its port:

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/8.2.34" port_service_version[22]:"9.6p1 Ubuntu"

Of the ~3.5K IPs whose banners show both LiteSpeed and PHP 8.2.34, about 500 also have port 22 open. Across all PHP 8.2.34 hosts, the OpenSSH package on port 22 matches Ubuntu 24.04 on 269 IPs, Ubuntu 22.04 on 112 and Debian 12 on 65. For a defender, that is the difference between "patch everything" and "these are the machines that match the leaked target profile, patch them first". Keep in mind that port 22 reveals the host operating system: PHP may still run inside a container built on a different base image.

Adversaries run PHP too

The exposed surface also includes attacker infrastructure. Around 5.7K PHP hosts with at least one open port have five or more detections in VirusTotal, 729 of them disclosing PHP 8.x. One of them is an old acquaintance: the NOX Stealer panel (rebranded as BOMBAY) on 5.175.221[.]206:8443, which we profiled in our Internet Scanning post, runs nginx 1.24.0 with PHP/8.3.33.

What the VirusTotal corpus saw

The leak left traces across VirusTotal. The archive referenced in the write-up was first submitted at 02:29 UTC on October 21, less than 15 minutes after the first submission of the write-up URL. By the time of writing, 21 crowdsourced reports covering the vulnerabilities had been ingested as collections. Following entity:collection collection_type:report "CVE-2026-109618" is the fastest way to keep up with new reporting as it appears.

What to do now

Patch. Upgrade to the fixed release of your branch (8.2, 8.3, 8.4 or 8.5) as soon as it is available on php.net or through your distribution.

Plan the EOL migration. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive security fixes. If you are on 5.4 to 8.1, upgrade the branch or check whether your distribution or vendor ships a backport.

Disable upload progress until you patch. Set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini (or the pool configuration) and reload PHP-FPM, Apache or LSAPI. It only breaks upload progress bars that rely on the feature. Community analysis suggests it may not cover every vector, so treat it as a stopgap, not a fix.

Filter multipart at the edge. Where an application doesn't need file uploads, block or inspect multipart/form-data requests before they reach PHP. Cloudflare shipped emergency rules to its Managed and Free rulesets on October 21, and its CTO stated that they cover known payloads, while stressing that only updating PHP fully protects a site.

Make sure the WAF can't be bypassed. Edge rules only help if the origin is not directly reachable. Search your own ranges in VirusTotal (for example, entity:ip port_service_cpe:php asn:<your ASN>) to find origins that expose PHP directly to the Internet.

Don't rely on hiding the version. expose_php = Off hides the header, not the vulnerability.

Queries used in this post

Query

What it finds

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php

All IPs where VirusTotal fingerprinted PHP on any port

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_status:open

PHP hosts with at least one port currently open

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/"

PHP hosts that disclose their version in an HTTP header

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/7.4."

PHP hosts on a given branch (repeat for each branch from 5.2 to 8.5)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/8.3.35"

PHP hosts on the latest release before the fix (repeat for 8.2.34, 8.4.26 and 8.5.11)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_service_cpe:nginx

PHP hosts by web server (also "apache:http_server", lighttpd, internet_information_services)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"LiteSpeed"

PHP hosts by Server header (also openresty, Caddy)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_service_cpe:wordpress

PHP hosts by application (also laravel, nextcloud, drupal, joomla, roundcube, phpmyadmin...)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_status:open country:US

PHP hosts with an open port, by country

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_status:open asn:16509

PHP hosts with an open port, by hosting provider ASN

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php open_port:22

PHP hosts with another port open (also 3306, 3389, 445, 8443, 8000)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"LiteSpeed" port_banner:"PHP/8.2.34"

Hosts whose banners show both LiteSpeed and PHP 8.2.34, the profile referenced in the leak

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_banner:"PHP/8.2.34" port_service_version[22]:"9.6p1 Ubuntu"

PHP 8.2.34 hosts whose OpenSSH package on port 22 is Ubuntu 24.04's (use 8.9p1 Ubuntu for Ubuntu 22.04 and deb12 for Debian 12)

entity:ip port_service_cpe:php port_status:open positives:5+

PHP hosts with an open port and five or more detections

entity:collection collection_type:report "CVE-2026-109618"

Crowdsourced reports about the vulnerabilities

Note: All counts in this post were taken on October 21, 2026. For large result sets VirusTotal returns estimated totals that vary between runs, so we report the median of seven runs, rounded. Port modifiers without a port in brackets match per IP, not per port: port_service_cpe:php port_status:open means PHP was fingerprinted on the IP and at least one of its ports is open.

References

PHP, Supported Versions and Unsupported Branches

PHP, Downloads and PHP 8 ChangeLog
