articles.full_text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Its modes and the flags that matter: Build the package locally only, performing no network access at all: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --build-only --out demonstration.pkg Refuse a filename that would break the hand-off. The tool rejects any name containing a space or a path separator before it builds anything, because SubProgram_Start splits its argument string on spaces before execvp, so an extra token would change what /bin/mv is asked to do: --filename "payload.pkg" accepted --filename "pay load.pkg" rejected by the tool itself Build the negative control, for an operator who owns the hardware to confirm that the success path really is gated by the product string and by nothing else: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --control --build-only --out control.pkg Build the account-database variant as a local file, which is never sent unless --send is also given: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --passwd-mode --passwd-entry "marker:*:0:0:INERT-DEMONSTRATION-ENTRY:/root:/bin/sh" Deliver the built package to a management listener the operator owns and is authorised in writing to test, over HTTP or HTTPS, with optional HTTP Basic credentials: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 80 --user <user> --password <pass> python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 443 --https --user <user> --password <pass> The default payload is deliberately non-destructive: pre touches one marker file and writes the executing uid into a second, post touches a third, and the inner archive writes a single marker entry under the root of the filesystem. Nothing is deleted, encrypted or modified beyond those markers. The tool also prints the sha256 of what it built, so an operator can record the digest of a package before installing it, which is the one detection control that works after the fact. The script's own documentation carries a warning that applies to every reader of this submission: the network half of this chain was never exercised against an appliance, and running it against hardware you do not own or hold written authorisation to test will reboot and reimage that device, because a successful install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. PoC location in the public repository: product/prosoft-technology/rlx-ifh24e-v2244/unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce/exploit/prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish Full analysis, including the sink and source inventories with offsets, the end-to-end data flow marked at the line between measurement and inference, the verification transcripts, the negative control, the authentication boundary and its limits, the detection notes, the remediation set and the derivation of every one of the six CVSS readings: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce ProSoft Technology, Inc. was notified unconditionally through the mailbox its own website publishes for reporting a potential vulnerability, under a Security Assurance heading on its Quality and Environment page, with a copy to the North America technical-support address published on its Regional Technical Support page. The research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested, nothing is withheld pending a reply and nothing is asked in return. No report was filed with any third party and no national coordination body was involved. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

articles.title: PHP2Shell - Critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): detection, analysis, and remediation
articles.context: What happened On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

PHP disclosed two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. We independently reproduced them and confirmed that application-level authentication can't block an attack: PHP processes the malicious request before any application code runs.

AWS reported PHP2Shell exploitation attempts in the wild as early as October 17, 2026, four days before public disclosure and the release of patches.

Only patching fixes these vulnerabilities. Mitigations circulating in the community, such as setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in the PHP configuration file, don't fully protect you.

Successful command execution doesn’t necessarily crash the worker. Memory disclosure, including the PHPSESSID technique, can provide addresses needed for exploitation.

To investigate, look for large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors during request initialization, and unexpected shell processes.

Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both have a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2. PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 contain the fixes. Older PHP branches are also affected. Although PHP 8.1 and earlier are outside normal upstream support, the PHP security team provided source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Users of older branches should check their vendor’s security advisory for patched packages or upgrade to a supported version.

Before the public disclosure, our team built exploits for the vulnerabilities so we could analyze them and develop detections. Our reproduction triggers the out-of-memory corruption described in CVE-2026-109618 on PHP 8.5.11 with an unauthenticated HTTP POST request. The request never reaches the target application's code. Instead, PHP runs the attacker's command while it cleans up the failed request. Any PHP script exposes the vulnerable path, even one that only prints a response.

The two flaws affect different stages of the request life cycle:

CVE-2026-109618: After a memory allocation fails, PHP leaves invalid data behind for its cleanup routine to process.

CVE-2026-109619: A PHP worker can reuse stale state from a previous request.

Our detailed walkthrough primarily covers CVE-2026-109618, although we will discuss CVE-2026-109619 as well.

How to know if you're affected

Any PHP runtime that serves HTTP requests is in scope. PHP's release announcement warns that all web deployments are affected, including Apache modules, PHP FastCGI Process Manager (PHP-FPM), php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

When you build your inventory, include containers and applications that bundle their own PHP interpreter. Don't rely solely on the command-line PHP installation: it can use a different version or configuration than the runtime that serves your web application.

Fixed versions

The advisories for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 list the same fixed versions for each supported branch:

PHP branch

Affected releases

First fixed release

8.2

Before 8.2.35

8.2.35

8.3

Before 8.3.36

8.3.36

8.4

Before 8.4.27

8.4.27

8.5

Before 8.5.12

8.5.12

Remediation steps

For each deployment:

Record the PHP version, the package or image source, the owner, and the update process.

Apply the upstream or distributor update. If you use a vendor package, check the vendor's advisory, because vendors sometimes backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

Rebuild and redeploy affected container images.

Restart or replace every worker that still runs the old runtime.

PHP 8.1 and older

PHP 8.1 and older are outside the PHP project's normal support window. To address this vulnerability, PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, but expect slower fixes for these branches as vendors have more work to do in order to validate the fix. If you run those older branches, check whether your vendor covers it or move to a supported PHP branch.

If you can't patch immediately

Restrict public access to exposed applications. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, CERT-EU recommends isolating internet-facing applications. Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

PHP's temporary mitigation guidance also describes measures for each vulnerability:

CVE-2026-109618: Enforce memory_limit=-1 at the administrator level, and pair it with request limits at the frontend and memory limits on the container. Limit the size of decoded request bodies, including requests without a usable Content-Length header. Don't substitute process limits such as RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, because they can trigger the allocation failures this vulnerability depends on. Even with these measures, allocation failures can still happen, and an attacker who exhausts system memory can destabilize the host.

CVE-2026-109619: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. Apply both settings in configuration that loads before PHP parses the request, then restart every worker. Remove any per-request settings that generate early diagnostics. Hiding the errors doesn't prevent access to stale state.

These measures reduce your exposure while you update, but none of them fully fixes the vulnerabilities. Patching is the only complete fix.

How the vulnerabilities work

Both vulnerabilities follow the same pattern: a fatal error interrupts PHP partway through an operation, and PHP later treats the incomplete state as valid.

CVE-2026-109618: Interrupted initialization after memory exhaustion

PHP converts form submissions into the $_POST array. Internally, PHP stores the array's keys and values in a hash table, in entries called buckets. Before application code reads a submitted field, PHP allocates memory for the field name, creates any nested arrays, and inserts the values into those hash tables.

The flaw appears when an insertion stops halfway through. In the version we tested, _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i() increments the hash table's entry counters before it allocates a copy of the new key. Here is the relevant sequence in PHP's source:

idx = ht->nNumUsed++; ht->nNumOfElements++; p = ht->arData + idx; p->key = key = zend_string_init(str, len, GC_FLAGS(ht) & IS_ARRAY_PERSISTENT);

If the key allocation exceeds memory_limit, PHP raises a fatal error and abandons the insertion. At that point, the counters already include the new bucket, but PHP never initialized the bucket's key or value.

PHP still cleans up the failed request. When it destroys the array, it visits every counted bucket and interprets its contents as PHP values. The unfinished bucket holds bytes left over from an earlier allocation. An attacker who controls those leftover bytes controls what the cleanup code does next, up to running a shell command.

This hash table bug is one instance of the broader flaw that PHP's CVE-2026-109618 advisory describes: a memory error abandons an operation while the internal state is incomplete, and cleanup then treats that state as valid. Multiple public PoCs have demonstrated other code paths with the same flaw, so don't build defenses around the specifics of the hash table exploit.

CVE-2026-109619: Stale state crosses request boundaries

A PHP worker handles many requests over its lifetime. Some worker-wide fields point to memory that belongs to a single request. If PHP frees that memory without clearing the fields, a later request can follow a stale pointer into freed memory. This class of bug is called a use-after-free.

According to the PHP advisory, stale state appears in two ways: a fatal error interrupts PHP while it resets state, or a late shutdown diagnostic recreates state after cleanup. The advisory confirms two exploitable cases:

Fatal-error backtraces (PHP 8.5 only): Fatal-error reporting keeps backtrace state after shutdown. A configuration diagnostic in a later request reads that state before PHP initializes it. PHP confirmed that this case leads to command execution on mod_php.

Upload processing: After a fatal error, upload processing can leave session or decoder state behind. A later upload reads that state before normal initialization. PHP confirmed command execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM. On PHP-FPM, the attack also needs the application to perform a suitable operation after startup succeeds.

The upload case matters because of session upload progress, which tracks uploads before the target script runs. PHP enables this feature by default, and it runs even if the application never calls session_start().

To exploit CVE-2026-109619, an attacker's requests must reach the same worker. A larger worker pool lowers the success rate of each attempt, but it doesn't remove the flaw.

Exploitation walkthrough for CVE-2026-109618

Our reproduction runs PHP 8.5.11, built from commit 678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8, on Debian 12 (ARM64). It uses Apache's prefork worker model with mod_php, and sets memory_limit=16M, post_max_size=64M, and automatic POST parsing. To make allocations and failures easier to observe, our lab runs a single worker, disables OPcache, and shows errors in responses. The exploit ends by calling glibc's system().

The exploit works in three stages: reach the interrupted insertion, fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data, and turn request cleanup into a system() call.

Stage 1: Reach the interrupted insertion

The request carries three form fields:

=<binary value>&a=1&<very long field name>[x]=1

Each field plays a role:

The empty-name field prepares memory for reuse.

The a=1 field makes PHP allocate hash table storage.

The oversized name field triggers the incomplete insertion.

The array syntax tells PHP to create a nested array. In the version we tested, that path reaches a string-key insertion helper that allocates the key after it updates the hash table's counters. A plain field name takes a different path that uses an already-created key that is not vulnerable.

PHP's filter extension registers the submitted variable in an internal array and then in $_POST. We size the field name so that PHP's first key allocation succeeds and the second exceeds memory_limit. The failed insertion leaves an incomplete bucket in $_POST, which PHP destroys during request shutdown.

The failure happens during request initialization. Nothing in the target script can impact or defend against the exploit (authentication, filtering…).

Stage 2: Fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data

The attacker needs the unfinished bucket to hold useful bytes, not random leftovers. Our reproduction arranges those bytes through heap grooming: a sequence of allocations and frees that steers PHP into reusing a chosen block of memory.

In this build, a small hash table uses a 320-byte allocation. The binary value in the empty-name field is 276 bytes, and once PHP adds a string header and terminator, its allocation lands in the same 320-byte size class.

PHP copies that value while it processes the field, then frees the copies because the field name is empty. The a=1 field that follows makes the hash tables reuse the freed memory, so most of the binary content survives past the first valid bucket. When the oversized field triggers the fatal error, PHP has counted the second bucket but not initialized it, so PHP reads its contents from the stale bytes the attacker planted. The payload shapes those bytes to resemble a PHP value that points to a fake array.

Stage 3: Turn array cleanup into a function call

PHP arrays hold a destructor callback, the function PHP calls to clean up each element when it deletes the array. The attacker sets the expected location of this callback to the address of system() and points the array's element at a command string.

During shutdown, PHP follows the stale value into the fake array and calls the supplied callback with the supplied element. In our lab, the call becomes system(<command>). The attacker controls the callback address and its pointer argument, allowing the cleanup routine to call system() with a command string.

Here is the full sequence:

Request initialization fails → Request shutdown destroys $_POST → PHP interprets the unfinished bucket as an array → PHP destroys the fake array → The destructor callback invokes system(command)

Our system-call trace records a shell running the command, and the process tree shows its children under an Apache worker. The command runs with the worker's privileges, which are www-data in our lab.

Our refined exploit returns HTTP 200 with the memory-exhaustion error in the response body, and finishes in 3.10 seconds. Process snapshots show the same Apache worker still running during and after the command. A successful HTTP status doesn't mean a request was harmless, and the exploit doesn't need to crash a worker. The process trace is stronger evidence of execution than the response delay alone.

Exploit requirements and limitations

An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses. Neither constraint prevents exploitation, and reports of active attacks are already circulating.

Request and memory limits

The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit. When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table.

PHP's default memory limits are vulnerable. Setting memory_limit=-1 blocks the known exploitation path, but don't treat it as a long-term fix: if the underlying allocation still fails, an attacker may still reach remote code execution.

Address discovery is a separate requirement

To turn the cleanup bug into command execution, the attacker needs valid memory addresses for the fake data structures and for the function they want to call, such as system(). Address space layout randomization (ASLR) randomizes those addresses, so guessing them can take repeated requests and crash workers.

A memory leak removes much of that guesswork. Wiz describes using the PHPSESSID cookie to leak process memory back to the attacker. If the leaked bytes include pointers that stay valid in the target worker, the attacker can use them to make the exploit more reliable.

Public reports of exploitation

As of October 21, we have multiple reports of active exploitation in the wild. We’re also aware of broad untargeted scanning going on.

How the patch addresses both flaws

The PHP security patch changes how memory exhaustion interrupts execution. A soft limit now defers the error until PHP reaches a safe point, which lets an in-progress operation finish initializing its data. If memory use crosses a higher hard limit, PHP terminates the worker at once with _exit(137) instead of running normal cleanup over a potentially invalid state.

The patch also resets request-owned global state before anything can reuse it. During shutdown, PHP clears error and exception state, and it initializes serialization and session state before early request processing can reach it.

The hash-table insertion still updates its counters before it allocates the key, even in PHP 8.5.12. The fix changes the surrounding error handling instead, so an allocation failure no longer leaves the halfway-initialized entry for ordinary cleanup to process.

The fix looks complete for the known exploit, but we consider the underlying pattern risky. Updating metadata before allocating the memory it describes leaves the door open to similar bugs. If an attacker finds another way to interrupt initialization so that the surrounding metadata still counts unallocated memory as valid (for example, an array that records a size of 2 when an allocation failure leaves only one item), the same class of flaw can return.

The patch suggests the PHP team knows about the pattern but judged the refactor to remove it too large to finish before the fix shipped. We expect more of these bugs to surface as researchers find exploitable instances of the pattern, and backporting each one may not stay sustainable. It’s also likely that instances of this pattern unique to older versions of PHP will be found and left unpatched.

How to detect exploitation

Look for signals at three layers: the incoming HTTP request, the PHP error log, and the processes that web workers spawn. No single signal is conclusive on its own, so correlate them. A successful exploit doesn't necessarily crash the worker or return an error.

Suspicious form submissions

While there are a number of ways to trigger the vulnerability, each of them relies on delivering attacker-controlled data through PHP's request parser, which runs before the target script. For detection, look for unusual field names, encodings, and transport behavior alongside request size. Start from what your application's legitimate submissions contain and flag departures from that baseline.

Based on an analysis of multiple public PoCs, the majority begin with a similar multipart form upload. An abbreviated request looks like this:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----XYZ ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" aabb00cc ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" pwn ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="a.txt" Content-Type: application/octet-stream ------XYZ ...hundreds more parts, or one multi-megabyte fill field... ------XYZ--

These field names are useful indicators when an application doesn't normally use them. They can also appear in legitimate submissions: PHP documents the upload-progress field in browser forms, and its transparent session handling can add session identifiers to forms. Investigate unexpected use of these fields, especially alongside the structural anomalies below.

The requests create memory pressure in different ways. Some public tools append fill fields of 100 MB or more. Others use deeply nested, machine-generated names, such as files[R00001][a][a][a], repeated across hundreds of parts. Public examples fit roughly 900 parts into less than 1 MB. PHP's allocations while parsing these fields can greatly exceed the size of the body on the wire, so body size alone is a weak signal. Also monitor parts per request, brackets per field name, and nesting depth.

Inspect upload filenames for PHP tags or serialized-object fragments, such as <?php or |O:. These chains can stage payloads in filenames because PHP stores the filename in the session record.

Another path to the vulnerable function can be reached through large application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST requests whose body carries a single field name of many megabytes (3-60 MB, depending on the memory_limit of the target), along with a binary value containing raw null bytes and control characters.

Two other traffic patterns can support these chains. Uploads that declare a large Content-Length and then trickle or never finish can keep a session record alive for the exploit. On deployments with multiple workers, a burst of connections that become slow or silent while other requests proceed normally can indicate an attempt to occupy every worker but one. This helps an attacker send both requests in a state-reuse chain to the same process.

Also inspect response headers. A Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID= header containing an unusually long, percent-encoded value or binary content outside the application's expected session-ID format can indicate the memory-disclosure stage returning heap contents. It can follow an otherwise unremarkable request. Compare the value against the application's normal format: valid PHP session IDs aren't limited to hexadecimal characters.

Configure your web application firewall (WAF) or reverse proxy around these behaviors, and verify what its inspection engine actually sees. A rule can't inspect bytes the engine truncates, fields its parser discards, parts it never enumerates, or bodies it handles differently because they arrived chunked.

Memory exhaustion errors

Our exploit attempt generated this fatal error in the PHP error log:

PHP Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 16777216 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 3500032 bytes) in Unknown on line 0

The Unknown on line 0 location means PHP failed during request initialization, before any script started running. Correlate these errors with oversized POST requests, upstream connection resets, and worker crashes. Memory exhaustion alone doesn't prove an attack, because legitimate workloads can also exhaust memory.

When the exploit guesses a memory address incorrectly, the Apache worker crashes with a segmentation fault. In our lab, the Apache error log recorded this message:

AH00052: child pid ... exit signal Segmentation fault (11)

Also treat a short burst of these errors as a possible setup event, prior to the actual exploit payload being sent. Because modern versions of these chains recover addresses without crashing workers and can leave a persistent include active after a single successful fire, a complete attack can produce as few as two to four memory exhaustion errors and then go quiet. A handful of these errors on one PHP worker in a short window (especially paired with any of the request indicators above) deserves investigation even if nothing crashes afterward.

Unexpected shell processes

A web worker that spawns a shell is the most direct evidence of successful exploitation. In our capture, an Apache worker spawned a shell, which then launched the attacker's commands:

apache2 (www-data) └── sh -c <reverse-shell command> └── bash [outbound connection to c2.example:443]

Investigate any shell that a web worker launches, especially when it coincides with the request or error log signals above. If your application runs external commands on purpose, build a baseline of expected activity so you can spot deviations.

Don't make your detection depend on our demonstration's command names, a specific HTTP status, or a worker crash. In our refined exploit, the request returns HTTP 200, and the same Apache worker keeps running after it executes the command.

Signals for CVE-2026-109619

For CVE-2026-109619, review early configuration warnings, shutdown diagnostics, fatal errors, and execution timeouts on routes that attackers can reach. These events can point to the state-retention paths that PHP's advisory describes.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Workload Protection has out-of-the-box coverage for PHP applications executing a shell. This detection will catch exploits of those vulnerabilities. You can check for suspicious activity using this query. Review uncommon or unusual command lines.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes detections that can help identify PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and associated command execution:

Shell spawned by web server or PHP process detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or PHP processes using process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

PHP2Shell session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or upstream crash on nginx uses nginx error logs to correlate PHP memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or upstream worker crashes on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell PHP-FPM session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or FPM worker segfault on the same host and service uses PHP error logs and PHP-FPM master logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or PHP-FPM worker segmentation faults on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell memory exhaustion with worker crash or session decode failure on an Apache host uses Apache and PHP error logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or worker crashes on the same host.

Datadog Cloud Vulnerability Management can help identify PHP vulnerability findings on supported hosts and container images. Its package scanning support covers official operating system packages; self-compiled runtimes such as our lab build need separate inventory checks. PHP application dependencies managed through Composer are also distinct from the interpreter itself.

Conclusion

Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. If you run PHP, update to a fixed release or your vendor’s patched package as soon as possible. Rebuild affected container images and restart or replace workers so they’re running the updated code. Configuration changes can block some attack paths, but patching is the only complete fix.

articles.title: LiteLLM supply chain compromise: What you need to know
articles.context: 0, latest, main-latest, main-stable What happened According to LiteLLM’s analysis of the incident, attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers' accounts...
articles.full_text:
On October 21, 2026, attackers published a malicious release of litellm, a popular Python proxy library for LLM providers with about 23 million weekly downloads. The malicious release, version 1.107.0, was available on PyPI and in LiteLLM's official Docker images for approximately two hours before being removed. It installed a credential stealer that runs whenever Python starts and also contained a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT) backdoor. The infostealer payload targets cloud, developer, AI-tool, browser and LiteLLM proxy credentials.

This marks the second supply chain compromise of LiteLLM in 2026, with the earlier incident (affecting versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8) being linked to TeamPCP activity by Datadog Security Research. No connection between the two compromises has been established at time of writing.

Package name

Platform

Affected releases

litellm

PyPI

1.107.0

litellm

GHCR, Docker Hub

Tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, main-stable

What happened

According to LiteLLM’s analysis of the incident, attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers' accounts to launch LiteLLM’s private release workflow. At time of writing, it was not yet clear how the affected credentials were initially compromised.

The three stolen credentials were used to launch, approve and subsequently delete evidence of an unauthorized run of the legitimate build pipeline against a malicious fork, Berri-AI/litellm, whose name differs from the legitimate BerriAI/litellm fork by one hyphen. The similarity of the malicious fork’s name to the real project seems intended to evade casual detection by a human reviewer. The resulting wheels and images were published through LiteLLM's normal release channels and with seemingly legitimate build provenance that faithfully recorded the malicious fork as the source.

Timeline

Time (UTC)

Event

11:39

Malicious release 1.107.0 published to PyPI

13:20

PyPI quarantines affected version 1.107.0

13:53

Affected Docker images removed

Payload analysis

The release adds three files to the victim Python installation’s site-packages directory:

cook.pth

cook.py

sitecustomize.py

Python runs .pth files and sitecustomize.py automatically every time the interpreter starts. Any Python process in the environment runs the malware, even if LiteLLM is never imported.

Credential stealer (cook.py): Collects secrets and sends them, encrypted with AES-256 and RSA-4096, to the lookalike domain www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck.

Backdoor (sitecustomize.py): Every hour, checks a certain file hosted on a fixed GitHub repository (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt, now removed) for a domain, then downloads and runs Python code from it. That file only ever held test values, so no second stage payload was observed in the wild.

Deleting the litellm package directory does not remove these files. Running the environment's own python or pip triggers the malware again. Instead, the dropped payload files must be manually removed.

Data exfiltration

Cloud: AWS, GCP and Azure credentials, including from instance metadata; Kubernetes, Docker, Vault and Terraform secrets

Developer: SSH, GPG and TLS keys, Git, npm and PyPI tokens, .env files, shell history

AI: LLM provider API keys, and sessions for Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot and other AI coding tools

Browsers: saved passwords and cookies

LiteLLM proxy: If a database is configured, it queries the tables where the proxy stores upstream provider credentials.

What to do if you are affected

Manually remove the malicious cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py from the site-packages directory.

Remove all code and data associated with the malicious litellm==1.107.0 release.

Revert to litellm==1.106.2, the latest safe version of the package.

From a clean machine, immediately rotate all affected credentials.

Audit relevant logs for use of exposed credentials during the exposure window.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Code Security customers can rely on the Security Research Feed to easily identify if your environment is affected by this compromise. Use Code Security to easily identify affected hosts, containers or build environments.

Final thoughts

In this case, stolen developer tokens were used to point a trusted release pipeline at the wrong source. In order to ensure the validity of build provenance, it is essential to put in place adequate controls on which branches are eligible for building. Maintainers should lock release workflows to approved repositories and treat developer CLI tokens as the high-value secrets that they are.
