Sovereign Private Cloud Tech Community blog

The post Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice appeared first on The Official Microsoft Blog.

articles.title: 181: Ricky
articles.context: Alright, so they somehow discovered your IP and then they attacked your IP, and that was enough to knock you offline and lose the game. He discovers a whole world of ddossers and booters and punters and griefers who use malware to attack other players in the game to make them lose so you can win.
articles.full_text: JACK: I think that when I was a kid I was a good liar. Don't ask me where it stemmed from; probably because I was always getting in trouble, and that — I learned that if I was a good enough liar that I could sometimes lie my way out of trouble. But I was reading this post on Reddit the other day, and so many memories came back to me. [Music] There was this post. Some dad was complaining about his son being a ding-dong. He’s like, my son, who’s fifteen, wanted to get some ice cream, so we gave him a few bucks and sent him to the store. It happened to be a buy-one-get-one-free sale, and we all knew that, too. So, he went, he bought some ice cream on his own, and he came back with just one tub of ice cream. The knucklehead didn't get the free one. He just paid full price for a single tub of ice cream. The store clerk even told him, hey, there’s a sale. You know you can get a second one free. But my boy just said, well, I only want one, and refused the second one. His dad on Reddit was all miffed about how his son could be so daft and ignore free ice cream. He even said, I know that as soon as the boy finishes his ice cream he’s gonna want another, so why didn't he just get two? He knows that we all love ice cream, so why didn't he get one for his mom or his dad? Why did he get just one ice cream and not the second free one? It was free ice cream. This Reddit post blew up. Everyone was piling on about how dumb this kid was, saying stuff like, in my state you could disown your child for far less. Someone else said this is probably because the kid doesn't go buy things very often and doesn't know how to handle money very well or deals. The dad wrote in the post that he was starting to feel worried because people were saying some real mean things about his son, but nobody was saying what I was thinking. I feel like I know exactly what happened here, because I was in the exact same situation when I was a teenager. If you would have talked to my mom then, she would have been just like this worried dad. She would have told you that I’m the worst shopper in the world. Because I’m almost certain that what happened is he ate a full tub of ice cream on his way home and then lied and said he only bought one. I mean, it all adds up. The boy was hungry for ice cream before even leaving the house. There’s no way he’s gonna wait until he gets home to have his first bite. Grab a spoon at the store and start on your way home. Also imagine the look on his face when the clerk told him, you know you can get a second one for free, right? No way. Dang, this is my lucky day. So, he must have gotten two, and on his way home he started thinking, shoot, mom and dad don't know I got two. They only gave me enough money to get one. So, if I come back with one, they won't even know there was a second. So, if I could scarf this second tub down before I even get home, it would be glorious. No rules. No regulations. No speed bumps. Just eat a whole tub of ice cream as fast as I can. Challenge accepted. I’ll tell you, teenage boys can crush a whole tub of ice cream real easy. They can make a dozen cookies vanish instantly. They have the power to inhale desserts like no one else can. The real tell here is that the dad on the Reddit post even said, we would never let him eat a whole tub in one sitting. That’s the thing; the boy had an unregulated container of ice cream, and he thought no one is gonna know. No one is gonna stop him from eating all this in one sitting. Let’s do it. So, he saw this as his big stroke of luck and secretly slurped it down, and then tried to lie about it when he got home by saying, no, no, I only got one, I swear. But little did he know the entirety of Reddit was gonna believe that lie. He’s probably okay with them calling him names and stuff, because being misunderstood isn't as bad as being caught in your lies. But I see you, kid. I’ve been in that same situation before. I’ve been in that situation many times. Two cupcakes I bought at the bake sale became one. Two chocolate bars from the fundraiser became one. Yeah, of course two ice creams from the ice cream truck became one, too. My mom could never understand why I would sometimes pay extra for a single cupcake. Intro: [Intro music] These are true stories from the dark side of the internet. I’m Jack Rhysider. This is Darknet Diaries. JACK: Imagine going to a high school baseball game in New Port Richey, which is near Tampa, Florida. You see one kid, a center-fielder, who’s absolutely tearing it up out there. He’s catching anything that comes his way. He’s got an arm like a rocket. He could hit anything thrown at him. He’s built like a tank but runs like the wind, and it just looks like he’s in a different league than the rest of those high school players on the baseball field. He’s eating them up. It’s like all the other kids are in a lower league than him, and they're just all playing in slow motion compared to him. You can tell this kid is the star. That is Ricky Handschumacher. RICKY: So, I played center field, but initially I was really known for getting on base, getting hits, and then stealing bases. JACK: Stealing bases. RICKY: Yeah. JACK: Is this where all this starts? This is where all of it starts, stealing bases. RICKY: Coincidentally, yeah. JACK: But were computers interesting to you or not at all? RICKY: No, I was your gamer, you know? Like I said, I wasn't your average nerdy kinda guy who’s antisocial or anything. I was always out with my friends. I was always out on the streets playing sports; you know, football, baseball, basketball with all my friends. Like, Friday night and Saturday night I would go roller skating. So, I was never like, home, but I did have a passion for actual gaming. JACK: Alright. So, let’s talk about gaming. What was your game of choice? RICKY: Halo 3 was my primary game. JACK: [Halo sound effects] In 2010, fifteen-year-old Ricky is up late on a school night. His headphones are tuned in as he plays Halo 3 on his Xbox that’s humming away. Ricky doesn't want to disturb his mom, who’s sleeping in the other room. On his glowing TV screen he’s trying to escape what looks like a war zone. He’s destroying all the other players in the game. RICKY: I was good. So, I was always playing MLG and Team Slayer and all the ranked playlists against the pros and everything like that. Then, of course, naturally once you get to that level, there’s people who cheat on there and stuff. I was a high rank, but cheaters get high ranks, too, naturally because they're just cheating. So, it kept happening to me. JACK: People would go up against Ricky and see that they can't beat him, so they decided to cheat to win. He didn't know what was happening at first. RICKY: [Music] My screen would just go blank and then they would stop the attack when the game was over, which means they’d just win by default pretty much, 'cause we can't even move. Or if they hit you hard enough, we actually — our whole internet would just go out. I was with my mom. She’s like, why is the internet out? So, I had to play stupid. Like, I have no idea. I don't know what's happening. JACK: I’ve been in a similar situation. I remember the days when we had a family computer, and I downloaded a lot of random stuff and installed it on there. Time and time again I would break our computer. I didn't want to get in trouble, so I would try real hard to fix it before anyone noticed. Because of that, I got really good at detecting viruses and malware and fixing it on the family PC. But for Ricky, he was on an Xbox, and when he’d play, the internet would go down in the whole house, and it was just him and his mom living there. His dad left the picture a long time ago. But strangely, this pattern kept happening. When he would play Halo 3 against other players, the internet would go out. The game would disconnect, and then when he would finally get back on, he would see that he lost the match. RICKY: It happened to me again and again, and I’m like, alright. Then through the — through word of mouth I was like, oh, if they're DDoSing us, like, okay. So, I’m like, what the hell is that? I was getting DDoSed attacked over and over and over. JACK: Alright, so they somehow discovered your IP and then they attacked your IP, and that was enough to knock you offline and lose the game. RICKY: Yeah, and that’s kinda where it all started. Then curiosity — I was like, okay, how are they doing this? JACK: Remember, outside of gaming Ricky is not a computer guy. He doesn't know what's going on at all. So, he just turns his Xbox off and jumps on the family PC and starts trying to look for answers. RICKY: I started browsing some forums, and I was like, okay, it’s called DDoSing attacks. So, I started looking that up. I’m like, hm, okay, seems pretty simple. There’s a bunch of different kind of booters, like an IRC booter or a putty booter. You could just — or you could just go online to a website and use that booter, which was less powerful, but it would get the job done. I browsed the forums, found out what it was, downloaded the programs myself. So, I was like, okay, well, if they do it to me, I’m gonna do it back to them. JACK: Eventually he gets to the bottom of it. He discovers a whole world of ddossers and booters and punters and griefers who use malware to attack other players in the game to make them lose so you can win. Ricky decided, well, hey, I want to win, too. I want to try. [Music] So, he downloads a tool. He says it was Cain & Abel, and decides to try to use it to attack other players. He started a match, ran the tool to disconnect another player, then bingo; he sees they just freeze in the game and he can easily kill them, and he wins the match with almost zero effort. This was way easier than actually playing by the rules. RICKY: That’s kinda where I got introduced to that world. JACK: Yeah, so, at that point you were really competitive in baseball, you were really competitive at Halo. I just wonder, 'cause you had a sense of pride, of ranking up on your own and being competitive in sports — and where’d that sense of pride go with cheating? RICKY: I don't know. I just let it take over, pretty much. I was like, well, this is easier than actually trying. JACK: Yeah, but that’s not the sportsmanlike way. RICKY: Yeah. I don't know. I just took the easy way out and got the advantage. JACK: Were you cheating in sports at all? RICKY: No, that I was not cheating in. JACK: Alright. RICKY: No, I was naturally good. JACK: Yeah, well, you were naturally good at Halo, too. You were in MLG and all that stuff. RICKY: Yeah, I don't know. JACK: [Music] Who would have thought that this innocent little victory in Halo was going to lead Ricky down a long, dark path? From here he tried more Halo cheats like wall glitches, fast travel, reduced hitbox, and more. It was fun. This was the new game, not to compete competitively in Halo but to get around the game rules, to do things you weren’t supposed to, to be a god in the game. It gave him a sense of power. He saw the game differently now. He stopped seeing things on the screen like Covenant and Banshees and Needlers. Now he was seeing bytes and ones and zeros and the data behind the game, which gave him an incredible win streak. You know, the type of win streaks that you just have to take a screenshot of so that you can look back at from time to time and remember those matches. But even being a god can get boring after a while, and even though he was the winner in those screenshots of his, he would notice that some people seemed to be even cooler than him somehow. Everyone looks the same in Halo 3. You're all the same player, Master Chief. It’s just, everyone has a slightly different color. But there’s one thing that sets you apart from everyone else; your name, specifically your gamer tag. These are special, actually. They're unique. There’s only one person in the world with your gamer tag. Some people call themselves cool things like Shadow Strike or Nebula Storm or Blade of Odin. Fine, but what about that guy that’s just called Wolf? How did he get that name, Wolf? Now that is fricking cool. Well, it’s a first-come, first-serve kinda thing. So, Wolf must have made that gamer tag a long time ago when Xbox Live was first created, when gamer tags first came out. They probably made the name in the first week or maybe even the first day, which makes them OG, right? But instead of Original Gangster, they're the Original Gamer. Ricky wanted one of these short, cool gamer tags. That would really set him apart from the other normies playing in the game by the rules, but all the good names were taken. So, he goes back online into the hack forums and starts looking to see, how do you get one of these? It turns out there’s a whole underground marketplace of people buying and selling Xbox gamer tags, but not in the way you might think. See, a typical online market, you'll see people selling things that they've had for a long time or something that they've bought from someone else or something they made, right? But this was an underground hack forums marketplace. It operates differently. These gamer tags weren't ones that sellers were sitting on for a while. No, all these gamer tags were stolen. When Ricky found that out, he leaned in closer. How do you steal a gamer tag? Well, there are a few ways, but the easiest is just to get someone’s password and username and take over their account, change their password, and now that gamer tag is yours. But getting someone’s password is tricky. Maybe an easier way to get it is to trick Microsoft that you're the actual owner of the account and you just lost the password. Ricky saw some people were doing that and decided to try it himself. RICKY: There was a company called Zune, which is like Microsoft’s music app. Come to find out what you could do is you could call up Zune, and then halfway through the call you just tell them your gamer tag that you're targeting, and you say, okay, hey, my gamer tag is Jack. Then you just stop the conversation and be like, I have to go real fast. I’ll call back. JACK: Before hanging up, though, Zune support would give Ricky a reference number for the case that they were working on. Then he’d hang up and call a different number, Xbox Support this time, and they'd say, how can I help you? He’d say, oh, well, I was on a call but it dropped. I have a reference number if you want to pull the case details up. RICKY: Correct, yeah. You'd just simply say, yo, I have a reference number. Can you pull up my case? Then they would just give you the information right then and there. There was no questions asked. JACK: Ah, interesting. So, it’s almost like a bypass of a verbal authentication. So, then when you call Xbox and say, I have this reference number, then they give you the e-mail address. RICKY: Yep. JACK: Then you say, can you reset the password? RICKY: You would just be like, hey, yeah, here's my reference number — validate the account. Then just — you could just literally ask them, hey, what's the e-mail that I have on file? They'd read it off to you. JACK: How do you get the password? RICKY: Okay, so, back in the day AOL and Yahoo were your most popular domains. What's their proof of ownership of an account of an e-mail, was literally — AOL was like, your billing zip code would verify the account, and then they would be able to reset the password for you. Same with Yahoo. I think Yahoo was security questions, which back in the day was terrible because people would — a lot of the time chicken or pizza would be your favorite food that people would put, and stuff like that. So, they were pretty much takeable. JACK: See, that’s the thing that amazes me about these teenage hackers. They see the world differently than us, kinda like when you see motorcycles lane-splitting. You ever get stuck on a highway and there’s bumper-to-bumper traffic and you're standing still in your car and a motorcycle comes zooming past you right in-between the two lanes? You're like, come on. The motorcycle rider just looks back at you like you're a chump waiting in traffic like everyone else. They just whiz by like there’s no cars on the highway at all. These teenage hackers find ways through roadblocks that we just don't see. Like, you don't need someone’s password when the password reset question is ‘What's your favorite food?’ and you put ‘pizza’ up there. Now anyone can just write ‘pizza’ on there, and they could reset your password for you. It’s like, come on, what's the point of passwords if they could just be bypassed so easy? Sometimes it would try to validate it’s really you by asking for your zip code. Well, if you have their e-mail address, it’s not too hard to use some kind of people search tool online to look to see what someone’s zip code is. You and I don't think like that, though, but Ricky does. He’s the kind of guy that looks at us like we’re chumps for choosing an easy password recovery question. This was all happening in 2012, and Ricky was sixteen years old when he stole his first gamer tag. [Music] He found the one he wanted, Wolverine. Yeah, that sounds cool. He wasn't an X-Men fan; he just liked the sound of it. So, he called up Zune support, which is a Microsoft product, and is like, I have a problem with my account. They ask him for his e-mail address associated with the account. He says, well, I don't know. Can you just look up my Xbox gamer tag? They said, you know what? That works. What's your gamer tag? Ricky says, Wolverine. Zune support says, ah, yes, I see your account, sir. What can I help you with? Ricky says, okay, well, the problem is that when — you know what? Actually hold on; something just came up. Can I call you right back? Zune support says, yeah, sure. Do you want a reference number for when you call back? It’ll be easier for us to find your details. Ricky says, yes, yes, I do want that. He hangs up, and then he calls Xbox Support this time, and tells them, I was on with support but I got disconnected. Can you look up my case if I give you a reference number? They said, yeah, go ahead. He reads the number to them, and they see his details. Xbox Support’s mode of operation then was that if someone had a reference number, they must have already verified they are the account holder. So, they ask him, what's the problem? How can I help you? Ricky says, I just forgot what e-mail address I used for this account. He makes up some story about why he can't remember. He happened to be a good liar. Maybe it was that he got a new computer and didn't have those details on his new one. Xbox Support thinks, you know what? This is a harmless request. Sure. Your e-mail address is blahblahblah@aol.com. Great, he says. That’s all I wanted, and he hangs up. Now he has an e-mail address associated with that gamer tag. All he needs now is the password. Trying to get the password for an Xbox account is tricky, though. So, he has a better solution; try to reset the password on aol.com’s e-mail address. Once in there, he can reset the Xbox account and get control of that gamer tag. This is where he uses different tricks to get into an AOL account, by telling the website, I forgot my password, and it asking for his favorite food or zip code to verify it’s him. From there, bingo. He can now access the e-mail account and reset the password for that Microsoft gamer tag and get into it. This is how he became Wolverine. RICKY: Yeah, I thought it was cool, like a cool alias to have, and that was the first one I ever took. So, I was like, you know what? That’s what it is. JACK: So, Wolverine. RICKY: Yeah. So, that’s my alias. JACK: Ricky didn't have steel claws like Wolverine did. His weapons were his keyboard and telephone. Once Ricky got his first taste of stealing a gamer tag, he wanted more. He went back to that marketplace on hack forums where people were selling gamer tags. People were selling things like Gang or Spirit or Booty or Boss for a few hundred bucks each. Ricky started stealing gamer tags and then selling them for money on the site, for Bitcoin specifically. He started making some money off this, not bad money, either. A couple good gamer tags might sell for around $1,000. But many were just a few hundred bucks. He’d play with them, too, just to dunk on people. He’d log in with a stolen gamer tag, totally pwn some other players in Halo 3 by knocking them offline with some DDoS attack, and then just laugh at it all. But sometimes people would report him for abuse, and this would bring the party to a screeching halt. RICKY: I thought it was funny just to hit them offline and stuff like that. But eventually you just get banned. Like, back then Xbox was big on just banning your accounts and stuff for DDoS attacks. So, I would just get banned over and over, which then led to my consoles being banned. So, I was always at GameStop and whatnot just trading in consoles for new consoles and selling my banned consoles and stuff like that. JACK: He told me this happened over a dozen times, and he would just keep selling banned Xboxes at the same GameStop, and then go to another one across town and buy another. I just can't believe that they didn't catch on to him for constantly selling them banned Xboxes. RICKY: They would plug it in to make sure it turned on, which was fine with me, but they never checked like — connected to Xbox Live and stuff like that. JACK: He would do this again and again. RICKY: So, I would typically trade it in at one store and then go to a different GameStop and then buy the new console. I’ve probably went through at least ten, maybe closer to twenty. JACK: You would think after a while that Ricky would be like, alright, alright, enough of this getting banned. I’ll stop attacking people. But for some reason he was just so addicted to it that he would not stop attacking people and just kept getting reported for abuse again and again and again. You would think after five times, it’s like, okay, I’m tired of going down to get a new Xbox, but not Ricky. He would just keep doing it. Now, eventually he graduated to stealing something even more malleable. It wasn't just gamer tags anymore. [Music] His attention turned to Instagram handles. RICKY: I was always the old-school Halo guy, like Xbox guy. Like, I didn't want to transition into Instagram. I just stuck to what I know. Then just one day, a couple of my people were like, yo, why are you not doing Instagram? It’s a new wave. So, they kinda persuaded me. They were like, listen, here's an AOL e-mail address. It’s for the Instagram @bro, just like B-R-O. Nobody can take it. I’m like, dude, it’s an AOL. What do you mean nobody can take it? JACK: At the time, Ricky felt like he could steal any Xbox gamer tag he wanted. So, what do you mean you can't steal this Instagram name @bro? It’s tied to an AOL address account. Those are easy to get into. But this idea sparked something in Ricky. If he could get any gamer tag he wanted, then how different would it be to get Instagram names? It’s the same social engineering techniques that he figured out how to recover someone’s password, but there’s just way more money in it. RICKY: With the Instagram @bro, how nobody could get it that was trying to get it, it’s because it was linked — it was an adult account on AOL, but it had — it was like the parent account, and under the parent account it had other accounts. It was one of those e-mails under the parent account. That’s why nobody could get it. I was able to realize that. I realized it. Once I reset the main e-mail, and I was like, yo, this isn't my e-mail — like, you have other accounts under that e-mail. JACK: [Music] Ricky said that he would sometimes pay an employee at a cell phone store a couple hundred bucks to help them do a SIM-swap, an insider who could bypass the security protections, just like what happened to Mark. This insider, he says, didn't know exactly how much was being stolen in crypto. They were just happy to get a few hundred bucks to change someone’s phone number in the system. But that was nothing compared to the lion’s share that Ricky and his crew would get from the heist. RICKY: So, once I had a couple million, I was like, damn, my moral compass checked in. I’m like, actually screwing people’s lives up. I have my own kid. My kid’s gonna be set for life, like just living life now. But we just kept going. It was like — almost like an addiction at this point. JACK: While all this was going on, Ricky was living a double life. He had just turned eighteen. He had just finished high school. He did not get the baseball scholarship for college. He did get a girlfriend, and they had a kid together, and he was still living at home with his mom. He had a 9:00 to 5:00 job for the county’s park and recreation department, you know, to keep up with the ruse that he’s got some normal job with a regular income. But of course, that job was boring compared to his online world, where millions of dollars were passing through his fingers. RICKY: So, I was just changing trash bags and stuff like that at a park, sitting in a work truck. So, I had all the time in the world to just be on my phone, like talking to everybody on Discord or Skype or something like that. While I’m at work, we're just hitting targets for crypto. DEBBIE: I had no idea, a boy that works for the city. JACK: This is Debbie, Ricky’s mom. DEBBIE: He had a county job. It wasn't the best money, but I was happy he had it. He had good benefits, he had retirement with it, and he went to work every day. JACK: She had no idea her son was living this double life, bringing in anywhere from $100,000 to a million dollars from victims. But having all this Bitcoin was pointless unless Ricky could spend it, and this is where he had to be careful. Crypto exchanges require KYC, which stands for ‘know your customer’. They want your full name and picture of your ID before they will let you exchange cryptocurrency for cash. So, that wasn't going to work. His Bitcoin wallet was likely marked as fraudulent, and if he used an exchange and gave them his name, then they would probably call the cops on him. So, he needed a new plan, a way to cash out Bitcoin without using an exchange, and basically he just found another person in the world who would do it. Like, he would send them the Bitcoin and they would hand him cash. He met them through localbitcoins.com. RICKY: I had a guy in the Tampa area. If I needed $20,000 cash or less, I can go to him, or if I needed more, I had a guy that was in Miami, and he never scammed me, but I would send him the crypto and he would mail me the cash. JACK: Yeah, let’s talk about both of these, right? So, when you go to meet someone, how does this meet go down? RICKY: Typically it was at a McDonald’s or something. We would just go sit in the booth. I would send him the Bitcoin. We would wait for the confirmations and for him to get it in his account, and he would give me the cash. Prior to that, though, we had the deal locked in at a certain amount, 'cause Bitcoin would go up and down. But I would typically just lock in the deal, and I’d be — okay, we’ll meet at 7:00. This is where we’re going. He would send me an address, and I would just go there. JACK: And then he’d just hand you an envelope? RICKY: Yeah, or just straight cash or an envelope and whatnot. But it was always a public place. It was never in a dark alley or anything crazy like that. JACK: That’s the classic way LocalBitcoins worked; you meet someone in person, you send them the Bitcoin, and they hand you the cash. Of course, they’d take a percentage for doing this deal. Maybe they'd give Ricky 95% of the money and keep 5% for themselves for the trouble of having to launder these Bitcoins. So, he actually had a lot of people making decent money on LocalBitcoins just buying crypto off people. But eventually Ricky needed to cash out bigger and bigger amounts, and this person he was working with wasn't able to cash out what he needed, so Ricky had to find someone new, and this new person was like, send me the Bitcoin; I’ll send you the cash in the mail. RICKY: It typically would just come in a vacuum-sealed, clear envelope wrapped in another envelope kinda thing. Sometimes it would be inside of a book, like a big Harry Potter book or something like that, and the pages would be cut out and the money would be in there. What's funny is I lived with my mom, so packages are coming to the house, but I’m eighteen years old. She’s not going through my mail. So, she would just take the envelope, put it on my bed, and she’d be like, hey, the mail came for you. She had no idea what was inside of it. JACK: Alright, so you're loading it up in crypto here. Things are coming in, $100,000, $1 million at a time. So, you're leading a double life here. You're living with your mom. Does she have any idea that you're doing any of this stuff, involved with this? RICKY: First of all, she doesn't really understand what the hell crypto was, and she was like, Ricky, what are you doing? How do you have all this money? I bought a $100,000 F-250 Ford truck, I had jet skis, I had side-by-sides. I had a lot of toys and stuff like that. DEBBIE: It really got my attention when he came home with the truck. I said, what is going on? RICKY: I would just lie to her. Like, yo, I invested back then. At the time when I started, Bitcoin was a couple hundred dollars, and now it’s, let’s say, $3,000, $6,000. So, I made a lot just from that, that little growth. So, I was able — but that’s what I told her. Meanwhile I’m stealing it, but — so, she has really no idea the severity of it. So, my mom, she believed me. She believed that I was saying there’s no reason for her not to believe me. DEBBIE: He never gave me a reason not to believe what he was doing was wrong, 'cause he wasn't that kinda kid. JACK: Ricky’s crypto investment explanation wasn't a total lie. He did have Bitcoin investments, and Debbie didn't have any reason to question it. After all, her own mother, Ricky’s grandmother, dabbled in Bitcoin, too, so she knew it was real. Ricky also had a young kid at home, and Debbie thought why would he do anything to throw his life away? DEBBIE: I was a single mom. I did the best I could growing up with him. He was a very honest child, never got in trouble, never was in the principal’s office. He didn't get in fights. So, when he came home with the truck, I just said, I don't know what you're doing or what's going on, but that’s not normal, and all I know is if you get in trouble, there’s not much I can do. I mean, I — and I said — at that time it was just his daughter, and between the mom and my son being the parents to this child, they were both younger, and I was fairly involved with my granddaughter. I just said to him, it’s just not your life anymore. You have a child involved here. JACK: Debbie believed her son and was proud of him, and had no reason to think he would lie to her. In fact, she thought Ricky’s crypto savviness could actually help others. At the time she worked as a nurse in the Pasco County Jail, and one day she overheard some sheriff’s deputies yapping about crypto. DEBBIE: I assumed at this point my son was doing really good with crypto, 'cause that’s what — the vision I was getting. I kinda went into work and was saying, yeah, my son does crypto, Bitcoin, and he’s done really well, and they've matured. I remember one of the deputies was really interested. He’s like, really? RICKY: They were like, oh, we’d love to talk to him. DEBBIE: I was like, yeah, he’s doing really good with it. One of the guys, one of the deputies, wanted to get with him and speak with my son. RICKY: So, next thing you know my mom is having me call these police officers and they're coming to the house to ask me about crypto. They're asking me about investing. They're asking me like, what do I think? I just went along with it. Like, yeah, crypto’s great. This is what I recommend. I recommend Bitcoin or Ethereum. I think XRP was actually blowing up at that time, too. I think I made a lot off XRP, actually, which — not legitly, but I used my dirty money and put it into XRP, and XRP blew up. I was telling them about that, and they were loving it. So, they were just like, okay, cool, thanks for chatting. They had no idea I was stealing it. JACK: And how were you feeling inside? RICKY: Oh, I’m nervous. I’m like, mom — that’s when I told her. Like, yo, never again. Don't tell people what I do. DEBBIE: [Music] I said to Ricky, and you let this deputy come to the house and talk to you? JACK: By 2018 the walls started closing in on Ricky. He says he has a hunch of when it all started to unravel. One night he was doing a SIM-swap, a crypto heist with some other guys online, his crew. One of the guys was a younger kid, and this younger kid was posing as an AT&T employee trying to social engineer someone into doing the SIM-swap for him. But little did this kid know, his mother was listening through the door, and she heard him trying to scam someone on the phone. That kid’s mom called the cops on her son, and that kid got arrested in Michigan. Ricky and his crew did not know this. All they knew was that kid suddenly went missing. That’s strange. But they had no idea he got arrested. But then that kid came back out of the blue and really, really, really badly wanted to get in on the action again. Ricky suspected that’s really weird that this kid got a bunch of money from a crypto heist and then disappeared for a while and now really wants back in. They kept that kid at arm’s length, but that didn't matter. Another one of Ricky’s friends was arrested shortly after, who was also present on that same call where the kid’s mom overheard them. Joel Ortiz was arrested for SIM-swapping and stealing millions of dollars in crypto from victims. He pled guilty, and a judge sentenced him to a decade behind bars. Prosecutors said that he was the first SIM-swapper to ever be sentenced to prison in the US, and after hearing about Joel’s arrest, Ricky was worried that he might be next. RICKY: I’ve known Joel. I’ve talked with him and I’ve done stuff with him and stuff where it was like, hold on, this is a huge red flag. I remember I was eating at Ford’s Garage when it happened when I found out that Joel got arrested. So, that’s what kinda raised my suspicion. I’m like, oh shit, Joel got caught. JACK: After hearing Joel went down, you would think that it would give you a spook of some kind and be like, okay, I’m gonna lay low for a couple weeks or clear some stuff or get rid of some evidence. RICKY: Yeah. JACK: But you didn't do any of that. RICKY: Um…no. JACK: Just a day after learning about Joel’s arrest, the dominoes started to fall. There are moments in our life that stand out forever. Maybe it’s when your first child is born or first kiss or playing a video game for the first time. For Ricky, that day was July 18, 2018. On that day, Ricky was still living at home with his mom, and he had broken up with his girlfriend that he had a child with, but he had a new woman and a new child with her. I think the baby was a few months old at that point. The day started just like any other day. Ricky was getting ready to go to work at the parks and recreation department, and his girlfriend left the house just before him so that she could go to work. RICKY: I used to live by a cul-de-sac area. [Music] When she went to work, she’s like, hey, there’s a lot of cops in this cul-de-sac. I was like, okay, come back. Like, that’s weird. That’s off to me. So, when she went around the block the other way, she’s like, yo, they're also on this side of the house, like on this block. I was like, alright, I’m pretty sure they're coming. I walk outside to go — just act like I’m going to work. Like, I knew at that point that they were probably coming for me. I could see them coming down the road. I was like, just try to play it off. I went to go get up in my truck, and they were like, don't go in your truck. Don't run, don't run. JACK: Ricky stayed still, standing next to his truck as officers handcuffed him. OFFICER: You wanna lean against your truck or something? RICKY: Yeah, if — whatever. I mean, just whatever. [Background talk] OFFICER: You have anything on you that might hurt us if we pat you down or whatever? Alright. Just hang tight. You understand right now you're just being detained. JACK: This is body cam audio from Ricky’s arrest by the Pasco County Sheriff’s Office. It’s the very same sheriff’s office where his mom Debbie worked as a nurse. DEBBIE: When they came here that day — and, you know, they — I guess it would be to raid the house, but they were very — doing the search warrant stuff, but they did not break down our doors. They didn't do anything. So, now I kinda get up out of my bed and I look into the kitchen area, and there’s two cops standing in the doorway. They're like, hey, Debbie. I need you to come out here. JACK: They know you? DEBBIE: Yeah, they knew my name, they knew everything. Now, yeah, I knew some of them from coming in and out of work. I think I kept saying, what is going on? What is going on? What is happening? JACK: And when they finally tell you this is what we think is going on, what was your reaction to that? DEBBIE: We have — my reaction to that was, well, isn't Bitcoin — isn't this legal? That was my first reaction; but I thought it was legal. So, I kinda looked at him and he goes, he was not — those coins and the money that he was getting, Debbie, did not belong to him. He was stealing them. That’s when I really realized like, oh, okay. So, now what? JACK: Debbie sat outside the front of the house with Ricky as deputies collected evidence. Some of Ricky’s burner phones, his iPhone, his crypto wallets, and some other SIM cards were taken. RICKY: They took my truck, they took two side-by-sides, they took a trailer I had, the trailer I haul everything. JACK: Ricky was taken away in the back of a squad car to jail. … OFFICER: I have one male adult, 1012. Nothing else is in your pockets? RICKY: No, sir. JACK: They drive off to jail. The twenty-five minute ride is mostly quiet. Ricky is alone with his thoughts, but he does ask the officer behind the wheel what to expect. RICKY: Do you know how all this all goes? Like, do I see a judge and then…? OFFICER: You’ll have advisors. RICKY: I will? Okay. OFFICER: That’ll be done by video, on chat or whatever. RICKY: That’ll be today, right? OFFICER: Should be. JACK: I can't get over how calm Ricky sounds. He had been cooking up these schemes for years to steal things from who knows how many victims, starting with a few hundred dollars in gamer tags to millions of dollars in crypto wallets, and it all came to an end here in the back of the squad car. Maybe he was feeling relief, like his big secret’s out. He doesn't have to lie to his mom anymore or try to walk quietly in the shadows of his double life. But sitting in the back of the car, you have to wonder what else is going through his head. What’s gonna happen to me, and what about my family? What about my money? But he quietly listens as the officer driving him to the jail spells out the next steps for him. OFFICER: I would think it would be this afternoon. That’s when they’ll basically just announce what you're charged with, and then whether you're gonna retain your own attorney or whether you're asking for a public defender. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: And then — but that is — again, I don't know if you're being charged federally. RICKY: Okay. OFFICER: Which makes it different, so… RICKY: Alright, thank you sir. JACK: Ricky was booked in the county jail. His mom was so distraught, though. She didn't want to see her son in jail. What mother would? So, she went down to jail to see if she could bail him out. DEBBIE: I just — it had to be done. I wasn't leaving him in jail. JACK: Did he go to the very jail you worked at? DEBBIE: Oh yeah, he sure did. All my nursing staff, friends, they were all like, oh my god, Debbie’s son is here. What’s going on? Then the sergeant — they all knew once I posted bond for him, get him outta here. Yeah, they did do a little bit of, let’s say, courtesy. I shouldn't say courtesy, but they treated him knowing that he was my son. Like, let’s move him along. You know? JACK: Yeah, that must have been embarrassing. DEBBIE: But yeah. Yeah, a little bit embarrassing, a little bit of shocking, embarrassing. The only thing — and I wasn't actually physically working there anymore. I had just left like six months prior. But I mean, it was still fresh. I had worked there for almost ten years. JACK: They said his bail was $110,000. The cost of a bail bond is usually 10% to 15% of the total amount. Debbie ended up paying that to a bail bondsman to get him out. She didn't even hesitate. She just immediately was there for him. Prosecutors charged Ricky with grand theft and money laundering. The case against him dragged on for four years. He had to wear an ankle monitor during that whole time and follow a strict curfew. He pled guilty to federal charges of computer misconduct and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. By the time he went before a judge for sentencing, Ricky didn't know what to expect in the courtroom or how it would affect his family. His mom and fiancé were there during the sentencing. DEBBIE: It was horrible. It was I think one of the saddest days of my life. I remember standing in front of that judge. I just cried and said, look, I know my son did wrong. I know he did wrong, believe me. I can't believe he did all this, but he’s — that’s not my — that’s not the kind of kid he is. It was horrible. JACK: What did the judge say to that? DEBBIE: She was a woman, and I could almost feel her sympathy for me and getting it, but the law is the law, and I agree. The law is the law, and my son broke the law, and he had to pay his consequences. I let him know you did not just do this to yourself. You did this to your whole family. We're all suffering through this. We're suffering more than you are. JACK: The judge sentenced Ricky to four years in federal prison and ordered him to pay $7.6 million in restitution, which is what the courts accused him of stealing. RICKY: I knew it could have been worse and it should have been worse, and I was thankful that I got the forty-eight months. Like, I knew it was coming. I knew it had to happen because all the havoc I caused. I was like, you know, I gotta deal with it. I did what I did and now I gotta do it. I lost — I had to leave everybody, my family, my mom, my grandparents, my kid, everybody. JACK: Okay, so your child was four or five months old when you went away. RICKY: Correct, and that’s super hard because all those — I’ve always said the money, whatever, the money can't buy back those memories that I missed. Like, there’s nothing I could do; his first walk, his first talk, stuff like that, that money can't buy. DEBBIE: It was so hard coming to see him in prison and having to leave knowing that my kid’s in prison. Me and his fiancé, we went and saw Ricky at least once a month if not twice a month. We’d pack up the car, we’d leave early one morning, get there. We drove six hours, whatever it was, with two kids in the car, me and her only. No men, nobody to help us. We drove down there and had to do what we had to do, and then spend the night in a hotel. It was horrible, embarrassing, horrible, a combo of everything. JACK: So many criminal hacker stories go the same way. There’s a video game, a cheat, an underground community, an exploit, a payday, and then the knock on the door. They don't usually have the foresight to see how it will inevitably end. What do those millions of dollars really buy you? A couple of years of wealth that you can't really show anyone? Some screenshots of good old times? The skills to find gaps in security through social engineering? Whatever it is, the windfall was worth a lot less when you factor in what you lose. That’s the real cost. No cryptocurrency can buy back lost time or memories with your children. That’s what Ricky learned. [To Ricky] What was the worst part of this whole experience? RICKY: The worst part was the victims, because they didn't deserve it. So, that was the worst part, dealing with — I was doing terrible things. But I guess you have a chance in prison; you're like, dude — looking back on the shit that you caused — I can only imagine if I was in there and she was with a kid. That could have been used for my — their kids’ college funds or retirement or whatever the case may have been that they had that much money for, and I just came by and took it all. JACK: If it was me, I think I would have been — the saddest or the worst part of it was just not seeing my child in those early day — in those early years. Did that have an affect on you? RICKY: Yeah, that’s the second part of it. The first part was how I ruined innocent people’s lives. The second part now is I went to prison, I affected more people than just myself. I lost — I had to leave everybody, like my family, my mom, my grandparents, my kid, everybody. They were devastated. I know they were devastated, and it hurt me knowing that I hurt them like that. Like, my actions caused all that. JACK: After serving just a little more than two years in prison, Ricky got out early in 2024. These days he’s thinking a lot about the time he has now. Since his release he’s tried to turn his story into something useful, to reach out to the very gamers like him who may follow a darker path of social engineering. He’s spoken at anti-fraud events and security conferences like Black Hat and DEF CON. SPEAKER 6: Ricky, what would have made a difference to you as a teenager that would have stopped you going down this pathway? RICKY: Probably companies who could intervene, like get you before you're — it’s too late. If you had a chance to use your skills for good and after you help companies and whatnot, where they could be like, hey, we offer you a job, said job, into this world where you don't have to do what I was doing. JACK: I agree with that. The people in his bubble at that time were all criminals, and they used their skills for bad. But if he had more exposure to people, mentors, for instance, who could show him that these hacking tricks he knows, the cleverness of his social engineering skills and his OSINT skills, can be used for good and here's how, I think that kind of stuff does influence a lot of people to turn away from their life of crime and to find a new home, to be a productive member of society. So, he’s trying to do that now. He’s trying to build a pen testing company with another former SIM-swapper named Joseph Harris, one of the people Ricky met in the hacker forums. They're hoping to get this company up and running next year. [Outro]: [Outro music] A big thank you to Ricky and Debbie Handschumacher for sharing this story with us, and also thanks to Mark Kreitzman for telling us about one of the worst days of his life. You can learn more about what he’s working on at efani.com. If you liked this episode, go listen to our most popular episode we’ve ever made, Episode 112, called Dirty Coms, which goes into more details about this whole underground world, or listen to Joseph Harris’ story, which is Episode 118, called Hot Swaps. Hey, have you listened to my other podcast yet, LOW? It is wild. A lot of feedback from people are saying, pssh, I’ll pass, which is fine. It’s not for everyone. But I’m getting even more feedback from people saying — well, here, let me actually pull up one of the quotes that came in today. "The end of Episode 1 left me speechless." Someone else wrote, "it has moved me in a way that I did not think a podcast could." I mean, when is the last time you heard a show that moved you in a way that you didn't know was possible? If you need that in your life, open your podcast player and type in LOW, L-O-W. I made it as easy as possible to find. Go find it, go listen to it, and tell me what you think. This show is created by me, the ghost in the groceries, Jack Rhysider. This episode was written and produced by the packet-snacker, Sean Powers, assembled by the fridge phreaker, Tristan Ledger, mixing by Proximity Sound, theme music by the mysterious Breakmaster Cylinder. Alright, question; if you dug up a tomb that was in a pyramid, does it become unencrypted? This is Darknet Diaries.

articles.title: Beyond Passwords: How Attackers Abuse Device Code Authentication
articles.context: As the digital threat landscape continues to shift and threat actors exploit new attack vectors, practicing good cyber hygiene and staying informed about emerging threats remain...
articles.full_text:
By: Adriane Andaya, Cofense Phishing Defense Center

The Cofense Phishing Defense Center (PDC) has analyzed several emails that may look like ordinary spam to the untrained eye. Threat actors attempt to mimic routine corporate emails and blend into everyday inbox traffic. As aware of the common phishing tac tactics grows, threat actors are turning to techniques such as device code phishing. To understand how this technique works, it is important to understand what access codes are and how they differ from the common username-and-password method of authentication. Access codes are temporary codes that are entered instead of the users’ credentials on devices that are requesting authentication. While this method can simplify sign-ins, attackers can abuse it. If a victim completes the sign-in process, they may unknowingly authorize the threat actor’s session, which potentially grants access to the account and associated resources.

Figure 1: Fake bid invitation email

Cofense PDC analysts have handled several of these malicious emails that use subjects designed to capture the recipient’s interest. As illustrated in Figure 1, the email appears to be a regular bidding invitation, but when the recipient clicks on the link to view the project details, they’re redirected to a fake login page and prompted to enter their email. Microsoft branding is used to make the page appear more trustworthy.

Figure 2: Syncfusion phishing login page from the embedded URL

Figure 3: Spoofed Mimecast device enrollment page

As shown in Figure 2, the threat actors leveraged familiar brands such as Syncfusion and Microsoft to give the phishing page an appearance of legitimacy. The attack then proceeds after the victim has entered their email address. As seen in Figure 3, a very convincing spoofed Mimecast page adds another layer of legitimacy, encouraging the victim to enroll their device under the guise of an IT policy.

It is important to note that despite these familiar brands being used, the URL in the address bar does not match any of these brands’ registered domains. This mismatch should be an immediate red flag. By incorporating well-known brands, threat actors exploit familiarity to increase the likelihood of a successful phishing attempt.

Figure 4: Access code generation

Figure 5: Microsoft pop-up window

Figure 4 shows that a code will be generated, and a button to “view the document” will be presented to the user, which opens a Microsoft window (Figure 5) prompting the user to enter the code to allow access. Microsoft warns that entering the code will grant the originating application or device access to the account without requiring the user’s password and may bypass the protection normally provided by MFA. The second warning advises users not to enter codes from unverified sources. If a code from an untrusted source has been entered, it must be treated as an account compromise, and you must immediately notify your IT department. You can also take these steps to prevent or minimize the account breach:

Change the account password.

Sign out of all active sessions or revoke existing sessions.

Review recent account activity for suspicious or unauthorized access.

Review authorized applications and remove any unfamiliar or suspicious entries.

Re-verify registered security and MFA methods.

Check for unauthorized account changes, including sent emails, deleted items, forwarding rules, recovery addresses, or other modified settings.

This tactic targets decision-makers, management-level personnel, and key figures, but anyone can fall victim to this phishing campaign. It is crucial to verify any agreement, contract, or other related documents, especially if they are from an unfamiliar sender. In some cases, even familiar emails have been compromised and have been used to send emails that contain malicious URLs or attachments. To prevent your account from being compromised, you must check for any suspicious signs on the website you will be redirected to before entering any credentials.

As the digital threat landscape continues to shift and threat actors exploit new attack vectors, practicing good cyber hygiene and staying informed about emerging threats remain essential. While no security measure can eliminate all risks, staying vigilant and adopting safe digital habits can go a long way toward keeping you and your credentials secure.

However, as sophisticated tactics like device code phishing demonstrate, individual awareness alone is not enough. Organizations also need the ability to detect and respond to threats that slip past traditional security controls. Cofense combines real-world threat intelligence, AI-driven detection, and human expertise to help organizations identify and respond to these evolving phishing threats.

Learn how Cofense can help strengthen your organization's phishing defenses: https://cofense.com/platform.

articles.title: Introducing pathrunner: An AWS privilege escalation framework
articles.context: If your detections only support a specific post exploitation action, like creating a new administrative user and granting administrator access to it, you will be blind when an...
articles.full_text:
In December 2025, we released pathfinding.cloud, a catalog of AWS IAM privilege escalation techniques. Pathfinding.cloud defines the sets of permissions that would allow an AWS IAM principal to gain access to another AWS IAM principal. In May 2026, we released Pathfinding Labs, a collection of intentionally vulnerable AWS environments that can be deployed into a sandbox account, exploited, and torn down. You can use these labs to learn how the techniques documented in pathfinding.cloud are exploited.

Today, we're releasing pathrunner, a modular, cloud-native offensive security framework designed to help automate the exploitation of the paths defined in pathfinding.cloud and instantiated in Pathfinding Labs.

Full documentation for pathrunner and all of its commands and exploit modules can be found at https://pathfinding.cloud/pathrunner/.

Why build an offensive tool?

Every defender has more security vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on their plate than they have time to resolve, which means they must triage and carefully choose where they spend their finite remediation time. An offensive tool demonstrates the impact of an attack, enabling defenders to prioritize exploitable misconfigurations based on how impactful they are.

When assessing software vulnerabilities, we look for publicly accessible Proof of Concept (PoCs) exploits. If those exist, we increase the severity of related findings. When it comes to misconfigurations, exploitability can be more difficult to determine. For example, what's an exploitable misconfiguration vs. simply a missing best practice?

Offensive security approaches can pinpoint the specific misconfigurations that are exploitable and show exactly how they can be exploited in your environment. Defenders and offensive security teams alike both widely use offensive security tools like Metasploit and Bloodhound. There is nothing quite like seeing a vulnerability or misconfiguration in your environment actually exploited!

Pathrunner in action

The best way to understand what pathrunner can do is to watch it in action. In the following clip, we'll walk through the following actions:

Importing the credentials for an AWS IAM user identity that we've gained access to

Selecting an exploit module that our victim identity has permission to execute

Selecting the target identity that we want to access

Executing the attack and capturing the credentials of the target identity

Automatically importing the new credentials and switching to them

Validating that we have successfully accessed the target identity

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Identities are the sessions of the cloud

In traditional on-prem Active Directory environments, when attackers compromise a workload, the best and most likely path to the next hop in the attack path is usually through another workload, which is often a server or user workstation. Each connection between a workload and the attacker is called a session, because it is usually a TCP session between the two hosts. Not all escalations pivot through workloads, of course (e.g., kerberosting), but "attacker to workload" sessions are certainly very common in traditional Active Directory environments.

In cloud environments, the script is flipped. There are still occasional times where an attack hops from one workload to another and sends network sessions back to the attacker's command and control servers, but more often than not, penetration testers and real attacks are hopping from one cloud identity to another by accessing credentials. Sometimes this happens by executing code on a remote workload, and sometimes no workload is involved at all.

For these reasons, identities are fundamental to pathrunner. The very first pathrunner feature we created was the ability to import identities from multiple text-based formats by using a simple command: pathrunner identity add --from-clipboard. The second feature was the corresponding pathrunner identity switch [name] command, which enables you to easily switch between multiple identities.

Here's a look at two configured identities in pathrunner. The identity named bedrock-001 is associated with the initial set of credentials, which we first gain access to as the "attacker." The identity named bedrock_codeinterpreter_1790097483 is associated with the post-exploitation identity that we gain access to after running the bedrock-001 exploit in pathrunner.

Modular by design

Pathrunner's modular design was heavily influenced by a few successful exploitation frameworks of years past, like Metasploit, CrackMapExec (now NetExec), and Empire (now forked and maintained here). And even in the AWS cloud realm, we have Pacu and Nebula. These modular tools allow the operator to exploit multiple misconfigurations or vulnerabilities within the same user interface, which makes them much easier to use.

As of October 2026, there are over 80 exploit modules in pathrunner.

Modular payloads make for better detections

Another foundational decision that we made when building pathrunner was to support modular payloads. For an offensive security practitioner, sometimes certain payloads just don't work. Maybe there are network access restrictions or organizational service control policies in place. Providing multiple payloads for each module lets the user pick the payload that makes the most sense.

Another key benefit of having multiple payloads in an offensive security tool is that it allows you to build and evaluate more detections. If your detections only support a specific post exploitation action, like creating a new administrative user and granting administrator access to it, you will be blind when an attacker goes in another direction. Instead, if you walk through each and every pathrunner payload in your environment and build detections for each of them, you will have a much greater chance of catching malicious activity.

Use pathrunner to manage your "attacker" infrastructure

In cloud compromises, it is a common practice for attackers to stage their payload or exploit artifacts on external sources or to exfiltrate data or credentials to those external sources. They often use additional compromised cloud accounts to host their infrastructure.

Offensive security practitioners often use additional cloud accounts that they own to replicate this pattern. Done manually, this can be a tedious task. In pathrunner, we built this functionality in! We included support for adding an "attacker" identity and the ability to deploy "attacker" infrastructure in an AWS account that you control, separate from any "victim" AWS accounts.

In practice, if you configure your attacker identity with pathrunner attacker identity add and then type attacker infra ec2 create, pathrunner will create an EC2 instance in your own "attacker" account, deploy a second instance of pathrunner on that instance, put the right security groups in place, and show you how to connect to it via SSH or SSM.

Once you connect, you can then start a remote listener on the publicly accessible EC2 instance by using attacker listener start and start collecting credentials. In other words, with pathrunner, you can set up a remote endpoint to catch credentials with just three commands.

Here's the end-to-end flow showing how it all works. In the video, pay attention to the iTerm2 tabs at the top. I'll switch between MY MAC and ATTACKER AWS when showing how I can run an exploit from MY MAC, but catch the credentials on the "attacker" infra instance of pathrunner.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Alternatively, if you initially run pathrunner on a remotely accessible host that already has some public callback ports open, you can skip all of the remote deployment steps and just start the listener with attacker listener start. That's it!

Be a team player: Give your blue team an audit log

As mentioned earlier, it is quite impactful to show a defender exactly how you were able to exploit a misconfiguration in their environment. It's even more helpful to show exactly what audit log events your activity generated, along with timestamps for when those events occurred. We have good news! Pathrunner has this functionality built in as well. If you type workspace report --output pathrunner.html, you will get a report that is ready to hand over to the defenders.

There are two main parts to this report. First, it shows you the resources that were created or modified during your use of pathrunner. You can manually clean these up when you are done, or you can use the workspace cleanup all sub-command.

Second, the report includes a table that lists all of the CloudTrail events that we think pathrunner would have triggered, along with timestamps and descriptions.

What's Next?

We hope that pathrunner helps you improve your cloud detection capabilities, as well as the overall security posture of your environment. Please head over to the pathrunner repo if you would like to suggest features, let us know about bugs, or contribute to the project, and don't forget about the complete command reference guide at https://pathfinding.cloud/pathrunner/.

articles.title: The ballot box meets the bot.
articles.context: Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections.
articles.full_text:
State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security. Stolen credentials force ConnectWise to suspend cloud services. Fake calendar invites steal Microsoft logins. Temu settles Texas privacy allegations. Toronto police arrest seven in a cryptocurrency kidnapping case. The G7 sounds the alarm on quantum threats. Monday business briefing. Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

Today is Monday October 19th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security.

According to ProPublica, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked CISA to secretly acquire and hack a voting machine, then report its findings to the White House. Career employees resisted, concerned the results could be used to challenge election outcomes. The request was eventually dropped.

The revelation comes amid a dramatic retreat from CISA’s election security mission. Since President Trump returned to office, the agency has lost more than a thousand employees, roughly a third of its workforce, while cutting critical monitoring and support services.

State election officials say CISA was largely absent during preparations for November’s midterms. Meanwhile, the administration’s release of previously confidential election security information has damaged relationships built over years of cooperation.

CISA finally released an election security plan in late September, but state officials say it arrived too late to make much difference. Several now question whether they can trust the agency with sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations are attractive targets because of their access to sensitive voter and campaign information.

Attackers are using AI to produce convincing emails, text messages, and deepfake audio and video, eliminating traditional warning signs like poor grammar.

The agencies recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, stronger email filtering, and independent verification of suspicious requests.

The alert describes an emerging threat rather than a specific ongoing attack.

ConnectWise suspends its Cloud Backup service following stolen credentials.

ConnectWise has suspended its Cloud Backup service and taken two other cloud services offline after attackers stole credentials associated with seven application identities, potentially exposing customer Microsoft 365 environments.

The stolen credentials allowed attackers to impersonate trusted ConnectWise applications without needing customer passwords.

Security firm Huntress identified suspicious sign-ins across roughly a thousand Microsoft tenants, including approximately 300 successful authentications. Researchers also observed a targeted campaign against 16 organizations in sensitive sectors, though those attempts failed.

ConnectWise says it has disabled the compromised credentials and found no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed.

However, backups and restoration services remain unavailable. Huntress warns that attackers may have established persistent access inside affected tenants before the credentials were revoked, making additional investigation essential.

Calendar invites steal credentials.

Cybercriminals are turning ordinary calendar invitations into credential-stealing traps. Researchers at Check Point identified more than 300,000 unique phishing emails targeting over 40,000 organizations, disguised as Microsoft Teams meetings and other workplace appointments.

The invitations contain links to counterfeit Microsoft login pages designed to capture usernames and passwords. Some include legitimate calendar attachments, making the invitations appear more convincing.

The campaign has accelerated dramatically, with Check Point recording more than 740,000 messages during the first two weeks of October alone.

Researchers emphasize that attackers aren’t exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. Instead, they’re exploiting employees’ familiarity with routine meeting requests.

Check Point recommends checking unexpected invitations carefully and using phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys, to protect accounts against credential theft.

Temu settles with Texas over privacy allegations.

Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to pay Texas three million dollars to settle allegations that it improperly collected user data potentially accessible to the Chinese government.

The agreement requires Temu to store personal data on U.S. servers and restrict transfers to China. It also mandates independent product safety testing and stronger consumer protections.

Violations of certain data security provisions could trigger annual penalties of eight million dollars.

Temu denies wrongdoing. Several other states have filed similar lawsuits, making Texas the first to reach a settlement.

Toronto police make arrests in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner.

Toronto police have arrested seven men in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, including three active members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Investigators say the victim was abducted at gunpoint in July, handcuffed, and assaulted as his captors attempted to access cryptocurrency holdings and business security systems. He was eventually released after being threatened not to contact police.

The investigation uncovered an extensive collection of weapons, including firearms with 3D-printed receivers, silencers, and more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition. Approximately 2,500 rounds were allegedly stolen from the Canadian military.

Police also seized substantial quantities of illicit drugs, GPS tracking devices, and other equipment.

The seven suspects face a combined 82 charges. The investigation remains ongoing.

The G7 urges post-quantum readiness.

The G7 is urging governments and businesses to accelerate their transition to post-quantum cryptography, warning that quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used encryption systems.

In a call to action led by France’s national cybersecurity agency, the group argues that quantum threats should be treated as a near-term concern, even though the timeline for developing cryptographically capable quantum computers remains uncertain.

The recommendations include identifying critical systems, inventorying cryptographic assets, and developing phased migration plans. Organizations are encouraged to incorporate quantum-safe technologies into routine equipment upgrades to reduce costs.

The G7 also calls for national strategies, additional research, public-private partnerships, and updated cybersecurity requirements.

France plans to begin rejecting security products without quantum-safe encryption during certification reviews starting in 2027.

Monday business briefing.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with eight companies announcing rounds totaling nearly $143 million.

San Francisco-based Harmonic Security leads the pack with a $50 million Series B, followed by Israeli startups Pluto Security, raising $42 million, and Rein Security, securing $25 million.

Other recipients include France’s Netsec and Fleuret AI, Tennessee-based Hilt, London’s CodeWall, and Utah’s Guardrail Technologies. The funding will support product development, hiring, and international expansion.

On the acquisition front, quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to purchase zero-trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.

CrowdStrike is reportedly negotiating a $500 million acquisition of Israeli data loss prevention startup Orion Security.

Meanwhile, government contractor SAIC has acquired cryptographic software provider Information Security Corporation, and Singapore-based V-Key has announced a majority investment in AI security firm CloudsineAI.

MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

MapQuest, the venerable mapping service that once helped drivers navigate the world with printed directions and a healthy supply of printer ink, has found a new way to stay relevant.

Its latest mobile app update introduces a surveillance layer that shows users the locations and directions of known license plate readers and outdoor security cameras.

The feature covers equipment from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon, Verkada, and several other surveillance vendors.

Flock alone reportedly operates at least 120,000 cameras across the United States, and independent projects have already been mapping their locations.

Now MapQuest is bringing that information directly into its navigation app, helping users identify surveillance infrastructure along their routes.

Apparently, the company that once helped you avoid getting lost can now help you see who’s watching you.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.
