articles.title: Exploited Vulnerabilities Typically Take Three Months to Patch, Moody’s Finds
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
AI-Driven Attacks Threaten to Widen the Patching Gap

The Moody’s report also warned that AI agents are already capable of exploiting vulnerabilities and compromising systems within days. It documented containment failures during developer testing at OpenAI and Anthropic, although OpenAI’s case involved an internal evaluation rather than an attack by a threat actor.

The report noted that no comparable threat-actor campaign at that scale has been publicly documented.

However, the barriers to fully autonomous cyber-attacks are likely temporary, Moody’s analysts noted.

High computing costs and restricted access to frontier AI models currently limit their use in large-scale campaigns. The report cited the UK AI Security Institute, which estimated that the cyber-capability gap between open-weight and frontier models had narrowed to four to seven months, from six to 10 months previously.

Organizations with weak patching practices face the greatest credit risk, according to the Moody’s report.

Those with large digital networks are particularly exposed because their broader attack surfaces create more opportunities for exploitation. Smaller and mid-sized companies could also become more economically viable targets as AI reduces the cost and effort required to carry out cyber-attacks, the analysts noted.

Published on October 19, this Moody’s report uses February 2026 data from Bitsight Technologies that accounted for vulnerabilities disclosed over previous two years.

“Meaningful advances in AI's offensive cyber capabilities since then may have further reduced the average time to exploit; remediation times may also have changed,” the Moody’s report noted.

articles.title: Conduent Agrees to Pay $80m to Settle Data Breach Class Action
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Digital platform provider Conduent has agreed to pay $80m to settle a class action lawsuit following a 2024 cyber incident that breached the personal and health data of around 62 million people.

The money will be divided up into covering material losses experienced by individual claimants whose personal data was breached, the costs of credit monitoring and medical data monitoring services for each of the claimants and the plaintiff’s legal fees.

A filing submitted to the US District Court for the District of New Jersey on October 16, 2026 explained that the agreement divides the claimants into two subclasses.

One consists of around 40 million individuals whose stolen data was stored in complex backup files that were not readily accessible to third party actors. The second relates to 22 million individuals who stolen data was stored in files that were readily accessible.

Only those plaintiffs who have documented losses relating to fraud and/or identity theft stemming from the incident can claim a direct cash reimbursement, up to a maximum value of $3500.

If the settlement receives final approval from the Court, Conduent will no longer be liable for civil claims relating to the cyber incident.

The business services firm has also agreed to strengthen its data security practices as part of the settlement.

The settlement agreement was confirmed by Conduent in an 8-K filing form submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on October 16.

It emphasized that the agreement is not an admission of fault or liability, which Conduent denies.

“The Company maintains cyber insurance and does not expect this settlement to have a material impact on its financial position, results of operations or cash flows,” the filing added.

Conduent provides third-party printing/mailroom services, document processing services, payment integrity services and other back-office support services. The company supports approximately 100 million US residents across various government health programs, operates many of the largest toll systems in the US and is a provider of government payment disbursements for federally funded benefit and payment card programs.

Third Largest Healthcare Data Breach of All Time

The attack on Conduent was allegedly perpetrated by the SafePay ransomware gang, which claimed it had stolen 8.5TB of data from the firm.

The incident took place in October 2024 but was not discovered by Conduent for almost three months.

Following analysis of the impacted files, Conduent told affected individuals that an unauthorized actor exfiltrated data that may have included names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, health insurance details and medical information.

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) journal ranks the incident as the third largest healthcare data beach of all time, as of October 2026, due the number of individuals’ protected health information that was compromised.

First place on that list remains the 2024 ransomware attack on the healthcare payment processing provider Change Healthcare, which has affected more than 192 million people.

This is followed by an incident which hit US health insurance giant Anthem in 2015, which HIPAA recorded as breaching the data of 78.8 million people.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.context: gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses,...
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

SHINYWIRE

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

GHOSTBYTE

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

CONFLICTING INTERESTS

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A security breach affecting open-source AI agent framework provider OpenCode could expose API keys linked to users of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google AI models.

On October 17, OpenCode confirmed a security breach that occurred the night before and affected its Console service, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Rather than exposing the underlying OpenAI, Anthropic or Google keys to individual team members, Console stores each workspace’s credentials and uses them to authenticate requests to the respective providers.

OpenCode is a widely used AI agent platform designed for software developers. It has 217,000 stars on GitHub.

In a July 2026 interview with Y Combinator – financial backer of Anomaly, the company which develops and maintains OpenCode – the founder and CEO Jay V claimed OpenCode had reached approximately 13 million monthly active users and 4.6 million weekly active users.

OpenCode Points to Unauthorized Access to Legacy System

The incident was “related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” said OpenCode on social media.

“We have notified them all this morning via email. If you did not get an email you were not impacted, it was a subset of users who had external providers linked,” the company added.

The email was made public by several OpenCode users on the dedicated subreddit forum and the official Discord channel.

The email said OpenCode had "identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that we were in the process of decommissioning" and that "third party provider keys (e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic) saved in your workspace may have been exposed."

Specifically, Dax Raad, one of the main contributors to OpenCode and co-founder of Anomaly, noted on X that the breach involved only "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself.”

OpenCode also notified Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to remediate the issue.

Recommended Steps to Mitigate OpenCode Threat

In an incident response report, software supply chain security firm Safeguard provided recommendations for OpenCode users to identify whether they have been affected by the incident and mitigate its impact:

Key steps include:

Checking whether you may be affected: search your inbox for the subject line “Action Required: Potential provider key breach.” If you have received the email, follow the guidance provided. If not, still review your keys as a precaution

Identifying all potentially exposed keys: list every OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Gemini API key that was ever stored in an OpenCode Console workspace, including keys added by other workspace admins

Reviewing API usage for suspicious activity: check each provider’s usage and billing reports from 16 October onward, and further back if possible. Look for unexpected usage spikes, unfamiliar models or unexplained charges

Creating replacement keys: generate new API keys for any potentially exposed credentials before revoking the old ones. Use project- or workspace-specific keys with appropriate restrictions and spending limits

Revoking potentially exposed keys: disable or delete the old keys through the relevant provider dashboard. Do not assume a key is safe simply because it has not shown suspicious usage

Updating all systems using the old keys: replace them in CI/CD secrets, environment files, local agent configurations, production applications, and team members’ machines. Ensure all consumers use the new keys before removing any remaining dependencies on the old ones

Verifying that old keys no longer function: test revoked keys against the relevant provider APIs and confirm they return an authentication error rather than a successful response

Applying additional security controls: restrict keys to the required projects and APIs, set appropriate spending limits and budget alerts, and review workspace access and permissions

Securing your OpenCode Console configuration: if you continue using Console with your own provider credentials, add a dedicated, restricted API key rather than reusing a production key.

OpenCode and Anomaly have been contacted with a request for comment.

articles.title: Securing the agentic insider
articles.context: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge wil
articles.full_text:
In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful.

While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents.

Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised.

Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise.

They are agentic insiders.

Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly.

To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7.

An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime.

In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise.

The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise.

Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic insiders, implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence:

Sensors/Signals/Actuators: bring together signals across the various sensors (identity, data, cloud, endpoint, network, runtime) to discover agents in the enterprise and bring them under management by assigning an identity, container and set of policy and permissions.

Context: use those signals to compute, dynamically, the risk associated with what the agents are attempting to do.

Harness/agents/models: based on dynamic agent risk, a team of Guardian Agents, with green and blue agents, actively and continually supervise every action of every agent and surgically respond as the risk profile increases, in real time.

This is where agentic security changes the equation for security practitioners.

Project Perception can supervise in real time while providing traceability for practitioners to examine what happened, understand why the risk emerged and apply the judgment needed to update their security system accordingly. Agentic security provides speed. Practitioners provide judgment. That is how defenders begin operating at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against.

Today, security systems can reliably observe the actions of the agents. Those signals are essential and tell us what we need to contain. Our security controls should increasingly be able to ask not only “What is happening?” but also “Why is it happening?” Is this consistent with the intent of the task?” This will require greater transparency into the model itself, not only the input and output tokens, but the thinking and chain of thought tokens. Only then can we truly understand whether the model’s intent is aligned with the purpose of the agent. Model transparency will not replace containment. It will make containment smarter and stronger. And it will allow us to better inform accountability and traceability. This needs to be the next step in securing agentic insiders.

With Project Perception, you can get started today on the journey to secure your agentic insiders. There should not be a choice between innovation and safety.

Hayete Gallot leads Microsoft’s work to help organizations operate securely in an AI-driven world. Her scope includes identity, threat protection, compliance and data security at global scale.

The post Securing the agentic insider appeared first on The Official Microsoft Blog.

articles.title: ConnectWise Shuts Off Cloud Services After ‘Unauthorized Access’ to Microsoft 365 Tenants
articles.context: IT management software provider ConnectWise has suspended access to several of its cloud services after it discovered that unauthorized actors had gained access to Microsoft 365...
articles.full_text:
IT management software provider ConnectWise has suspended access to several of its cloud services after it discovered that unauthorized actors had gained access to Microsoft 365 tenants.

A Microsoft 365 tenant is a dedicated instance of Microsoft services used by an organization to store their data separately from other organizations using Microsoft services. Each organization using a Microsoft 365 tenant has its own unique identifier assigned to it by Microsoft.

ConnectWise began investigating suspicious activity on October 15. By October 17, the company said that it had identified “unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment.”

The discovery has resulted in several ConnectWise cloud services including Cloud Backup (previously known as SkyKick), SaaS Security and Cloud Management being taken offline while the company investigates the incident, said a security advisory.

“We understand that this interruption affects your ability to support your customers. We do not yet have a confirmed restoration time and will share a timeline as soon as we can do so reliably,” ConnectWise said in an October 19 update.

The action has been taken due to the discovery of unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

An attacker could potentially abuse this access to gain unauthorized access to customers' Microsoft 365 environments. They would do this by authenticating to the app using the tooling of the tenant in the same way the backup service would, leveraging this access to obtain tokens with the app's existing permissions, therefore providing access to the environment.

With this access an attacker could access the same directories and data as a backup service, putting the tenant users’ corporate data at risk.

“The credential belongs to the application itself, so the attacker inherited the permissions granted to it. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) doesn’t apply because this is an application sign-in, so no user, device, or MFA prompt is involved,” said Justin Kohler, chief product officer at SpecterOps

“Backup tools need broad access to read and restore data. Anyone holding the app’s credential can reach the same mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information the backup service can,” he added.

Cybersecurity analysts at Huntress have been following the ConnectWise incident. In a blog post, they said that in at least one customer tenant being observed, the attacker provided themselves with a Global Administrator role, using this access in an attempt to modify permissions for other applications, including an MSP management application, and Huntress's own security application.

While ConnectWise has said it has yet to discover any indication that partner backup data has been compromised, the company said it will “continue investigating potential unauthorized access.”

There is currently no attribution as to who could be behind the attack. “We cannot discuss threat actor attribution at this time. Our focus is on investigation, remediation, and supporting affected partners and their customers,” ConnectWise said in the advisory.

ConnectWise has also advised its customers to take the following actions to help identify any potential incidents:

Verify the status of the listed application connections and keep affected applications disabled until ConnectWise provides restoration instructions

Preserve available sign-in and audit records promptly, while taking any urgent containment action

Review application and user authentication, application credentials and federation trusts, directory roles, owners, consent grants and recent policy changes

Check for unauthorized mailbox forwarding, inbox or transport rules and delegated mailbox access

Investigate any other identities changed or used during suspicious activity; disabling the original applications does not remove those separate access paths

articles.title: US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26%, Hitting Four Year Low
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity job postings in the US fell by 26.4% year-over-year from January to September 2026, according to analysis by CyberSN.

A total of 235,786 cybersecurity roles were posted on the job market intelligence platform JobSpikr in 2026. This is the lowest amount of US-based cybersecurity jobs advertised in the four years CyberSN has undertaken its analysis, compared to 273,498 in 2023, 244,911 in 2024 and 320,210 in 2025.

There was a particularly significant drop in leadership roles. CISO postings fell from 4632 in January to September 2025 to 2832 in the same period in 2026, a 38.9% reduction.

Other leadership roles that saw substantial dips included cybersecurity director (a 32.5% fall), cybersecurity lead (41% fall) and cybersecurity manager (24.4% fall).

Overall, nine of the 10 cybersecurity functions tracked by the researchers had fewer postings in 2026 compared to 2025. The only exception was research roles, which grew by 26.1%.

The CyberSN researchers said it is not clear whether the sharp decline in job postings reflects less demand for cybersecurity roles from employers or is simply a return from an unusually strong year in 2025.

The report, published on October 16, also highlighted that roles posted in the three quarters tracked in 2026 stayed within 1.5% of one another.

“That is consistent with demand having settled at a lower level rather than continuing to fall,” the researchers wrote.

A significant proportion (39.9%) of postings in 2025 came from small businesses, with 200 or fewer employees. Nearly half (47.3%) were from large firms with 1001 or more employees, and 12.7% from those with 201 to 1000 employees.

AI Security Engineer Postings Surge

AI security engineer roles, grouped in the cybersecurity function of “defense” by CyberSN, jumped by 268.3% in January to September 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

The share of job postings that mentions AI or machine learning in the job description was similar in 2026 compared to 2025, 14.6% versus 15.1%, respectively.

Read now: Cybersecurity Job Ads Requiring AI Skills Double

September 2026 also saw a surge in cyber data scientist postings, with 667 compared to 247 in the previous month, August. Of all these roles posted in 2026, 88% mention AI in the job description.

articles.title: Putting models to the secure coding test: Security rules
articles.context: However, I was disappointed to see that the first result was the same IDOR vulnerability found in the default-mode and plan-mode iterations
articles.full_text:
Engineers no longer write all the code. With coding agents, people who have never coded before now are empowered to create software. And honestly, can we still say people are writing code when agents are writing it for us? This shift brings many benefits, but it also worries me from an application security perspective. How can we ensure that agents write secure code?

This led me to investigate an overarching question: How well do coding agents write secure code, and what can be done to improve it? I'll spend the next few months trying to answer this question and will share my findings in this series of blog posts. If you missed the first part of this series where I tested how plan mode compared to the default mode when writing secure code, check it out here.

My second research question, and the focus of this post, is whether running a model with pre-set security rules has a significant security effect compared to not providing any security rules. It seems like this question should have an obvious answer—“of course!”—but I want to see just how impactful good security rules are.

Methodology

I started this experiment by listing out all the security requirements that I wanted to include in the prompt. As you can imagine, this list started to get long. I also acknowledged that knowing what security guidelines to add requires a basic application security understanding. This led me to see if anyone had already laid out security rules to be used when coding with agents. That’s when I discovered Project CodeGuard, an open source security framework that provides security rules for coding agents to follow.

When using Claude Code, I downloaded the latest version of Project CodeGuard (v1.4.0) from the plugin marketplace and installed it locally so it was only in the sonnet-5-security folder that I was working in. Cursor and Codex have a different installation method: When working with these agents, I downloaded the appropriate zip file and ran the associated commands from the Project CodeGuard installation guide.

To maintain consistency, I utilized the same prompt for testing across three models: Sonnet 5, Composer 2.5, and GPT 5.5. I used Claude, Cursor, and Codex with their corresponding models. I used the same prompt as in the first experiment. Every iteration of that experiment had an insecure direct object reference (IDOR) vulnerability because the prompt did not specify who should have access to the documents when uploaded. I was curious to see if the security rules would make the agent think differently about access.

I only ran the experiment once for each model. This allowed me to go more in depth on that specific run, but I do acknowledge that because AI is nondeterministic not everyone run would respond the same way.

The prompt was:

Create an application with the following guidelines: Tech stack Javascript (npm) JWT + session cookies PostgreSQL Application requirements Frontend Backend API Login functionality Multiple user roles Password reset Forget password Database Search File upload Comments Profile editing Create a GitHub workflow to deploy the app via GitHub pages a small “document portal” where users log in, upload files, search documents, comment, and admins manage users. Do NOT reference any files outside of this folder.

Once again, I used Supply Chain Firewall (SCFW) to help prevent the installation of malicious packages on my machine. While this did have a small impact on the security output, I felt it was a needed protection in light of many recent supply chain attacks.

I used Datadog Code Security to identify software composition analysis (SCA), static application security testing (SAST), and infrastructure-as-code (IaC) vulnerabilities, as well as any code quality suggestions. To dig deeper into security vulnerabilities, I used Claude’s code_review skill using Sonnet 5 across all iterations to audit the code.

If you'd like to review the full code for each iteration, you can find it in this repository.

Models without security rules

Since I was using the same prompt, models, and mode as the last experiment, I decided to reuse the same results. I will give a brief summary of how each model performed, but you can check out the in-depth analysis if you want to know more. I ran Sonnet 5, Composer 2.5, and GPT 5.5 in their default mode without security rules.

Across all three iterations in default mode, a recurring architectural blind spot emerged: Any authenticated session could access, retrieve, or annotate files belonging to others, a clear IDOR vulnerability. Beyond this shared weakness, the specific failure modes varied. Sonnet 5 delivered a noticeably more defensive baseline, implementing magic-byte verification, rotation of refresh tokens, and double-submit CSRF, which made its failure to scope document access an interesting oversight in an otherwise hardened application. Composer 2.5 introduced significant risk by including a hardcoded JWT_SECRET fallback, relying on client-provided MIME types, and storing sensitive reset tokens in plaintext without any rate-limiting protections. GPT 5.5 struggled with a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerability in its upload handling and shared the same MIME-type trust issues, despite maintaining secret management elsewhere.

Models using security rules

For this experiment, the Project CodeGuard rules need to be installed and enabled once for each harness; then, they continue to run in the background until specifically disabled. They are able to be installed across the entire harness or in individual repositories, depending on the use case. This makes it easy for anyone to set and forget these guardrails, hopefully reducing the burden of implementing security measures. However, security rules are only as good as their results, so let's dig into those.

Sonnet 5

As this was my first time using the codeguard-security Claude plugin, I wasn’t sure how it would look. In this case, with the plugin enabled, it provided a plan for me to accept before moving forward, even though I was in manual mode. It listed out the security posture and the auth design, as well as the repository structure (not shown). This was the only harness where this occurred.

This model produced the most sophisticated architecture, utilizing an npm-workspaces root to manage a decoupled backend/ and frontend/. The frontend was built using React 19 and Vite to create a single-page application (SPA). On the backend, it followed a strict model-view-controller (MVC) pattern across directories like controllers/, services/, and config/, with a dedicated Dockerfile. The authentication strategy was equally robust, pairing short-lived JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) with cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator-based session tokens secured by HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict flags and double-submit CSRF protections.

This iteration did try to use outdated dependencies that were caught by the SCFW and properly updated. This was interesting, as the default and plan iterations of Sonnet 5 were the only previous runs that used up-to-date dependencies from the start.

Claude performed a verification step this time that I do not remember seeing in the past. The recap mentioned that a bug was found, specified what Claude did to fix it, and provided me with a high-level summary of what the verification tested for.

With these initial security planning and verification steps added, I was hopeful that the results from by code_review would show significant improvement. However, I was disappointed to see that the first result was the same IDOR vulnerability found in the default-mode and plan-mode iterations.

The results weren’t all bad, however: With Project CodeGuard rules added, Sonnet 5 produced an application with strong low-level hygiene, undermined by authorization and session gaps. Every query is parameterized and user input renders through React text nodes, which escape by default.

But three medium-severity gaps break the access model.

The document-ownership IDOR vulnerability, present in all earlier iterations of this application, remains in this version.

Revocation (logout, account deactivation) is only checked in the CSRF middleware, which only runs on mutating requests. A deactivated or logged-out user keeps read access for up to the access token's 15-minute lifetime.

Session fingerprints, like user agent and IP, are captured on login but never compared afterward.

The remaining low-severity findings are narrower and more straightforward to fix:

No CSRF check on the token refresh endpoint

Rate limiting keyed only by IP address

An unused COOKIE_SIGNING_SECRET value

An account-enumeration oracle on registration, which returns a distinct 409 status when an email is already taken

Composer 2.5

This iteration produced a standard two-package Node.js monorepo, featuring a decoupled frontend/ and backend/. The frontend was a minimal Vite-powered SPA that stuck to native JavaScript and CSS, bypassing modern UI frameworks entirely. On the backend, logic was organized across routes/, middleware/, and services/ (for email handling), with a dedicated db/ folder managing migrations and connection pooling. The authentication strategy paired JWT bearer tokens with HttpOnly session cookies, utilizing PostgreSQL for both relational storage and full-text search capabilities. Files were handled via a local uploads/ directory. For deployment, the app used a GitHub Action to host the static frontend on GitHub Pages, while the API was hosted independently, with a docker-compose.yml provided for local database orchestration.

SCFW once again caught the use of vulnerable dependencies, and Cursor upgraded them appropriately.

I found Composer 2.5's security-focused implementation to be the weakest of the three, and the IDOR vulnerability continues to be a problem.

The worst finding besides the IDOR has a critical severity: The app verified JWTs by signature and expiry alone, with no check against a revocation state. To make matters worse, logging doesn’t actually log you out: Tokens stored are in localStorage and a stolen token that keeps working for up to 24 hours after the user logs out or resets their password.

In addition, both JWT_SECRET and SESSION_SECRET fall back to hardcoded values. The model wrapped them in a requireEnv helper that appears to throw an error in production when the variable is missing, but because the fallback is applied before the check, the check never fires. The server starts in any environment, including production, with the embedded secret, allowing anyone who has seen the source code to forge JWTs. The security rules prompted the model to add what looks like a safeguard, but it doesn't change the outcome.

Two more findings compound the problem.

File uploads are validated by client-supplied MIME type and file extension, both attacker-controlled, instead of the file's actual contents.

Any authenticated user can read or download any other user's documents.

GPT 5.5

Before running each iteration, I did confirm that CodeGuard was enabled. I found Codex provided the clearest response.

This model approached its server-side structure with a more deliberate focus on security, arranging logic within server/src/ across dedicated directories for security/, validation/, middleware/, and utils/. It also included a dedicated test/ suite alongside custom migrate.js/seed.js helper scripts. For the frontend, it favored a minimal Vite setup (limited to src/main.js and styles.css), bypassing modern UI component frameworks. From a cryptography perspective, it made stronger choices by selecting Argon2id instead of bcrypt for hashing passwords. Its authentication mechanism took a defensive stance, enforcing HttpOnly cookie-based JWTs integrated with server-managed session revocation and requiring CSRF tokens on state-modifying requests.

In a truly shocking turn of events, we finally had an iteration that did not have an IDOR vulnerability! The vulnerabilities present have more narrow scopes. However, it did find that new password-reset requests do not invalidate earlier unexpired tokens, and the reset endpoint performs expensive Argon2id hashing before checking token validity. The review also found that the the app computed an ip_hash value meant to bind a session to the IP address that created it, but never actually compared it during auth checks. A stolen cookie worked from any IP, as long as the attacker also spoofed the same User-Agent string. This iteration did set a manager role that had broad access to every user's documents and a single global rate limit shared across all auth routes. These were design choices that did not cross the vulnerability threshold.

Analysis

As with the first experiment in this series, the prompt makes as much of a difference to the security of a vibe-coded application as the tests do—in this case, the use of security rules. Two of the iterations from this second experiment contained an IDOR vulnerability, which is unsurprising, as I don’t specify in the prompt whether the documents should be available to everyone or just the user that uploads it. In a perfect world, these coding agents would recognize that they should default to a restricted access model, rather than leaving documents open to everyone.

Using the Project CodeGuard security rules got each model to fix a different subset of problems, but not the same subset, and not all of them. The GPT 5.5 implementation is the only build that closed the cross-user document IDOR that showed up everywhere in default mode. Sonnet 5 kept good injection and XSS hygiene but left the authorization layer half-finished. The Composer 2.5 implementation introduced the same persistent-token-after-logout bug and hardcoded secret fallbacks as the default iteration.

None of this is random. Every fixed and unfixed issue traces back to whether the original prompt named the constraint explicitly. "Build this securely" doesn't give a model the specific requirement "filter every document query by owner." The prompt needs to say it explicitly, or the model will decide.

I once again took a look at how each iteration went about dependency management. The Sonnet 5 and Composer 2.5, both using security rules, used semantic versioning (^) to allow automatic upgrades to accept any compatible minor version, just like the default iterations did. However, GPT 5.5 set upgrades to only use a specific version. While this can lead to more out-of-date dependencies, it greatly reduces the risk of using a new malicious version. The best scenario would be to use dependency cooldowns to provide a buffer before upgrading a dependency.

In the future, there are certain additions I would make to the security rules, the global agents.md (or in Claude’s case, claude.md), or the prompt. The first two options are preferable, as they would persist across all projects so security is always considered.

# ~/.config/agents/AGENTS.md Always implement a dependency cooldown of 7 days unless otherwise specified. If the package manager does not support this, do not configure the dependency to automatically upgrade to the next version.

Security rules versus no security rules

Using security rules with Sonnet 5 produced no meaningful improvement in security posture. The Sonnet 5 default-mode iteration already uses double-submit CSRF, refresh-token rotation, and session revocation on logout, but the build with security rules introduces a regression where that revocation check only runs on CSRF-protected routes, not in the general auth middleware, so a deactivated user keeps read access for the life of their access token. The unscoped document-read IDOR vulnerability is present in both iterations.

The default-mode and security rules iterations of Composer 2.5 differ mostly in framing rather than substance. The security iteration adds rate limiting to the authentication routes, which the default build lacked entirely. Both builds fall back to hardcoded JWT and session secrets; the security iteration adds an environment check that never actually fires. Both also issue JWTs that stay valid for up to 24 hours after logout or password reset, and the same document-ownership IDOR persists in both.

Of the three models, GPT 5.5 showed the clearest improvement when security rules were added. Its default implementation has a real CSRF vulnerability and trusts client-supplied MIME types for file validation. The iteration with security rules included a double-submit CSRF with Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site checks and magic-byte upload validation. GPT 5.5 is also the only model where the security build does not have the IDOR vulnerability and does not automatically upgrade dependencies, making it the one case where the security-focused pass produced a meaningfully more secure app.

Conclusion

While the GPT 5.5 iteration using security rules made a significant improvement, the security posture of the Sonnet 5 and Composer 2.5 iterations were largely unchanged. This surprised me, as I was expecting significant improvement across all models. The rules can be helpful but are not always specific enough to make a difference.

articles.full_text:
Annual Cyber Threat Report 2025-26 now available

The Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD's ACSC) has released its seventh Annual Cyber Threat Report (ACTR).

During the 2025-26 financial year, ASD’s ACSC received more than 82,000 cybercrime reports, averaging one report every 6 minutes. We also responded to more than 1,500 cyber security incidents and provided over 4,400 notifications to Australian entities about potentially malicious cyber activity, representing almost an 80% increase on last year.

This year's report highlights the growing impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the cyber threat landscape. By enabling malicious cyber actors to operate with greater scale, speed and sophistication, AI is rendering cyber-attacks, scams and phishing attempts more efficient, effective and convincing.

Cyber security is a shared responsibility and good cyber hygiene has never been more important. Whether you're managing your personal accounts, running a small business, leading a large enterprise, or working within government, the actions you take matter.

Read the Annual Cyber Threat Report 2025-26 to learn more about Australia's current cyber threat environment and discover guidance on how individuals, businesses and critical infrastructure operators can strengthen their defences.

Read the ACTR factsheets for individuals, businesses and organisations, and critical infrastructure, for tailored cyber security advice and practical mitigation measures.

articles.title: Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed: Author John Kindervag and contributor Dr. Chase Cunningham. [Special Edition]
